title: bug(examples/linearlite): whole-board :populates makes independent successful writes last-reply-wins
description:
SURFACE REVIEW: examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite at afe446ea71bf7d0eb2e4ce5960caca864a091778.

SUMMARY

Linearlite is the flagship optimistic-mutation example and explicitly promises that accepted writes settle from recorded facts, "not whichever reply landed last" (examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite/README.md:58-65). Its implementation teaches the opposite cache consequence: every create, title edit, and status change replaces the single board resource with a whole-board snapshot from that mutation's response. Because those writes use independent mutation instances, each response can be accepted and the last response to arrive replaces the aggregate cache, even when its snapshot predates another accepted write.

This is not the ordinary same-instance stale-reply case. Mutation generation/work-id suppression is intentionally scoped to the reply's instance. It protects a re-execute of one instance; it cannot order independent instances that all write the same resource key. `:on-conflict :invalidate` also does not help: that policy governs a failed rollback, whereas an accepted success applies `:populates` authoritatively.

EVIDENCE

- README.md:58-65 says success re-seeds the board and that "No wall-clock race decides which wins" / the result is not "whichever reply landed last". README.md:76-80 says an instance's `:optimistic?` means its optimistic value is still on screen.
- core.cljs:147-158 defines one shared board target/query. Each mutation returns `{board-key result}` from `:populates`: create at :208-231, edit-title at :237-246, and change-status at :252-261.
- core.cljs:426-451 deliberately gives those writes distinct instances: `[:create tmp-id]`, `[:edit id]`, and `[:status id]`. Different cards and even title/status writes on one card can therefore be live independently.
- core.cljs:481-541 leaves create, edit, and status controls enabled while writes are pending, so overlap is an ordinary interaction, not an unsupported programmatic edge.
- The demo server freezes a whole-board value per request: `apply-write!` mutates and returns the then-current board at core.cljs:310-341; the HTTP stub captures that payload and defers its delivery by 220 ms at :343-387. Two quick writes therefore hold two different aggregate snapshots.
- The runtime verifier looks up only the mutation instance named by the reply (implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_events.cljc:1536-1571). On each accepted success it runs `apply-populates` unconditionally (:1640-1702). `apply-populates` seeds the target with the supplied value (:208-249), and `populate-entry` replaces `:data` (:291-327 in mutation_runtime.cljc). There is no cross-instance resource-target freshness verdict; that is outside the documented instance stale-suppression contract.
- Linearlite's behavioral tests cover one mutation at a time (implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/linearlite_example_cljs_test.cljs:354-465) and the real-stub tests inspect one write at a time (:569-635). The generic test named `concurrent-submissions-do-not-clobber` (resources_mutation_cljs_test.cljc:414-439) uses mutations with no cache consequences and asserts only that the two instance rows retain independent pending/result state; it cannot catch aggregate cache clobbering.
- Git history shows the whole-board `:populates` pattern originated with the example in c0e4889344; later edits changed prose, APIs, mounting, and the canned-503 classification, but did not add an overlapping-success witness or alter this consequence shape.

CONCRETE FAILURE

Start from board S. Dispatch A, which optimistically produces S+A and whose stub response freezes S+A. Before its delayed reply, dispatch independent B, which optimistically produces S+A+B and freezes S+A+B. When A settles first, its accepted whole-board populate replaces the cache with S+A: B vanishes from the screen even though B's instance remains pending and `:optimistic?` still derives true. B's later reply restores it, producing a visible optimistic regression in the shipped demo.

A real transport makes the issue worse. If two writes are processed in one order but their already-built responses arrive in the other, both independent instances are current and both whole-board populates are accepted. The older aggregate snapshot can arrive last and permanently erase an already-successful change in the client cache. Final cache state is then exactly last-reply-wins, contrary to the example's central claim.

IMPACT

This is teaching-surface correctness, not polish. The example invites SPA programmers and coding agents to copy independent per-control instances plus aggregate `:populates`, a combination that can lose accepted edits. It also makes the `:optimistic?` badge semantically dishonest during the overlap window. Because the README presents this as the safe answer to hand-written optimistic races, the example needs an honest concurrency shape before it is used as canonical guidance.

BOUNDED FIX

Keep the example small and choose one explicit, honest policy. Recommended: retain concurrent controls, but make success consequences commute at the same granularity as the writes. Have POST return the created issue plus enough correlation to replace its own temporary card, have title/status writes return the changed issue or field, and use surgical `:patches` over the board instead of replacing the whole aggregate from each independent response. Same-card/same-field re-executes should continue to reuse an instance so the existing stale-suppression rule applies. If the intended API only returns coarse board snapshots, an explicit invalidate/refetch or deliberate single-writer serialization is acceptable instead, but the example must not present independent whole-board response snapshots as order-independent.

Update the local README/comments to state the guarantee actually implemented. In particular, distinguish "the commit/rollback verdict uses recorded facts" from "independent successful server snapshots are globally ordered"; the latter is not supplied by mutation instance generations.

ACCEPTANCE

1. Add a focused Linearlite regression that dispatches two writes under distinct instances against the board, parks both transport replies, and settles them in both normal and reverse order.
2. After both accepted successes, the board contains both server-accepted changes; neither completion can revert the other's accepted field/card.
3. While the second write remains pending, settling the first does not erase the second optimistic change (or, if serialization is the chosen explicit policy, the UI cannot originate that overlap and the test pins the lock).
4. Preserve the example's headline behavior: each allowed write paints immediately, an unconflicted failure rolls back, a successful create reconciles its temporary id/marker, and existing single-write tests remain green.
5. README and source comments describe the bounded guarantee without claiming cross-instance whole-response ordering the runtime does not provide.
6. Exercise the actual example registrations/consequence functions, not test-local copies; the regression must fail against the current three whole-board `:populates` registrations.

NON-GOALS

- No generic cross-instance transaction scheduler, CRDT, vector-clock, or server version protocol in the resource runtime.
- No redesign of all resource granularity or every example.
- No change to the existing failed-rollback `:on-conflict` semantics.
- No broad UI polish, disabling campaign, or attempt to litigate every distributed-systems edge.

DUPLICATE AUDIT

Targeted `rg` searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` for Linearlite plus whole-board/populate/out-of-order/last-reply/cache-clobber found no matching issue. Nearby beads are distinct: rf2-pqt5f fixed canned-503 classification; rf2-k4oe and rf2-djqm concern example-test registration ordering; rf2-ujdn0 concerns launch instructions; rf2-iy3d6 concerns RealWorld route/detail reply placement, not cross-instance mutation consequences.

UNCERTAINTY / VALIDATION NOTE

No runtime or browser command was run during this review, per the review fence. The static acceptance path is enough to prove that two distinct current instances can both replace the same resource entry; exact timer ordering in the canned browser should be pinned by the parked-reply regression rather than assumed. The recommended `:patches` shape is intentionally a bounded teaching fix; if maintainers prefer invalidate/refetch or explicit serialization, acceptance is behavioral rather than prescriptive.
close_reason:
REPRODUCED AND FIXED in the example. PR https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9197.

PREMISE HOLDS, and both halves of it. Two temporary tests planted in implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/linearlite_example_cljs_test.cljs (driving the example's own registrations, not copies) were RED on the unmodified example and GREEN after the fix, with identical inputs — captured exit 1 then 0, 13 tests / 61 assertions, the 11 pre-existing tests green in both runs. (a) Settling an accepted write erased another instance's STILL-PENDING optimistic change: srv-2 read :in-progress where :done was expected. (b) The older whole-board snapshot arriving LAST permanently reverted an already-ACCEPTED change: same read, both successes accepted. So the transient optimistic regression and the permanent last-reply-wins are both real, not one or the other.

OWNER: THE EXAMPLE, not the framework. implementation/ is untouched. :populates is documented as an authoritative load that seeds an entry from the reply and populate-entry does exactly that; :patches — (fn [params result] -> {target patch-fn}) — is the framework's existing tool for a fine-grained consequence, and the example's own README already called :optimistic 'the exact-target twin of a mutation's success-time :patches'. The bug was the example choosing the aggregate consequence for fine-grained independent writes.

FIX (examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite/** only, 2 files). Each mutation commits at the granularity it wrote at, so the three consequences are disjoint and commute: edit-title sets the saved title on its own card, change-status the saved status on its own card, create-issue drops its temporary card and merges in the server's row. The demo backend answers a write with just the row it changed, in the board's own {:issues [...]} envelope; a read still answers with the whole board. patch-issue is variadic so one shape serves both hooks. README and source comments now state the BOUNDED guarantee — the commit-or-roll-back verdict and same-instance stale-reply suppression are per-instance, independent instances writing one entry are not ordered for you and cannot be from the client, and keeping their consequences disjoint is the application's job — plus the honest alternatives (invalidate/refetch, or deliberate serialisation) when an API only returns coarse snapshots.

ACCEPTANCE 2-5 MET. Acceptance 1 and 6 met AS A REPRODUCTION but not as a landed test: examples are test-free by ruling (rf2-8cevm) so the witness cannot live under examples/, and its real home — the adapter test tree — was outside this worker's fence. The tests were run there and removed; that file is byte-identical to its committed blob f7c581dd8e8ec8d703b4456b6e58e5f13af1285a, verified by content hash. rf2-chl2 carries the verbatim test source so the durable regression is a paste-and-run job, and notes the two stale :populates references left behind (the passing-but-misnamed successful-write-commits-the-server-board-via-populates, and the frozen, uncompiled pilot baseline under docs/design/hicasso/product/pilots/baseline/linearlite/).

GATES on the final rebased base, captured exits: npm run test:cljs 0 (11176 tests / 55753 assertions / 0 failures); npm run test:examples-compile 0 (58 builds, zero warnings, [:examples/linearlite] among them); scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci 0, and that gate was checked for discrimination rather than trusted — a planted broken anchor in this README returned exit 1 naming file and line.

title: Reject remote open-in-editor callers that spoof a loopback Host
description:
## Problem

`re-frame.testbed.open-in-editor-server/local-request?` authenticates a request as local from its `Host` header and optional `Origin`, but never checks the TCP peer exposed by Ring as `:remote-addr`. `Host` is supplied by the client, and a direct HTTP client may legitimately omit `Origin`, so a non-loopback peer can send `POST /__rf-open-in-editor` with `Host: localhost:<port>` and pass the guard.

This is a reachable boundary failure, not a hypothetical proxy configuration. All 14 handler-wired `:dev-http` entries in `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn` omit `:host`. The source inside the pinned `thheller/shadow-cljs` 3.4.10 jar defaults that missing host to `0.0.0.0`, while its Ring adapter places `(str (.getRemoteAddress request))` in `:remote-addr`. Thus the testbeds listen beyond loopback and already provide the transport fact the guard needs.

After the guard, `handle` resolves the caller's `file` and calls `launch!`; absolute paths pass through and any existing path can launch the developer's editor. A reachable network peer can therefore trigger editor/Node processes repeatedly and probe coarse path/launch outcomes. CORS does not protect this route from a direct client.

## Evidence

- `tools/testbed-support/src/re_frame/testbed/open_in_editor_server.clj:399-407`: `local-request?` destructures only `headers`; its docstring claims locality from loopback Host/Origin.
- The same file at `:479-508` calls that check before resolving the requested path and invoking `launch!`; `resolve-file` at `:93-112` explicitly passes absolute paths through.
- `tools/testbed-support/README.md:63-69` documents the endpoint as local-only.
- `tools/testbed-support/test/re_frame/testbed/open_in_editor_server_test.clj:68-77` builds requests without `:remote-addr`; tests around `:130-149` reject non-loopback/missing Host but cannot exercise a remote peer spoofing a loopback Host.
- `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn` contains 14 `:dev-http` entries using this handler and no `:host` setting. The installed, lock-pinned shadow-cljs 3.4.10 source was inspected: `start-build-server` uses `"0.0.0.0"` when host is absent, and the AOT Ring adapter supplies the remote socket address.
- Ring's request-map specification defines `:remote-addr` as the client or last proxy IP: https://github.com/ring-clojure/ring/blob/master/SPEC.md

A minimal failing regression is a request map with `:request-method :post`, a valid existing file, `"host" "localhost:8031"`, no Origin, and a non-loopback `:remote-addr`; current code reaches the launch spy instead of returning 403.

## Recommended shape

Make the endpoint's one central launch guard require a loopback transport peer in addition to the existing Host/Origin checks. Parse the concrete Ring/shadow representations deliberately (including IPv4 and IPv6 loopback), fail closed when the peer is missing or malformed, and do not trust forwarding headers: these shadow dev servers are direct listeners. Keep this narrow; there is no need for tokens, sessions, middleware, or a redesign of the testbed API. Update the request fixture to provide a loopback peer by default and document the transport check alongside the existing local-only contract.

Targeted searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` and this path's git history found no current owner for remote-peer validation or Host spoofing. Commit `4e6f05d33c` introduced the Host/Origin guard intending to cover public binding/DNS rebinding, but did not inspect `:remote-addr`; this completes that intended boundary rather than duplicating the coordinate, cwd, or tier-classpath work.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A POST from a non-loopback `:remote-addr` returns 403 before path resolution or process launch even when `Host` is loopback and Origin is absent or loopback.
2. Missing and malformed peer addresses fail closed; do not consult `X-Forwarded-For` or similar client-controlled headers.
3. Direct IPv4 and IPv6 loopback peers continue to support the existing cross-port local testbeds, Host validation, and optional loopback-Origin behavior.
4. Focused tests cover the spoofed-Host/non-loopback-peer case and assert the launch spy is untouched, plus accepted IPv4/IPv6 loopback representations actually emitted/allowed by the Ring adapter.
5. The testbed-support README's security contract mentions the peer-address requirement, and `clojure -M:test` from `tools/testbed-support/` plus `npm run test:testbed-support` pass.
close_reason:
Fixed by PR #9198 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9198).

The premise held. `local-request?` destructured only `:headers` and never consulted `:remote-addr`, so a POST from 203.0.113.7 carrying `Host: localhost:8031` with no Origin answered 200 with the launch spy fired against `file=/etc/passwd`. That exact assertion is now the regression test, and it was red before the change (25 assertions red across the new tests, 0 after).

`loopback-peer?` now gates the whole endpoint on Ring's `:remote-addr`, ahead of the method branch and the OPTIONS preflight. The Host/Origin check is retained as non-authoritative defence in depth (it still narrows a loopback peer's browser to same-machine pages and closes DNS rebinding).

Accepted set, each with a reason recorded in the docstring: all of 127.0.0.0/8 (a client may connect to any of it; the kernel never routes it off-box); `::1` AND its expanded spelling `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`; and the IPv4-mapped `::ffff:127.0.0.1`.

CORRECTION to the description's mechanism detail. The pinned adapter is thheller/shadow-undertow, whose `exchange->ring` fills `:remote-addr` from `(.getHostAddress (.getAddress (.getSourceAddress exchange)))` — a BARE numeric literal — not `(str (.getRemoteAddress request))` as the description states (verified in the installed 0.3.1 and 0.3.4 sources; identical in both). That distinction matters: `getHostAddress` emits IPv6 loopback EXPANDED as `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`, so a check for the `::1` spelling alone would have refused every genuine IPv6 caller. It also means no port is ever appended, so a `host:port` value is refused.

Missing and malformed values fail closed, and `X-Forwarded-*` is ignored (a `:dev-http` server is a direct listener). Parsing runs only on strings already shaped like numeric literals, because `InetAddress/getByName` resolves `localhost` — measured 3ms — and any attacker-chosen name pointing at 127.0.0.1, to a loopback address; an unguarded parse would have been a second way in.

Workflow note: running a testbed off-box no longer works by pointing a browser at it. The seam documented in the README is an SSH local port-forward (`ssh -L 8031:localhost:8031 <host>`), which presents a genuine loopback peer and needs no configuration; the default was not widened.

Gates: `clojure -M:test` from `tools/testbed-support/` — exit 0, 41 tests / 228 assertions before; exit 0, 47 tests / 295 assertions after. `scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci` exit 0, with a planted broken target confirming it returns exit 1 and names the line. `npm run test:testbed-support` was declined for want of `implementation/node_modules` in the worker worktree — its `:ns-regexp` selects only `.cljs` suites and this diff touches no `.cljs` file (the server namespace is `.clj` and never enters a browser or Node bundle); CI runs it on the PR.

title: mcp-conformance: Windows hermetic cleanup grades the npx wrapper, not the shadow-cljs JVM
description:
## Correctness finding

The live hermetic runner can emit its GREEN sentinel and exit 0 on Windows after only the direct `cross-spawn` wrapper exits, while the shadow-cljs JVM descendant remains alive.

`makeCleanup` grades shadow teardown solely from `hasShadowExited()` (`tools/mcp-conformance/scripts/run-re-frame2-pair-live-hermetic-suite.cjs:367-414`). That predicate is driven solely by the `exit` event on the child returned by `crossSpawn(...)` (`:1013-1021`, wired at `:1041-1044`). On Windows, the exact installed cross-spawn 7.0.6 parsing path turns the trusted bare `C:\Program Files\nodejs\npx` into `C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /d /s /c ...` targeting `npx.CMD`. The returned handle therefore represents the command wrapper, not the downstream shadow-cljs JVM. Node's official child-process documentation explicitly warns that killing a shell child does not terminate the child processes it launched.

The current unit model collapses those separate lifetimes into one EventEmitter: `makeFakeShadow().kill()` emits that same fake object's `exit` (`tools/mcp-conformance/test/runner-cleanup.test.cjs:61-71`). It proves direct-child timing and escalation, but cannot detect a wrapper that exits while a grandchild survives.

## Impact

This defeats the verifier's defining hermetic guarantee. A false-green run can leave the shadow/JVM/watch server holding the fixture's fixed port 8030 (`run-re-frame2-pair-live-hermetic-suite.cjs:65`) and runtime metadata, contaminating or wedging the next human/AI run or causing it to exercise stale state. This is a certification defect rather than cosmetic cleanup: `finalizeConformance` converts `report.clean` into the pass sentinel and exit 0 (`:420-440`, `:1361-1368`).

## Evidence and history

- Read-only execution of the exact installed cross-spawn parser yielded command `C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe`, `/d /s /c` arguments, and `file=C:\Program Files\nodejs\npx.CMD` for the runner's spawn shape.
- Read-only local process-table inspection confirmed shadow's ordinary Node-to-Java descendant shape.
- Node's primary documentation covers both Windows `.cmd` shell handling and the fact that killing a shell does not terminate its child processes: https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html
- Cross-spawn's primary source/documentation confirms its `.cmd` shim handling: https://github.com/moxystudio/node-cross-spawn
- Commit `ba8c8a20d6` introduced dirty teardown grading specifically so a leaked shadow JVM/port-8030 owner cannot pass, but the implementation equates wrapper exit with JVM exit.
- The repository already has a scoped Windows process-tree precedent: `scripts/test-core-jvm-windows.ps1:163-171` uses `taskkill.exe /pid <owned-root> /T /F`; `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh:697-762` documents and handles the native descendant tree.

## Bounded fix

Make Windows teardown own, terminate, and grade the process tree rooted at the exact PID spawned by this runner. Adapt the existing scoped `/T` pattern, or use a graceful shadow stop with that verified fallback, while the root relationship is still observable. Do not mark cleanup clean merely because the npx/cmd wrapper emitted `exit`. Keep current POSIX behavior unless an equivalent demonstrated defect requires a change.

Add a small regression fixture/test that separates wrapper exit from grandchild liveness. Prefer an outcome-focused local helper or test seam over a generic process-supervision abstraction.

## Posture fit

This is a narrow truthfulness and ergonomics repair using a process-tree pattern already proven in the repository. It makes the powerful one-command hermetic verifier trustworthy and removes expensive rerun contamination for programmers and their AI tools, without adding public API or framework machinery.

## Non-goals

- Dynamic or parallel port allocation.
- A generic cross-platform process supervisor.
- Global stale-process reaping or killing unrelated Java/Node processes.
- Redesigning the fixture or MCP wire contracts.
- Expanding the host matrix.

## Duplicate check

Focused `rg` searches over `.beads/issues.jsonl` for mcp-conformance combined with Windows, cleanup, teardown, orphan, JVM, 8030, npx, and server.pid, plus exact symptom phrases, found no issue owning this outcome. Related closed `rf2-j538f7.19`/commit `ba8c8a20d6` established the intended guarantee but did not handle descendants; closed `rf2-ahjbc` and `rf2-a9l6e` have different scopes. A tracker memory records prior observed Windows false-green leftovers, but this finding was independently established from the runner, dependency source, platform semantics, process hierarchy, tests, and history.

## Uncertainty

The live suite was not booted in the review worktree because that would require the prohibited dependency link/install and runtime mutations; no process was listening on 8030 during inspection. The exact cross-spawn transformation, direct-handle control flow, official Node semantics, repository process-tree precedent, and observed Node-to-Java hierarchy establish the mechanism. The implementer should choose the smallest graceful-stop/tree-kill detail and verify the outcome below.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A regression launches or faithfully models a Windows wrapper with a separately long-lived grandchild; wrapper exit alone cannot produce `shadow.clean === true` or the overall GREEN sentinel.
2. Normal cleanup and SIGTERM/SIGKILL/watchdog paths terminate the runner-owned shadow process tree within the existing bounds; unrelated Node/JVM processes are never targeted.
3. Cleanup returns dirty, exit 2, and no pass sentinel whenever owned-descendant teardown cannot be proven.
4. Two consecutive Windows hermetic-suite runs both pass from their own state; after each, no fixture-owned process/listener remains on port 8030 and the next run does not trust stale runtime metadata.
5. Existing browser cleanup, live-test inventory, trusted-executable checks, wire assertions, sentinels, and exit-code contracts remain green.
notes:
AUDIT PR #9213 (2026-09-05): REOPENED. The new creation-time ownership fence is not applied to the root PID. `ownedDescendants` unconditionally includes `rootPid` whenever that numeric PID appears in the live table (`if (byPid.has(rootPid)) owned.push(rootPid)`), even if that row's `createdMs` predates `spawnedAtMs`; `makeShadowTreeReaper` then calls `taskkill /pid <rootPid> /T /F`. Once the short-lived cmd/npx wrapper exits and Windows recycles its PID, cleanup can therefore kill an unrelated process and its descendants, directly violating AC2 and the PR's safety claim. Deterministic probe at merge 2c08156e85: table root `{pid:100,createdMs:1000}` plus child `{pid:200,createdMs:6000}`, `spawnedAtMs=5000` returned owned `[100,200]` and invoked treeKill(100). The added recycled-PID test covers only a stale child, not the root. Bound the root row by the same creation-time check (and handle a missing/invalid creation timestamp fail-closed), while retaining discovery of legitimate orphans whose dead parent PID remains in `ParentProcessId`; add a regression that proves a recycled root is never targeted. Focused all-status search found no more exact owner than rf2-kzbf.
AUDIT PR #9247 (2026-09-05): REOPENED. The reproduced dated-root case is repaired, but the new algorithm is not actually fail-closed for ambiguous lineage.

1. For an undated root row, classifyRootRow returns unprovable and makeShadowTreeReaper sets rootError, but ownedDescendants still walks from that PID. With root {pid:100, createdMs:0} and child {pid:200, ppid:100, createdMs:6000}, the child enters owned and line 454 tree-kills pid 200 before the function returns the dirty error. If the undated root is a stranger, that is the stranger's child. Reporting dirty after the kill does not satisfy AC2 or the source/PR claim that unprovable ownership is not killed. The added test gives the undated root no child, so it misses this path. The close reason acknowledges this residual but closes the safety criterion anyway.

2. When our wrapper has exited and a stranger subsequently reuses the number, spawns a child, and itself exits before enumeration, rootClass is absent and strangerCeilingMs is Infinity. That stranger's surviving child retains the recycled number as PPID, passes the spawn floor, enters owned, and is killed. A boolean rootExited cannot distinguish it from our orphan; an observed wrapper-exit time provides the natural upper bound because our direct child had to be created before the wrapper exited.

Bounded repair: when the current root is unprovable, kill nothing and return dirty. Bound orphan discovery with positive ownership evidence such as the observed wrapper-exit instant, and add table-model teeth for an undated root with a child plus an absent recycled root with a post-exit child. Then satisfy AC4 on Windows: neither test.yml nor expensive-tests.yml can do so today because both suite jobs run on ubuntu-latest, where makeShadowTreeReaper is inert; the PR explicitly did not run the required two consecutive Windows hermetic suites and port-8030 checks.
IMPLEMENTED (PR #9256, 2026-09-05). Both PR #9247 audit residuals repaired, each reproduced red first.

(1) Unprovable root: ownedDescendants now refuses the walk entirely when classifyRootRow returns 'unprovable', so no child of an undatable root is ever handed to treeKill. Previously owned=[200] for {root 100 createdMs 0, child 200 ppid 100 createdMs 6000} at spawnedAtMs 5000, and line 454 killed 200 BEFORE the dirty error returned.

title: surface-review(ssr): hiccup emitter drops false ARIA and booleanish attrs, leaving SSR DOM semantics unlike React
description:
## Scope Correct the boolean-value classification used by the hiccup-to-HTML path in implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/html_helpers.cljc. This helper feeds both the public non-streaming re-frame.ssr/render-to-string path and the streaming hiccup walker. Keep the change at attribute serialization plus focused parity coverage. ## Correctness finding html-helpers/attr-string currently applies one rule to every attribute: true emits a bare name, while false and nil are omitted. HTML/React attributes do not share one boolean class. In particular, aria-* and data-* boolean values stringify, and booleanish attributes such as contentEditable, draggable, and spellCheck stringify both true and false. The current path therefore turns aria-expanded=true into a present attribute with the empty string, drops aria-expanded=false entirely, turns contentEditable=true into a bare attribute, and drops contentEditable=false. This is not a theoretical edge. Boolean ARIA state is ordinary SPA authoring, and contentEditable=false is the way a child opts out of an editable ancestor. Omitting that false marker changes the server DOM's semantics. Spec 011 also records that React attribute-only hydration mismatches are not guaranteed to be patched and do not reach onRecoverableError, so the wrong server attribute can survive hydration without the framework's mismatch signal. The separate structural-tree serializer already models the needed categories in implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/ui_tree.cljc. This is drift in the stock-Reagent-compatible hiccup emitter, not a missing design. ## Verified evidence Verified at source tip 52283022e9; the relevant html_helpers.cljc, ui_tree.cljc, and ssr_emit_test.clj blobs are byte-identical to origin/main at 82c112928c. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/html_helpers.cljc:563-626 — attr-string branches on the value alone. Lines 595-597 emit every true bare and omit every false/nil before considering the attribute name. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/emit.cljc:778-794 — the standard renderer sends DOM attrs through attr-string. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/streaming.cljc:391-404 — the streaming shell uses the same helper, so both hiccup SSR modes are affected. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr.cljc:48 and implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/emit.cljc:883-920 — this is the public render-to-string implementation installed into the headless/Reagent-compatible adapter path. - Focused JVM probe of the current emitter: aria-expanded true -> aria-expanded false -> contentEditable true ->
...
nested contentEditable false -> the child has no attribute - Focused probe against the repository's installed react-dom 19.2.0: aria-expanded true -> aria-expanded="true" aria-expanded false -> aria-expanded="false" contentEditable true -> contentEditable="true" contentEditable false -> contentEditable="false" For the nested editable-parent case, React emits the child's explicit false marker; the current SSR emitter emits
locked
, so the section inherits editability. - implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/ui_tree.cljc:598-650 already distinguishes aria/data, booleanish, overloaded-boolean, true boolean, and ordinary boolean-valued attributes. - implementation/ssr/test/re_frame/ssr/emit_ui_tree_cljs_test.cljc:238-256 pins contentEditable="false" and aria-hidden="false" on that serializer. - implementation/ssr/test/re_frame/ssr_emit_test.clj:716-735 covers only the true-presence class (disabled/required) and therefore stays green while the other classes are wrong. - spec/004B-UI-Tree-and-Conversion.md:552 and 565-567 records the React 19.2 attribute classes; spec/011-SSR.md:842 records the consequence of attribute-only hydration drift. ## Recommended minimal fix Make html-helpers/attr-string classify boolean values by attribute name before emitting them, using the already-shipped ui_tree classification as the local reference. Prefer one small shared classifier/roster if that reduces drift cleanly; a faithful local reuse is also acceptable if sharing would distort the two deliberately separate emitters. Preserve the existing public API and the current escape, security-strip, and attribute-name-validation order. At minimum, aria-* and data-* booleans and the booleanish contentEditable/draggable/spellCheck family must stringify true and false; true boolean and overloaded-boolean attributes must retain presence semantics; booleans on ordinary non-boolean attributes must not become arbitrary bare attributes. The implementation should remain a small serialization correction, not a renderer redesign. ## Posture rationale Excellent SSR ergonomics means authors can write the same natural SPA hiccup they use on the client, especially normal accessibility state such as aria-expanded open?, without hand-stringifying booleans to compensate for the server. The fix is compact and already has a correct sibling implementation to follow. It adds no abstraction users must learn and avoids a broad compatibility project. ## Non-goals - No new public API, protocol, renderer option, or hydration detector. - No rewrite of the structural-tree serializer, component resolution, style serialization, attribute ordering, or DOM-property alias system. - No emulation of React development warnings. - No attempt to exhaustively clone every React DOM implementation detail beyond the boolean attribute classes needed for server/client semantic parity. - No unrelated security-filter or escaping changes. ## Related and duplicate search Searched every bead status and full issue text for ARIA, aria-*, contentEditable, booleanish, overloaded boolean, attr-string, generic boolean, false attribute, attribute semantics, and render-to-string. No issue owns this defect. rf2-51tgp is the closed oncommand security-filter gap and does not concern value classification; the Hicasso contenteditable beads concern controlled-input documentation and are unrelated. Git history across all local and remote refs found the generic value-only branch introduced by 9cfc27065c (2026-05-14), the focused presence-only coverage, and the later richer structural-tree serializer (260fe87d57). It found no commit that adds name-aware boolean classification to html-helpers/attr-string. The latest relevant source blobs match origin/main. ## Uncertainty The exact internal sharing shape is intentionally left to the implementer because render-to-string and emit-ui-tree consume different tree representations and Spec 004B says not to conflate their pipelines. The behavioral requirement is certain from direct output comparison. A browser may canonicalize bare true attributes differently by element, but that does not rescue false ARIA/booleanish values: the emitted marker is absent, while React explicitly emits "false".
acceptance_criteria:
1. Add focused JVM tests through the public hiccup render path showing aria-expanded true and false serialize as quoted "true" and "false", never bare/absent.
2. Add a nested editable-parent regression showing an explicit false child remains contentEditable="false"; include true and false rows for at least one other booleanish member or a table-driven family check.
3. Preserve controls: disabled true remains a presence attribute, disabled false remains absent, download true/string/false retain overloaded-boolean behavior, and a boolean on an ordinary non-boolean attribute does not become a bare attribute.
4. Exercise the shared helper through both emit/render-to-string and streaming/render-shell (or an existing focused streaming DOM-tag seam) so neither hiccup SSR mode can drift.
5. Use the existing ui_tree serializer's classified outputs as parity references without coupling the two render pipelines incorrectly.
6. Prove non-vacuity by running the new focused assertions against the current implementation and observing failures on the exact aria false/contentEditable false rows, then green after the change.
7. The focused SSR JVM suite passes; any affected CLJS parity lane also passes.
notes:
--- FOLLOW-ON (PR #9194 ssr-ring collision, ruled) ---

The fix reddened ONE downstream job, `JVM ssr-ring (clojure -M:test)`:
`default-shell-attr-string-handles-booleans-and-nil` (ring_test.clj:2160) asserted
`:data-off false` omitted from <html> and `<body class="ok">` bare. RULED as ONE
contract; the ssr-ring test's prose was a stale downstream restatement, not a
second contract. Corrected the test.

Why not two contracts (the tempting read: the shell is static config for <html>/
<body>, which React never renders or hydrates, so false-means-omit could be a
deliberate authoring convenience):

1. There is no second serialiser to carry a second contract. ssr-ring
   shell.clj:78,86 calls `html/attr-string` — literally the function the hiccup
   element emitter uses — and its own docstring says the bags are "stamped via the
   shared attr-string serialiser". Two contracts would mean forking the function or
   adding a mode flag: inventing a divergence, not preserving one.
2. The test never claimed a shell rule. Its section comment introduced the block as
   "Serialisation goes through the shared re-frame.ssr.html-helpers/attr-string
   helper - boolean true -> bare attribute name, false/nil -> omitted", i.e. it
   states the DELEGATION and then transcribes the delegate's then-current rule. The
   deftest is even named for the helper. Its subject is "the shell delegates", so
   correcting the delegate correctly moved it.
3. "React never renders <html>/<body>, so false is meaningless there" does not hold.
   What reads a shell data-* is CSS and boot JS, not React: `[data-hidden="false"]`
   selects differently from `:not([data-hidden])`, and `<html data-js="false">` is
   the canonical no-JS marker. aria-* on <body> is read by assistive tech. The false
   value carries meaning on the shell for exactly the class the fix changed.
4. The omission convenience is not lost and never was spelled `false`: `nil` omits,
   unchanged, and the same deftest still pins it green. In Clojure `nil` is absence
   and `false` is a value.
5. The shell change is narrow and lands only where it should. Genuine HTML boolean
   attributes keep presence semantics under the classifier, so `:body-attrs {:hidden
   false}` is still OMITTED - `hidden="false"` is truthy to a browser and would hide
   the document. Only aria-*/data-*/booleanish moved, which is where omission
   asserted the opposite of what the author wrote.
6. Two rules for one map shape would be the friction: `{:data-hidden false}` meaning
   omitted on <body> but `data-hidden="false"` on a <div>, with no cue at the call
   site.

CORRECTION, NOT RELAXATION - the test got stronger, +1 assertion (1163 -> 1164):
the data-* rows now assert `="true"` / `="false"` POSITIVELY where the old
`data-flag` row passed on a bare substring and would have stayed green either way;
<body> gained the presence class the test never covered (`:hidden false` omitted,
`:inert true` bare) plus an explicit negative that `hidden="false"` never appears;
and the exact `<body class="ok" data-collapsed="false" inert>` open tag still pins
that nothing else leaks. `:data-hidden` was renamed `:data-collapsed` so the
`hidden="false"` negative could not be satisfied by a substring of the stringified
data-* row.

SPEC: 011 §Head/meta step 4 now states the bags carry no shell-specific rule and
points at §The render-tree -> HTML emitter. 004B untouched (read-only) - and its
scope statement supports the ruling rather than limiting it: its conversion table is
declared "one table, two consumers", and the shell is a third caller of the same
helper, not a surface the table excludes.

GATES (final base a30393e51b, each redirected, own exit captured):
ssr-ring BEFORE exit 1, 231 tests/1163 assertions, 2 failures (CI's two lines
reproduced exactly); AFTER exit 0, 231/1164, 0 failures. ssr exit 0, 628/3215, 0
failures. mkdocs build --strict exit 0. check_doc_slugs.py exit 0 with an EMPTY log,
disbelieved until a planted broken anchor reddened it exit 1 naming
spec/011-SSR.md:1256 (the new sentence's own line, so the gate demonstrably read the
worker tree), then restored and verified byte-identical to the committed blob.
NOT RUN: npm run test:cljs - no node_modules in this worktree, not linked. CI's 86
checks cover it; the CLJS lanes were already green on the pre-fix push, with
ssr-ring the only red.
REOPENED BY PR #9194 AUDIT — the new shared classifier is internally consistent but incomplete against the installed react-dom 19.2.0 source it says it tracks. The presence roster omits disablePictureInPicture, disableRemotePlayback, scoped, and seamless; the booleanish/stringifying roster omits autoReverse, externalResourcesRequired, focusable, and preserveAlpha. Current public JVM SSR drops all eight boolean values, while React 19.2 emits presence markers for the first four and quoted "true"/"false" values for the latter four. Because both re-frame serializers now share this roster, their parity test agrees on the same wrong output and cannot expose the external mismatch.

Minimal acceptance: reconcile these bounded roster omissions against the repository's installed React 19.2 serializer and add table-driven public-emitter coverage (plus the independent React fixture/golden seam where practical) so both presence and stringifying cases are pinned. Keep this a roster/test correction, not a broader React-DOM clone. Separately document/dispose React's generic boolean `value` grouping rather than silently assuming it belongs in or out.
close_reason:
SECOND CARRIER — the PR #9194 audit reopen answered. PR #9207 (worker/ssrbool-b), gates green, opened not yet merged.

WHAT LANDED. (1) The eight roster omissions the audit named, reconciled against the INSTALLED react-dom 19.2.0: presence gains disablePictureInPicture, disableRemotePlayback, scoped, seamless; the stringifying family gains autoReverse, externalResourcesRequired, focusable, preserveAlpha. (2) An external anchor, which is the part that matters — implementation/ssr/test/react_dom_probe/boolean_attr_classes.cjs renders every boolean-valued attribute react-dom accepts and writes react-dom's OWN markup to a committed .edn beside it; re_frame/ssr_boolean_attr_react_parity_test.clj derives the class from those bytes in Clojure and compares it with boolean-attr-class IN BOTH DIRECTIONS (a name React classifies that the roster omits, and a name the roster carries that React does not, both red), then drives all 48 evidence rows through all three public emitters — render-to-string, render-shell, emit-ui-tree. (3) spec/011-SSR.md gains the structural lesson and both dispositions. 004B untouched.

WHY THE PROBE IS NOT CIRCULAR, since that is the thing a third carrier should check first. Both halves come from react-dom, not from us: candidate NAMES are the values of react-dom's own possibleStandardNames table (scraped from the dev build), and "is this a boolean attribute?" is React's own dev-build "Received `true` for a non-boolean attribute" warning. A candidate list taken from our roster would have reproduced the audit's blind spot verbatim. That warning is also what BOUNDS this to a roster correction rather than a react-dom clone: the numeric attributes (cols, rows, size, span, rowSpan, start) coerce a boolean into markup through arithmetic — `size={true}` really does render size="true" — but React warns on them, so React's own verdict excludes them and we do not model a fourth class.

THE TWO DISPOSITIONS, both DECIDED not deferred, and both PINNED so the premise changing is itself a failure. `value` stays :ordinary — react-dom stringifies a boolean `value` because `value` shares a serialiser branch with the booleanish names, not because it is one; that branch is the generic push-what-you-were-given path and a string or number `value` (the only kinds a form control carries) serialises identically under :ordinary, so the classification bites only for a boolean `value`, which on a form control is an author error rather than a state; and `value` is a 004B form-control special form whose meaning already varies per element, so reclassifying it from the shared SSR roster would have changed ui-tree's handling of that special form from outside 004B. `ismap` stays :presence on 004B's word, and that word is FALSIFIED against the installed React — react-dom 19.2 accepts no boolean ismap at all (warns, emits nothing), so it cannot appear in the evidence; ismap IS a real HTML boolean attribute so presence is HTML-correct, and what is unsettled is whether the grammar tracks HTML or react-dom where they part. Both are recorded in the test's `divergences` map with reasons, in the boolean-attr-class docstring, and in 011.

NON-VACUITY WITNESS. Roster reverted to its eight-name-short state with the new tests left in place: exit 1, 40 failures — 8 in boolean-attr-class-agrees-with-installed-react-dom (exactly the eight names), 12 each in the two hiccup emitter tests (4 presence x true, plus 4 stringifying x true and false), 8 in the structural-tree test. EVERY pre-existing #9194 boolean deftest stayed GREEN through that run, which is the audit's point made mechanically.

GROUND A THIRD CARRIER STILL HAS. (a) rf2-u6zw — 004B's ismap row is falsified against the installed react-dom, and 004B may want to carry the `value` disposition; a spec decision, deliberately out of this bead's fence. (b) rf2-4hjw — implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/dom/server.cljs carries its OWN boolean roster with the same class of omission (missing inert, noModule, scoped, seamless, disablePictureInPicture, disableRemotePlayback, and no stringifying or overloaded class at all); its react-dom parity test is corpus-driven so it only catches what the corpus contains. title: surface-review(http): frame-scope managed request cancellation and supersession
description:
## Scope

Correct the frame isolation of implementation/http managed-request lifetime tracking: raw app-authored :request-id supersession, :rf.http/managed-abort, and actor-destroy cancellation. Keep the public :rf.http/managed args map and :rf.http/managed-abort effect shape unchanged.

## Correctness finding

The HTTP registry is process-global but both of its cancellation indexes use frame-local identifiers without the frame: in-flight is request-id -> handle and actor-in-flight is actor-id -> handles. managed-handler correctly captures the issuing frame, yet passes the raw request-id to next-issuance! and supersede!. managed-abort-handler receives frame-ctx but deliberately ignores it and aborts by the raw id. The actor-destroy hook likewise accepts only actor-id. Consequently two isolated frames running the same application code are not isolated at the managed-HTTP lifetime boundary.

A frame B request using the same ordinary stable id as frame A supersedes and suppresses A's live request. A manual abort dispatched in B can abort A even when B owns no request. Generated/fixed actor ids are also frame-local, so destroying an actor in one frame can walk the same actor-id slot containing another frame's handles. This is especially exposed by documented per-request SSR frames, Story/test variants, and side-by-side mounts: reusing code naturally reuses ids such as :articles/load.

## Steps to Reproduce

From implementation/http on current tip, the following read-only registry probe records a frame-A handle, then exercises the same production supersede selector a frame-B managed-handler calls:

  clojure -M -e "(require '[re-frame.http.registry :as r]) (r/clear-all-in-flight!) (let [seen (atom []) _ (r/record-in-flight! :shared nil {:frame :frame/a :abort-fn #(swap! seen conj [:frame/a %])})] (println (pr-str {:before (select-keys (r/lookup-in-flight :shared) [:frame]) :cross-frame-supersede-found? (boolean (r/supersede! :shared)) :aborts @seen :after (r/lookup-in-flight :shared)}))) (r/clear-all-in-flight!)"

Exit 0 output:

  {:before {:frame :frame/a}, :cross-frame-supersede-found? true, :aborts [[:frame/a :request-id-superseded]], :after nil}

A second probe invokes the real abort effect handler with frame B's context over frame A's registered handle:

  clojure -M -e "(require '[re-frame.http.registry :as r] '[re-frame.http.handlers :as h]) (r/clear-all-in-flight!) (let [seen (atom []) _ (r/record-in-flight! :shared nil {:frame :frame/a :abort-fn #(swap! seen conj [:frame/a %])})] (h/managed-abort-handler {:frame :frame/b :event [:cancel]} :shared) (println (pr-str {:caller-frame :frame/b :aborts @seen}))) (r/clear-all-in-flight!)"

Exit 0 output:

  {:caller-frame :frame/b, :aborts [[:frame/a :user]]}

This is not merely a test helper artifact. transport/run-attempt! publishes every live/backoff handle through registry/record-in-flight! using the raw normalized request-id; handlers/managed-handler calls supersede! with that same raw id before each fresh issuance.

## Source evidence

- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/handlers.cljc:207-220 and 253-267 capture :frame in the normalized context, proving frame identity is available.
- handlers.cljc:381-410 nevertheless calls next-issuance! and supersede! with request-id alone.
- handlers.cljc:413-428 names managed-abort-handler's first arg _frame-ctx and calls abort-in-flight! with request-id alone.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/registry.cljc:36-73 defines process-global atoms keyed only by request-id and actor-id.
- registry.cljc:87-179 clears, looks up, and aborts by unqualified request-id; 201-289 keys issuance and supersession the same way.
- registry.cljc:391-428 aborts actor work by actor-id alone, while the hook contract receives no frame.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc:1082 and 1701 are the live/backoff record-in-flight! sites; handles carry :frame, but the lookup key does not.
- spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:790 promises replies remain in their issuing frame; docs/core/frames.md:138-140 defines SSR and repeated mounts as isolated worlds. The lifetime side channel currently breaks that same isolation before reply routing.
- The repository already proved this class for higher-level consumers: commit 450cdd44a1 (rf2-sxyrzk) had resources/mutations synthesize [:rf.req frame-id work-id] because the process-global HTTP registry otherwise cross-cancelled identical frame-local work ids. That workaround does not protect direct :rf.http/managed users, whose ergonomic API accepts ordinary stable ids.

## Recommended bounded repair

Make the issuing frame part of HTTP's internal cancellation identity while preserving the caller's raw :request-id as the public correlation value echoed in replies and traces. Thread frame through request lookup/supersede/manual-abort/issuance and through actor-destroy cancellation (or use an equivalent compound internal key). A programmer should be able to write :request-id :articles/load once in reusable app code; the runtime, which already carries frame identity, should provide isolation automatically.

Keep the existing process-global atoms if compound keys are the smallest repair. Reuse the existing identity-conditional cleanup, retry handoff, finalisation CAS, and frame-destroy sweep. Update Spec 014 and internal comments that currently describe request-id keying as process-global to state the intended same-frame supersession law. Existing resource-generated qualified ids may remain if removing that redundant qualification would broaden the change; compatibility matters less than keeping this repair focused and mechanically safe.

## Posture rationale

This is a correctness and ergonomics repair, not extra machinery. Requiring every direct HTTP caller (and AI-generated app code) to remember to bake a frame id into an otherwise simple stable request id leaks a runtime implementation detail and makes reusable event code unsafe in the exact multi-frame/SSR modes the library advertises. Internal compound identity uses information already present and keeps the public API minimal. Do not add namespaces, registries, lease objects, user-facing tokens, or configuration switches.

## Non-goals

- No new public request-id type, frame argument, cancellation verb, failure kind, or compatibility alias.
- No transport, retry, decode, privacy, reply-envelope, or stale-trace redesign.
- No requirement to move process-global atoms into every frame; correct compound keying is sufficient.
- No attempt to make explicit cross-frame cancellation possible through this local effect. If such orchestration is ever needed, it deserves a separate explicit surface rather than accidental raw-id reach-through.
- No cleanup of the resources workaround unless required to keep its current behavior green.

## Related and duplicate search

Searched all-status beads with bd search/list across titles and descriptions for request-id, managed HTTP, in-flight registry, frame isolation, cross-frame, frame-qualify, frame-scope, supersede, and abort. No current or closed bead owns direct managed-HTTP cross-frame cancellation. The closest current HTTP issues are closed rf2-rsv2n (abort during body preparation), closed rf2-o9e15 (supersede-test flake), and closed rf2-lddbk (successful response metadata); all are distinct.

History search found commit 450cdd44a1 / historical rf2-sxyrzk, which fixed only resources and mutations by pre-qualifying their generated transport ids and explicitly documented the still-process-global HTTP registry. Commit d4f85afcac added frame-destroy aborts but its tests use distinct request ids per frame. The existing spec/conformance/fixtures/http-managed-frame-isolation.edn uses canned replies with no :request-id, so it never enters this registry. The full implementation/http JVM suite is green (506 tests, 3882 assertions, 0 failures/errors), confirming the current suite lacks this adversarial same-id/two-frame case rather than contradicting the reproduction.

## Uncertainties

The minimal internal signature migration needs care because resources calls the late-bound abort-by-id seam with its already-qualified token, and machines currently calls the actor-destroy hook with actor-id alone. The implementer should choose whether those internal hooks gain frame-id or accept a compound selector while leaving app-facing effects unchanged. CLJS is single-threaded but the same key collision exists; JVM/SSR additionally needs existing atomic/identity-conditional cleanup preserved under concurrent frames.
acceptance_criteria:
- A deterministic direct-managed-HTTP test creates two live frames, issues overlapping requests with the same raw :request-id in both, and proves both remain live; neither receives :request-id-superseded merely because the sibling frame reused the id.
- Reissuing that id inside frame A still supersedes exactly A's prior attempt, emits one stale-suppressed row with carried/current ids for A, and leaves frame B's handle and eventual reply untouched.
- Dispatching [:rf.http/managed-abort id] in frame A aborts only A's request; the identical id in frame B remains live and completes into B. The symmetric B case also passes.
- A cross-frame actor case uses the same generated or fixed actor-id in two frames; destroying A's actor aborts only A-owned HTTP and leaves B's actor request live. The actor-destroy hook carries enough frame identity to make this structural, not naming-convention-dependent.
- Frame destroy and epoch restore still abort every handle owned by the selected frame, including two sibling frames that reused a request id; retry-backoff handles remain continuously cancellable and clean only their own registry entry.
- App-visible replies/traces continue to echo the caller's original :request-id, not an internal compound key. Existing single-frame request-id, abort, supersede, retry-race, actor-destroy, and resource/mutation qualified-id tests remain green on JVM and CLJS.
- The two reproduction probes above no longer resolve or abort frame A from a frame-B selector through the supported production path; a negative control restoring raw global keying makes the new same-id/two-frame tests fail.
- Spec 014 and API/docs describe same-id supersession and managed-abort as frame-scoped, consistent with the isolated-world frame contract, without asking callers to manually qualify ids.

## Verdict (PR #9195)

PREMISE HOLDS, and was reproduced at tip before any edit. Spec 014 was SILENT
on cancellation scope — it said neither "frame-scoped" nor "process-global" —
so this settled the contract and implemented it (outcome 2 of the three the
dispatch named).

### Reproduced at tip (afe446ea71 / 835ea4804f), all four probes exit 0

- `supersede!` driven from frame B resolved and aborted frame A's handle:
  `{:cross-frame-supersede-found? true, :aborts [[:frame/a :request-id-superseded]], :after nil}`
- `managed-abort-handler` with frame B's ctx aborted frame A's handle:
  `{:caller-frame :frame/b, :aborts [[:frame/a :user]]}`
- `abort-on-actor-destroy :actor/x` aborted BOTH frames' handles.
- FOURTH finding the bead did not record: the issuance counter was shared too —
  frame B's FIRST issuance under a shared raw id read **2**, not 1, perturbing
  B's `:work/id` for a supersession that never happened to it.

Frame-scoping was chosen because process-global contradicts what 014 already
says: §Frame awareness promises multi-frame apps "work without extra
ceremony" (false unless every caller hand-qualifies ids); §Chain order and
frame scope already makes the sibling HTTP surface — the interceptor chain —
per-frame; §Sibling actors are not affected already asserts inter-actor
isolation. Spec 014 gains §Frame scope — a `:request-id` is frame-local, a
§Frame scope note under Abort on actor destroy, §Frame awareness extended from
reply routing to request lifetime, and the snapshot helpers' new arities.

The issuing frame is now part of the INTERNAL key (`[frame-id id]`) for both
indexes and the issuance counters, derived from the `:frame` stamp the
transport already puts on every handle. Public `:rf.http/managed` args map and
`:rf.http/managed-abort` effect shape unchanged; the caller's raw
`:request-id` stays the correlation value echoed in replies and traces. No new
namespace, registry, lease object, user-facing token or config switch.

`implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_frame_scoped_cancellation_test.clj`
(9 deftests, deterministic — latched localhost `HttpServer`, no timing-
sensitive assertion). AC 7's negative control was run: restoring raw global

structural" needs the HOOK'S CALLERS to pass a frame, and both are outside the
dispatched fence: `machines/lifecycle_fx/finalize.cljc`

bound one line above) and `core/frame.cljc` ~3983's machines-absent fallback.
The registry half IS done — the actor index is keyed `[frame-id actor-id]` and

line per call site. Its `[actor-id]` arity is retained as the documented
ANY-FRAME sweep so no flag day is needed. Filed rf2-wjfm (P2,
discovered-from rf2-o8ek) with both call sites named.

The resources any-frame seam (`:http/abort-in-flight!`) was left unchanged and
is correct as-is: its token is already frame-qualified
(`[:rf.req frame-id work-id]`, Spec 016), so at most one frame can match.

Both production `record-in-flight!` sites stamp `:frame (:frame ctx)` from a
ctx whose value came through `require-frame-stamp!` (throws on nil), so a real
handle can never lack one. `flows_http_integration_test.clj`'s
`prime-in-flight!` and the `managed_http_counter` example's demo-only seed fx

1. `examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs` was changed to stamp `:frame` on its seeded handle, yet its `:abort-fn` still calls one-arg `(clear-in-flight! request-id)`. #9195 redefined that arity as an ANY-FRAME sweep. With the demo mounted in frames A and B under its stable `:http-counter/long` id, cancelling A invokes A's abort closure and deletes BOTH registry slots; B's fake long request becomes unregistered/unabortable and its UI can remain loading. A deterministic JVM registry probe using that exact closure shape produced `{:aborts [[:frame/a :user]], :a-live? false, :b-live? false}`. 2. `clear-in-flight!`'s 2-arg nil-handle branch also delegates to the ANY-FRAME sweep. Both live-fetch host paths acknowledge a publication window between `record-in-flight!` and `reset! handle-holder`; on the JVM another thread can fire the just-published abort-fn there. A nil handle from frame A can therefore delete an already-live same-id frame-B slot. The comment that the window "precedes any successor" covers only same-frame succession, not a sibling frame that was already live.

Keep rf2-wjfm as the existing owner of the deliberately deferred actor-hook call sites. On this owner, make every cleanup path that possesses an issuing frame frame-exact, including the demo and nil/publication path, and add same-id/two-frame witnesses for both. REOPENED by merged-PR audit of #9202. The cross-frame cleanup paths are fixed, but the new frame-exact fallback does not close the publication race across the registry TWO indexes. record-in-flight! publishes the stamped handle to in-flight first (registry.cljc:142-143), then actor-in-flight in a separate swap! A JVM abort between those swaps invokes the handle while its forward-reference cell is still nil; clear-in-flight-in-frame! removes the request slot and tries to remove the actor slot before that slot exists, then record-in-flight! resumes and publishes the already-aborted handle into actor-in-flight. Preserve the frame-scoped and identity-conditional laws, but make publication plus cleanup coherent across both indexes (or make the stamped handle identity available to the abort closure before either publish). Add a controlled midpoint interleaving witness asserting both indexes are empty after the abort; the landed tests call cleanup only after record-in-flight! has finished and therefore cannot see this gap.
## Round 3 verdict (PR #9251) — the #9202 audit finding

PREMISE HOLDS, reproduced at tip (150805f821) before any edit with the
audit's own recorded output, byte for byte:

  {:abort-fired? true, :request-slot nil, :actor-slot-count 1}

Governing note confirmed by probe rather than by reading the title: at the
LAST closed snapshot notes=6241, newest=7667 — 1426 characters written while
closed, so the newest note is the audit and it governs. Control rf2-y1jkm
varied across the same walk (status and notes length both moved).

### Fix

record-in-flight! publishes to in-flight and actor-in-flight in two swap!s
over two atoms. Cleanup cannot close the gap between them — it cannot remove
a slot the future has not written — so PUBLICATION observes it instead,
using the identity law the rest of the registry already runs on: once both
swaps are done, if this handle is no longer the one in-flight holds under its

retracted from the actor index by identity. Only a handle carrying BOTH ids

After: {:abort-fired? true, :request-slot nil, :actor-slot-count 0}.

### Also measured, and it bounds the severity

The ghost is confined to the ISSUING frame — a sibling live under the same

({:aborts [[:frame/a :user]], :b-request true, :b-actor-count 1}). #9202's
frame-scoped keys hold; this was an incoherence within one frame.

### Witness

Four deftests appended to
implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_frame_scoped_cancellation_test.clj.
An atom's watches run on the swapping thread BEFORE swap! returns, so a watch

Three assert both indexes empty (abort door, supersede door, and with a

publication is never retracted, which an unconditional reconcile would fail.
Each carries a precondition assertion so a case whose interleaving stopped
happening fails rather than passing vacuously.

Negative control: removing the reconcile and nothing else takes the suite to

fourth correctly still green. Byte-copied before, cmp-verified on restore.

### Example checked, NOT changed

examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs is correct at tip: it stamps
:frame and its :abort-fn calls the frame-exact clear-in-flight-in-frame!
(#9202's repair for the previous round). It also seeds with actor-id nil, so
it publishes into ONE index, has no midpoint, and cannot reach this finding.
check-examples-compile.cjs therefore not a gate for this diff.

### Gates (captured exits, re-run on the final rebased base)

- implementation/http clojure -M:test: exit 0, 525 tests / 3969 assertions
- npm run test:cljs: exit 0, 11,220 tests / 56,708 assertions
- npm ci from the lockfile in the worker worktree; node_modules verified

The OTHER door is blind at the same midpoint: abort-on-actor-destroy landing
between the two swaps finds no actor slot and fires nothing, so the handle
survives its actor's destroy. Measured:
{:case :actor-destroy-at-midpoint, :abort-fired? false,
 :request-slot-present? true, :actor-slot-count 1}.
