title: TRUNK RED: the new require-alias ratchet fails on origin/main itself — two surfaces sit BELOW their baseline floor, and every open PR is blocked
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-04 09:4x AUSEST by the mayor, ON THE MAYOR CHECKOUT AT origin/main WITH NO PR INVOLVED, captured exit 1:

  python scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py --verbose
  -> 2 surface(s) now BELOW their baseline floor - lower the floor in
     scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn (--write-baseline) so the ratchet holds
     the ground that was won:
       implementation/flows: 155 violation(s), floor 156
       implementation/ssr:   399 violation(s), floor 402

HOW IT GOT HERE. PR #9135 (rf2-ydpr, worker/ratchet-a) merged at a48586caf5 and armed the ratchet as a NEW REQUIRED lint.yml job. Its baseline was captured before two other sweeps landed, so flows is one below its floor and ssr is three below. The ratchet is deliberately two-sided - it refuses when you drop below the floor as well as when you rise above it, so that ground won is held - and that second side is what is firing.

BLAST RADIUS: EVERY OPEN PR. The job is required, and lint.yml's aggregator 'Lint required' consumes it (its log reads 'needs results: success, success, success, skipped, success, failure'), so both go red on any branch whose content is irrelevant to require aliases. Confirmed on PR #9139, a documentation-only change: rebased onto the new trunk it came back 87 checks with exactly these 2 failures. No merge can pass clause 2 of the merge criterion until this is fixed.

THE FIX is small and the tool names it: lower the two floors. scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py --write-baseline is the affordance the error message points at.

BUT DO NOT RUN --write-baseline BLIND, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE CARE OF THE BEAD. A ratchet floor may only ever go DOWN. If --write-baseline rewrites every row from the current tree, it will also RAISE any row whose count has risen since the baseline was captured - which silently grants permission for a regression that has already happened and destroys the ratchet's purpose on that surface. Read what --write-baseline actually does at source BEFORE running it. Diff the file it produces against HEAD and confirm every changed row moved DOWNWARD; if any row would rise, do not accept that hunk - lower the two failing rows only, and report the rising row as a separate finding with its numbers.

ALSO CHECK, DO NOT ASSUME: whether more than two rows are stale in the downward direction. The tool reported two because two crossed their floor; a row sitting well below its floor without crossing reports nothing at all. Compare every row against a fresh scan and say which rows are slack and by how much.

RELATED, AND NOT YOURS: rf2-ttss covers implementation/http's row, which reads 272 while PR #9142 (unmerged) takes that surface to 0. Do NOT touch the http row - #9142 has not landed, so 272 is still correct at tip, and lowering it now would red the ratchet a second way. Leave it and let rf2-ttss handle it after #9142 merges.

GATE: scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py itself, captured exit 0 after the fix, plus a planted non-canonical alias in one of the two repaired surfaces proving the tightened floor still bites (a green after tightening proves nothing on its own). Its --self-test if it has one. Read .github/workflows/lint.yml for how CI invokes it and match that invocation.

URGENT: this blocks the whole merge queue.
close_reason: PR #9144 lowers the two crossed floors (implementation/flows 156->155, implementation/ssr 402->399) in scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn. --write-baseline was diffed rather than accepted blind: it changes only those two rows plus :min-edges 9692->9691, and NO surface row would have risen. :min-edges left at 9692 because for that key lower is looser (blind-scanner floor, total<min-edges), not tighter. A --report census confirms no other row is slack — after the change every surface sits exactly at its floor, none under, none OVER. implementation/http untouched at 272 (rf2-ttss owns it post-#9142). Gate: --self-test exit 0 (40 passed) and --verbose exit 0 on the final rebased base; planted non-canonical alias in implementation/flows took it to exit 1 naming 'implementation/flows: 156 violation(s), floor 155', proving the tightened floor still bites.

title: realworld-resources: the example's app-db never seeds in a development build (same boot-window defect as rf2-2xzc)
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-04 on worker/dispatchlater-a, not inferred. A dev build of
`:examples/realworld-resources` (shadow-cljs compile, served over HTTP, headless Chrome):
app-db is `{}`, zero article cards, `#app` is a 1698-character shell. Zero page errors.

SAME MECHANISM AS rf2-2xzc, whose full write-up is on that bead. examples/real-apps/
realworld_resources/schema.cljs registers four NON-NILABLE app-db path schemas against
:rf/default at ns-load:

    [:auth]                AuthSlice
    [:auth :login-form]    FormSlice
    [:auth :register-form] FormSlice
    [:settings-form]       FormSlice

app-db starts {} and the candidate validator walks EVERY registered path over the WHOLE
candidate app-db at EVERY :db commit (spec/010 §Per-step recovery row 4) with no exemption
for a path nothing has written yet. `:app/initialise` (core.cljs) fans out to
[:auth.login-form/initialise] and [:auth.register-form/initialise] as separate dispatches,
and `:auth/initialise` is its own :initial-events step - so each seed is its own commit and
each is rejected by the siblings still absent.

WORSE THAN THE SIBLING IN ONE RESPECT: [:settings-form] is never seeded at boot at all, so
that path reads nil forever. Every :db commit in that application is rejected permanently,
not only during the boot window. And because a rejected candidate does not walk :fx either,
nothing downstream of a :db-bearing handler fires.

DEV ONLY, for the same reason: validate-app-schema!'s whole body is inside
(if interop/debug-enabled? ... true), so a release build installs every candidate.

WHY NO TEST SEES IT: reg-app-schemas is frame-local to :rf/default and
realworld_resources_cljs_test.cljs drives anonymous frames (it re-registers [:auth] against
its own frame by hand at line 550, which is the tell).

THE FIX is the one PR #9134 applied to the managed-HTTP sibling: wrap each registration in
:maybe for the boot window with the rationale written out (the idiom
examples/patterns/boot/schema.cljs already documents), and name the registry as a value so a
harness can install it on its own frame. Then add the matching contract test in the framework
tree - examples are test-free (rf2-8cevm) - mirroring
implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_realworld_boot_seed_cljs_test.cljs. Note that ns
cannot co-load both apps' auth/settings nses (duplicate ids under the image-assembly guard),
so the resources coverage needs its own ns.

P1 because it is the same class of failure as rf2-2xzc: total, silent, application-wide, and
only in the build every consumer develops against.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #9143 (branch worker/resboot-a), open against main. examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/schema.cljs now wraps all four app-db path registrations in :maybe and names the registry as the value app-db-schemas so a harness can install it on its own frame. The two reasons are kept apart at the site: a boot WINDOW for [:auth], [:auth :login-form] and [:auth :register-form] (each seeded by its own event, so its own commit), and PERMANENT absence-by-design for [:settings-form], which :settings/load seeds from the authenticated user on settings-route entry behind an auth guard - so it reads nil for the whole life of the app for an anonymous visitor, and bare it rejected every :db commit in the application forever, not only during boot. Judged on the stance: [:settings-form] is deliberately NOT also seeded at boot, because a boot seed would manufacture an empty draft from a user who is not signed in yet, to be overwritten on entry, and would defeat the route-entry seed that keeps the form a pure Form-1. Contract test added in the framework tree (examples are test-free, rf2-8cevm) at implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_realworld_resources_boot_seed_cljs_test.cljs - a NEW file, not the sibling's. It is differential: boot-under-the-shipped-registry is paired with boot-under-the-pre-fix-bare-registry, so a soft-passing validator fails the pair rather than silently passing the positive half. Gate: npm run test:cljs, captured exit 0 on the final rebased base, 11173 tests / 55748 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 warnings. Planted-fault control: unwrapping all four :maybe values (the pre-fix registration verbatim) gives captured exit 1 with 17 failures and app-db stuck at {} - the on-screen symptom reproduced; restore verified by git blob hash. Two mechanism findings recorded in the new ns docstring for the next person adding a RealWorld-touching test to the core tree: (1) requiring the resources app's EVENT nses from a core-tree ns that sorts early puts a second provenance row for the ids both RealWorld apps register into the shared source store from that ns's load onward, failing default-image assembly with :rf.error/image-duplicate-id across nine later namespaces; (2) sequestering the sibling tree from there does not fix it, because sequester-app-namespaces! memoizes its capture and a call that early becomes an incomplete memo for every later suite. reg-app-schemas writes no registrar or source-store row, so requiring the example's schema ns alone is collision-free, and that is what the test does. Separately observed and NOT introduced here: the new require-alias ratchet reports implementation/flows (155, floor 156) and implementation/ssr (399, floor 402) below their floors on trees this branch does not touch - already tracked as rf2-ril5.

title: realworld: the Global Feed renders zero articles - silently, while Popular Tags from the same demo backend populate (pilot 1's nominated screen)
description:
FOUND 2026-09-03 ~17:40 AUSEST by the rf2-t4jpz PRE-PILOT rehearsal, running the
OPERATOR half of docs/design/hicasso/product/pilots/workspace.md at pin
6e9bb105fc9b1569d63fdebc212b7787a2a023ba.

SYMPTOM. The RealWorld/Conduit example's Global Feed renders NO ARTICLES. The
page shows the RealWorld empty state, "No articles are here... yet.", and it
never changes. Nothing complains: 0 page errors, 0 console errors of any level
(the only two console messages are React DevTools' banner and shadow-cljs'
"#6 ready!"), 0 failed or 4xx requests, and the stylesheet resolves (52 rules).
#app innerHTML is 2350 characters - the same number the previous operator run
recorded and read as a pass.

WHY IT MATTERS. The feed is pilot 1's FIRST NOMINATED SCREEN. brief-realworld.md
tells the blinded pilot "it works today. Run it before you change anything" and
then asks it to migrate "the feed" to Hicasso. A pilot meeting an empty feed has
no article card to port, no before/after to compare, and a false premise in its
own brief. This is not scaffolding the operator got wrong - it reproduces from a
workspace assembled literally from the manifest, with every step green.

THE POPULAR TAGS SIDEBAR ON THE SAME PAGE RENDERS, and that is the discriminator.
Tags come back through the SAME in-page demo backend and the SAME
:realworld.demo/http-stub override of :rf.http/managed (realworld_http/http.cljs),
and they populate: intro, demo, clojure, re-frame. So the stub is installed, the
managed-HTTP path works, and the demo world has articles in it (the tag list is
derived from the seeded articles' :tagList - demo_backend.cljs line 544-545 -
so a populated sidebar PROVES the seed corpus is present and reachable).
Whatever fails is specific to the article-list read.

MEASURED, four ways, all on one build and one server:
  /                            #app 2350, empty feed, 0 errors
  /realworld                   #app 2350, empty feed, 0 errors
  click "Home" (route-link)    URL unchanged, still empty, 0 errors
  click the "clojure" tag      URL -> /realworld/tag/clojure, heading shows
                               "clojure", STILL "No articles are here... yet."
The tag click is the important row: the route matched WITH its path param (the
heading proves it), so :realworld/home-tag's :on-match [[:home/load]] fired,
and :home/load's own :fx dispatches [:tags/load] and [:articles/load] together
(tags.cljs). Tags updated. Articles did not.

NOT A BASE-PATH ARTEFACT. routing.cljs:254 wires
(routing/with-base-path routing/history-url-strategy "/realworld"), so the app
is served from a sub-path in the repository's own example site. The workspace
serves public/ at the root of :dev-http instead. That mismatch is real and is
filed separately, but it is NOT this: the tag row above is at a URL where the
base path is correct, and the feed is empty there too.

NOT AN ERROR PATH. The view renders the machine's :empty state, not its error
state, so :articles/load-failed did not fire and :articles/error is nil. The
fetch "succeeded" and produced nothing.

THE BEHAVIOURAL BASELINE CANNOT SEE THIS, which is why it has survived. Both
pilot baselines are green at this pin (realworld npm test exit 0, Ran 4 tests
containing 123 assertions, 0 failures). But baseline_test.cljs drives
:articles/load with :fx-overrides {:rf.http/managed :realworld.test/canned-articles}
- CANNED replies, not the demo backend - so it asserts the slice fills from a
reply it supplied itself and never exercises demo_backend/handle at all. Examples
are test-free by policy and no CI lane renders this app, so nothing in the tree
watches this screen.

ROOT CAUSE NOT PINNED. Two candidates were opened and neither closed: the
demo backend's dispatcher matches the article list with
(str/ends-with? path "/articles") after stripping the query (demo_backend.cljs
:438, path-of/query-params at :385ff), and paged reads :limit/:offset back out
of the query string via query-int. Either could be it; so could something above
them in :rf.http/managed. Left for the fix dispatch rather than guessed at here.

REPRODUCE. Assemble pilot 1's workspace per workspace.md steps 1-4 at this pin,
npx shadow-cljs watch app, load http://localhost:8080/ in a browser and read the
Global Feed. Expect the empty state beside a populated Popular Tags sidebar.
Control: pilot 2 (LinearLite) through the identical harness renders its three
issue cards across three status columns, #app 3535, 0 errors - so the harness
and the assembly procedure are sound and the discriminator is this application.
notes:
SCOPE IS FAR LARGER THAN THIS BEAD'S TITLE, and the discriminator is DEV vs RELEASE, not the feed. Established 2026-09-03 by pilot 1 of the rf2-t4jpz rehearsal - a BLINDED agent that had never seen this bead, reading only the 29 published pages - which lost roughly a third of its run to it before isolating it. Same pin, 6e9bb105fc9b1569d63fdebc212b7787a2a023ba.

THE RULE. In a DEVELOPMENT build the demo backend's HTTP replies do not settle in Chrome. In a RELEASE build, same machine, same browser, same commit, they all do.

Development build, headless Chrome, four screens:
  the feed                  Hicasso (migrated)   "No articles are here... yet."
  article detail (deep link) Reagent, UNTOUCHED  "No article loaded."
  profile (deep link)        Reagent, UNTOUCHED  "No profile loaded."
  sign in                    Reagent, UNTOUCHED  stays `anonymous`

Release build, same browser, same driver:
  the feed        10 cards, "Hello, Conduit", pagination 1/2/3
  article detail  a real backend reply - "Couldn't load article: Article not found."
  sign in         `authed`
  the editor      renders, publishes, navigates

TWO UNTOUCHED REAGENT SCREENS FAIL IDENTICALLY TO THE MIGRATED ONE. So this is neither the view layer, nor the migration, nor the feed - it is application-wide and substrate-independent, and my own operator measurement (the description above) was taken on a `shadow-cljs watch` build, which is why it looked like a feed defect. The Popular Tags sidebar populating while articles did not is the one fact that still needs explaining against this rule, and it is the loose end worth pulling.

WHAT THE PILOT RULED OUT, each measured: headless timer throttling (`setTimeout(...,0)` at 0 ms, `requestAnimationFrame` at 0 ms, microtasks running); a stale bundle (reproduced on a clean watch restart); the reply delay (`reply-delay-ms` is 20); an SPA fallback artefact (reproduced before any fallback existed).

THE PILOT'S ONE UNTESTED LEAD, and it could not test it without reading source the fence bars: the demo backend defers every reply through `:dispatch-later`, and `:dispatch-later` is the common factor in everything that fails. That is where a fix dispatch should start.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE EXAMPLE. If deferred effects do not settle in development builds generally, every developer meets it on every async path, and the symptom is an empty screen with no error - the most expensive failure shape there is. The pilot graded its own entry `none` for defect class because it could not honestly attribute a cause; that is the right grading and it is not a judgement that the finding is small.

CROSS-REFERENCE: the pilot's own entry is P1-F21 in ai/findings/2026-09-03.pilot-b-rehearsal-realworld.friction-log.md (local-only), and the same log's outcome-6 row records the release build passing both halves against this bundle.

MECHANISM PINNED 2026-09-04 (worker/dispatchlater-a, PR #9134). NOT :dispatch-later,
and no request was ever issued. :dispatch-later, the demo backend, the canned-reply
path and managed HTTP are all healthy; the after-fix event stream shows both
:rf.http/deliver-canned-reply hops through :dispatch-later working exactly as designed.

THE MECHANISM. examples/real-apps/realworld_http/schema.cljs registers NINETEEN app-db
path schemas against :rf/default at ns-load, all of them non-nilable. app-db starts {},
and each slice is seeded by its OWN feature's :*/initialise, fanned out from
:app/initialise - separate events, therefore separate commits. The candidate validator
(re-frame.router/run-candidate-validation! -> re-frame.schemas.validate/validate-app-schema!)
walks EVERY registered path over the WHOLE candidate app-db at EVERY :db commit,
(get-in db path), with NO exemption for a path nothing has written yet - spec/010 line 73
states this outright ('a normal [:map ...] schema over the nil app-db slot ... detonates
every dev commit'). An unwritten path reads nil, which is not a [:map ...]. So the FIRST
seed was rejected by the eighteen siblings still absent; every later seed was rejected the
same way; app-db never left {}. Measured: app-db is {} on a live page while
[:rf.runtime/routing :current] is fully populated.

WHY IT LOOKED LIKE 'REPLIES DO NOT SETTLE'. A rejected candidate does NOT walk :fx
(spec/010 row 4). So :articles/load's [:rf.http/managed ...] never fired - no request, no
:dispatch-later armed. Measured two ways on the same dispatch: a :trace listener showed
:rf.event/dispatched, :run-start, :db-pending, 17 x :rf.error/schema-validation-failure
(:rollback? true, :where :app-db), :run-end - and NO :rf.fx/handled at all; and a patched
re-frame.interop/set-timeout! recorded zero timers armed.

WHY DEV ONLY. validate-app-schema!'s entire body sits inside
(if interop/debug-enabled? ... true) - goog.DEBUG. A release build returns true without
walking anything and every candidate installs. That is the whole dev/release split the
pilot found; it is not timers, not the view layer, not the migration.

THE POPULAR TAGS LOOSE END, EXPLAINED. The tags lifecycle lives ENTIRELY in the
:realworld/tags state machine. Its snapshot is runtime-db, validated by the machine-data
boundary against the machine's own [:schemas :data], whose :data the machine spec seeds
itself. :tags/load and :tags/loaded return ONLY :fx, never :db, so app-effect? is false and
the app-db validator never ran for them. The one panel on the page that never touches
app-db is the one that worked. The pilot's LinearLite control renders because it registers
no app-db schemas at all (grep: no reg-app-schema under examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite).

WHY THE BASELINE COULD NOT SEE IT. reg-app-schemas is FRAME-LOCAL and the example registers
against :rf/default. Every existing test drives the example in an anonymous frame
(make-anon-frame-record!), which carries no app-db schemas - so the registry that kills the
real app is inert in the harness. realworld_cljs_test.cljs even re-registers [:auth] against
its own frame by hand for one regression, which is the tell.

VERDICT: EXAMPLE DEFECT, not a framework defect. The semantics is documented (spec/010) and
the corpus already teaches the correct usage with a written rationale -
examples/patterns/boot/schema.cljs: 'Each slot below starts out nil - the boot machine fills
it in later - so every registration wears a :maybe to stay valid through the loading phases.'

FIX (PR #9134): every registration in realworld_http/schema.cljs now wears :maybe for the
boot window, with the rationale written out, and the registry becomes a named value
app-db-schemas so a harness can install the app's real registry on its own frame. Plus a new
substrate contract test, implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_realworld_boot_seed_cljs_test.cljs
(examples stay test-free), which drives the example's own boot fan-out under its own registry
AND pins the framework semantics underneath it.

WITNESS. dev build, headless Chrome, real shadow-cljs bundle over HTTP:
  before  #app 2350, 'No articles are here... yet.', app-db {}
  after   #app 13236, ten article cards + pagination, app-db seeded
  release after: #app 9130, ten cards - dev and release now agree.
Article detail, sign-in and post-login home all render in dev after the fix. Zero page errors
either side.
Same instrument both sides on the identical dispatch: before {:event [:articles/load]
:outcome :rolled-back}; after {:event [:articles/load] :outcome :ok} plus five more events
ending in :articles/loaded with ten articles.
Test witness: with the pre-fix registrations planted back (17 sites), the new ns is exit 1
with 15/17 assertions failing and app-db {}; with the fix, exit 0. The two assertions that
pass either way are the ones pinning framework semantics. Restore verified by blob hash.
Gates (exit codes captured to files): shadow-cljs compile node-test 0; node out/node-test.js
--test= the new ns + the five existing realworld nses 0, 'Ran 90 tests containing 899
assertions. 0 failures, 0 errors.'; clj-kondo on both changed files 0; shadow-cljs release
:examples/realworld 0.

THREE THINGS FILED SEPARATELY RATHER THAN FIXED HERE (outside this fence):
  1. examples/real-apps/realworld_resources has the SAME defect - MEASURED, not inferred:
     dev build, app-db {}, zero cards, page renders a 1698-char shell. Four non-nilable
     schemas at ns-load ([:auth], [:auth :login-form], [:auth :register-form],
     [:settings-form]) and [:settings-form] is never seeded at boot at all, so that app's
     every :db commit is rejected permanently rather than only during boot.
  2. :rf.error/schema-validation-failure reaches ONLY the dev-only :trace stream
     (schemas/validate.cljc calls trace/emit-error!, not the both-axes emitter), never the
     always-on :errors stream. Measured with a control on the same frame: an :errors listener
     saw 0 records while :trace carried all 17, and the same listener DID receive
     :rf.error/no-such-handler for an unregistered event id. That silence is what turned a
     one-line schema mistake into an invisible app-wide rollback loop and cost the pilot a
     third of its run - worth a ruling even if the current behaviour is deliberate.
  3. A React duplicate-key warning on the article-card tag list, visible only once cards
     render (dev React only).
close_reason:
CLOSED 2026-09-04 by the mayor (backlog-reread loop): the fix is on the trunk and all three carried findings are re-homed. Nothing remains on this bead.

THE FIX. PR #9134 merged as 627d6da0a1, 'fix(realworld): the example boots under its own app-db schemas'. examples/real-apps/realworld_http/schema.cljs now wraps each app-db path registration in :maybe for the boot window with the rationale written out, names the registry as a value so a harness can install it on its own frame, and is pinned by a differential contract test in the framework tree at implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_realworld_boot_seed_cljs_test.cljs (examples are test-free, rf2-8cevm).

THE MECHANISM, for the record, because it is nothing like this bead's title. Not :dispatch-later and not HTTP: nineteen NON-NILABLE app-db path schemas registered at ns-load, against a candidate validator that walks EVERY registered path over the WHOLE candidate app-db at EVERY :db commit with no exemption for a path nothing has written yet. app-db starts {}, :app/initialise fans out to separate dispatches, so each seed is its own commit and each is rejected by the siblings still absent — app-db never leaves {}. DEV ONLY, because validate-app-schema!'s whole body sits inside (if interop/debug-enabled? ... true), which is what makes it so disorienting: the app works in release and is dead in dev. And because a rejected candidate does not walk :fx either, no request is ever ISSUED — a patched set-timeout! recorded zero timers armed, which is why the :dispatch-later lead was a dead end.

THE THREE CARRIED FINDINGS, all re-homed and none lost:
1. The same defect in examples/real-apps/realworld_resources -> rf2-ghxt, CLOSED, PR #9143 merged.
2. :rf.error/schema-validation-failure reaching only the dev-only :trace stream and never the always-on :errors stream -> rf2-xpd8, OPEN and HELD FOR MIKE. It needs a product ruling on which stream carries a rollback, not a worker.
3. The duplicate React key warning on the article-card tag list -> rf2-sefb, OPEN and dispatched to worker/exfix-a.

The DOCUMENTATION half also landed: rf2-aaam put the whole-registry-per-commit rule, the nil-reads-as-a-value trap, both escapes and the dev/release direction into docs/core/how-to/validate-with-schemas.md.

WHY CLOSE RATHER THAN HOLD: keeping a P1 open whose every part is either merged or re-homed keeps it at the head of the ready list drawing dispatch attention it cannot use. That is the 'item already DONE in the tree' case this loop exists to catch.

title: hic: workspace.md step 6 says copy the brief FROM brief-<pilot>.md, not the block INSIDE it — a literal copy hands the blinded pilot 4 bead ids and a link to the operator page
notes:
FOUND 2026-09-03 by the rf2-t4jpz PRE-PILOT rehearsal, operator half, re-run after PR #9050 and #9049. Workspace pin cfcc30ae93. This is a BLINDING LEAK on the dispatch path and should be fixed BEFORE the two pilots are dispatched.

THE DEFECT. workspace.md step 6 reads: "Copy the brief and the blank log into <pilot-root>/, from brief-realworld.md or brief-linearlite.md, and from friction-log.md's template section." Note the asymmetry inside that one sentence. For the friction log it names the SUB-PART ("template section"). For the brief it names the WHOLE FILE. But brief-realworld.md's own line 3 says "Copy the block below into <pilot-root>/BRIEF.md. Everything inside it is written to the pilot agent and is the only thing that agent is given" -- the pilot's brief is the content of the fenced markdown block, not the file.

So an operator executing step 6 literally runs "cp brief-realworld.md <pilot-root>/BRIEF.md" and hands a BLINDED pilot all of the following, none of which is inside the fence:

  1. Four tracker ids -- rf2-v04s, rf2-hic-063, rf2-xkhul, rf2-lpfz -- where the read fence's "Not allowed" column explicitly bars "Reading the tracker, git log, or any branch".
  2. A relative link to README.md#what-governs-this-directory -- the governance page, under docs/design/, out of bounds by the fence's own mkdocs rule.
  3. A relative link to workspace.md -- THE OPERATOR PAGE, of which workspace.md line 5 says "A pilot agent is never sent here". The pilot's own brief links it.
  4. The meta-paragraph explaining that the brief "is deliberately free of in-tree references" and that "a brief that leaks in-tree knowledge does not bend a rule, it invalidates the evidence the pilot exists to produce". That tells the pilot it is inside a blinding experiment being measured -- which is itself the leak the paragraph warns about.
  5. The enclosing markdown code fence, left as literal lines 11 and 157 of the delivered file.

MEASURED, BOTH PILOTS, AND THE TWO OPERATORS DIVERGED -- which is the evidence the instruction is ambiguous rather than merely terse:

  source brief-realworld.md ................ 8738 bytes, 4 bead ids
  my LITERAL step-6 copy ................... 8829 bytes, 4 bead ids, starts "# Brief -- Pilot 1: RealWorld/Conduit"
  the PREVIOUS rehearsal operator's copy ... 7066 bytes, 0 bead ids, starts "# Your brief"

The previous operator INTERPRETED step 6 and extracted the fenced block. I executed it literally and did not. Same page, same step, two different artefacts, and only one of them is blind. Both pilots are affected: the linearlite copy carries 2 bead ids by the same route.

WHY IT FAILS OPEN. The copy succeeds, exits 0, and produces a file that reads like a brief -- the pilot-facing content is all present and correct, just preceded by front matter. Nothing errors, nothing is missing, and the operator has no reason to look. The damage is invisible until somebody re-reads the delivered file, and by then the pilot has read it.

MINIMAL FIX, and it is one clause. Make step 6's brief half name the sub-part the way its friction-log half already does: "from the fenced block inside brief-realworld.md or brief-linearlite.md". Optionally add the same "Copy from here into <pilot-root>/BRIEF.md" pointer that friction-log.md's template section carries, so the two halves of step 6 are shaped alike. Do NOT restructure the briefs, move the front matter, or touch the fence -- the briefs are correct as written and say so themselves on line 3; it is workspace.md that under-specifies.

RELATION TO rf2-lpfz. Distinct. rf2-lpfz's reopened residue is pilots/README.md line 30, an operator-facing page a pilot never receives. This bead is about a pilot-facing artefact that step 6 mis-specifies, and it is the one that reaches the agent.

NOT A BLOCKER for the boot check or the baselines, both of which pass; see the rehearsal report on rf2-t4jpz. It IS a blocker for a CORRECT dispatch: per rf2-hic-063's revisit trigger (a), a leaky rehearsal finds no friction and is worthless, so dispatching on the literal artefact would burn both pilots.
close_reason: FIXED in PR #9058. workspace.md step 6 now names the sub-part for the brief exactly as it already did for the friction log: 'from the fenced block inside brief-realworld.md or brief-linearlite.md, and from the fenced block inside friction-log.md's template section', plus one sentence saying it is the block that is copied and why the front matter above it is a leak. The briefs' front matter, the fence and the briefs themselves are untouched, as the bead directs. PROVEN BY EXECUTION, not by reading: I ran the corrected step 6 literally against both briefs and the log template and asserted on the products -- realworld/BRIEF.md 7433 bytes/143 lines, linearlite/BRIEF.md 8967/170, FRICTION-LOG.md 1290/54, and all three carry 0 lines with a bead id, 0 links to workspace.md and 0 stray fence lines. The same three patterns run against the source pages as controls and all bite (brief-realworld.md 2/1/2, brief-linearlite.md 2/1/2, friction-log.md 6/4/6), so the zeroes are checks that passed rather than patterns that missed. Extraction boundaries checked at both ends. For contrast the pre-fix literal copy is 8738 bytes carrying 4 unique bead ids and a workspace.md link.

title: machines/SSR: hydration leaves pre-existing timers absent from the replacement snapshot
description:
## Scope

Repair the SSR-to-client handoff for state-machine `:after` transitions. The scope is active singleton and spawned snapshots under `[:rf.runtime/machines :snapshots]`, including flat/compound states, active paths in root-parallel regions, and a root-parallel `:after`. Keep ordinary transition semantics and epoch restore semantics unchanged.

## Correctness finding

The server intentionally suppresses machine wall-clock timers, but the client hydration path only installs the serialized runtime-db snapshot. It does not reconstruct the host-side timer table for active `:after` declarations and does not re-run machine entry. A machine hydrated while sitting in an `:after`-bearing state therefore has the right durable `:state`, `:data`, and `:rf/after-epoch`, but no live timer. It can remain in that state forever unless some unrelated external event moves it.

This contradicts the local contract that timers begin on the client after hydration. It is also the relevant conformity lesson from XState v6 persistence: durable state and host work are distinct, and restoring a snapshot must explicitly reconstruct the timer runtime without replaying historical effects.

## Evidence

- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc` (`build-after-fx`, around lines 2059-2144) emits `:rf.machine/after-schedule` only while processing newly-entered nodes. In server mode the effect carries `:server? true` and the timer is skipped.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/timer.cljc` keeps timer handles/watchers in a process-local timer table; they are not part of the hydration payload.
- `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/hydrate.cljc` (`hydrate-event-handler*`) installs the payload's runtime-db and has one late-bound reconciliation hook for Resources. There is no Machines hydration/re-arm hook or machine scheduling effect.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/late_bind/directory.cljc` inventories Machines hooks for SSR projection, timer cleanup on frame destroy/epoch restore, and timer scheduling, but no hydration reconstruction hook.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/ssr.cljc` projects durable machine snapshots only; it cannot carry host timer handles.
- `spec/005-StateMachines.md` lines 1323 and 2444-2448 say server timers no-op and the client schedules them after hydration.
- `spec/011-SSR.md`, section “`:after` is no-op under SSR”, requires `:after` timers to begin running on the client against the preserved snapshot epoch.
- `docs/machines/automatic-transitions.md` states: “The client re-arms timers after hydration.”
- XState v6's official persistence contract includes timers in the durable snapshot shape and restores without replaying historical entry effects: https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/persistence and https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/how-xstate-runs-machines . Exact comparison baseline: `xstate@6.0.0-alpha.50` (`0b52534e`), released 2026-08-27.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Failure scenario/invariant

Given a server-rendered machine whose active state declares `:after {5000 {:target :timeout}}`:

1. Server entry bumps/stores the node's `:rf/after-epoch`, emits the skipped-on-server trace, and schedules no host timer.
2. The hydration payload carries the active snapshot and epoch.
3. `:rf/hydrate` installs that snapshot on the client without entering the state.
4. No client timer exists, so advancing beyond 5000 ms never dispatches the synthetic elapsed event and the machine remains stuck.

Required invariant: after a successful client hydration commit, every live active `:after` declaration represented by the hydrated snapshot has exactly one client timer/watch armed for that snapshot's existing epoch, without replaying unrelated entry behavior.

## Recommended minimal fix

Add one hydration-only Machines reconciliation seam, analogous in ownership to the existing Resources hydration hook:

- Have the Machines artefact publish a late-bound hydration hook/effect that runs only after a valid client `:rf/hydrate` has committed the payload runtime-db.
- Walk the hydrated live snapshots, resolve each actor's registered/inline machine definition using existing resolver paths, enumerate only the currently active nodes (plus the root-parallel node), and schedule their declared `:after` entries through the existing timer scheduler.
- Reuse the persisted `:rf/after-epoch`; do not bump it.
- Resolve literal/function/subscription delays on the client. Because the wire does not carry a schedule timestamp or due-at value, arm the full declared client-relative delay, matching the repository's existing SSR contract.
- Do not re-run `:entry`, actions, raises, spawns, or other effects. Do not reuse the epoch-restore callback: epoch restore deliberately cancels host work and must continue not to revive it.
- Make repeated hydration/scheduling idempotent by the existing timer-table key or an equally small guard, so it never leaves duplicate handles/watchers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A focused hydration integration test registers an `:after` machine, produces/installs an SSR-shaped runtime-db snapshot, hydrates on a client frame, and proves exactly one timer is armed with the persisted epoch and its callback performs the declared transition.
- The test proves the timer was not armed on the server and that hydration does not re-run an entry action, raise, or spawn.
- Coverage includes a compound active path and root-parallel coverage sufficient to prove active region nodes and root-owned `:after` declarations are enumerated correctly.
- A dynamic subscription/function delay is resolved on the client through the existing scheduling path; watcher teardown/cancellation remains correct.
- Negative controls prove that a snapshot with no active `:after`, a rejected malformed/wrong-frame hydration, and a server-side hydrate arm no timers.
- Existing epoch-restore coverage continues to prove `:machines/on-frame-restored!` cancels timers and does not re-arm them.
- Existing timer traces remain coherent; hydration-created timers emit one normal scheduled trace (with actor, path/state, delay source, epoch, and frame) rather than a misleading state-entry replay.
- Relevant spec/docs wording and late-bind directory inventory match the implemented hydration-only seam.

## Non-goals

- A general durable workflow engine, snapshot migration framework, elapsed-time/due-at persistence, or cross-process clock reconciliation.
- Replaying all machine entry behavior during hydration.
- Reviving timers during epoch/time-travel restore.
- Serializing browser timer handles or subscription objects.
- Matching XState's actor API or persistence wire format.

## Related/duplicate search

All-status tracker searches covered titles/descriptions containing: `machine timer`, `after hydration`, `hydration timer`, `re-arm`, `rearm`, `skipped-on-server`, `after-epoch`, `hydrate`, `restore`, `SSR`, and `rf.runtime/machines`. No bead owns this outcome. Closed `rf2-1vlyg` concerns reverse-creation teardown after restore, not hydration timer reconstruction; closed `rf2-ys42` is a documentation review that repeated the client-rearm promise but did not implement it.
acceptance_criteria: After client hydration, the frame's host timer table contains exactly the timers implied by the installed machine snapshots: stale pre-hydration/previous-hydration entries and dynamic-delay watchers are cancelled, live declarations are armed once at their persisted epochs, and no entry/cascade is replayed. A changed-snapshot regression distinguishes this from the existing identical-snapshot idempotence test; restore semantics and other frames remain untouched.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8915: reopened after the three-lens review. The new hydration seam reconstructs every live declaration correctly, but it does not reconcile away host timers that are absent from the replacement snapshot. :rf/hydrate replaces runtime-db wholesale; timer/after-timers is separate host state. rearm-after-timers! only walks the newly installed snapshots and calls schedule-after-timer! for their active declarations. That function supersedes an old entry only when the new declaration has the same {actor, invoke-id, delay-key}; there is no frame-level cancellation or set difference. The idempotence test repeats the identical snapshot, so it proves only the same-key case.

A frame with a pre-hydration timer, or a documented direct second :rf/hydrate, can therefore replace an :after state with a no-:after state, remove an actor, or shrink a delay set while leaving the old host handle in after-timers. Literal handles linger until firing; subscription-delay entries can keep a reaction/watcher alive and reschedule. Epoch/active-path checks may suppress the eventual stale transition, but they do not release the host work or give the replacement operation coherent scheduled-to-cancelled tracing.

Minimal repair: after the payload runtime-db commit, reconcile this frame's timer table to the exact declaration keys enumerated from the installed snapshots: cancel entries not in that set, then retain/supersede or arm the live set. Preserve the client/payload/hook gates, existing epochs, no-entry-replay rule, and epoch-restore semantics. Add a changed-snapshot control (active :after to no :after or absent actor) and a dynamic-delay watcher/ref-count control; do not add a general persistence layer or public API.

---

AUDIT REPAIR (2026-09-01 21:47 AUSEST) — PR #8930, branch worker/timerrec-jqvgp.

PREMISE VERIFIED AT TIP BEFORE BUILDING. Both halves of the audit note hold exactly as
written. schedule-after-timer! computes its slot as
(after-timer-key parent-id invoke-id delay-key) => {:parent <actor> :spawn (vec invoke-id)
:delay <delay-key>} and issues ONE cancel-after-timer-entry! against that single key with
:reason :on-supersede — so the supersede is keyed on {actor, invoke-id, delay-key} and
there is no frame-level cancellation and no set difference anywhere in the arm path.
rearm-after-timers! walked only the newly installed snapshots. And
hydration-re-arm-is-idempotent in machine_after_hydration_rearm_cljs_test.cljc installs the
SAME runtime-db value twice into one frame, so it proves only the same-key case.

THE REPAIR. rearm-after-timers! is now a two-phase reconcile.
  1. hydrate/live-declarations (new, pure) enumerates the live declarations of every
     resolvable snapshot ONCE, each carrying its :actor-id and its :snapshot. Both halves
     read that one list, so a table entry is cancelled if and only if the walk did not
     produce it — the two phases agree by construction rather than by two parallel walks.
  2. timer/cancel-timers-absent-from! (new) takes the set difference over this frame's
     inner table and releases every entry outside the live set.
  3. The live set is armed exactly as before, at the persisted epoch.
Cancel runs BEFORE arm, so a surviving declaration is superseded in place by its own
re-arm rather than swept and re-created.

NO NEW TRACE VOCABULARY, SO NO SPEC CHANGE IS OWED. The cancellations reuse the closed
six-value :reason set (reply/timer-cancel-reasons; Spec 005 §Trace event catalogue,
line 2477): :on-destroy when the replacement snapshots no longer hold the actor at all,
:on-exit when the actor survived but its declaring node left the active configuration.
Both are the ordinary readings of those two values. spec/005-StateMachines.md is NOT
touched (it was held by another worker besides). The only file outside the machines
artefact is the ONE description string for :machines/rearm-after-hydration! in
late_bind/directory.cljc, which described the hook as arming only.

transition.cljc WAS NOT NEEDED AND WAS NOT TOUCHED. The seam is hydrate.cljc and the
cancellation primitive is timer.cljc; spawn_order.cljc and machines.cljc were not needed
either.

THE FOUR NAMED INVARIANTS, EACH PRESERVED AND EACH PINNED BY A TEST.
  - client/payload/hook gates — the :platform :server refusal is read once, ahead of BOTH
    phases, so a server-side hydrate neither arms nor cancels. The ssr/hydrate.cljc gating
    (client? + payload-rt + hook presence) is untouched. Pinned by
    a-server-side-hydrate-reconciles-nothing.
  - existing epochs — never bumped; the arm path is unchanged and reads the snapshot's own
    :rf/after-epoch. The cancelled row is stamped with the epoch the cancelled timer was
    armed at, asserted in the changed-snapshot control.
  - no-entry-replay — neither phase runs a cascade, an :entry, an :exit, an :action, a
    :raise or a :spawn, and neither writes a snapshot. Asserted on the :entries counter
    after the second install.
  - epoch-restore semantics — :machines/on-frame-restored! ->
    cancel-frame-timers-on-restore! is untouched and still cancels without re-arming;
    it shares no callback with this seam. implementation/epoch's full JVM lane is green.

CONTROLS. New namespace
implementation/machines/test/re_frame/machine_after_hydration_reconcile_cljs_test.cljc
(6 deftests, 47 assertions). Every test installs runtime-db TWICE into the SAME frame,
which the existing namespace never does, and both snapshots are produced by running the
machine on a real :platform :server frame rather than hand-written. Every assertion reads
the TIMER TABLE, the released subscription or the cancellation trace — never "no wrong
transition fired", which passes on the broken code because the epoch gate already
suppresses the stale transition.

SABOTAGE RESULT (the deliverable). Phase 1 reverted to the union by replacing the
cancel-timers-absent-from! call with a no-op of the same arity:
  - machines lane exit 1, 1226 tests / 4336 assertions — the SAME totals as the clean run,
    so no namespace was skipped or crashed — with 17 failures, ALL of them in the new
    namespace: 8 in hydration-cancels-a-timer-the-replacement-no-longer-declares, 4 in
    hydration-cancels-timers-for-an-actor-the-replacement-drops, 4 in
    hydration-releases-a-dropped-dynamic-delays-watcher-and-subscription, 1 in
    the-reconcile-is-frame-scoped.
  - GREEN under the same plant: every pre-existing machines test including all nine of
    machine_after_hydration_rearm_cljs_test; and, within the new file,
    an-identical-re-hydration-retains-rather-than-cancels and
    a-server-side-hydrate-reconciles-nothing, plus every precondition assertion in the
    four failing tests.
  - ssr lane under the same plant: exit 0, 609 tests / 2990 assertions, 0 failures.
  - The dynamic-delay failure printed the audit's exact mechanism verbatim: a
    :rf.machine.timer/cancelled with :reason :on-resolution fired from the SURVIVING
    watcher when the delay's value changed, one hydration after the declaration was
    dropped — the reaction and its (frame, query-v) ref-count were still held.
  - The plant was restored by checkout and verified by git BLOB hash against the committed
    object (identical before and after), not by reading a diff.

GATES, all re-run on the final rebased base, each exit code captured on the same command
line as the redirect:
  machines JVM  clojure -M:test   1226 tests / 4336 assertions   0 fail   exit 0
  ssr JVM       clojure -M:test    609 tests / 2990 assertions   0 fail   exit 0
  epoch JVM     clojure -M:test    543 tests / 7176 assertions   0 fail   exit 0
  CLJS          npm run test:cljs 11156 tests / 55201 assertions 0 fail   exit 0
The CLJS lane printed its shadow-cljs config path and it named this branch's own checkout.
Diff is implementation/machines/** plus the one directory.cljc description string — no
markdown, no spec/, no workflows — so check_doc_slugs.py and check_readme_links.py are out
of scope and mkdocs build --strict is not a candidate (docs_dir is docs).
AUDIT PR #8930: REOPENED exact owner; no duplicate. Completeness: the ordinary changed-snapshot, dropped-actor, dynamic-delay, identical, sibling-frame, and server cases are well covered, but no control exercises a cancellation callback that replaces the frame. Correctness: rearm-after-timers! computes frame A live declarations, then cancel-timers-absent-from! captures an A incarnation guard only inside its own loop and returns nil. If a :rf.machine.timer/cancelled listener destroys A and publishes same-ID B, that helper stops, but the caller unconditionally walks the old live vector. rearm-hydrated-after-timer! then captures B as its current owner and installs A-derived timer work into B. The same gap exists across the arm loop: the first live declaration can emit :on-supersede and publish B; its per-entry guard aborts correctly, but the next iteration captures B and arms another A declaration. Implementation quality: the entry-level token and incarnation fences are sound, but the batch owner is not threaded across phases or iterations. Minimal completion: bind the whole reconcile to one frame incarnation and recheck it across every callback-bearing cancellation and arm, with a mixed retained/dropped or multi-live regression whose first cancellation publishes same-ID B and proves B receives no A timer, watcher, subscription hold, or scheduled trace. Preserve the normal reconcile and avoid a new mechanism.
AUDIT PR #8942: REOPENED exact owner; no duplicate. Completeness: the new regressions replace A only from :rf.machine.timer/cancelled; none exercises the hydration arm's own :rf.machine.timer/scheduled fan-out. Correctness: schedule-after-timer! checks the threaded owner before resolving the delay, but hydration sets :emit-scheduled-trace? true and trace/emit! synchronously invokes listeners after that check and before the timer-table sentinel is reserved. A /scheduled listener can therefore destroy A and publish same-id B; execution then unconditionally reserves the A-derived slot under B's frame id, arms the host timer, and attaches its watcher. For a subscription delay, resolution already acquired B-addressed subscription work before the trace, so abort must balance that hold too. Implementation quality: threading one predicate across phases is the right mechanism, but it does not yet span every callback boundary as the new contract claims. Minimal completion: recheck that same batch predicate immediately after the /scheduled fan-out, release any just-resolved dynamic-delay resources on abort, and add one focused /scheduled-listener A-to-B regression proving B receives no timer-table entry, host arm, watcher, subscription hold, or later re-resolution. Preserve the ordinary live-owner path; no new mechanism or vocabulary.

--------

AUDIT REPAIR (2026-09-02 00:36 AUSEST) — PR #8955, branch worker/tracefence-jqvgp.

VERDICT ON WHETHER A THIRD PASS WAS WARRANTED: YES, and the reason is the FALSE
CONTRACT rather than the reachability of the scenario. Both halves matter and they
point the same way.

The scenario itself is narrow. It needs a trace listener on
:rf.machine.timer/scheduled that destroys the frame and republishes a same-id
successor, during hydration. No application writes that; it is the same class of
contrivance as passes one and two. But the pass-two docstring in hydrate.cljc said
outright that the reconcile "captures the owning incarnation ONCE, before either
phase, and every callback-bearing step is fenced by that ONE predicate", and
schedule-after-timer!'s said its recheck meant "a superseding reschedule installs NO
A-derived host work (or subscription ref-count) into successor B". Both were false as
written, verified at tip: the /scheduled emit inside schedule-after-timer! is a
callback boundary with the same reach as /cancelled, and it had no recheck. Narrowing
the claim was the alternative repair, and it was the worse one — the fence would then
read "every boundary except this one, for no stated reason", and the gap it left is a
genuine leak. Widening the fence is four lines using the mechanism already present, so
the honest repair is to make the claim true.

THE EXPOSURE IS ALSO WIDER THAN THE AUDIT SAID, IN ONE RESPECT THAT ARGUES FOR THE
FIX. /scheduled is the FIRST callback-bearing trace of the whole reconcile whenever
the frame holds no prior timer — the ordinary first hydration of a page. On that path
phase 1 cancels nothing and the single arm supersedes an empty slot, so neither
existing tooth fires at all. It is not a deeper corner than the /cancelled ones; it is
the shallower one.

PREMISE VERIFIED AT SOURCE BEFORE BUILDING. trace/emit! delivers "to the ring buffer,
epoch capture, and all registered listeners synchronously". schedule-after-timer!
emits /scheduled inside the (let [token ...]) AFTER the post-supersede recheck and
BEFORE the (swap! after-timers assoc-in [frame-id k] ...) sentinel reservation, with
no guard between them. The slot is keyed by the BARE frame id, shared by A and B.
:emit-scheduled-trace? true has exactly two src call sites (searched line-oriented AND
over whitespace-collapsed text, with a :emit-scheduled-trace? false control returning
non-zero): rearm-hydrated-after-timer! and on-sub-changed!. Both are now covered,
since the recheck lives inside schedule-after-timer! rather than at the hydration
caller.

THE REPAIR. One (when-not (owner-gone?) ...) immediately after the /scheduled emit,
rechecking the SAME predicate — the batch caller's when supplied, never a fresh
capture, which would name B and pass. Slot reservation, host arm, publish and watcher
all move behind it. No new abstraction, no cancellation framework, no epoch system, no
new trace vocabulary. spec/005-StateMachines.md is NOT touched and none was owed: the
ordinary live-owner path is unchanged in behaviour. The only other edits are the two
docstrings whose claims were false, which now ENUMERATE the two boundaries instead of
asserting coverage of them.

ONE CLAUSE OF THE AUDIT IS NARROWED, AND THIS IS THE IMPLEMENTATION-GOVERNING PART.
The audit asked to "release any just-resolved dynamic-delay resources on abort". The
abort must release NOTHING, and adding the release would be a new bug. The one hold in

subs/unsubscribe addresses the frame by BARE ID, which now denotes B, so a decrement

reaction. That is precisely the rf2-i4aj9c hazard, and the established rule in this
file (release-entry-resources!'s owner-gone? guard) is to SKIP the shared decrement
once the owner is lost. Recorded as a comment at the recheck, and pinned by an
assertion, so a later reader does not "complete" the fix by adding the unsubscribe.

title: migration: path lowering misclassifies custom */path interceptors
description:
## Scope

Repair the v1-to-v2 event-registration migration path where the shipped M-73 scanner/codemod encounters interceptor-bearing reg-event-db or reg-event-fx calls. Scope includes migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod, its focused tests/README, the directly coupled re-frame-migration reference/eval, and one focused integration proof against the actual v2 reg-event contract.

## Correctness finding

The guide promises that M-73 composes with M-70, but the implementation performs a head/handler-only rewrite and deliberately preserves every middle slot. For the canonical path-interceptor example it emits an rf/reg-event whose metadata still contains the removed inline (rf/path ...) call; for historical positional chains it emits a reg-event with the retired vector middle slot. Both outputs are invalid v2 and hard-fail while the namespace loads. The codemod then reports the site as :rewrite/:rename rather than an unresolved M-70 finding, so its green unit suite certifies a broken migration.

## Evidence

- skills/re-frame-migration/references/auto-call-site-rewrites.md:482-505 tells users to prefer the shipped codemod and specifies the mechanical conversion from {:interceptors [(rf/path :counter)]} to {:interceptors [[:rf.interceptor/path [:counter]]]}.
- migration/from-re-frame-v1/README.md:883-903 calls the codemod first-class/tested and gives the same positional [(rf/path :counter)] to metadata-ref conversion.
- migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/src/re_frame/migration/reg_event_codemod.clj:31-33 instead states that path-interceptor metadata is preserved untouched. analyse-call at 301-342 classifies every reg-event-fx as a pure rename and simple reg-event-db solely by its last handler; it never analyses middle-slot shape or entries. apply-rewrite-at at 665-688 replaces only the registrar head and db handler.
- migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/test/re_frame/migration/reg_event_codemod_test.clj:102-114 and 125-134 explicitly assert that {:interceptors [(rf/path :counter)]} survives while the call is renamed to reg-event, pinning the invalid output.
- implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc:1962-1983 makes rf/path a throwing removal stub (:rf.error/path-removed). implementation/core/src/re_frame/events.cljc:71-82 and 126-165 require interceptor refs and reject inline values with :rf.error/inline-interceptor-removed; 803-837 rejects a positional vector middle slot with :rf.error/reg-event-bad-middle-slot.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the shipped codemod rewrite over this v1 source:

       (rf/reg-event-db :counter/inc
         {:interceptors [(rf/path :counter)]}
         (fn [db _] (update db :value inc)))

2. Observe that it reports :action :rewrite and emits reg-event while preserving {:interceptors [(rf/path :counter)]}.
3. Load/evaluate the emitted registration with the actual v2 re-frame.core namespace.
4. Observe the namespace-load hard failure :rf.error/path-removed before the handler registers. The positional-vector variant is also retained and is rejected as :rf.error/reg-event-bad-middle-slot; a custom inline value retained in metadata is rejected as :rf.error/inline-interceptor-removed.

## Failure scenario / invariant

The current successful rewrite is:

    (rf/reg-event :counter/inc
      {:interceptors [(rf/path :counter)]}
      (fn [{:keys [db]} _] {:db (update db :value inc)}))

Loading it against v2 calls the removed rf/path stub before the handler can register. A positional v1 chain is likewise left as the now-illegal vector middle slot, and a custom inline value carried into metadata is rejected by reg-event.

Invariant: every site the codemod reports as mechanically rewritten must be a valid v2 registration shape, or it must remain an explicit unresolved M-70 finding. A source transform is not successful merely because it parses and no retired registrar name remains.

## Recommended minimal fix

Teach the codemod one small middle-slot normalization that composes M-70 with M-73:

1. Recognize the standard path constructor in bare, positional-vector, metadata-interceptors, and metadata-plus-vector source shapes; lower each (rf/path p...) to [:rf.interceptor/path [p...]], create or merge the metadata map, and preserve chain order/comments.
2. Preserve entries that are already v2 refs.
3. For any other inline/bare interceptor whose stable registered id cannot be derived without author intent, emit an explicit M-70 Type-B finding and do not claim the event migration complete. Do not leave an invalid inline value hidden behind a successful M-73 result.
4. Scan both retired reg-event-* forms and already rewritten reg-event forms for these invalid middle-slot/inline survivors so a rerun can recover a partially migrated tree.
5. Replace the string-only preservation assertions with exact normalization tests plus a focused registration integration test using the actual v2 core.

## Acceptance Criteria

title: implementor skill: foundation gate can pass a reference-keyed live sub-cache
description:
## Scope

Correct the completion and EP-006 verification workflow in `skills/re-frame2-implementor/**` so a non-CLJS port cannot be declared foundation-complete while its live subscription cache is keyed by host reference identity. Keep the corpus score as an honest corpus score; add only the one port-owned live witness needed for the observability gap already acknowledged by the pinned Spec. Limit supporting checks/evals to this outcome.

## Correctness finding

The skill makes the conformance corpus the acceptance test and its Done gate accepts a green `:core/* + :identity/* + :data-classification/*` run as foundation completion. Its EP-006 row specifically calls the two `:identity/cedn1` Mode-B fixtures "sub-cache fixtures." Those fixtures never touch a frame, `subscribe`, a cache slot, ref-counting, or disposal: they call the canonical-identity primitive directly. The owning Spec explicitly says the missing live assertion would subscribe one query through two distinct host allocations and observe one cache-slot creation.

A TypeScript port can therefore implement CEDN-1 correctly, use Immer for structural sharing, but store query arrays in a native reference-keyed `Map`. Every required fixture can pass and the skill can report v1 completion even though equal freshly allocated queries create separate derived containers forever. This is a false-green proof of a pattern-required runtime contract, not a request for broader coverage.

## Evidence

- `skills/re-frame2-implementor/SKILL.md:9-10,31,52,70-75` repeatedly says the corpus is the acceptance test and defines Done as the three required fixture families being green.
- `skills/re-frame2-implementor/references/phase-2-impl-order.md:35` describes `:identity/cedn1` as the EP-006 "sub-cache fixtures"; lines 40 and 68 make fixture-set greens acceptance gates, and line 78 permits completion after those discovered gates.
- `skills/re-frame2-implementor/references/conformance.md:78-90` requires a port-owned self-test only when a mandated surface has no fixture. It does not cover a fixture that exists but observes only a prerequisite, and line 90 equates `N / N` with conformance against the claim.
- `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:793-820` requires `rf=`-keyed live lookup and explains that native JS `Map`/array identity breaks de-duplication, ref-count convergence, and disposal. It also notes that Immer supplies neither value equality nor a value-keyed map.
- `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:824-829` says the two fixtures assert only canonical cache-key identity and explicitly leaves the deeper live-runtime assertion as follow-up because the current Mode-A DSL cannot subscribe two distinct host allocations.
- `spec/conformance/fixtures/sub-cache-dedupes-equal-query-v.edn:36-76` is a Mode-B `:fixture/calls` file containing only `:canonical-identical` and `:canonical-distinct` calls. Its companion `sub-cache-key-map-arg-order.edn` likewise tests canonical bytes/identity only.
- `implementation/core/test/re_frame/conformance_runner.cljc:1026-1039` executes those calls through `identity/identical-identity?`; no subscription-cache code is reached.
- `skills/re-frame2-implementor/evals/evals.json:4-25` is trigger-only, so no outcome regression prevents the skill from accepting this corpus-green/runtime-red port.
- The focused implementor guards are currently green, but they check EP order, required family names, partition vocabulary, and bead leakage; neither exercises this completion invariant (`python scripts/check_skill_implementor_order.py --self-test`, `python scripts/check_skill_implementor_order.py --verbose --ci`, `python scripts/check_skill_implementor_partition_drift.py --self-test`, and `python scripts/check_skill_implementor_partition_drift.py --verbose --ci`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a minimum TypeScript-shaped port, implement the CEDN-1 canonical operations correctly and use a native `Map<QueryVector, CacheEntry>` for the live sub-cache.
2. Run all claimed required-family fixtures. The two named sub-cache fixtures pass because they invoke only the canonical identity functions, and the required-foundation score can reach `claimed-applicable / claimed-applicable`.
3. Allocate two separate arrays with equal contents, for example `q1 = ['editor/field-error', 'title']` and `q2 = ['editor/field-error', 'title']`, and subscribe both in one frame.
4. Observe two native-Map keys, two derived containers, and two first-run computations. Releasing the readers cannot converge on one slot's last-reader disposal even though the skill's current completion proof is green.

## Failure scenario / invariant

A React view constructs its query array afresh on every render. Under reference-keyed lookup, every render misses the cache, repeats the subscription computation, and leaves an independently referenced entry whose lifecycle cannot converge with the prior readers. The port is reported conformant despite violating the required invariant: two separately allocated query vectors that are `rf=` must resolve to one live cache entry, one shared computation, and one ref-count; that entry disposes exactly once after the last equal reader releases it. A non-equal query must remain a different entry.

## Recommended minimal fix

Add one explicit EP-006 completion proof to the skill: on a host whose ordinary map keys collections by reference (or whenever the selected cache mechanism does not intrinsically provide `rf=` keys), run a port-owned live test using two separately allocated but `rf=`-equal query values. Require the result at the EP-006 checkpoint and in the v1 Done gate alongside the corpus score. In `conformance.md`, name this as the pinned Spec's known observability gap: the existing identity fixtures prove the canonical-key prerequisite, not live cache wiring, so a port-owned self-test is required even though fixture files exist.

Keep the proof mechanism-agnostic. The port may use an `rf=`-keyed persistent map or an interned canonical key; the skill should require the observable one-slot/one-lifecycle result, not prescribe a library. Add a focused outcome regression for the skill so a corpus-green/live-red TypeScript-shaped port is diagnosed as incomplete.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The published EP-006 workflow and Done checklist explicitly distinguish canonical-identity fixture success from live sub-cache success. A non-CLJS/reference-keyed host cannot be called EP-006-, foundation-, or v1-complete until the live witness below has run green; the reported conformance fraction remains the fixture result rather than being silently inflated.
2. The required executable witness creates `q1` and `q2` through separate host allocations, first proves `rf=(q1,q2)`, subscribes both in the same frame through the public/runtime subscription path, and observes exactly one cache slot, one derived container/first-run computation, and a shared ref-count. Releasing one reader keeps the slot live; releasing the second removes it and invokes disposal exactly once.
3. Negative control: a third query with a different argument value is not `rf=` to `q1` and produces a second cache slot and second first-run computation. This prevents a degenerate implementation that interns or collapses every query from satisfying the positive witness.
4. Non-vacuity mutation control: temporarily replace the value-keyed lookup in the test port with the host's native reference-keyed `Map`. The existing `sub-cache-dedupes-equal-query-v.edn`, `sub-cache-key-map-arg-order.edn`, and required-foundation corpus run remain green, while the live witness exits nonzero on two slots/two first-runs. Restore the conforming lookup and record the same witness green.
5. A focused checked-in skill outcome eval presents that exact corpus-green/live-red TypeScript-shaped checkpoint. The expected result withholds EP-006/v1 completion, names reference-keyed live lookup as the port bug, and asks/runs the live witness; a paired one-slot control is accepted. The eval must execute through the skill's normal route, not merely search for a phrase in Markdown.
6. Existing implementor order/partition self-tests and CI modes remain green. Any focused guard added for this invariant has its own red control (remove the live-proof requirement and the guard/eval fails) and does not pin a copied fixture catalogue or implementation token.

## Non-goals

- No new Mode-A conformance operator, cross-host fixture protocol, generated fixture translation, or rewrite of the conformance corpus.
- No mandate for Immutable.js, CEDN interning, or any one cache implementation.
- No expansion into every subscription invalidation/performance law; this issue owns only equal-query live cache identity and its reader lifecycle.
- No change to CEDN-1, `rf=` semantics, capability tags, scoring arithmetic, or the CLJS reference implementation.
- No broad behavioral-eval platform, generic conformance hardening, compatibility layer, or documentation polish.

## Related / duplicate search

All-status census covered 1,133 beads. Exact title/description/notes searches for `sub-cache`, `value-keyed`, `reference-keyed`, `rf=`, `Immer`, `sub-cache-dedupes`, `live-runtime assertion`, `Mode-A harness primitive`, `cache key`, and implementor/conformance acceptance found no bead owning this false-green port-completion outcome.

- `rf2-nuy8x` (closed) reduced the implementor skill to the pinned-spec/fixture loop and added the current required-family gates; it did not require a live two-allocation sub-cache proof. This bug is a correctness residual of that completed workflow, not a duplicate of its ergonomic reduction.
- `rf2-rzeko` (open) owns exactly-once disposal of stock Reagent `Reaction`s in the CLJS adapter. It does not cover non-CLJS query-key equality, duplicate live cache slots, or implementor-skill completion evidence.
- `rf2-a9l6e` (open) owns the MCP conformance tool's compatibility-profile UX, not a port runtime or this skill's proof boundary.
- The owning Spec's line-829 follow-up note is prose, not a tracked bead, and it proposes a future corpus primitive; this task deliberately takes the smaller skill-level port-owned witness.
