title: ssr-node crossing (C/6): render-state contract (project/restore, two partitions) + protocol v1 revision
description:
Slice C of the ssr-node crossing programme. Parent rf2-8arzr's RULING note (2026-09-02, delegated by Mike) is the canonical record: read its shared contract S1-S7 (S3 and S4 especially) first; this description carries only C's own brief. This is the slice both reviewers agreed carries the real risk — reconstructing the SAME settled render state in Node — so it lands BEFORE the adapter (D) consumes it.

## Scope (fence)

- New `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/render_state.cljc` (+ JVM test under `implementation/ssr/test/` and a CLJS test in the same tree — `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn` ~:102 already lists `ssr/test`, so NO build change).
- `implementation/ssr-node/src/protocol.cjs`, `test/protocol.test.cjs`, `test/fixtures/**`, README section `### A gap this protocol does not paper over` (~:355-365; rewrite it — the door now exists, decided by the framework, not by the sidecar).
- NOT `implementation/ssr-ring` (D consumes this), NOT `implementation/hicasso` (E). Parallel with A and B; B edits different README sections — rebase, don't fight.

## Do

JVM side (`render-state/project`): given a frame-id and a `:render-state` policy, return the partition map `{:rf/app-db {...} :rf/runtime-db {...}}` — the SAME envelope shape the hydration payload already uses (`implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/payload.clj` ~:5-13) under a DISTINCT policy. The policy is declared like `:payload`: a fail-closed allowlist per partition — top-level app-db keys, and top-level runtime-db keys (the route slice, machine snapshots) — plus a `(fn [frame-id] -> partition-map)` escape hatch for a projector the allowlist vocabulary cannot express. Absent policy = construction-time error (mirror `:rf.error/ssr-missing-payload-policy`). Reuse `payload_policy.cljc`'s apply/project machinery, including derived sensitivity the way `project-runtime-db` already applies it. Also a per-key `pr-str` serialization helper producing the wire form (key text -> EDN text) for both partitions; the serialization DOMAIN is the payload's existing EDN domain — reuse it, do not invent a second one.

CLJS side (`render-state/restore!`): seed a FRESH per-request frame's app-db and runtime-db from the partition map, with NO boot-event replay (the JVM drained them), reusing `hydrate.cljc`'s partition-install path minus verification and DOM concerns. This is the "second install door" the ssr-node README declined to invent in a sidecar; the framework now decides it, here.

Node protocol v1 (pre-alpha: revise directly, no compatibility layer, `protocol` stays `1`): the request carries the runtime partition beside `state`, per-key EDN text, gated by an ENTRY-owned allowlist for that partition too — absence = unrenderable, mirroring `stateAllowlist` (~:264-273). Invariants: the service never decodes application data; allowlists stay entry-owned so a caller cannot widen its own allowance (the fail-closed guarantee stays in Node; it does not move to the JVM); `initialEvents` / `payloadPolicy` / `head` stay refused with their existing reasons. The wire spelling (`runtime` + `runtimeAllowlist`, or one two-partition `snapshot` object) is the worker's call within those invariants. Update the fixtures (e.g. `bad-no-allowlist.cjs` gains a runtime-partition sibling) and the protocol rows.

## Acceptance

1. Round-trip corpus: every value class the hydration payload's EDN domain supports goes JVM `pr-str` -> CLJS `read-string` -> `restore!` -> identical, for BOTH partitions; a route slice and a machine snapshot are in the corpus.
2. ONE negative fixture: an unsupported value (a fn / a Java object) fails at projection with a named error — never a silent nil.
3. One omitted-required-key fixture: restoring with an allowlisted key absent renders the honest "wrong page" (nil where the value should be) and is documented as the operator's allowlist mistake, not a framework failure.
4. `protocol.cjs` revised, `npm run test:ssr-node` green, README section rewritten.

## Gates (foreground, to completion)

`clojure -M:test` in `implementation/ssr`; the CLJS lane that compiles `ssr/test` (`npm run test:cljs`, or the focused build — name which in the PR); `npm run test:ssr-node`.

## Stop and report to Mike (do not improvise a framework decision)

If restoring runtime-db turns out to require replaying boot events, or the route/machine slices cannot be expressed as top-level runtime-db keys. Leave the PR open with what works and say so on this bead.

## Traps

Two partitions, two allowlists — never derive the render-state projection from `:payload`, and never the reverse; the whole point is that they differ. No `git stash`; commit then rebase. Worker worktree guard first; report `WORKTREE_ROOT`.

description:

## Do

Introduce the render-body seam exactly as the parent's S1 states:

- `ssr-handler` gains ONE construction opt, `:renderer` — a plain fn, no protocol, no registry, no multimethod: `(fn [{:keys [frame-id request opts]}] -> {:body-html <string> :render-hash <string-or-nil>})`. It is called by `build-full-response*` at today's hard call (`pipeline.clj` ~:564, `ssr/render-to-string`) INSIDE the existing `rf/with-frame` scope, AFTER `drain-blocking-resources!` and the boot-event drain, BEFORE head resolution and the payload build consume its result. Its input is the live post-drain frame (by id), the handler opts and the Ring request — never a JVM hiccup value.
- The DEFAULT renderer wraps today's `lifecycle/resolve-root-view` -> `lifecycle/render-document-hash` -> `ssr/render-to-string` unchanged. Extract it as a named fn (public `re-frame.ssr.ring/local-renderer` or private — the worker's call; the public surface added by this slice is the one `:renderer` opt).

A nil `:render-hash` means no `data-rf-render-hash` marker and no payload `:rf/render-hash` — exactly today's unresolved-root behaviour (rf2-q1b96). Keep the `(and emit-hash? (some? hash-str))` guard: `:emit-hash?` with no hash re-stamps a constant (rf2-atmvj).
- `lifecycle.clj` (~:361, `:rf.error/ssr-ring-missing-root-view`): `:root-view` is required iff no `:renderer` is supplied. With a custom renderer it is optional and ignored.

The handler calls it once per request inside the request frame's scope, after the boot-event drain and the blocking-resource settle and before head resolution and the payload build consume its result, with the live post-drain frame (by id), the host request and the handler opts — never a hiccup value. The renderer owns body markup plus an optional locally-derived render hash, and nothing else; the server keeps the request frame, head, `__rf_payload`, shell, status, headers, cookies, redirects, error projection and frame teardown. A nil `:render-hash` omits both the `data-rf-render-hash` marker and the payload's `:rf/render-hash` — the unresolved-root behaviour of [§Hydration-mismatch detection](#hydration-mismatch-detection). The default renderer is the local one (the CLJS reference's `re-frame.ssr.ring.pipeline/local-renderer`: resolve `:root-view` → hash → `render-to-string`), whose bytes and errors are unchanged by the seam; `:root-view` is required exactly when the renderer is the default. not the item, so an item can carry a second sequencing the lift says nothing about; its newest
layer then reads "released" while a live precondition sits underneath. The failure is not
re-blocking clear work - it is dispatching into a surface somebody else holds, or one gated by a
decision nobody has made.

2026-09-01T18:30:25Z, absent from `bd list --status open`. The history is three entries,
newest-first: 04:30:26 closed / 04:14:24 open / 04:11:22 open — an ordinary create, notes
update, close.

TWO INSTRUMENTS FAILED, AND THE SECOND APPEARED TO CONFIRM THE FIRST, which is what made it
convincing.

  (1) The status probe was `bd show <id> | head -1 | grep -oE 'OPEN|CLOSED' | head -1`. THIS
  BEAD'S OWN TITLE CONTAINS THE WORD "OPEN" — "...the inverse ... fails OPEN" — and the title
  precedes the status field on that line, so the probe returned the title's word. The bead was
  the only one of twenty in that sweep whose title could poison its own status read, and it is
  the one that flagged.

  (2) The corroborating check was a status-transition walk over `bd history --json`. It reported
  "closed -> open" at the newest index. The history is NEWEST-FIRST, so walking indices upward
  walks BACKWARDS in time: a pair reading closed-then-open forward-in-index is open-then-closed
  forward-in-TIME. The detector printed every transition reversed. On any bead that has ever been

can contain the words a status probe looks for. And before trusting a transition walk over a
history, establish which end is newest by reading the timestamps — the ordering is a property of
the tool, not something to assume, and an ordering error inverts every answer while producing
well-formed output.

title: [method] gate-artefact cleanup uses a variable-expanded rm, which stalls on a permission prompt
notes:
FILED 2026-09-02 03:39 AUSEST from an OPERATOR REPORT (Mike, in chat), not from an audit.

THE FRICTION. Workers clean their gate artefacts with a variable-expanded deletion -
  rm -f "$SP"/*<worktree>*
- and a static permission check cannot evaluate $SP, so it must stop and ask. The ask lands
on an operator who may not be watching, and the worker stalls mid-turn with everything queued
behind it. Mike's words: "that results in the session locking up and asking me for permissions
to continue because the rm operation is potentially dangerous if $SP is blank."

THE HAZARD IS REAL, WHICH IS WHY THE CHECK IS RIGHT TO ASK. An unset or empty variable turns
"$SP"/*name* into a glob rooted at the top of the filesystem. So the repair removes the
AMBIGUITY, not the check.

SHIPPED as PR #8971 (mayor/rm-literal-path): one paragraph in the gate-mechanics block of
dispatch-prompt-template.md, beside the artefact-naming rule that generates this cleanup -
delete by the LITERAL path, never through a variable; and where a variable is genuinely
unavoidable, make the shell itself refuse an empty one ("${DIR:?}"), named as the FALLBACK
because it removes the hazard without removing the prompt.

A SECOND, STRUCTURAL OPTION WAS OFFERED TO MIKE AND IS NOT TAKEN HERE - it is his call, and
this bead is not authority for it. The template currently sends artefacts to the SESSION-shared
scratch directory, which is why the worktree-and-attempt naming rule exists and why a cleanup
command is needed at all. Writing them inside the worker's own worktree instead would let
scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh take them out on reap: no cleanup command, no glob, no
prompt, and the peer-collision half of the naming rule becomes unnecessary.

I MEASURED THE ONE THING THAT COULD HAVE BLOCKED THAT OPTION, so the decision is informed:
*.log is ALREADY gitignored repo-wide (.gitignore:14), so a gate-*.log written inside a
worktree is invisible to `git status --porcelain` (verified: clean tree with the file present)
and does not block removal (verified: the removal script's --dry-run accepted the tree). So the
structural option needs no tooling change - only a change to the instruction.

SCRIPT WART NOTED IN PASSING, not filed: remove-worker-worktree.sh --dry-run prints its
ordinary success line "OK: worktree removal complete." A reader could take that for a real
removal. It is inert - the worktree and branch were both verified intact afterwards - and not
worth a change on its own, but worth knowing before trusting that line.

title: [method] route-vs-queue names one queue trigger and leaves the actual discriminator implied: is there an open change to land in?
notes:
FILED 2026-09-02 02:10 AUSEST by the acting mayor, from the Method reread loop (loops.md
§6), about a decision I had made correctly twenty minutes earlier for a reason the document
does not give.

THE SECTION. loops.md §2, "Routing a finding onto a live worker's file". It offers two
moves. Route-and-note: "message the worker that holds the file, and the fix lands inside the
change that is already open". Queue-and-note: "Sometimes routing is the wrong move
altogether. It widens a deliberately bounded fence mid-flight, which is how a bounded repair
becomes an unbounded one."

THE GAP. The route branch's clause "the change that is already open" reads as DESCRIPTION of
the happy path, not as a PRECONDITION to test - and the queue branch names exactly one
trigger, fence-widening. So a mayor holding a finding whose surface is held by a live agent
WHOSE CHANGE HAS ALREADY MERGED finds neither branch obviously applicable, and the default
pull is to route, because routing is the section's headline move and the agent is right
there and messageable.

WHY THAT FAILS OPEN. Routing into an agent with no open change hands fresh work to a
transient owner with nothing to carry it - which is the precise shape the section's own next
paragraph says evaporates ("the message lives in one agent's transcript, so if that agent
dies, times out, or reasonably declines the extra item ... the finding evaporates"). The
section records that hazard against the AGENT (it may die or decline) and not against the
CHANGE, so a reader who has satisfied himself the agent is alive - which is easy, and which
I had done - reads the warning as discharged.

MEASURED TODAY, and this is what I want on the record because I nearly took the wrong
branch. rf2-7htk7 was reopened by the PR #8963 audit with two concrete findings. The agent
that wrote #8963 was STILL RUNNING and still holding tools/xray/, I had messaged it an hour
earlier, and its PR was MERGED. Route was the reflex; queue was correct. I reached queue by
reasoning from the clause rather than by reading a rule, which is exactly the situation §6
exists to catch.

APPLYING THE DOCUMENT'S OWN DISCHARGING TEST to this finding, since #8962 just installed it:
what would I expect to SEE that is different if this claim were false? A sentence in that
section naming a merged, closed or finished change as a queue trigger, or naming the absence
of an open change at all. Searched the section as a flat string: "already open" and "landed"
are present; "merged", "no open change", "has closed", "finished" and "not open" are all
absent. So the claim is not merely un-refuted, it has a positive check behind it.

PROPOSED - ONE CLAUSE, and it belongs inside the existing route paragraph rather than as a
third branch. Say that routing works BECAUSE there is an open change for the fix to land in,
so that is the thing to check first; where the holder's change has already landed, there is
nothing to route into and the queue branch is the one to take even though no fence is being
widened. Keep both existing branches and both existing reasons exactly as they are - this
adds a second trigger to the queue branch, it does not replace the first. Add no mechanism:

title: test(websocket): integration fixture shadows the example registrations it claims to cover
description:
Audit finding from PR #8959 across completeness, correctness, and implementation quality.

The focused WebSocket integration fixture does not consistently exercise the runnable example registrations it claims to protect. `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs` calls `register-all!` for every test, and that function re-declares registrations from `examples/patterns/websocket/messages.cljs` inline. Because `reg-*` is last-write-wins, the fixture copies replace the example's own handlers before assertions run.

This is measured, not hypothetical: PR #8959 records that a fault planted in the example's `:ws.app/request-reply` handler body left the whole focused suite green. The same ownership split also weakens the boundary checks by construction: `inbound-boundary-structural-test` reads `handler-meta` only after `register-all!` has installed the fixture's copied `:schema` and `:rf.schema/at-boundary` metadata, so the suite can certify the copy while the runnable example drifts.

Completeness: machine/schema/mock vars are genuinely reused, but the source registration bodies and metadata are not. Correctness: a regression in the shipped example can remain green while its test-local twin behaves correctly. Implementation quality: the docstring now tells maintainers to mirror changes into both copies, preserving the drift mechanism instead of removing it.

Minimal outcome: make the example registrations re-invocable from one source of truth and have test setup call that source (or reuse named handler/metadata values directly). Add one focused mutation/control proving that changing the example's ingress handler or boundary metadata makes the suite red. Keep this local to the WebSocket example; do not build a generic registrar reload framework or broaden the public API.

Duplicate search covered all-status terms for `websocket register-all handler bodies`, `websocket test fixture mirrors example`, `request-reply body left suite green`, `websocket handler drift`, `websocket inbound boundary test`, `websocket at-boundary fixture`, and `websocket example registration test`; no existing owner was found.
acceptance_criteria: The WebSocket focused suite registers the example's handler bodies and boundary metadata from the same definitions the runnable example uses, with no independent test-local copy that can drift. A controlled fault in the example's `:ws.app/request-reply` body or removal of its `:rf.schema/at-boundary` metadata makes the focused suite red; the restored focused and adapter suites pass. The repair stays local and adds no generic reload framework.
notes:
VERDICT (PR #8969, worker/wsfixture-idv1m) — finding CONFIRMED at source and repaired; premise held in full.

REPRODUCED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING, both directions, on the pre-fix tree:
- gutting the example's :ws.app/request-reply body ({:db db}) -> focused suite exit 0, 29 tests / 240 assertions / 0 failures. Matches what PR #8959 recorded.
- deleting the example's :rf.schema/at-boundary from :ws.app/request-reply -> focused suite exit 0, 29 tests / 240 assertions / 0 failures. This second direction was NOT previously measured; it confirms the 'weakened by construction' half — inbound-boundary-structural-test was reading handler-meta back for metadata register-all! had installed moments earlier.

REPAIR (minimal outcome, first option): each example ns (websocket.schema / .connection / .messages / .core) now installs its registrations through a named re-invocable (defn register! ...), still called once at ns-load, so the production-app ns-load idiom and core/run are unchanged. Ignoring whitespace the diff to the four example files is exactly the wrapper — defn + docstring + one closing paren + (register!) — no registration content changed. The fixture's register-all! calls the four entry points and keeps no copy. Registered ids in the fixture: 30 -> 5 (four :ws.test/* reply-log targets it genuinely owns, plus the two framework :rf.machine/* runtime subs no example ns owns). Verified line-oriented AND over whitespace-collapsed text, with origin/main as the positive control. No generic registrar-reload framework, no public API change, nothing outside the WebSocket example.

The docstring instructing maintainers to mirror body changes into both copies is deleted with the mechanism it described.

CONTROL ADDED: websocket-example-registrations-are-live — three assertions, one per way the coupling can be lost: registered :doc (identity: which definition won the last write), registered :schema + :rf.schema/at-boundary read off the live registry, and the handler body driven through a real dispatch.

BOTH PLANTS REPLAYED ON THE REPAIRED TREE:

- at-boundary removal -> exit 1, 2 failures (websocket-inbound-boundary-structural + new control)

Acceptance criteria met in full. Left open for the mayor to close on merge.

title: [method] the reap route stops at the empty sink: an id keys TWO locations and the doc names only the expensive fallback
notes:
FILED 2026-09-02 01:28 AUSEST by the acting mayor, from the Method reread loop (loops.md §6),
against a rule I had just spent a whole Hygiene loop enforcing. This is the §6 category
"hazards recorded without their discriminating test" — the hazard is on the page, the cheap
test that discharges it is not, and the doc jumps straight to the expensive fallback.

WHAT THE DOC SAYS TODAY. loops.md §5 Reaping records the empty-sink hazard correctly and at
length: "beware a per-agent scratch sink that merely shares the id"; "An empty file keyed by
the id says nothing whatever about whether a report exists - it is a fact about that file";
"the sink read empty for fifteen of seventeen worktrees, every one of those fifteen
transcripts sat complete elsewhere". It then says "the id names a FILE only once you know
which file is the agent's OWN; until then it names a directory to search", and the NEXT
paragraph - headed "When no id was recorded at all" - gives the path search: grep every
transcript for the worktree path, rank by hit count, confirm by the report's own claimed root.

THE GAP. Between "the sink is empty" and "grep 4.6 GB of transcripts" there is a step the doc
never names: TRY THE ID AT ITS OTHER LOCATION. An agent id is not one path. Here it keys both
a per-task scratch sink AND the real session transcript store, under different roots and a
different filename convention. The doc's own evidence already implies a second location exists
- "their real transcripts sat complete elsewhere" - but it never turns "elsewhere" into a step,
so a reader who has just been told the sink lies goes to the path search, which is two orders
of magnitude more expensive and, per the doc's own warning, many-to-one and misrankable.

MEASURED TODAY, one hygiene pass, 40 candidate worktrees.
  - 38 had a ledger id; 2 had no row at all.
  - Scratch sink keyed by id: NON-EMPTY for 9, exactly 0 bytes for 31. Consistent with the
    doc's "fifteen of seventeen", so the recorded constant is NOT stale - the remedy is
    incomplete.
  - Second id-keyed location: held a complete transcript for ALL 31 of the empty-sink ids.
    Zero misses. 29 of the 31 opened their final message with a quotable completion sentence;
    the other 2 (adapterswitch, twosmall) ended on interim status and were correctly REFUSED
    the reap - the route works in both directions, which is what makes it a test rather than
    a shortcut.
  - Path search was needed for exactly 2 of 40, both unindexed: timerincarn-jqvgp resolved
    cleanly (92 hits in the worker's own transcript against 1 in each peer, and its report's
    claimed root matched), and http-issuance did not (every hit was 1 - peers naming it and
    nothing else), so that tree stays.

So the expensive fallback earned its place once in forty, and the doc points at it thirty-one
times too often.

PROPOSED, small, and it belongs inside the existing Reaping paragraph that already warns about
the sink rather than as a new block. Say that an id can key MORE THAN ONE location; that an
empty one is a fact about THAT location and not about the id; and that the step between them is
to enumerate the id's other locations before falling back to the path search. Keep the path
search exactly where it is, as the route for an id that was never recorded - which is what it
is actually for.

GENERICITY. State it as "an agent id may key several locations" rather than naming this host's
directory layout. A transcript path the platform documents as an implementation detail is not a
contract - loops.md says so itself two paragraphs later - so the durable instruction is
"enumerate the id's locations", not "look in <path>".

SEQUENCING - MANDATORY. docs/the-mayor-method/ is SOLE-TOUCHER hot-zone. PR #8962
(worker/methodstep-ute0q, rf2-ute0q + rf2-f7fby) is OPEN against loops.md and
dispatch-prompt-template.md right now. DO NOT DISPATCH until #8962 merges.

GATE: python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py plus python -m mkdocs build --strict (exclude_docs
does NOT hide the-mayor-method/). Run mkdocs as "python -m mkdocs" - bare mkdocs returns 127
here, which is NO VERDICT rather than a pass. Neither gate reads prose, tables or rendering:
verify those by hand and say so in the PR body.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8966, verified on main at b99e95fefa (docs(method): name the id's other locations as the step between an empty sink and the path search). Verified by MERGE, not by PR state. The repair sits INSIDE the existing empty-sink paragraph in loops.md section 5 Reaping - an id may key several locations rather than one, an empty one is a fact about THAT location and not about the id, and the step between them is to enumerate the id's remaining locations before falling back to the path search, which is left verbatim and in place as the route for an id that was never recorded. Carries the forty-worktree measurement including the both-directions discrimination (29 quotable reports found, 2 correctly REFUSED on interim status). title: [method] the mayor briefs from the bead's oldest layer — make the newest-mutation read and hold-banner sweep a STEP, not a thing to remember
notes:
FILED 2026-09-02 by the acting mayor, against my own practice. This is at least the THIRD recorded instance of one failure class and the memories have not stopped it, which is the argument for a mechanical step.

THE PRIOR RECORD, found while filing this: bd memories 'mayor-brief' returns three keys, two of them predating today - mayor-brief-accuracy-stop-asserting-file-paths-i (2026-07-18, 'three times in one session') and mayor-brief-premises-must-be-verified-at-head (2026-08-17, whose own text says 'fifth instance'). Today added a third. A note that has been written three times and re-learned each time is not working as a control.

TODAY'S THREE, all the same shape - briefed from the bead's Scope/description rather than its newest text-bearing mutation, all three caught by the WORKER rather than by me:
- rf2-y8jjk: dispatched onto an unstruck '*** AWAITING MIKE - NOT DISPATCHABLE. ***' banner that WAS the newest text-bearing field. Worker refused, wrote nothing, opened no PR. A sweep then found ELEVEN of 27 open beads carrying a hold banner - I had been reporting two of them as dispatchable.
- rf2-9n43e: the newest note split the work into A (dispatchable) and B (sequenced behind two open beads sharing a test file). The brief asked for both; the worker did A only.
- rf2-i3og0: ruled from a skill page's prose without checking the owning spec or the history. Ruling was backwards. Worker refused and filed rf2-lspr9.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS WORTH A STEP: the dispatch preamble ALREADY orders the worker to read by tracker timestamps, at length, with the reasoning. The mayor writes that preamble and then does not do it. So the knowledge is present, written down, and pasted verbatim into every dispatch - what is missing is that nothing makes the mayor execute it before the brief exists. That is the same property the stash ban, the beads-boundary hook and the draft interlock all have and the reason they hold: enforced where it cannot be forgotten.

PROPOSED (small, and it belongs in the existing 'Write the brief in this order' section rather than as a new section): make step one of writing a brief a READ of the item's newest text-bearing mutation plus a fixed-string hold sweep - probes short enough to survive the ~76-column wrap ('NOT DISPATCHABLE', 'AWAITING MIKE', 'OPERATOR CALL'), exercised once against a bead known to carry one, because a zero from a wrong pattern reads exactly like a clean bead. State that a hold banner is the newest field often enough that the Scope section cannot be trusted to mention it.

SEQUENCING - MANDATORY. docs/the-mayor-method/ is SOLE-TOUCHER hot-zone per rf2-ttu8i, never parallel with another method-file bead. PR #8949 (mayor/one-rule-draft-interlock) is open against BOTH method pages right now. Do not dispatch until #8949 merges.

GATE: python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py plus python -m mkdocs build --strict (exclude_docs does NOT hide the-mayor-method/, verified by a planted-link red on #8949). Run mkdocs as 'python -m mkdocs' - bare mkdocs returns 127 here, which is NO VERDICT rather than a pass.
FIFTH INSTANCE, 2026-09-02, and a DIFFERENT SHAPE worth naming separately — a blanket fence in the brief that the bead had already lifted.

rf2-fmns2 (PR #8954). My brief said: 'Do not touch implementation/shadow-cljs.edn. If a new example build-id is genuinely required, that lives in the hot-zone top-level shadow-cljs.edn, so STOP and report rather than editing it.' The worker edited it anyway and was RIGHT to:

- the item's AC4 requires :examples/login-hicasso to exist and enrol automatically, which is only possible in that file;
- the bead's own TRIAGE NOTE had already anticipated the hot-zone touch and SEQUENCED this task behind rf2-3xq1v (shadow-cljs.edn) and rf2-39rc5 (package.json) - both closed and merged before dispatch;
- it checked every open PR first and found none touching either file.

I verified all three claims after the fact: rf2-3xq1v and rf2-39rc5 both read CLOSED, and a sweep of every open PR's file list found #8954 is the only one touching implementation/shadow-cljs.edn or top-level deps.edn.

WHY THIS SHAPE IS DISTINCT from the four already recorded. Those were the brief carrying STALE instructions - a hold banner not read, a work split not read, a ruling made without checking the owning spec. This one is the brief carrying a fence the mayor invented generically and correctly by default, which the ITEM had already discharged by naming the predecessors that had to land first. A blanket 'do not touch X, STOP and report' is the right default and is WRONG whenever the bead has already sequenced X - and the bead is where that sequencing lives, so the mayor cannot know it without reading the newest layer.

IMPLICATION FOR THE PROPOSED STEP: the newest-mutation read must look for SEQUENCING as well as for holds. A triage note that names predecessors is an authorisation with a precondition, and re-stating a fence over it converts a satisfied precondition back into a blocker - which either strands the work or, as here, costs the worker a justification round it should not have had to write.

Cost this time: nothing, because the worker read the item and overrode the brief. That is five for five on workers catching it, which is the safeguard working and not a reason to keep relying on it.
CORRECTION TO THE PROPOSED REMEDY, 2026-09-02 — the marker sweep I proposed has a FALSE-POSITIVE mode, and I hit it within hours of proposing it. Do not build the step as written.

WHAT HAPPENED. I ran the fixed-string sweep over dispatch candidates and it flagged THIS BEAD as held, carrying both 'AWAITING MIKE' and 'OPERATOR CALL'. I wrote this bead and put no banner on it. The probe was matching (a) my own note QUOTING rf2-y8jjk's banner, and (b) the proposed remedy's own list of probe strings. It also flagged rf2-6c12m, whose text says outright 'its AWAITING MIKE banner is struck, so it is DISPATCHABLE' - the opposite of held.

I then tried to discriminate automatically - active marker vs 'struck' nearby vs a banner attributed to another bead id - and THAT failed too, because the standing banner text itself ends 'WHOEVER RULES STRIKES THIS BANNER IN THE SAME ACT', so the word 'struck' appears in every ACTIVE banner as an instruction. rf2-y8jjk, which is definitely held, scored active=2 struck=2. A second instrument, same shape of failure.

THIS IS THE HAZARD THE METHOD ALREADY NAMES, and I walked into it while building a check meant to prevent a different error. loops.md Tracker mechanics: 'An instrument can be RIGHT and still answer a different question from the one you asked... a marker scan finding a banner read as this item is held.' It lists that exact instance. The scan answers 'does this text contain these characters'; the question is 'is this item currently held', and the gap is invisible in the answer.

CONSEQUENCE FOR MY EARLIER REPORT: I told the operator '11 of 27 open beads carry a hold banner'. That number is UNRELIABLE and at least two of the eleven (this bead, rf2-6c12m) are false. Do not carry it forward. The two I can stand behind are reads rather than scans: rf2-y8jjk (a worker read it, refused the dispatch, and quoted the unstruck banner) and rf2-zq34m (I read its banner and its diverged-blockers note directly).

WHAT THE STEP MUST BE INSTEAD. A marker scan is a CANDIDATE FILTER, never a verdict. It narrows 27 items to a handful; the hold is then established by READING each candidate - which is cheap at that size and is the only thing that distinguishes an active banner from one quoted, discussed, or struck. Write the step that way, and write beside it the question the scan actually answers, so the gap is on the page rather than in the reader's head. If a machine-checkable hold is wanted, the durable fix is a STRUCTURED FIELD on the item rather than a marker in prose - but that is a tracker change and a separate decision, not this bead's.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8962, verified on main at commit 2a018d54fd (docs(method): make the newest-mutation read a dispatch step...). Verified by MERGE, not by PR state. Built with the bead's own CORRECTION note governing, not its original proposal: the step reads the item's newest text-bearing mutation for a hold AND for sequencing, and a hold-marker sweep is written as a CANDIDATE FILTER with the hold established by reading each candidate - the question the scan answers stated beside the question being asked. The structured-field idea stayed out of scope. Worker pointed at loops.md Tracker mechanics rather than restating it, and correctly reported that #8958 had landed MORE there than my brief credited.

THE FAILURE, verbatim from a local run of the actual gate command (the CI run was still `in_progress` when this bead was filed, so nobody had the text; the job log became retrievable via `gh api repos/day8/re-frame2/actions/jobs/99865809057/logs` even while the run was not):

title: WebSocket stale timeout can settle a newer same-ID request
description:
Audit finding from PR #8936 across completeness, correctness, and implementation quality.

The PR correctly makes a live-socket timeout explicit, but the worked and runnable machines correlate a timeout only by `request-id` plus the socket actor id. That rejects timers from an old connection, not an old registration on the same live socket.

At merged commit 23e25e4040:
- `:register-request` stores `[:in-flight request-id]` and schedules `:ws/request-timeout` carrying only that id and `:source-socket-id`.
- `:clear-request` looks up whichever entry currently occupies that id, removes it, and now dispatches its reply-event a local `:ws/timeout`.
- The spec permits any `=`-comparable id and explicitly recommends reusable per-feature vectors such as `[:feature/load slug]`; uniqueness for a socket lifetime is not a contract.

Concrete failure: request A with id R completes; request B reuses R on the same still-live socket before A's uncancelled deadline; A's timer passes `:current-socket?`, deletes B, and fires B's callback with a premature timeout. Registering B while A is still pending also overwrites A's callback without settling it. Both violate the page's new exactly-once/terminal-outcome promise.

Keep the repair local to the WebSocket pattern: correlate scheduled timeouts to the specific registration they came from and state the duplicate-in-flight policy. Do not build a generic timer-cancellation layer or managed WebSocket abstraction.
acceptance_criteria: A timeout or wire reply can settle only the exact in-flight registration it belongs to; an uncancelled timeout from an earlier same-ID request on the same socket cannot clear or notify a later request. Concurrent duplicate IDs have an explicit policy that does not strand a displaced caller. The spec, runnable example, schema if needed, and focused tests agree, while preserving socket-epoch rejection and the existing local/server provenance shapes. No generic cancellation facility or new public WebSocket abstraction.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8946 (2026-09-02) — REOPENED BECAUSE WIRE REPLIES STILL CORRELATE TO THE REUSED ID, NOT THE REGISTRATION.

The timeout half is sound: `:own-request-timeout?` checks both socket epoch and registration token. The same token never reaches the wire-reply path, though:

- `:register-request` still sends `(assoc body :request-id request-id)` with no registration discriminator.
- `ReplyMessage` carries only `:request-id`.
- `:receive-message` looks up and removes whichever entry currently occupies `[:in-flight (:request-id body)]`, without a token check.

Concrete failure: A is pending under `R`; B re-registers `R`, locally superseding A, and both requests are now on the wire with the identical correlation value. When A's server reply arrives first, `:receive-message` finds B's slot, removes it, and fires B's callback with A's body. B's actual reply later becomes unsolicited. The callback count can remain exactly once while the reply is attached to the wrong registration—the more fundamental correlation failure.

This directly contradicts this bead's acceptance criterion: "A timeout or wire reply can settle only the exact in-flight registration it belongs to." The merged spec instead disclaims which server reply answers which registration and says the reply settles whichever registration holds the slot; that narrows the required end state rather than satisfying it. The two new tests use `:silent-no-echo`, so neither injects A's wire reply after B takes the slot and the missing fence is unobserved.

Completeness: the registration identity protects deadlines only. Correctness: last-write-wins plus an unchanged wire id can deliver stale data as B's successful response. Implementation quality: an explicitly ambiguous request/reply contract is a sharp edge in the recommended reusable-id pattern, and the focused tests avoid the ambiguous branch.

Minimal outcome: preserve exact wire correlation either by ensuring two registrations with one wire id are never concurrently outstanding (for example, reject/serialize the newcomer) or by putting a registration discriminator on the wire and requiring it back; add the A-reply-after-B-registration regression. Keep this local to the example—no managed-WebSocket abstraction or generic cancellation layer.

Duplicate search: `rf2-tb442` owns this exact same-id registration-correlation contract and already names wire replies in its acceptance criteria, so it is reopened rather than duplicated.
close_reason:
Second pass (audit PR #8946), PR #8959. The reopen was about the WIRE-REPLY half of the correlation, and that is what this addressed: :register-request now stamps the registration :token onto the outbound frame as :request-token beside :request-id, schema/ReplyMessage REQUIRES it echoed back, and :receive-message settles the [:in-flight rid] slot only while the echoed token is still the slot's token. A mismatch is treated as an unsolicited reply (nothing cleared, no :reply-event fired, frame still reaches the inbox), not an error. Duplicate-in-flight policy (last-write-wins, displaced caller settled :ws/superseded) is unchanged; the displaced registration now leaves two inert leftovers rather than one -- its armed timer and the reply its request will still draw from the server.

REGRESSION PROVING A WIRE REPLY CAN NO LONGER SETTLE A LATER SAME-ID REGISTRATION: deftest websocket-wire-reply-cannot-settle-a-later-same-id-registration in implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs. A registers under the reusable id [:feature/load "gamma"] and stays pending; B re-registers the same id (A settled :ws/superseded, A's request still on the wire); A's SERVER reply then arrives carrying A's token. Asserted: the slot still holds B's token, B's callback count is still 1, and A's reply reaches the inbox as an unsolicited vetted frame -- then B's own reply settles B with B's OWN body and B's token. RED BEFORE / GREEN AFTER measured: with :receive-message's token check reverted to (get-in data [:in-flight rid]) and everything else left in place, the focused suite returned captured exit 1 with 4 failures, ALL in that test, on the same 29 tests / 240 assertions -- including 'expected (= {:type :request :tag "B"} (:echo outcome)) / actual (not (= {:type :request :tag "B"} {:type :request :tag "A"}))', which is the defect in one row: B's caller handed A's body as its answer. Restored (verified by git blob hash against the committed object), recompiled, re-run: captured exit 0.

Gates, captured exit codes from the runner: node-test compile 0 (1877 files, 0 warnings); node out/node-test.js 0 (11197 tests, 55483 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors); focused websocket ns 0 (29 tests, 240 assertions); check_doc_slugs.py 0; check_readme_links.py --ci 0. Both link gates exercised against a planted broken target first and returned exit 1 naming the planted file and line, so their greens are measured rather than silent.

EP-0011 CANARY HELD. The app-level/no-uniform-envelope boundary is intact: :request-token is an ordinary unqualified app key on the app's own wire frame, not :work/id or :rf/reply-to. The five 'app-level reply carries no EP-0011 ...' assertions pass, and they are live -- planting the five envelope keys onto the reply body reds all five. ServerReplyOutcome is also a :closed map, so envelope vocabulary on this path is a schema rejection as well.

WIRE COMPATIBILITY, stated because the outbound body changed: a server that ignores :request-token echoes only :request-id, its reply then fails the closed ReplyMessage arm, and the frame takes :refuse-frame -- nothing in the connection moves, the slot is not cleared, no callback fires, and the ingress mints the canonical :rf.error/schema-validation-failure naming the missing key on the very first reply; the request then settles on its own deadline with the documented {:origin :ws/local :ok false :error :ws/timeout}. So it degrades to a loud, terminal, documented outcome, never to silence and never to wrong data. Admitting an untokened reply and correlating by id would have restored the exact ambiguity the field removes. The escape hatch is documented in ReplyMessage's docstring and Pattern-WebSocket item 6: an app whose server cannot echo the field drops it from BOTH ReplyMessage and :register-request and then owes its ids uniqueness for the socket's lifetime. A new boundary case pins this -- a reply omitting only :request-token is refused and the in-flight slot survives it.

Scope kept local to the WebSocket pattern per the bead: one wire field, one required schema entry, one equality check, plus spec/example/skill/README prose. No managed-WebSocket abstraction, no generic correlation or cancellation layer, no new public surface.

SPEC CHANGE OF NOTE: Pattern-WebSocket item 6 previously DISCLAIMED this ('the wire reply settles whichever registration holds the slot'), which narrowed the acceptance criterion rather than meeting it. That disclaimer is removed and item 6 is restructured around both settling paths, with a new anti-pattern for fixing the timer and leaving the reply.

title: CLAUDE.md prescribes naming remote+branch as the fix for 'Cannot rebase onto multiple branches'; measured insufficient
notes:
MEASURED 2026-09-01 22:4x AUSEST by the acting mayor, in the mayor checkout, six worker worktrees live.

WHAT HAPPENED. Ran the checkpoint sequence's third step in its PRESCRIBED named form - 'git pull --rebase origin main' - and it aborted:

  From https://github.com/day8/re-frame2
   * branch                  main       -> FETCH_HEAD
  fatal: Cannot rebase onto multiple branches.

Tree was clean and undiverged. HEAD == origin/main afterwards and the push landed, so no damage this time - but the rebase silently did not happen, which is the step the sequence exists to perform.

WHY THE PRESCRIBED REMEDY DOES NOT HOLD. CLAUDE.md's Beads-durability bullet says a BARE 'git pull --rebase' takes its target from FETCH_HEAD and therefore aborts this way, and prescribes naming remote and branch. But naming them does not immunise the pull, because a pull is TWO steps: it fetches into FETCH_HEAD, then rebases onto what FETCH_HEAD says. FETCH_HEAD lives in the SHARED common git directory - 'git rev-parse --git-common-dir' returns .git from the mayor checkout, and linked worktrees do NOT get their own copy. So any concurrent fetch from any of the six live worker worktrees rewrites it inside that window, and the rebase step reads the peer's multi-ref version no matter how the pull was invoked. Naming the remote and branch controls only the FETCH half.

The doc's own measured instance (2026-08-29 22:31) was the bare form, which is why the named form was taken to be the fix. This is the named form failing identically.

THE FIX IS ALREADY IN CLAUDE.md FOR THE OTHER CASE. The post-merge bullet deliberately replaced 'git pull --ff-only origin main' with 'git fetch origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main', reasoning that 'A ref can't be captured that way' - FETCH_HEAD is a scratch file any concurrent git process rewrites, an explicit ref is not. That reasoning applies verbatim to the rebase pull, but the checkpoint sequence still prescribes the pull form. The merge case was fixed and the rebase case was left.

PROPOSED: in the Beads-durability sequence and the session-completion block, replace 'git pull --rebase origin main' with 'git fetch origin main && git rebase origin/main', keeping the && so a failed fetch cannot be followed by a rebase against a stale ref. Then rewrite the naming guidance to say what it actually buys (the fetch half) rather than presenting it as the remedy for this abort.

SECOND, SMALLER FINDING - the abort was INVISIBLE. It was run as 'git pull --rebase origin main 2>&1 | tail -3 && bd dolt push && git push'. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, so tail returned 0 and the && chain continued straight past a fatal abort. This is the same hazard the dispatch template's gate-mechanics block states for gates ('Never pipe a gate through a filter'), reached through git rather than through a gate runner, and it is what made the doc's phrase 'inert only because the push that follows still lands' literally true here. Worth a line where the sequence is written down: do not pipe the steps of this sequence.

---

RESOLVED by PR #8964 (draft -> ready), CLAUDE.md only, 14 insertions / 10 deletions.

The bead's PROPOSED action was carried out as written. Three sites prescribing the
pull form now run 'git fetch origin main && git rebase origin/main' with the &&
retained: the Session Completion block, the Beads-durability sequence, and -- a
site the bead did not name -- the fast-forward bullet's own 'Not possible to
fast-forward' remedy under Workflow, which still prescribed 'git pull --rebase
origin main'. The naming guidance is rewritten to say what naming buys (the fetch
half); the 2026-08-29 measurement is kept as evidence about that half. The
no-piping line is added where the sequence is written. The reasoning is stated
once, in Beads durability, pointing at the fast-forward bullet for "a ref can't be
captured that way".

TWO OF THIS BEAD'S OWN PREMISES WERE MEASURED WRONG AND ARE NOT REPRODUCED IN THE DOC.

1. FETCH_HEAD IS PER-WORKTREE, not shared across worktrees. The bead reasoned that
   because 'git rev-parse --git-common-dir' returns the mayor checkout's .git,
   linked worktrees have no FETCH_HEAD of their own and any peer worker's fetch
   rewrites the mayor's. Measured on git 2.53.0.windows.2: 'git rev-parse
   --git-path FETCH_HEAD' resolves INSIDE the linked worktree's own git directory,
   and a 'git fetch origin main' run from a linked worktree wrote that per-worktree
   file while leaving the common-dir FETCH_HEAD byte-identical and its mtime
   untouched. So a peer worktree is not the contaminating process.

   THE BEAD'S CONCLUSION SURVIVES ANYWAY, and CLAUDE.md already had the accurate
   wording: the fast-forward bullet says FETCH_HEAD is "a scratch file any
   concurrent git process IN THE SAME CHECKOUT rewrites". The mayor checkout runs
   several git processes at once, which is where this bites -- and it is where the
   abort was measured. The doc now carries the same-checkout framing plus one
   clause recording that FETCH_HEAD is per-worktree, because the old phrase "the
   shared fetch-head file" invites exactly the wrong mental model.

2. THE ABORT MESSAGES ATTRIBUTED TO THE SEQUENCE WERE WRONG, pre-existing and now
   corrected. Measured in a throwaway repo:
     - dirty tree, 'git rebase origin/main'      -> "cannot rebase: You have
       unstaged changes" (exit 1), and it refuses on ANY unstaged change, not only
       one the incoming commits would overwrite;
     - dirty tree, 'git merge --ff-only origin/main' -> "local changes would be
       overwritten" (exit 1);
     - diverged but clean, 'git rebase origin/main'  -> no abort, rebases the
       checkpoint on top, exit 0.
   So "local changes would be overwritten" is a merge-family message: correct where
   the fast-forward bullet uses it, wrong where Beads durability and the Workflow
   summary attributed it to the checkpoint step. And "Not possible to fast-forward"
   cannot arise from the rebase step at all. Both are now attributed correctly, and
   the stricter rebase behaviour is noted, since it makes clearing .beads more
   necessary rather than less.

GATES (captured exit codes, redirect + echo on one command line):
  python scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci  -> 0
  scripts/test-fast-pr.sh                    -> 0
check_doc_slugs.py was NOT nominated: CLAUDE.md is repo-root markdown, outside its
roots, where it exits 0 on a broken link. Gate discrimination was checked by
planting a broken anchor at the edited line -- check_readme_links.py went red,
exit 1, naming CLAUDE.md:66 and the planted anchor -- so the green is earned.
Restore verified by blob hash against the committed object.

VERIFIED BY HAND (no gate covers it): neither link gate reads inside fenced code
blocks, and this change touches two fenced command blocks; both were read by hand
and neither contains any link or anchor, so the fence-blindness is inert here. The
one added link, [Workflow](#workflow), resolves to the unique '## Workflow'
heading; no heading slug in the file is duplicated, so no GitHub -N suffix is in
play. The file contains no tables.
AUDIT PR #8964: REOPENED.

COMPLETENESS / IMPLEMENTATION QUALITY — the command is corrected in `CLAUDE.md`, but the same active workflow still prescribes the retired pull form elsewhere. `AGENTS.md:237-242` is the sibling agent-facing Session Completion block and still says `git pull --rebase`; `scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh:338-342` and `scripts/beads-checkpoint.ps1:655-660` still print `git pull --rebase` as the recovery sequence when they refuse an unsafe clear. Those are executable guidance that users and agents follow, not historical citations or tests. The edited generated block even warns that regeneration may restore the bad form, which confirms the repair was applied to a copy rather than durably reconciled across its active carriers.

Keep this small: make the AGENTS block and both checkpoint-script messages prescribe `git fetch origin main && git rebase origin/main` (or the platform-equivalent two checked steps), reconcile the generator/template if it is repository-owned, and leave genuine hook tests/history that intentionally exercise `git pull --rebase` alone. A semantic active-instruction census, not a global string purge, is the control. No new wrapper or retry framework.

Second pass, closing the AUDIT PR #8964 reopen. title: WebSocket teaching surfaces disagree on timeout delivery and reply-envelope shape
description:
Audit finding from PR #8907 across completeness, correctness, and implementation quality.

The PR correctly synchronizes the three active-exit doors with the runnable WebSocket example, but the request-outcome contract is still internally contradictory on the same edited teaching surface.

At merged commit 9445bfeb3c:
- spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md's worked :clear-request action only dissocs the slot. Item 4 says the caller's reply event never fires on timeout.
- The canonical runnable example examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs does the opposite: action-clear-request reads reply-event, clears the slot, and dispatches one machine-stamped :ws/timeout failure. Existing rf2-b2jpr acceptance and tests explicitly require a live-socket timeout as an explicit terminal outcome.
- Two lines after the stale item 4, the spec says a locally minted loss/timeout failure reaches the caller's reply-event. Thus the page contradicts itself and copying its worked machine restores the caller-hang that the canonical example already removed.
- The edited skill still emits the runnable example's bespoke {:origin :ws/local :request-id ... :ok false :error ...} outcome, while its correlation guidance on the same page mandates the uniform reply envelope with closed :status and :rf.reply/work-id. The runnable schema/RequestOutcome and spec use the bespoke shape. A programmer or AI cannot tell which contract is canonical.

No existing Bead owns WebSocket timeout documentation or this reply-envelope conflict; all-status searches covered websocket timeout, clear-request, reply-event, RequestOutcome, uniform reply, and rf.reply/work-id. rf2-0g60h owns only the fatal-door listing drift, rf2-b2jpr the already-fixed clean-disconnect runtime leak, and rf2-iyjae the already-fixed inbound trust/provenance boundary.

Keep this small: rule the one callback contract and align the runnable example, spec, and skill. Do not build a generalized WebSocket facility or a new reply abstraction.
acceptance_criteria: The spec worked :clear-request, its request-reply sequence, the runnable example/test, and the skill agree whether a live timeout invokes reply-event; no copied canonical form can silently clear a request while leaving its caller waiting. The WebSocket RequestOutcome uses one documented envelope shape across source schema, spec, and skill (either the uniform managed envelope or an explicitly justified pattern-local contract). Loss and timeout remain machine-stamped, server outcomes remain unforgeably distinct, and existing exactly-once/stale-epoch controls stay intact. No new abstraction or compatibility layer.
notes:
MAYOR RULING 2026-09-01 22:07 AUSEST — THE UNIFORM REPLY ENVELOPE IS CANONICAL. Settled from the page's own normative text, not by preference.

BOTH HALVES OF THIS BEAD ARE REAL, and neither is a taste call once you read the sources.

HALF 1 — THE SELF-CONTRADICTION. spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md's item 4 says the caller's reply event never fires on timeout. Two lines later the same page says a locally minted loss/timeout failure DOES reach the reply-event, and the runnable example (examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs) dispatches one. So item 4 and the worked :clear-request action are the wrong side of the contradiction: the example and the page's own later text already agree with each other, and rf2-b2jpr's acceptance requires a live-socket timeout as an explicit terminal outcome. RULED: correct item 4 and the worked action to fire the reply-event. Copying the current worked machine restores the caller-hang the canonical example already removed, which is the whole cost here.

HALF 2 — THE ENVELOPE. skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md:200 already states the rule, with its reason and a citation: 'Because this is the completion of an async request, model it on the uniform reply envelope (Managed-Effects property 9), not a bespoke ack: dispatch the :reply-event with a reply map carrying a closed :status {:ok :partial :error :cancelled :stale} and the request id as :rf.reply/work-id ... so your socket replies read the same as every other async completion in trace/Xray.' Line 64 of that same file, and spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md at 181/505/575, emit {:origin :ws/local :ok false :error :ws/connection-lost} — the bespoke ack the page forbids. RULED: the envelope is canonical and the bespoke shape is the drift. A page carrying its own rule plus worked examples that violate it is worse than either alone, because the reader cannot tell which is the contract.

:origin :ws/local IS NOT DROPPED — it is carried INSIDE the envelope. The same paragraph demands that two producers reaching one reply-event be told apart 'by a provenance key the machine stamps after receipt, never by the body's shape'. That is exactly what :origin is for, and it is the reason the two shapes must not remain alternatives: provenance belongs as a field, never as a rival envelope.

SCOPE, measured rather than assumed: seven files carry the bespoke spelling — spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md, skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md, examples/patterns/websocket/{connection,schema,messages}.cljs and its README, plus implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs. No framework source depends on it, so this is a teaching-surface correction plus one test, not a runtime migration.

NOT WANTED: any change to the reply-envelope contract itself; a WebSocket-specific exemption from it; a new outcome abstraction; a Playwright spec. Do not widen beyond the WebSocket surface.

---

WORKER VERDICT 2026-09-01 (rf2-i3og0, PR #8936, branch worker/wsenvelope-i3og0)

HALF 1 — IMPLEMENTED. Both premises confirmed verbatim at tip before acting.
Item 4 read: "The :clear-request action removes the in-flight entry; the
caller's reply event never fires." Two paragraphs later the same page reads:
"A correlated wire reply and a locally minted loss/timeout failure both arrive
at the caller's :reply-event." The runnable example already agreed with the
second. Fixed in spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md only: :clear-request now reads the
:reply-event, clears the slot and dispatches the :ws/timeout failure (guarded
for a nil reply-event); item 4 states the reply-event fires and why a silent
clear strands the caller; and the local-failure body is factored into a helper
as connection.cljs already does, so the lost-wire and elapsed-deadline
producers cannot drift into two shapes again. The example, the test and the
README needed no change — they were already on the correct side.

HALF 2 — STOPPED. THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD, AND THE DRIFT RUNS THE OTHER WAY.
skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md:200 does say what the ruling quotes, but
it is the residue, not the rule. Four independent sources say the opposite:

1. spec/Managed-Effects.md:281 — the envelope contract's OWN owning spec: "A
   WebSocket connection is a long-lived synchronous surface rather than a

title: machines tracing: preserve raised-event transitions in the macrostep cascade
description:
## Scope

Make the structured `:cascade` on `:rf.machine/transition` faithfully describe transitions selected by same-macrostep raised/internal events, including synthetic compound/parallel done-state signals. Cover flat, compound, and root-parallel machines plus the Xray consumers of this trace. Keep the state/effect fold unchanged.

## Correctness finding

Raised-event execution is semantically correct, but its inspection record is not. In the flat/compound drain, a dequeued raise is processed through a nested `machine-transition-single`; the resulting snapshot and real effects are retained, but that result's structured cascade is discarded because the loop recurs with `cascade` unchanged. The parallel parent queue retains the rebroadcast result's cascade by flattening it into the accumulator, but records no boundary or trigger event, so those exit/action/entry rows are indistinguishable from the external event's transition.

The outer trace can therefore say an external event moved a machine from A to C while its `:cascade` explains only A to B; the raised event that actually moved B to C is invisible or misattributed. That violates the local “complete configuration walk / one trace, one place” contract and prevents Xray from showing why the final state was reached.

XState v6 gets the important boundary right: one `@xstate.transition` inspection event carries every selected transition definition in its ordered `microsteps` collection, including eventless and internally raised processing. re-frame2 need not copy that wire protocol, but its one-macrostep trace should be equally lossless.

## Evidence

- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc`, `drain-to-fixed-point` around lines 4060-4138: after dequeuing a raised event, `step-result` supplies `snap2` and `fx2`, then the `recur` passes the old `cascade` unchanged. By contrast, the `:always` branch around lines 3988-4039 emits `:rf.machine.microstep/transition` and appends a nested `{:kind :microstep ... :steps ...}`.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/parallel.cljc`, `drain-parent-queue` around lines 1320-1370: raised-event rebroadcast appends `(result/cascade step)` directly into `acc-casc`, losing the event boundary/identity even though the geometry survives.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/registration.cljc` around lines 711-734 describes and emits `:cascade` as the ordered explanation of how the macrostep reached `:after`.
- `spec/005-StateMachines.md`, “The structured transition cascade”, promises a complete configuration walk and says one trace is the place tooling reads to understand the transition. Its closed step vocabulary explains external and `:always` work but has no raised-event boundary.
- `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/machines/trace_state.cljs` reads only this structured cascade to distinguish handled regions and derive fired edges. It assumes non-`:microstep` rows belong to the dispatched event, which makes the parallel flattening actively misattribute raised work.
- XState v6's official inspection contract says each `@xstate.transition` carries the triggering event, final snapshot, and `microsteps`: https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/inspection . Its execution contract defines one externally observed snapshot after all internal steps settle: https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/how-xstate-runs-machines . Exact source baseline: `xstate@6.0.0-alpha.50` (`0b52534e`), whose `packages/core/src/stateUtils.ts` appends the selected transition set for the seed event, eventless rounds, and internal-queue events to the same macrostep `microsteps` array.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Failure scenario/invariant

Use a machine where external `:go` takes `:idle -> :working` and its action raises `[:settle]`; `:working` handles `:settle` with `:target :done` and entry/exit actions.

1. Dispatch `:go`.
2. Observe the committed snapshot is `:done`; FIFO raise semantics worked.
3. Inspect the single `:rf.machine/transition` trace. `:before` is `:idle` and `:after` is `:done`, but on a flat/compound machine its `:cascade` contains only the `:go` geometry (and any `:always` wrappers), not the `:settle` transition.
4. Repeat in a parallel machine: raised transition rows appear flattened with the external rows, so Xray may light them as if `:go` selected them.

The same omission applies when the runtime synthesizes a raised done-state event after entering an embedded final state.

Required invariant: the macrostep inspection record preserves, in execution order, the event boundary and transition geometry of every handled dequeued internal event needed to explain the final snapshot. An ignored raised event contributes no fictional transition.

## Recommended minimal fix

Extend the existing structured cascade with one nested internal-event boundary rather than adding a second trace protocol. For example:

```clojure
{:kind   :raised-transition
 :source :raise
 :event  [:settle]
 :from   :working
 :to     :done
 :region nil
 :steps  [ ...the nested exit/action/entry and `:always` steps... ]}
```

- Append one such wrapper after each handled dequeue in both the flat/compound and parallel parent queues, in actual FIFO execution order. Preserve nested `:always` structure from that step.
- Use one schema-approved name/shape across both engines; the example spelling is a recommendation, not a request for aliases.
- Keep the outer trace's external `:event`, `:before`, and `:after` as the macrostep headline.
- Keep the current `:microsteps` scalar as the `:always`-iteration count for compatibility unless a separate design explicitly changes it. Do not emit an extra dispatch envelope or notify observers mid-macrostep.
- Teach Xray to traverse the wrapper, attribute nested edges/actions to its internal event, and exclude those rows when determining which regions handled the external event.
- Update Spec 005, the trace schema/ratchet, and focused tool documentation to make the internal-event boundary part of the closed cascade shape.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A focused pure-engine test proves a flat/compound `external -> raise -> transition` macrostep records the external geometry and then one internal-event wrapper with the raised event, from/to state, and nested ordered steps.
- A two-raise chain proves wrappers are ordered by actual FIFO dequeue order; an `:always` transition enabled by a raised transition appears inside/after the correct boundary according to runtime order.
- An ignored or guard-blocked raised event does not fabricate a handled-transition wrapper; a targetless handled raised transition still records its action boundary even when from equals to.
- Root-parallel tests prove raised rebroadcast geometry is grouped under the internal event and Xray no longer counts it as evidence that a region handled the original external event.
- A synthetic embedded done-state signal is represented by the same mechanism, without a special parallel trace dialect.
- Xray projection/view tests show the dispatched event and the internal event as distinct causal transition steps and light the correct graph edges.
- Snapshot, data, effect order, raise FIFO, eventless-before-next-raise ordering, atomic rollback, and subscriber/dispatch behavior are byte/value-identical to pre-change behavior.
- Spec 005, relevant Spec-Schemas/Spec 009 trace rows, runtime comments, and Xray consumers agree on the new closed shape; trace privacy projection still scrubs nested `:data-delta` values.

## Non-goals

- Adopting XState's `@xstate.*` event names or actor inspection protocol.
- Changing transition selection, microstep order, effect order, raise depth limits, or observer notification.
- Adding an actor mailbox, emitted-event channel, or JavaScript transition-function API.
- Recording unhandled internal events as successful transitions.
- Redesigning the public `re-frame.machines/machine-transition` result shape.

## Related/duplicate search

All-status tracker searches covered titles/descriptions containing: `microstep`, `raised event`, `raise`, `cascade`, `structured`, `inspection`, `trace`, `machine transition`, and `XState v6`. No bead owns lossless raised-event macrostep inspection. Closed `rf2-v4xjh` changed the public pure-transition result map and explicitly excluded transition semantics; it does not repair runtime traces. Closed `rf2-sxw06` concerns static Mermaid topology export. Closed `rf2-zk1xu` reconciled Spec 009 tag rows but does not add this missing runtime evidence.

title: realworld-http: late article delete success overrides the reader's newer route
description:
DISCOVERED-FROM rf2-84iek (PR #8898), named in source by that worker as a suspected same-class defect it deliberately did not fix.

THE SUSPICION (verify at source before acting; this is a CLAIM, not a finding). rf2-84iek corrected three optimistic comment WRITE paths in examples/real-apps/realworld_http/ that mutated shared state without checking the reply belonged to the current route. While doing so its worker observed that :article/author-follow-rollback looks like the same shape: a failed follow on article alpha, settling after navigation to beta, would flip the on-screen author flag for BETA.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED THERE. rf2-84iek non-goals it, and the worker had no reproduced defect for it. It named the suspicion in the source rather than acting on an unverified premise, which is the right call and is why this is a separate bead rather than scope creep on that PR.

WHAT MAKES THIS NON-OBVIOUS, and the reason it should not be fixed by pattern-matching the sibling: rf2-84iek established that gating alone was NOT sufficient for the comment paths. The comments slice is route-owned and resets on slug change, but the comment FORM was not -- so refusing a stale settle left the next articles form permanently locked with its textarea and Post button disabled. The fix needed a gate AND a reset, as two halves of one change. Whoever takes this must ask the same question of the author/follow state: is it route-owned and reset on navigation, or does it ride across? If it rides, a gate alone reproduces that same lock-out bug in a new place.

FIRST STEP IS TO REPRODUCE OR REFUTE. If the author-follow state turns out to be route-owned and already reset by :article/load, there is no defect and saying so with the evidence closes this. Do not fix it on the strength of the resemblance.

SCOPE: examples/real-apps/realworld_http/ plus the existing production-source CLJS suite at implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/realworld_cljs_test.cljs. No framework work, no new mutation abstraction, no Playwright spec.
acceptance_criteria: `:article/delete-success` carries the issuing slug and navigates home only while that slug still owns `[:article]`. A held alpha delete settled after navigation to beta leaves beta current; the same success settled while alpha is current still navigates home. Reuse the existing slug gate and request target shape; no new framework machinery.

title: docs(story-mcp): three pages still promise false-empty browser reads
description:
## Scope

Align the three remaining Story-MCP documentation statements for unreachable browser-only capabilities with the shipped `capability-unavailable` error contract. Documentation only: `tools/story-mcp/README.md`, `tools/story-mcp/spec/002-Tool-Registry.md`, and `tools/story/spec/Principles.md`. No runtime, schema, tool, or transport change.

## Correctness finding

PR #8865 correctly rewrote `docs/story/api/mcp-surface.md` to say that the headless JVM cannot inspect the CLJS substrate registry or a11y-panel atom and therefore returns `isError true` / `:rf.error/story-mcp-capability-unavailable`, never a false-empty success. Three committed authorities still state the retired opposite:

- `tools/story-mcp/README.md:18-20`: browser-only surfaces return an explicit empty result.
- `tools/story-mcp/spec/002-Tool-Registry.md:462-463`: `read-a11y-violations` returns an empty list plus a hint.
- `tools/story/spec/Principles.md:168-170`: substrates/a11y violations return empty plus a hint.

The implementation, tool descriptors, focused tests, `tools/story-mcp/spec/API.md`, and the opening host-boundary section of `002-Tool-Registry.md` all enforce the error. The stale prose is operationally material: an empty violations vector means a reached provider observed no findings, while capability absence means the host could not look.

## Deduplication

All-status searches over `read-a11y-violations`, `capability-unavailable`, `false-empty`, `empty list`, and the exact sentences found no issue owning these residual pages. rf2-udumn / PR #8865 owns the public chapter and retired `record-as-variant` residue; its enumerated scope is complete and closed, so this narrowly owns the separate capability-result contradiction.

## Recommended minimal fix

Replace the three stale clauses with one consistent rule: unreachable provider -> machine-readable capability error; empty collection -> a reached provider genuinely reported none. Keep the canonical links rather than adding another catalogue.
acceptance_criteria:
1. README, Tool-Registry §read-a11y-violations, and Story Principles all describe the same `isError true` / `:rf.error/story-mcp-capability-unavailable` result for an unreachable browser provider.
2. Each distinguishes capability absence from a reached provider returning an empty substrate/violation collection.
3. No runtime, descriptor, schema, tool inventory, or transport behavior changes.
4. The applicable documentation link gate passes; tables/links touched are hand-checked where the gate does not cover prose.
notes:

rf2-akg45 was filed 16 SECONDS after this bead (06:53:23Z vs 06:53:39Z) with the same three files,
the same three line ranges and the same source PR #8865. Closed as a duplicate of this one. Its own
description records that an all-status search over read-a11y-violations, capability-unavailable,
false-empty, empty list and the exact sentences "found no owner" -- which was true when it ran,
because this bead was seconds old. The search was not careless; the race was too tight for it.

TWO THINGS akg45 CARRIED THAT THIS BEAD DID NOT, preserved here so nothing is lost by the close:

1. THE OPERATIONAL RATIONALE, which is the reason this is a bug rather than a wording preference:
   for a11y, EMPTY means no observed findings, while UNAVAILABLE means the host could not look.
   A reader who takes a false-empty as authoritative concludes a component is accessible when in
   fact nothing inspected it. That distinction is what the three pages currently destroy.

2. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: README, Tool-Registry and Story Principles consistently return the
   machine-readable capability error for an UNREACHABLE provider, and reserve empty substrate and
   violation collections for a REACHED provider that genuinely reported none. No behaviour or

akg45 also confirms the surrounding scope is settled: the implementation, descriptors, tests,
spec/API and Tool-Registry own opening section already reserve empty collections for a reached
provider, and rf2-udumn enumerated public-chapter/retirement scope is complete and closed. So the
three clauses named here are the whole of the remaining work.

All three line references held on the tip of the day: tools/story-mcp/README.md:18-20 said browser-only surfaces return an explicit empty result; tools/story-mcp/spec/002-Tool-Registry.md:462-463 said the JVM stdio server returns an empty list plus a documented hint; tools/story/spec/Principles.md:169-170 said substrates / a11y violations return empty plus a documented hint. docs/story/api/mcp-surface.md was NOT touched -- it is the authority the other pages were aligned to.

- tools/story-mcp/deps.edn, the JVM-only header comment: CLJS-only registries and panel state degrade explicitly to empty results.
- skills/re-frame2-pair/references/stories.md:175: JVM-standalone story hosts return an empty list + a documented hint that axe-core requires the browser ... expect the no-op. This is the worst of the five for a reader, because it told an agent to EXPECT the no-op from a call that reports isError.
