title: [uix] adapter/wrap-view is also consulted at registration, so a pre-init registration misses the substrate wrap
description:
## Scope

The :adapter/wrap-view (rf2-00li) consultation in views/apply-adapter-wrap-view, on the same registration pipeline rf2-oz7wr fixed one layer above.

## Finding

Found while fixing rf2-oz7wr and deliberately left out of that PR (#8909) rather than widening it.

:adapter/wrap-view is published through substrate-adapter/route-hook!, so like :adapter/componentize-view it answers only while ITS adapter is the rf/init!-installed one. views/apply-adapter-wrap-view consults it at REGISTRATION. Under the canonical boot order in docs/core/how-to/boot-and-mount-an-app.md the registration namespaces load first and run calls rf/init! afterwards, so under UIx a top-level reg-view* gets nil back, wrap-applied? is false, and build-frame-aware-view falls through to the inline hiccup walk (source-coord/inject-source-coord-attr).

That walk exists for Reagent hiccup. On UIx the render-fn output is a React element, which is precisely why the UIx adapter publishes wrap-view at all — its own cloneElement path. The docstring on apply-adapter-wrap-view says the inline walk mis-classifies such a root and skips annotation.

## Severity, and why it is P3 rather than P2

Dev-only degradation, not a mount failure: the affected surface is the data-rf2-source-coord attribute (click-to-source in Xray and re-frame2-pair), which is elided from production builds anyway. Nothing throws and nothing renders wrongly. Contrast rf2-oz7wr, where the same routing/ordering mismatch made the advertised mount impossible.

## Suggested repair

rf2-oz7wr's fix moved the componentize step to lookup and memoized it on (wrapper identity x adapter spec) in views/view-head. wrap-view cannot simply move there — it is composed BELOW the frame-aware wrapper, so re-deriving it means rebuilding the wrapper, which changes the wrapper's object identity and therefore the cached head's. That is workable (re-derive the whole pipeline from the original render-fn, keyed the same way) but it is a bigger change than rf2-oz7wr's, and it needs its own check on what depends on wrapper identity across a re-derivation.

## Verification

Confirm before building: plant a top-level reg-view* under UIx, mount it, and read the rendered root for data-rf2-source-coord. Assert the attribute is ABSENT pre-fix and PRESENT post-fix, in a browser row (the annotation is a real-DOM fact).
notes:
VERDICT (PR #8919)

Dev-only classification: HOLDS at source, but the extent is wider than the description states. The spine's wrap-view body sits entirely inside (if interop/debug-enabled? ... user-fn), so :advanced + goog.DEBUG=false collapses it to the bare user-fn either way -- nothing throws, nothing renders wrongly, no production behaviour differs. P3 is right. But declining the wrap costs FOUR things, not one:
  1. data-rf2-source-coord -- the annotation the description names.
  2. data-rf-view -- Spec 006 view tagging contract, the view-hierarchy fallback when Fiber inspection is unavailable.
  3. the React-hook unmount sentinel (rf2-te71r), so :rf.view/unmounted never fires for that view. interop/make-reaction returns nil on a React-hook substrate, so the phase-A reaction-dispose hook cannot cover for it.
  4. a one-shot console.warn asserting the root element is not a DOM root -- about a view whose root is an ordinary span. The only one of the four that is actively misleading rather than merely missing.

Mechanism: REUSED #8909's lookup-time mechanism rather than building a second one, by generalising it. The description is right that wrap-view cannot simply move to view-head as-is: it composes BELOW the frame-aware wrapper where the shell composes ABOVE it, so re-deriving the wrap means rebuilding the wrapper, and rebuilding the wrapper means re-deriving the shell. That is an argument for ONE derivation, not for a parallel one. compose-view runs apply-adapter-wrap-view, view-coord-attr, build-frame-aware-view and apply-adapter-componentize-view against the adapter installed at call time; reg-view* runs it once to seed, view-head re-runs it when the seed was taken against a different substrate.

Two consequences the description's what-depends-on-wrapper-identity question asked for:
  - The cache key moved. #8909 matched the slot's handler-fn against either face of the entry (wrapper or head) because its re-derivation KEPT the wrapper object. This one rebuilds it, which would fail that check on every lookup and mint a fresh component type each render. The entry now records :registered, the exact object registration stored in the slot, and matches identity against that. One key instead of two faces.
  - Reagent keeps its object. A re-derivation whose wrap answer was nil before and is nil now has identical inputs to build-frame-aware-view, so it reuses the previous wrapper outright. Reagent publishes neither hook, so it takes that branch in every ordering and (rf/view id) hands back the very object registration built. Reagent behaviour unchanged; the Reagent adapter was not touched.
The registrar slot is still not rewritten on the lazy upgrade -- registrar/register! emits :rf.registry/handler-replaced on every call, and a phantom hot-reload on the first lookup after boot would be worse than the bug.

Evidence: new browser file implementation/adapters/uix/test/re_frame/adapter/uix_boot_order_source_coord_dom_cljs_test.cljs, three rows, asserting on the OUTPUT. reg-time-composition-is-unwrapped-while-the-lookup-is-not is the ABSENT half on the same registration (registration runs at ns-load with no adapter, premise asserted; the value registration stored is still readable and invoking it directly yields a root with NO data-rf2-source-coord, while the head (rf/view id) hands back post-init yields an annotated one). boot-order-registration-annotates-the-mounted-root is the PRESENT half as a real-DOM fact -- mounted through the documented route and read back off the committed node with getAttribute, plus a console check that the false non-DOM-root warning is gone. post-init-control-annotates-the-mounted-root is the non-vacuity control.

Gates, captured exit codes, on the rebased base: node-test compile 0 (1870 files, 0 warnings); node out/node-test.js 0 (11129 tests / 54979 assertions, 0 failures); shadow-cljs compile browser-test 0 (1012 files, 0 warnings); serve-and-run-browser-tests.cjs 0 (760 tests / 4168 assertions, 0 failures); clojure -M:test -n re-frame.late-bind-drift-test 0 (8 tests / 686 assertions). No markdown changed, so neither check_doc_slugs.py nor check_readme_links.py has a surface here.

Controls, both red: (a) planting the pre-fix behaviour -- always reuse the reg-time wrapper, which is #8909's shape -- gave exit 1, 5 failures, ALL in the two boot-order rows, with both attributes nil off the committed node and the false warning back verbatim naming a span root; the post-init control and every #8909 row stayed green. (b) restoring #8909's own defect under the new structure gave exit 1, 11 failures and 1 error, with boot-order-registration-yields-a-mountable-head-after-init contributing 9 -- the same count #8909's own plant produced, so this change has not defanged it. Both plants recompiled 314 files; both restores verified by git blob hash against the committed object.

Two stale prose spots found and deliberately LEFT (both outside the fence, neither load-bearing for any assertion): implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/view_alias_registry_cljs_test.cljs says core consults :adapter/wrap-view AT REGISTRATION TIME, now registration-and-lookup; and the late-bind directory lists re-frame.hicasso.substrate as a :adapter/wrap-view producer, which is true only transitively (hicasso reaches it through spine/make-react-adapter, not by its own route-hook! call).

title: docs(api/machines): canonical API doc teaches the bare :as machines alias Conventions reserves for application namespaces
description:
Found by rf2-3lhuj (PR #8902) while choosing which alias to give M-28's require
in the migration guide. Out of that dispatch's fence.

spec/Conventions.md has a normative section, "Require-alias dialect — a
framework subsystem namespace is aliased rf.<leaf>" (landed by d848371f60,
rf2-lgeron; no later commit touches it). It says the canonical alias for a
framework subsystem namespace re-frame.<leaf> is the dotted rf.<leaf>, shows
re-frame.machines :as rf.machines in its own worked require, and then states:

  A **bare** leaf alias (:as routing, :as machines, :as schemas) is
  **reserved for application namespaces**.

It names :as machines specifically as the form the framework yields to apps.

The published API doc teaches the opposite. docs/api/re-frame.machines.md:7
opens with [re-frame.machines :as machines] and spells every helper machines/...
throughout; docs/machines/tutorial.md:321 and
docs/machines/inspecting-machines.md:131 do the same, and
inspecting-machines.md:208 puts it in a troubleshooting table as the recommended
require. A repo-wide count of ':as machines' at tip returns 124 files, mostly
implementation tests, plus a comment in
implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc:76.

So a reader who follows Conventions and a reader who follows the API doc write
different code, and the API doc's form is the one Conventions reserves for the
app's own myapp.machines.

NOT ASSERTING WHICH SIDE IS WRONG — that is the ruling this bead wants. Either
Conventions' dialect rule is the standard and the docs plus (over time) the
tests should move to rf.machines, or the rule has been overtaken in practice by
a 124-file majority and Conventions should be amended to match. Deciding it is
cheap; leaving two published spellings is what costs.

Note the migration guide was moved to the Conventions form by PR #8902, on the
grounds that a normative spec outranks an API page. If this bead rules the other
way, that one line in migration/from-re-frame-v1/README.md M-28 moves with the
rest.
close_reason:
Done in PR #8912. RULED: Conventions wins; the docs move to rf.machines. Not amended.

This item asked which side was wrong - Conventions section Require-alias dialect (normative, landed under rf2-lgeron), which reserves the bare :as machines for APPLICATION namespaces and makes rf.machines canonical for the framework subsystem namespace, or the practice of a 124-file majority. Conventions is followed rather than re-litigated. That is the same call PR #8902 made for the migration guide and PR #8905 made for the spec tree, so the published corpus now carries ONE spelling instead of two rather than a third precedent.

18 call spellings and 7 require clauses corrected across six documents: docs/api/re-frame.machines.md (9 calls, 2 requires), docs/machines/inspecting-machines.md (4 calls, 2 requires), docs/machines/tutorial.md (2 calls, 1 require), docs/machines/concepts.md (1 call), spec/008-Testing.md (1 call, 1 require), spec/Construction-Prompts.md (1 call, 1 require). The last two were not named in this item and were found by the same census - a spec file teaching the reserved form is strictly worse than an API page doing it.

The API page Surfaces split two ways bullet already said the helpers are reached as re-frame.machines/<name> and not rf/<name>; it now names the alias and links Conventions section Require-alias dialect, so the page sources its own spelling instead of asserting it.

NOT CHANGED: live :as machines require aliases in implementation/ and tools/ source. Roughly 124 files, a real compile surface, for a defect that is entirely about published prose - and a mass rename would foreclose the amend-Conventions option this item deliberately left open. Prose was corrected; live aliases stand. If a future ruling amends Conventions instead, only documents move back, not code.

CENSUS TRAP worth keeping: a loose search for bare machines/<name> in markdown returns about 90 hits, nearly all of them NOT call sites - the late-bind hook keywords (:machines/teardown-on-frame-destroy!, :machines/spawn-fx), the MCP op names (machines/list, machines/describe), and source file paths (machines/transition.cljc). title: spec(Conventions): roster :rf/settle-flows in the reserved :rf/* row
description:
rf2-kh73v added a second member to `re-frame.events/reserved-event-ids`: `:rf/settle-flows`, the framework-private flow-settle event the `:fx` walk enqueues after `:rf.fx/reg-flow` / `:rf.fx/clear-flow` (Spec 013 §Sequencing — settling on the dispatching frame).

spec/Conventions.md line ~46 is the normative reserved-namespace roster and its `:rf/*` row names the framework-wide pattern events individually, including `:rf/set-db` at length. `:rf/settle-flows` is not there.

Deliberately NOT taken by rf2-kh73v: spec/Conventions.md is a hot-zone one-toucher and is outside that item's enumerated scope (which named Spec 013, the API/core guides and the cart example). Filed rather than smuggled in.

Note the entry is not simply another `:rf/set-db`. `:rf/settle-flows` is reserved but NEVER REGISTERED — not in the registrar, not in the EP-0023 image standard registry. It resolves through the router's unresolved-handler seam (`router/framework-private-handler-metas`), which is what keeps it off `registrar/registrations :event` and therefore out of every app's event catalogue. It is listed in `reserved-event-ids` for a different reason than `:rf/set-db` is: the registrar is consulted BEFORE the seam, so an app `(reg-event :rf/settle-flows …)` would silently shadow the framework's settle and strand every flow-lifecycle effect. The roster entry should say that, not imply a second registered standard.

Applications must not depend on the id; the observable contract is the settle boundary, not the transport. Spec 013 §Sequencing states this already — Conventions just needs the roster row to agree.
notes:
VERDICT 2026-09-01 AUSEST (worker, PR #8902). PREMISE HELD, TAKEN.

VERIFIED AT SOURCE, not assumed. :rf/settle-flows exists at tip in
implementation/core/src/re_frame/events.cljc (the reserved-event-ids value, the
settle-flows-event-id def, the handler and its handler-meta), fx.cljc:842 and
router.cljc:493. A fixed-string census of the id across ALL tracked markdown
returned ZERO hits, so Conventions did not merely omit it from one row - the id
appeared nowhere in the doc corpus. The census instrument was controlled: the
same flattened, whitespace-insensitive search returned 53 files for
rf/reg-machine, so the zero is a real zero and not a bad pattern.

THIS WAS A DANGLING CROSS-REFERENCE, not a cosmetic omission - which the item
did not know and which raises its value. spec/013-Flows.md:474 deliberately
does NOT name the private id, and instead says its "id is nonetheless reserved
(per Conventions Reserved namespaces) so an application registration cannot
shadow it". Spec 013 was delegating the reservation to a roster that was
silent, so at tip NO normative document recorded that the id is reserved.

THE ROSTER ENTRY DOES NOT IMPLY A SECOND REGISTERED STANDARD, per the item's
explicit instruction. It states the distinction: unlike :rf/set-db it is
reserved but NEVER registered - no registrar row, no EP-0023 image-standard row
- because it is materialised through the router's unresolved-handler seam, so
it never reaches an application's event catalogue, tooling projection or
generated code. It is reserved for a DIFFERENT reason: the registrar is
consulted BEFORE that seam, so an app reg-event on the id would silently shadow
the settle and strand every flow-lifecycle effect, and fails loud instead. The
row also carries Spec 013's own caution that applications must not depend on
the id, the observable contract being the settle boundary and not the
transport. Spec column gains 013.

The row already had vocabulary for this case - :rf/head and :rf/public-error
are described in it as "reserved-but-not-registered" - so the entry mirrors an
existing shape rather than inventing one.

ONE THING CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT DONE. Conventions rule 3 in the same
section reserves the bare :rf/* root for framework-wide pattern events that no
single AREA owns, and a reader could ask whether a flow-settle event should
have been :rf.flow/settle. It is defensible as-is: the event is defined,
enqueued and resolved entirely in core (events.cljc, fx.cljc, router.cljc), not
in the flows artefact, so it is core-owned like :rf/set-db rather than
area-owned. Recording the question rather than reopening a shipped id.

title: ci(http): no lane runs a solo-namespace ordering, so latent load-order hook dependencies are ungated
description:
DISCOVERED-FROM rf2-zvbm9 (PR #8889), reported by that worker as an observation it deliberately did not file itself.

THE FINDING (verify at source before acting): the jvm-http CI job runs a bare "clojure -M:test", i.e. the full-suite ordering only. rf2-zvbm9 was a namespace that passed in that ordering and failed when run ALONE, because it depended on a late-bind hook published by a namespace load that an alphabetically earlier test namespace happened to perform. No gate would have caught it, and none will catch the next namespace that acquires the same kind of latent dependency.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ONE BUG: the failure is silent and it accumulates. A namespace acquires an unnoticed dependency on somebody else load-ordering before it, the suite stays green, and the defect only surfaces when someone runs that namespace alone — which is exactly what a developer does when iterating, so the cost lands on the person least equipped to explain it. The specific hook here fails OPEN too: extract-paths returns an empty map when unbound rather than erroring, so the classification silently does nothing.

SCOPE IS A JUDGEMENT AND NOT OBVIOUS — this is filed to be RULED ON as much as fixed. Running every namespace solo multiplies the lane cost; running none leaves the hole. Candidate shapes worth weighing before building anything: a nightly rather than per-PR solo sweep; solo runs for a named set of namespaces with known late-bind dependencies; or making the hook fail LOUD when unbound, which converts a silent misclassification into an error and may remove the need for a solo lane at all. The last one is the smallest change and may be the right one — the stance prefers it over new CI machinery.

NOT URGENT: the specific instance is fixed by #8889, which requires the schemas namespace in the fixture that needed it.
notes:
MAYOR RULING, 2026-09-01: make the hook fail LOUD when unbound. Do NOT build a solo-namespace lane, nightly or per-PR, and do not add a named-set sweep.

The bead names three shapes and already leans at the right one. Confirming it as the ruling: extract-paths returning an empty map when unbound is a fail-OPEN, and that is the actual defect - the silent misclassification, not the absence of a lane. Convert it to an error. A namespace that has acquired a latent load-order dependency then fails immediately and says so, on the developer's own solo run, which is where the cost currently lands and where the message is most useful.

This is the smallest change, it removes a silent failure mode rather than adding machinery to detect one, and it may make a solo lane unnecessary - which is the point. New CI machinery to catch a class of bug that a two-line fail-loud converts into an ordinary error is exactly the over-engineering the stance rejects, and it would put a recurring toll on every PR forever.

If, having made the hook loud, you find a case it cannot reach, file that as its own bead with the case - do not widen this one into a lane.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #8943 (branch worker/cilanes). Followed the ruling exactly: the hook now fails LOUD when unbound, and NO CI machinery was added — no solo lane, no nightly, no named-set sweep.

THE DEFECT. privacy-body/extract-paths (implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/privacy_body.cljc) returned an empty marks map when the late-bind schema-walker hook was unbound. An unbound hook means the marks are UNKNOWN, not EMPTY, and answering {} for it is the fail-OPEN the ruling names: a :decode schema marking a slot :sensitive? classified nothing and the secret rode the trace verbatim, green either side of it. rf2-zvbm9 was exactly that — four assertions reading their own secret back, visible only in a solo-namespace run because the full-suite ordering happened to load re-frame.schemas first.

THE LOUDNESS IS GATED ON WHETHER A MARK IS DECLARED, AND THAT MATTERS — an unconditional throw would have been wrong in both directions, checked at source rather than assumed. (1) day8/re-frame2-schemas is a TEST-ONLY dep of the http artefact, and the artefact resolves malli.core directly (decode.cljc, which WARNS rather than throws when Malli is absent), so an app can legitimately use a Malli :decode with no schemas artefact at all; an unconditional throw breaks every such app on every successful response, and on the production accept-failure path (transport.cljc, not debug-gated) too. (2) In-tree, http-decode-test, http-managed-test and http-empty-body-parity all use vector :decode schemas WITHOUT requiring re-frame.schemas, so an unconditional throw reddens all three on a solo run for schemas carrying no marks at all.

So extract-paths separates the two cases with declares-marks?, a presence probe asking only whether the schema's EDN form writes a :sensitive? / :large? PROP anywhere — a MAP KEY, so a field merely named :sensitive? is not a mark. It reads no Malli semantics, resolves no registry, derives no paths: not a second walker (the ns doc forbids one), it only decides whether the shared walker is REQUIRED. Declares no mark → {} as before, and a schemas-less app is untouched. Declares a mark with the hook unbound → throws :rf.error/schemas-artefact-missing via the canonical error/throw-error! builder, naming the require that fixes it. Probe and walker agree on the opaque cases (keyword registry ref, compiled m/schema object): both read them as markless leaves, so neither throws.

REUSING THE EXISTING ERROR ID leaves spec/009-Instrumentation.md — hot-zone — untouched; the id is already catalogued there. The contract is recorded in its owning tracked record, spec/014-HTTPRequests.md §Privacy, as a new rule 5 (old rule 5 Composition becomes 6; nothing in the repo references these by number, checked).

NO CASE FOUND THAT THE LOUDNESS CANNOT REACH, so no follow-up bead was filed. title: flake(http): supersede-stale poll-until backstop times out under CI load, redding unrelated PRs
description:
implementation/http test `re-frame.http-reply-lowering-test/supersede-distinct-work-ids-and-canonical-stale-trace` (http_reply_lowering_test.clj) fails intermittently on loaded CI runners with `poll-until timed out — supersede-stale`, reported as `0 failures, 1 errors` and exit 1 from `clojure -M:test` in implementation/http.

## Observed

- 2026-09-01, PR #8873 (a routing-only diff that cannot reach this code path): `:elapsed-ms 30022`, i.e. the full 30 s backstop elapsed. Re-running the identical tree on a fresh CI head was green with no code change.
- The test`s own source comment records a PRIOR occurrence of the same class and the mitigation taken then: the backstop was raised from 5 s to 30 s because "the async supersede landed AFTER the window, timing the machine, not the canonicalisation (it redded unrelated PRs, e.g. #6817)".

So the 5 s -> 30 s raise reduced the rate but did not remove the failure mode; 30 s is now demonstrably marginal too.

## Why it matters

This test is inside a surface-gated job, and implementation/http declares day8/re-frame2-routing as a {:local/root} dependency, so ANY routing-only change schedules the http job. A flake here therefore reds PRs whose diff provably cannot reach the code under test, and each red costs a diagnosis dispatch. PR #8873 cost exactly one.

## Shape of the problem, not a prescribed fix

The wait is already signal-based rather than a fixed sleep (`poll-until` on a predicate over delivered replies plus a `:rf.http/stale-suppressed` trace row), which is the right structure — the remaining `:timeout-ms` is a pure backstop. The question is whether the supersede round-trip can be made deterministic at the test boundary (await the transport reply and the trace row on a latch rather than polling), so the backstop is unreachable rather than merely generous. Raising the bound a third time is the option to weigh against that, not the obvious answer.

Deliberately NOT diagnosed here: whether the timeout indicates real contention in the supersede path under load, or purely runner scheduling. Worth one look before choosing a remedy — a genuinely slow supersede under load would be a product finding rather than a test one.

## Non-goals

- No change to supersede/stale-suppression semantics; those are what the test correctly pins.
- Not a licence to delete or weaken the assertion.
notes:
VERDICT (PR #8889, branch worker/http-robust-o9e15): FIXED, and the theory recorded on this bead and in the test source was WRONG.

FINDING 1 - the stale-suppression trace is NOT async. handlers/managed-handler calls registry/supersede! and then transport/emit-superseded-stale-trace! inline in the fx phase, so the :rf.http/stale-suppressed row has already landed before the SECOND dispatch-sync returns. Probed: present with ZERO wait. The source comment claiming a real async round-trip (transport reply -> reply lowering -> app dispatch -> stale trace) was factually wrong and is removed.

FINDING 2 - the failure mode is ABSENCE, not lateness. registry/supersede! returns nil when nothing is in flight under the request-id. The test gate was a CountDownLatch(1) whose FIRST act inside the handler was its own .countDown, so the following .await returned immediately and the gate never held request #1 at all. Request #1 was free to finish its whole loopback round trip in the gap between the two dispatch-sync calls; two app replies were then delivered, no supersede ever happened, and poll-until sat out its full backstop waiting for a row that could not arrive. That is why the 5s -> 30s raise reduced the rate without removing the mode, and why a third raise cannot help: no bound is large enough for an event that is never emitted.

REPAIR - a new start-held-server! holds every exchange until the TEST releases it, so #1 cannot finalise before #2 is issued and the supersede becomes a property of the ordering rather than of machine speed. The stale row is then asserted SYNCHRONOUSLY (the 30s poll is gone entirely), and the one genuinely async step, the surviving request app reply, is awaited on a CountDownLatch the reply handler itself counts down. The sibling supersede-suppresses-prior-app-reply carried the identical no-op gate and the identical latent race and moves to the same harness.

PRODUCT FINDING - none. This bead deliberately left open whether the timeout indicated real contention in the supersede path under load. It does not: the supersede path is correct and synchronous, and the test simply was not exercising it when the race was lost. The one seam worth recording is that a superseded attempt TRANSPORT completion offers no observable completion signal a test can await, which is why the repair holds the server rather than awaiting the abort.

EVIDENCE (a flake is not proved gone by one green, so stated in tiers). STRONGEST: the same planted 300ms pause widening the gap between the two dispatch-sync calls, applied to both structures. Old structure = exit 1, poll-until timed out - supersede-stale, :elapsed-ms 30017, 0 failures 1 errors - matching the CI signature of :elapsed-ms 30022 on PR #8873. New structure = exit 0, 25 tests 137 assertions. ARGUMENT: the timed wait for the stale row became a synchronous assertion. WEAK: five consecutive solo runs, exit 0 and a stable 137 assertions each.

GATES on the final rebased base, all captured exit codes: full suite (= jvm-http in test.yml, clojure -M:test from implementation/http) exit 0, 508 tests 3883 assertions; solo re-frame.http-reply-lowering-test exit 0, 25 tests 137 assertions. Sabotage control planted at http_reply_lowering_test.clj:640 drove exit 1 naming the planted value at the planted line, which also establishes the gate read this branch checkout. Restores verified by git blob hash.

Test-only change: no production source touched, no assertion weakened, no spec change. Related: rf2-zvbm9 rode the same worker; the two turned out INDEPENDENT.
AUDIT PR #8889: REOPENED. The held-server ordering correctly removes the original race, but the regression still does not prove that the one delivered app reply belongs to the superseding issuance. Both server responses are identical, while both tests assert only reply count 1 and :status :ok; canonical replies carry :rf.reply/work-id, so a broken path that delivers issuance 1 while losing issuance 2 can satisfy the advertised request-#2 claim. The final Thread/sleep 200 is also only a timing window for absence of a delayed second delivery. Minimal completion: assert the delivered reply work-id is [:rf.work/http :search 2 1] and make the existing harness's no-second-delivery observation deterministic. Keep the held-server harness; no production change or new abstraction.

VERDICT (PR #8923, branch worker/httpwid-o9e15, 2026-09-01 20:52 AUSEST): AUDIT COMPLETED. Both things the PR #8889 audit asked for are done, test-only, held-server harness kept, no production change, no new abstraction.

PREMISE HELD AT TIP. Verified before editing: both supersession tests asserted only reply count 1 and :status :ok (the stale-trace test asserted only the count -- not even :status), both closing Thread/sleep 200 lines were present, and canonical replies do carry :rf.reply/work-id (already pinned at success-reply-is-canonical). Nothing had been fixed in the interval.

AUDIT LITERAL WAS RIGHT. Read from the code rather than the note: reply.cljc work-id builds [:rf.work/http logical-id (or issuance 1) (or attempt 1)], logical-id = the caller's :request-id when non-nil (here :search); registry/next-issuance! bumps issuance per fresh request under one request-id, and neither request retries. So the superseding attempt is exactly [:rf.work/http :search 2 1], as the audit quoted.

THREE DEVICES, NONE OF THEM A CLOCK.

(1) ISSUANCE IDENTITY. Both tests now assert the DELIVERED reply's :rf.reply/work-id is [:rf.work/http :search 2 1]. Issuance is the only fact distinguishing the two byte-identical server responses, so this is what convicts a path that delivers issuance 1 and loses issuance 2.

(2) THE SUPERSEDE IS AN ORDERING, read while both exchanges are still HELD: the :search in-flight slot already holds issuance 2. registry/supersede! cleared issuance 1 out of it and fired its abort-fn INLINE during the second dispatch-sync's fx phase; that abort-fn wins the once-only :finalised? CAS and routes through dispatch-aborted!, where :request-id-superseded is in reply-suppressing-abort-reasons -- no app dispatch, and the won CAS makes issuance 1's later transport completion bail at already-replied?. There is therefore NO LATER MOMENT at which a second reply could originate. That is the real content of the no-second-delivery claim; the 200ms window was allowing for an event that cannot occur.

(3) A FIFO DRAIN BARRIER replaces Thread/sleep 200. dispatch-sync seeds at the FRONT of the frame's queue and then runs the drain loop to fixed point (router.cljc drain-block!), so every envelope enqueued before it has been PROCESSED by the time it returns. Honest scope: the barrier is a barrier for anything already enqueued; the guarantee against a genuinely later delivery is device (2), not any wait. Both are now stated in the source.

ALSO: registry/reset-issuance-counters-for-test! (an existing test-only helper, already used by http_managed_test.clj) now runs at the top of each test. issuance-counters is a process-global defonce and http_managed_test.clj ALSO uses :request-id :search, so the issuance literals held only because eviction happened to clear the counter -- a latent load-order dependency of exactly the kind rf2-ohfym observes the single full-suite jvm-http lane cannot see. The reset makes the new literals independent of what ran first. Group 3's second test also gains the :status :ok assertion it lacked.

GATES on the final rebased base (163aefb4c4, merge base 3cc654e45c), every exit code captured on one command line and quoted from the .exit file: full suite (= CI jvm-http, clojure -M:test from implementation/http) exit 0, 508 tests 3890 assertions; solo re-frame.http-reply-lowering-test run FIVE consecutive times, exit 0 each, a stable 25 tests / 144 assertions each. Baseline was 137 solo / 3883 full; the seven new assertions are the whole delta. The namespace was run solo deliberately, per rf2-ohfym: a full-suite ordering can supply a load-order dependency the namespace does not declare.

THE CONTROL BIT WHERE IT HAD TO. A plant that reds everything would not demonstrate the audit's gap, so the control makes the harness genuinely deliver issuance 1: one registry/reset-issuance-counters-for-test! inserted BETWEEN the two dispatch-sync calls, re-minting the superseding request as issuance 1. The supersede still happens (it keys on request-id, not issuance), one reply is still delivered, and it is still :status :ok. Exit 1, 25 tests 144 assertions, 2 failures 0 errors -- same assertion count as the clean run, so nothing was crashed out.
  RED (both new): "the surviving in-flight request is issuance 2..." (device 2) and "the delivered reply belongs to the SUPERSEDING issuance (2)..." (device 1), both actual [:rf.work/http :search 1 1].
  GREEN under the same plant -- the assertions that existed BEFORE this PR: reply count 1, ":status :ok", "the superseding request #2 is the live in-flight request", and the whole of supersede-distinct-work-ids-and-canonical-stale-trace. That green-beside-red IS the audit's finding, reproduced.

A FIRST SABOTAGE ATTEMPT CAME BACK GREEN and was treated as a reason to stop, not to proceed: the plant had landed AFTER both dispatch-sync calls, where both issuances were already minted, so it was inert. Moved between the two dispatches, it bit. Restores after every plant verified by git BLOB hash against the committed object (e27fd9f7aa3b14dd8011e275d1314bef137e50a5) -- line endings are translated in this checkout, so a byte digest of the working file would not be sound. The red also establishes the gate read this branch's checkout, since the fault existed nowhere else.

NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY: no production change was needed and none was made; implementation/http/src is untouched. The adjacent rf2-ohfym (jvm-http runs no solo-namespace lane, .github/workflows, hot-zone) stays open and untouched -- but its concern is answered for THIS namespace by the counter reset plus the five solo runs recorded above.
close_reason: PR #8923 (draft->ready): audit completion. Both supersession tests now pin the DELIVERED reply's :rf.reply/work-id to [:rf.work/http :search 2 1] (verified against reply.cljc work-id, not the note - the audit literal was right), and the Thread/sleep 200 quiescence windows are replaced by two non-timed devices: an in-flight-slot ordering assertion read while both exchanges are still HELD (proving supersede! cleared issuance 1 and won its once-only :finalised? CAS inline, so no later delivery can originate) and a dispatch-sync FIFO drain barrier for anything already enqueued. reset-issuance-counters-for-test! added so the issuance literals do not depend on JVM load order. Test-only; held-server harness kept; no production change. Gates on the rebased base: full suite exit 0 (508/3890), solo namespace exit 0 x5 (25/144 each). Control: a plant re-minting the superseder as issuance 1 reds BOTH new work-id assertions while the pre-existing count-and-:status assertions stay GREEN - the audit's gap reproduced.

title: spec/Pattern-WebSocket worked-example listing still teaches the :ws/fatal in-flight leak
description:
rf2-ni0ko composed fail-in-flight onto the :ws/fatal transition in examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs, so every door out of :active reachable from :connected now settles :in-flight exactly once.

spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md's worked-example listing was NOT updated (hot-zone, outside that bead's fence) and still shows the unrepaired shape:

  :ws/fatal    {:target :failed
                :action :record-error}

That is precisely the shape rf2-ni0ko's witness proves strands every in-flight slot and its waiting :reply-event, including across a later manual :ws/connect out of :failed. A consumer copying the spec's recommended listing inherits the leak.

Nothing in the spec is FALSE today — its stated invariant (§5 item 5, and the 'Leaking in-flight requests when the socket drops' pitfall) is scoped to the DROP door, not to every door out of :active — so this is teaching-drift, not a contradiction. Two other pre-existing divergences in the same listing are worth folding in while there: it carries no :ws/disconnect transition at all (rf2-b2jpr added one with :action :fail-in-flight), and it still shows :on-socket-lost with the fail-and-clear INLINED rather than routed through the fail-in-flight helper rf2-b2jpr factored out.

Also skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md line ~114 shows ':ws/fatal {:target :failed}' with no action at all, and its parent-level :on summary row omits :ws/disconnect.

Suggested shape: update the listing's :ws/fatal row to the composed action, add the :ws/disconnect row, and show :on-socket-lost delegating to the shared helper — plus a sentence generalising the invariant from 'when the socket drops' to 'every door out of :active that destroys the socket'. spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md is HOT-ZONE: sequence, don't parallel.

title: changed-surfaces: migration_v1_codemod arm misses implementation/core changes its :integration lane now depends on
description:

PR #8857 wired `clojure -M:integration` into the jvm-migration-v1-codemod job, and that integration lane reaches implementation/core through a :local/root. So a change confined to implementation/core does NOT arm the codemod job even though the job now depends on that code — the classic surface-armed gate that is skipped on the very push that breaks it (loops.md clause 2 names this shape: a gate skipped on the breaking commit while the trunk rollup reads green throughout).

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED IN #8857: widening the arm means touching .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh AND its pinned mirror implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs — the one-toucher-by-construction pair (CLAUDE.md 'Minimise merge conflicts when dispatching'). A change that alters what the classifier OUTPUTS must move both halves in ONE commit, because the test pins those outputs. The worker was fenced out of that pair and stopped and reported rather than crossing, which was correct.

BEFORE DISPATCHING: verify the arm's current pattern at source, and confirm the :integration lane really does reach implementation/core (read the codemod deps.edn's :integration alias). #8857's own report notes that rf2-36u96's description was ALREADY wrong about scripts/test-jvm-tools.sh's roster, so this bead's premises deserve the same scepticism.

notes:
VERDICT 2026-09-01 — the bead HOLDS on both halves. Fixed in PR #8867 (branch worker/classifier-arm-fk5jy, commit ea167a2b94).

PREMISE (a) VERIFIED — the arm's actual pattern. Read at source rather than taken from the bead's wording. In .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh, 'migration_v1_codemod=true' appears in exactly ONE arm — 'migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/*)' — plus mark_all(). No arm earlier in the same case statement matches an implementation/core/... path (the nearest, the per-feature list, enumerates sibling artefacts and the exact files implementation/deps.edn, shadow-cljs.edn, package.json — not implementation/core/*). The job's gate in test.yml is 'if: needs.detect_changed_surfaces.outputs.migration_v1_codemod == 0x27true0x27' with NO implementation_jvm fallback, so nothing else could have armed it.

PREMISE (b) VERIFIED — the :integration edge reaches implementation/core. migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/deps.edn declares, under the :integration alias, 'day8/re-frame2-core {:local/root "../../../implementation/core"}', and its own comment says it outright: 'only this alias pulls implementation/core'. test.yml's jvm-migration-v1-codemod runs 'clojure -M:test' AND 'clojure -M:integration' as two separate steps (the second added by rf2-36u96 / PR #8857).

MEASURED BEFORE THE FIX (classifier run on this trunk):
  implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc -> migration_v1_codemod=false, implementation_jvm=true, tools_jvm_machines_viz=true
POSITIVE CONTROL on the same instrument, same run:
  migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/src/re_frame/migration/reg_event_codemod.clj -> migration_v1_codemod=true, implementation_jvm=false
So the false was a real negative, not a classifier that had stopped classifying.

THE FIX. One boolean, 'migration_v1_codemod=true', added to the existing 'implementation/core/*)' arm — which already carries three reverse edges of exactly this shape under rf2-wq17m, whose own comment says every reverse edge in the file is spelled out the same way. SCOPE JUSTIFICATION (why core and no wider): implementation/core/deps.edn puts only ':paths ["src"]' and two mvn coordinates on its BASE classpath. Its cross-artefact :local/root edges (schemas, machines, routing, flows, http, ssr, epoch, resources, test-quiet) all sit under ALIASES, and a :local/root dependency never activates its target's aliases. Core's own tree is therefore the whole of what the :integration lane reaches.

ONE-WAY EDGE, pinned in both directions: core changes now arm the codemod lane, but a codemod-only diff still must not arm implementation_jvm (the codemod is downstream of core). Verified after the fix: the codemod's own source still classifies implementation_jvm=false.

That red is also the proof the gate read the worker's own checkout, since the pin exists in no other tree. The covering gate is CI job js-harness-self-tests -> 'npm run test:scripts' from implementation/, which is UNGATED (no needs: detect_changed_surfaces, no if:) so it runs on every PR; the mirror is picked up by that script's scripts/*.test.cjs glob and spawns the REAL classifier bytes. title: patterns/websocket: :ws/fatal out of :active strands in-flight requests (same class as rf2-b2jpr)
description:
rf2-b2jpr routed clean :ws/disconnect through the shared fail-in-flight helper so leaving :active settles every in-flight request exactly once. One door out of :active still bypasses that invariant: :ws/fatal {:target :failed :action :record-error} (examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs, :active :on). Fired from :connected with a non-empty :in-flight, it destroys the socket actor and strands every slot exactly as the clean-disconnect bug did — the scheduled timeout carries the destroyed socket id, :current-socket? rejects it after teardown, and the slot plus its waiting :reply-event survive forever, including across a later manual :ws/connect out of :failed.

Mitigating context: nothing in the example currently dispatches :ws/fatal — it is the documented app-level escape hatch (spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md, ':active / * --:ws/fatal--> :failed'), so the leak is reachable only by consumer code using the pattern as written. :ws/auth-failed -> [:failed] is provably safe by contrast: :in-flight only fills in :connected, and every door out of :active from :connected settles it once this is fixed.

Fix is small now the helper exists: compose fail-in-flight with :record-error on the :ws/fatal transition (one action that does both), plus a wrapper deftest mirroring websocket-clean-disconnect-fails-in-flight-request with :ws/fatal as the exit door. Same fence as rf2-b2jpr: examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs + implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs.

title: reg-interceptor registration coords never reach the interceptor-exception trace (Xray chip gap for the supported authoring form)
description: The Xray Epoch INTERCEPTOR (exception) row's jump-to-source chip reads :source-coord off the :rf.error/interceptor-exception trace tag; the router takes it from the interceptor map's :source-coord (interceptor.cljc error-record). reg-interceptor (the ONE supported authoring form, EP-0022) captures registration coords into the REGISTRY meta (interceptor_registry.cljc reg-interceptor* -> source-coords/merge-coords), but descriptor->interceptor lowers {:before/:after} descriptors through ->interceptor* WITHOUT threading those coords onto the built value — so an interceptor authored the supported way never gets the exception-row chip; only a VALUE registered at the migration boundary carrying its own :source-coord does. Until rf2-93sxp the ->interceptor macro was the de-facto route to a coord-carrying value (tests and the standard_epochs testbed used it); with the macro gone (PR #8791) those sites author with reg-interceptor descriptors and the testbed's exception-row chip degrades to plain text (the INTERCEPTORS registry-read step's chip is unaffected — spec 021:426 documents it off handler-meta). Candidate fix: descriptor->interceptor stamps :source-coord from the registration meta's coords (registry resolver, one site), making the chip work for the authoring form everywhere. Touches interceptor_registry.cljc + tests; check spec/009 and tools/xray/spec/021 wording. Named as within rf2-93sxp's non-goals ('no redesign of source-coordinate diagnostics'), hence this follow-up.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #8817: resolve-ref threads the reg-interceptor registration meta's coords onto every resolved interceptor value as :source-coord (registration-coords helper; value's own coord wins; programmatic/framework/production paths stay coord-free), so a descriptor-authored interceptor's :rf.error/interceptor-exception trace now carries the registration coord the Xray exception-row chip reads. Regression pinned on the actual failing path (descriptor-authored throw -> trace :source-coord tag) plus factory/programmatic/framework/migration-precedence arms; control shown red with the threading removed, restore blob-hash-verified. tools/xray spec 021 unchanged - it already documents this behaviour; no spec/009 change needed.

title: schemas: malli.error's message table survives Closure after the humanizer gating — ruling wanted on an out-of-graph mechanism
description:
Follow-up from rf2-tiymn (PR pending). Measured 2026-08-30 on the matched schemas-bundle A/B, all gzipped, control 86851 B:

- unconditional humanizer publication (trunk before rf2-tiymn): margin 41595 B
- publication gated on interop/debug-enabled? (what rf2-tiymn lands): margin 40885 B (-0.7 KB). The :schemas/humanize-explain! keyword and malli.error/humanize's code leave the probe; malli/error.cljc drops 12.0 -> 10.5 KB optimized.
- adapter's [malli.error] :require deleted outright (counterfactual, not landed): margin 38333 B (-3.3 KB). Every malli.error literal gone.

The 2.5 KB between the last two is malli.error's `default-errors` message table (built through PersistentHashMap.fromArrays) plus its random-uuid negation prefix: top-level defs whose initialisers Closure cannot prove pure, so it keeps them with no reader. Gating cannot reach it; only taking malli.error out of the build's module graph does, and the library cannot do that for a consumer without a build-side knob (a dev-only :preloads ns that publishes the humanizer, a :reader-features conditional require, or an :ns-aliases stub). rf2-tiymn's brief ruled out a new knob and its non-goals rule out a dynamic loader, so the residue is recorded in Spec 010 §Bundle cost and priced inside the gate's margin.

Question for the mayor: is 2.5 KB gzipped per schemas consumer worth a consumer-side dev-only preload (the humanizer moves to a re-frame.schemas.malli.humanize ns wired via :devtools :preloads, with the JVM keeping the automatic publication)? If not, close this as recorded-and-accepted; Spec 010 already says what stays and why.

Spec 010 §Bundle cost and PR #8788 quote the same three in KB. Repeat builds of one tree vary by tens of bytes gzipped (raw identical), so the last two digits are noise.

The only thing left is a consumer-side dev-only :preloads knob for about 2.5 KB gz, a second wiring path through the template shadow-cljs.edn, the setup skill and the how-to for every consumer, against the stance. Recorded and accepted; reopen only if Mike wants the knob.

title: hicasso guide ch04: the owned-literal alternate-spelling claim is not delivered by the taught plain merge
description: docs/core/hicasso/04-controlled-inputs.md §Forward caller attributes safely (lines ~116-119 at 1af79839db) claims: 'A caller cannot replace the field's value, checked state, handler, key, or revision by supplying an alternative spelling such as :onInput or "value"; the controlled contract binds to the React slot reached by the authored literal.' (:1031-1033) is load-bearing only through inc - max cannot add correctness to a monotone term. The rest of the machinery (disposal hook, first-registration!, registry epoch, microtask rewire, acquire-cell! re-wire guard :956) each closes a named failure and should stay.

title: loops.md: FETCH_HEAD absence does not prove that no fetch ever ran
description:
FOUND BY THE MERGED-PR AUDIT OF PR #8721.

THE DEFECT. docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md now says each linked worktree gets its own fetch-head copy "the first time anything fetches from it", and that an absent file says "nothing has ever fetched from that tree". The first half of the correction is measured and sound: in the current repository, git rev-parse --git-path FETCH_HEAD resolves to a private metadata path for every linked worktree, and exactly four of seven linked worktrees have the file, matching the PR. The absolute inference from absence is not sound.

THE DIRECT COUNTEREXAMPLE IS PART OF GIT'S NORMAL INTERFACE, not a hypothetical deletion. Git 2.53's git fetch -h documents --[no-]write-fetch-head: a fetch can deliberately update refs without writing FETCH_HEAD. That is directly relevant to this paragraph's automated poller case. Such a poller can fetch forever while the per-worktree file remains absent. Therefore absence proves only that no fetch has written this clock in that worktree (or that the file is no longer there); it does not prove that no fetch has ever run.

IMPACT. The safe, load-bearing direction survives: movement is still proof that a writing fetch ran, while stillness proves nothing about liveness. The defect is confined to the new interpretation of absence, but that interpretation is the point of PR #8721 and can send a reader looking for the wrong history on an externally created tree.

MINIMAL REMEDY. Qualify the two new sentences in place: a linked worktree gets this file when a fetch writes FETCH_HEAD there, and absence means no fetch has written this particular clock. The paint-bounded window is ~96% frame grid, so a 1.25x difference in the arms' OWN work would displace the window-level ratio by only 0.3-1.1 percentage points, against an observed per-round spread of 1.5-7.5 points; a 1.5x difference (C4's line) by 0.6-2.2 points, still inside that spread. GATED. DO NOT DISPATCH UNTIL day8/re-frame2-hicasso IS PUBLISHED TO CLOJARS.

Clojars has never seen. A :hicasso scaffold emitted before then hands a new

Split off rf2-48rk3, which implemented that bead's OTHER ground (the two-value
substrate idiom) and is closed. The blocking work it left is only this.

WHAT rf2-48rk3 ALREADY PAID FOR, so do not re-cost it: substrate capabilities
(:xray?, :story?, :ssr?) are now DECLARED per substrate in hooks.clj's
substrate-registry and read through one fail-closed `capability` accessor. A

:ssr? false} on a hicasso entry is now the whole of that half of the job --
:xray? false is CORRECT because Hicasso rides the UIx adapter, where Xray's
panel cannot mount.

per-substrate transform emits exactly three files and a Hicasso variant changes
ALL THREE, which is why this is a VARIANT and not a flag on :uix:

Plus: the substrate-registry entry (with all capability keys), a template-fn

AXIS RULED — the "wants a ruling before code" hold in the description is discharged; the TAG GATE (first v* tag, rf2-kmqx3) still stands, and so does the sequencing behind rf2-zq34m recorded below.

DECISION — OPTION A. The template keeps exactly ONE template-specific selector, :substrate, and Hicasso becomes its THIRD VALUE. A user writes `:substrate :hicasso` (beside the existing `:reagent` default and `:uix`); no second selector (no :views, no :authoring, no :adapter key) is added, now or later, to express Hicasso-over-a-foreign-adapter — that pairing stays a documented recipe (docs/core/hicasso/00-installation.md's adapter section plus the use-uix-or-slim how-to), not a scaffold cell. Reagent stays the default. What the variant emits, on the collapsed rf2-zq34m shape: the three per-substrate files, and nothing else diverges — `_hicasso/deps.edn` (ONE view coordinate: the published re-frame2-hicasso artefact at {{rf2-version}}; core and ssr arrive transitively through its published :deps; NO re-frame2-uix, NO uix npm/clj pins), `_hicasso/core.cljs` (boot with Hicasso's OWN adapter: `(rf/init! substrate/adapter)` from `re-frame.hicasso.substrate`, then `(h/mount! el {:frame :rf/default :initial-events [[:counter/initialise]]} [views/counter-app])` with the handle retained in a defonce atom, and a `^:dev/after-load` that calls `(h/render! @!root [views/counter-app])`), and `_hicasso/views.cljs` (`h/defview` + `h/sub` + intent vectors at :on-click — hiccup, no hooks, no `$`). The shared files (events.cljs, subs.cljs, the shell, package.json, shadow-cljs.edn, README, the focused event-flow test) are substrate-invariant and stay shared; the substrate-registry entry declares every surviving capability key false (`:xray? false`, and `:story? false :ssr? false` for as long as those keys exist — zq34m is expected to delete the latter two with the flags they serve). Sequencing is part of the decision, not advice: this lands (1) AFTER rf2-zq34m's collapse has merged, on the collapsed shape, and (2) AFTER the first v* tag has made the Hicasso coordinate resolve from a clean consumer. The rf2-kmqx3 edge enforces the second mechanically; the first is a sequencing instruction to whoever dispatches, because both PRs touch the tools/template/** fence and zq34m explicitly excludes Hicasso from its own diff.

ONE PHYSICAL CONSTRAINT REMAINS AND IS NOT A DEFERRAL. A clock estimand needs a quiet box: one measurement at a time, controls arbitrating, no other worker compiling. That is a property of the instrument, not a scheduling preference — a reading taken against six concurrent compiles measures the fleet, not the library. COUNTER estimands have no such constraint; monotone counters read the same on a loaded box, which is why the deterministic censuses landed while the clock tables did not.

SO THE PLAN IS: build every instrument NOW, in parallel, on a loaded box — that work is edit-shaped and unconstrained. Then run the windows themselves back to back when the fleet is idle. That is the same split that produced rf2-w01c from rf2-hic-036 and rf2-d6ai8 from rf2-hic-088, and it means the quiet-box time is spent measuring rather than writing drivers.

WHAT THIS BEAD OWES, restated: if it needs an instrument that does not exist, that half dispatches immediately. If the instrument exists and only the window is missing, it queues for the next quiet period. Whoever picks it up should say which case it is in the first paragraph of its report.

Neither my brief nor this bead's description said gate 2 had become runnable. The worker found it by reading the dependency's close reason, which is the discipline working.

WHY. The gap is real — MET would record a verdict no comparison reached (a regression rule needs two readings across a CHANGE; what exists is one reading of an UNCHANGED tree), and UNPINNED has stopped being true now an instrument exists on the governed population. But a ledger's status vocabulary is a small taxonomy that every row is read against, and adding a term to it is a durable change to how all 49 rows are interpreted, in exchange for expressing one row's transitional state. Under the stance that is machinery where DISCLOSURE does the job: an annotated row saying 'anchored 3 runs, awaiting a second reading across a change' tells a reader strictly more than a new one-word status would, and it costs the taxonomy nothing.

base 2a93f2c112 (an ancestor of main). Nothing was built.

*** FIRST, TWO CORRECTIONS AT SOURCE. ***

1. THE DESCRIPTION'S STALE PARAGRAPH IS STILL STALE and this note does not fix it: the ORIGINAL

Five invocations of topo/clock_app.cljs through run.cjs, serial, nothing tuned, 04:52-05:13 AUSEST.

THE PRE-REGISTRATION WAS COMMITTED AND PUSHED BEFORE THE RUNNER WAS INVOKED ONCE (5caab9184f,
topology-tournament.md Part 3 sec 3.2, that page and nothing else). It carries sec 2.9.1's six

TWO OF THE FIVE WERE VOIDED, by the condition I registered before running: any file not this

RUN 3 COULD NOT BE RE-TAKEN because that peer then held the machine, and sec 2.9.2's

only run 1 -- forbids finishing it another time. TWO ADMISSIBLE RUNS OF A PRE-REGISTERED THREE.

*** RULE 1 -- THE INFERENCE SURVIVES. ***

sec 2.9.7's falsification is confirmed in all six readings (floor arm-specific, always larger on the
arm with more boundaries and reads). The narrow/broad reversal holds in ALL EIGHT readings. bulk

*** RULE 2 -- THE VALUES MOVED, AND AGAINST THE AUDIT'S PREMISE. ***

exclusive series reads SLOWER on 36 of 45 (median 1.094x the published centre, min 0.901, max 1.341)
and is THREE TIMES NOISIER on the published series' own statistic:
  raw cell spread   published median 9.0% / max 25.1%   exclusive median 28.6% / max 75.5%
  ratio-cell spread published median 3.9% / max 10.1%   exclusive median 3.8%  / max 22.0%
Three runs give a range more chances to widen than two, so a two-run series ought to score LOWER on
both. On the raw cells it scores three times higher; on the ratios it matches. THE ABSOLUTE CELLS
MOVED WITH THE BOX AND THE ARM-TO-ARM RATIOS DID NOT -- which is what within-round interleaving is
for and the first direct evidence on this lane that it works.

*** THE MECHANISM, MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED. ***

A 5s per-process CPU census: 2.29 busy cores of 24. Every AGENT process on the box summed to 0.52 --
23% of the busy time, 2% of the machine -- against 1.07 cores for ONE editor language service. THE
EXCLUSIVITY CONDITION REACHES A QUARTER OF THE LOAD. And the bracket counters do not predict the

*** THE RULING THIS ASKS FOR -- ONE SENTENCE, MIKE'S OR THE MAYOR'S. ***

DOES THE PRE-REGISTERED EXCLUSIVITY CONDITION BIND AGENT OVERLAP ONLY, OR THE WHOLE BOX?
  - Agent overlap only: sec 2.9's published series has a defect this window has now shown does not

*** WHICH ROWS ARE DISTRIBUTIONAL, AND HOW IT WAS ESTABLISHED. ***

DEFERRAL LIFTED — MIKE 2026-08-14: 'I want hicasso fully implemented, nothing deferred. I want a complete library. I want a sophisticated library.'

This bead was parked under the earlier direction to run measurement later. That direction is superseded. It is now live work.

ONE PHYSICAL CONSTRAINT REMAINS AND IS NOT A DEFERRAL. A clock estimand needs a quiet box: one measurement at a time, controls arbitrating, no other worker compiling. That is a property of the instrument, not a scheduling preference — a reading taken against six concurrent compiles measures the fleet, not the library. COUNTER estimands have no such constraint; monotone counters read the same on a loaded box, which is why the deterministic censuses landed while the clock tables did not.

SO THE PLAN IS: build every instrument NOW, in parallel, on a loaded box — that work is edit-shaped and unconstrained. Then run the windows themselves back to back when the fleet is idle. That is the same split that produced rf2-w01c from rf2-hic-036 and rf2-d6ai8 from rf2-hic-088, and it means the quiet-box time is spent measuring rather than writing drivers.

WHAT THIS BEAD OWES, restated: if it needs an instrument that does not exist, that half dispatches immediately. If the instrument exists and only the window is missing, it queues for the next quiet period. Whoever picks it up should say which case it is in the first paragraph of its report.

title: hicasso: the fused reader array costs 91-92 B/read — the largest term this page has attributed to a container rather than a value
description:
MEASURED, NOT SPECULATED. rf2-zei9w's ablation attributes 91 B/read (Reagent segment) / 92 (UIx) to the cell's fused reader array — the container itself, not the membership it holds. Per-round bands are disjoint across all six rounds, the R=0 shell does not move, and donors moved 0.05/0.19 B/read, so this is a per-KEY term and the attribution is solid. Published in docs/design/hicasso/studio/reads-per-boundary-heap-ladder.md (2026-08-04 section), PR #7452.

WHY IT IS WORTH A LOOK. rf2-dabt3's fusion banked -60 B/read in both segments — real, and it won — but that is only ~40% of the ~151 B/read the old reverse edge cost, because the replacement array is ~2x what ONE PersistentHashSet membership costs (+46/+47 B/read, PR #7418 run D). The design predicted the surviving array would be cheap residue; it is not. It is now the largest single term this page has attributed to a CONTAINER rather than to a value.

THE OBVIOUS SHAPE, and it is only a sketch. At the fan-out this table actually sees, the overwhelmingly common case is ONE reader per key. A scalar slot that holds the single reader directly and promotes to an array on the SECOND reader would retain a pointer instead of a JSArray-plus-backing-store for that case. arm1/runtime.cljs's own section header already argues a JS array beats a persistent set here; this asks the next question down, which is whether a container is needed at all in the common case.

THIS IS NOT A DISPATCH. It wants a ruling first, for three reasons:
• release-cell!'s .indexOf, arm-cell-reaper!'s alength and stats's alength all read .-readers directly, and cell-readers/stats are witness surfaces the six laws and the ladder's structural gate are written against — a polymorphic slot touches all of them.
• It is a byte shave on a pre-alpha arm, and the stance is explicit that not every measured term needs actioning.
• The bill it would attack is +331 B/read against Reagent; 91 of that is this term. Worth knowing the size before deciding it is worth the branch in a hot path.

Precondition if it is ever taken: a quiet box, p0_run.cjs --only ladder 6 rounds with both donors as same-run controls, and the same ablation discipline rf2-zei9w used — attribute, do not infer.

title: Consolidate 73 ad-hoc IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT set/restore sites onto one shared fixture
description:
Carried over from rf2-76lhy step 2, which closed on PR #7190 having delivered step 1 (the capture-time profile). This half was never done and should not be lost with the parent.

73 test files set and restore the process-global IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT by hand, with no shared fixture. A test that throws between the set and the restore leaks the flag into every subsequent namespace in the bundle - a cross-namespace coupling that no assertion can catch and that only shows up as unexplained slowness or flakiness later in the run.

IMPORTANT CONTEXT, so this is not over-sold. rf2-76lhy originally advanced the leak as the explanation for a suspected 3-4x CI slowdown. The per-namespace profile shipped in PR #7190 dissolved that: 73% of the lane's wall clock is 7 benchmark namespaces, the three recorded CI stop points all sit at 92-97% of the lane, and the CI/local gap is a uniform ~1.7x. There is no longer evidence pointing at the leak.

So this is a HYGIENE bead, not a bug hunt. It retires a real hazard class on its own terms - one use-fixtures with the restore in a finally - and it is worth doing, but nothing is currently known to be broken by it. Size it accordingly and do not let it grow into an audit.

Fenced away from the PR #7190 runner work; this is implementation/**/test/** across many artefacts, so it wants its own dispatch.
notes:
INVESTIGATED, NOT DONE (PR #7193 worker, 2026-07-28). Recommendation: leave it, or do it per-artefact later. This is the honest 'not worth doing now'.

CENSUS IS BIGGER THAN THE BEAD SAYS: 78 files, 175 `set!` sites, across NINE trees — freehand 43, ui 15, adapters 7, ssr 6, tools/story 2, tools/machines-viz 2, machines 1, core 1, scripts 1. Not 73, and not one artefact.

THERE IS NO SMALL, OBVIOUSLY-CORRECT CONSOLIDATION TO ADOPT. The nearest existing shared fixture is `re-frame.ui.test/act-operation!`, which already does exactly the right thing (reads the prior value, sets true, restores the PRIOR value — not `false` — after React settles). But it lives in implementation/ui/SRC, a published and EXPERIMENTAL artefact surface. Adopting it from freehand / ssr / adapters / machines test trees would make those artefacts' tests depend on re-frame.ui. That is an architectural decision, not hygiene, and it is Mike's. The alternative — mint a new shared test-support surface every artefact may require — is also a decision, not a sweep.

WHAT DOES EXIST is per-artefact convergence: freehand already has mount_support.cljs and bench/b6_harness.cljs; ssr has SIX files carrying byte-identical `disable-act-env!`/`restore-act-env!` pairs. So the tractable shape is PER-ARTEFACT, ONE PR EACH — freehand first (43 of the 78 files, landing spot already present), then ssr (6 files, pure duplication), then ui.

WHY NOT NOW. (1) The motivation is gone: PR #7190's profile dissolved the 3-4x CI-slowdown hypothesis this was step 2 of, and PR #7193 confirmed it on a second box — the whole gap was seven benchmark namespaces (71% of the browser lane's wall clock), and the CI factor is a uniform ~1.7x. There is still no observed instance of the leak. (2) A 78-file mechanical edit across nine trees is a maximal merge-conflict change against every open PR touching a mounted test. (3) Every one of those trees was outside PR #7193's fence, so it could not have been done there in any case.

If someone does pick it up: rule FIRST on whether re-frame.ui.test's act door may be the repo-wide answer, because that ruling decides whether this is one shared fixture or nine private ones.
RULING (delegated by Mike, 2026-07-28, dossier review):

DECISION — leave the sweep undone now; bead DEFERRED. No 78-file mechanical edit during the current mounted-test churn: the motivating CI-slowdown hypothesis was dissolved by measurement (seven benchmark namespaces + a uniform ~1.7x CI factor), and the sweep is a maximal merge-conflict change against every open mounted-test PR. Pick this up only when the high-conflict Freehand work settles AND either a real leak instance bites or an artefact's mounted tests are being reworked anyway — then land it artefact-sized, not repo-wide.

RECORD CORRECTION (from the Codex second opinion; commits verified in this checkout): "no observed instance" is true of the PERFORMANCE theory only. Flag leakage itself has occurred and been repaired — 43ce4cf9f6 and 1fff5b618b (shared-page act-discipline, ~361 warnings) and 0dd432b9ed (un-restored act boundary after a negative-control run, 755 warnings). The hazard class is real and observed; the slowdown attribution is what was disproved. P3 stands.

ARCHITECTURAL ANSWER (binding — do not re-litigate):
1. DONOR DEPENDENCY FORBIDDEN. No artefact's tests may require re-frame.ui (src or test): F6e deletes the artefact, and re-frame.ui.test/act-operation! is a private defn- coupled to donor internals in any case. Its invariant is the SHAPE to copy, never the namespace to require: capture the incoming flag value and restore the PRIOR value — not a blanket false — on every exit path (synchronous throw, Promise fulfilment, Promise rejection).
2. ONE repo-private implementation, NOT nine per-artefact copies. Home: the existing lightweight dependency-free shared surface implementation/core/test/re_frame/adapter/react_test_support.cljs (or a narrowly named sibling in the same core/test root). Verified: it is already required across an artefact boundary today (adapters/uix test) and sits on the consolidated Shadow classpath, so this mints no new architecture and survives F6e. Per-artefact is the DELIVERY boundary — artefact-sized PRs, freehand first (43 files, through its existing mount_support.cljs facade), ssr second (6 byte-identical disable/restore pairs) — not the implementation boundary. Nine permanent copies would reproduce at repo scale exactly the drift ssr's six copies already demonstrate.
3. Design floor for whoever lands it (from Codex, ratified): the helper takes the desired mode — both true (act-disciplined renders) and false (timing discriminators, hydration, deliberate un-acted negative controls) are legitimate, so no runner-wide constant. One save/restore engine with thin sync-wrapping and async-map fixture adapters (cljs.test forbids mixing the two fixture kinds; async tests need the map form) plus a Promise-aware operation bracket for callbacks that reject before done; overlapping async scopes rejected or serialized. Leave re-frame.ui.test self-contained until F6e and skip migrating ui test files the deletion gate removes.

Disposition: deferred (was open P3). Reopen against the conditions above.

BUT THE ARTEFACT ORDER IS DEAD. RULING 2026-09-02 10:23:48 AUSEST (delegated by Mike 2026-09-02, dossier review; ai/decisions/rf2-3t2nq.act-environment-fixture-home.md folded here and deleted — THIS NOTE IS THE CANONICAL RECORD). Tip at ruling: b26c5ad33e.

HOLD STRUCK — the placement question "held for Mike" in the 2026-08-21 comment is discharged by this ruling.

DECISION — CLOSE AS MINUTIAE. No fixture sweep, no hicasso-only dedupe, no publish on re-frame.test-support, no further deferral. Three findings carry it, each re-measured at tip b26c5ad33e rather than inherited from the bead's earlier numbers:

(1) The hazard the bead is written around — a throw between a set and a restore leaking the flag bundle-wide — has ONE candidate site in the whole repo, and it is not in hicasso. Repo-wide there are exactly two prior-value restores: implementation/core/test/re_frame/adapter/react_shared_suite.cljs:3280/3351 (act-prev, restored under `finally`) and implementation/ssr/test/re_frame/ssr/ssr_startup_recipe_dom_cljs_test.cljs:218-223 (prev, restored by `teardown!` at :243, called from the async continuation at :306 — NOT under `finally`; see PREMISE CORRECTIONS). Every one of the 43 `set!` lines under implementation/hicasso sets `false`; zero restore anything. There is no restore in that tree for a throw to skip.

(2) What the flag does makes the residual "hazard" a warning-policy leak, not a scheduler or timing leak (Codex's semantic correction, accepted — see WEIGHING). A `false` left behind suppresses "not wrapped in act" warnings in later tests of the same browser build; it does not defer renders or change what a test measures. The three repaired incidents the 2026-07-28 ruling cited (43ce4cf9f6, 1fff5b618b, 0dd432b9ed) were warning-state repairs of a `true` leaking across the shared page, consistent with that reading.

(3) What is left is a two-line duplicated helper (`leave-act-environment!` at checkpoint_support.cljs:161 and roots_frames_support.cljs:82) whose stated reason for existing twice — the freeze gate forbidding a `:require` of the bench helper — was retired by 8a10915ed8 on 2026-08-29, and whose 35 callers split 22/13 for structural reasons: 34 of the 35 use other functions from the same support namespace, and exactly one (state_dom_cljs_test.cljs) requires checkpoint-support solely for the setter. A dedupe would touch ~35 files in the repo's hottest test tree to remove one redundant require and one redundant defn, retiring no hazard. That is the trade that got the 2026-08-21 lift withdrawn, and the stance (pre-alpha, trust the programmer, do not drown in minutiae) says close it rather than action it.

The placement question that was held for Mike needs no ruling. The repo-private cross-artefact home implementation/core/test/re_frame/adapter/react_test_support.cljs already exists, is dependency-free (requires only clojure.string), sits on the consolidated Shadow classpath beside hicasso/test (implementation/shadow-cljs.edn:34 "core/test", :137 "hicasso/test"), and is required today from three places: implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/reg_view_devtools_dom_cljs_test.cljs, implementation/adapters/uix/test/re_frame/adapter/uix_source_coord_dom_elision_prod_test.cljs and implementation/core/test/re_frame/adapter/react_shared_suite.cljs. "Can hicasso's tests reach a core test-support namespace" is yes, today, without publishing anything. The 2026-07-28 ARCHITECTURAL ANSWER (items 1-3: no donor dependency; one repo-private implementation in that home; the save/restore design floor) stands as the SHAPE for any act-environment fixture that is ever genuinely needed; nothing here overturns it. What this ruling adds is that no such fixture is needed now, and the trigger for one is a diagnostic-policy decision, not this bead.

HOW THE OPINIONS WERE WEIGHED

Dossier author (sections "Summary" through "Evidence"; recommends A, close). Accepted on its main line: the census both ways, the disproven hazard, the drifted docstrings, the dead freeze gate, the existing home, and the rejection of C. Two of its facts are corrected at tip below: "both restore brackets are correct" (the ssr one restores the prior value but is not throw-safe) and "one parameterised on? helper" (there are two, one of them prose in docs). Its option B ("rule the home and dispatch a hicasso-only dedupe") is described as viable and it is, but its own cost line — a wide mechanical diff for zero hazard retired — is why it loses.

Codex ("Codex Recommendation"; also recommends close, and adds "do not dispatch a standalone hicasso dedupe as a substitute"). Weighed heavily on three points, each re-measured here rather than taken on trust. (a) The semantic correction: IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT is React's `isConcurrentActEnvironment()` predicate gating the "not wrapped in act" warnings, while the act queue is `ReactSharedInternals.actQueue`, controlled by `act()` itself. I did not re-read React's source; the citation (ReactFiberAct.js at the v19.2.0 tag, matching the installed react-dom 19.2.0) is specific and consistent with the three repaired incidents, and it changes the disposition in no direction, so it is recorded as Codex's reading, accepted. MAYOR 2026-08-18, BACKLOG REREAD — THIS IS A DEFERRAL WITH NO DATE AND NO STATED RELEASE CONDITION, WHICH IS THE ONE SHAPE THAT NEVER GETS RE-EXAMINED. Giving it a condition rather than a date, so a future tick can test it.

THE STATE I FOUND: status DEFERRED, defer_until NONE, untouched since 2026-07-28. Of ten deferred beads it is one of only two with no date at all; the other (rf2-2hpxo) has a real condition written into it — API-freeze. This one had neither.

THE BEAD IS HONEST ABOUT ITS OWN VALUE AND I AM NOT OVERRIDING THAT. It says so itself: rf2-76lhy originally advanced the flag leak as the explanation for a suspected 3-4x CI slowdown, and PR #7190's per-namespace profile DISSOLVED that — 73% of the lane's wall clock is 7 benchmark namespaces, the three recorded CI stop points sit at 92-97% of the lane, and the CI/local gap is a uniform ~1.7x. 'There is no longer evidence pointing at the leak.' It is a HYGIENE bead, and it says so.

SO WHY NOT CLOSE IT AS MINUTIAE. Because the hazard class is real and is exactly the kind this project takes seriously: a test that throws between the set and the restore leaks a process-global into every subsequent namespace in the bundle, and NO ASSERTION CAN CATCH IT — it surfaces later as unexplained slowness or flakiness, which is the hardest possible failure to attribute. The remedy is small and correct: one use-fixtures with the restore in a finally. Closing it would discard a real hazard on the grounds that it has not bitten yet.

THE RELEASE CONDITION, which is what was missing: DISPATCH THIS WHEN THE FLEET IS QUIET — no more than one other worker out, and no open PR touching implementation/ test namespaces. NOT because it is risky, but because 73 test files across the tree is the largest merge-conflict surface any single bead in this backlog carries, and a mechanical sweep that has to rebase past several landings will cost more in conflicts than the change is worth. Measured context for that: on 2026-08-18 the fleet ran 6 workers with 5 PRs open and the trunk moved 11 commits inside one worker's run.

SIZE IT WHEN IT GOES OUT: 73 files is above the single-dispatch comfort line here, so expect to split by artefact rather than send one worker at all of them.

NOT A NEW DEFERRAL DATE — deliberately. A date would fire on a day that may be just as busy. The condition is about fleet state, and the backlog-reread loop is the tick that can test it.

THE REASON IS THE NOISE FLOOR, and it was measured today by the compiled-tier report (rf2-lnecd, docs/design/freehand/studio/compiled-tier-browser-worth-it.md): THE NO-SUBSTRATE FLOOR ARM DRIFTED 37% ACROSS ROUNDS — larger than most of the effects being measured — which is why every claim in that report is stated as a RATIO TO THE IN-RUN FLOOR rather than an absolute. On the same box, the same primitive measured 10.4ns and 21.7ns across two JVMs.

A REGRESSION GATE ON A SUBSTRATE WITH A 37% FLOOR DRIFT IS A FLAKE GENERATOR. It would red on noise, and this repo has a standing rule that A FAILING TEST ON A TOUCHED SURFACE IS NEVER A FLAKE — which is exactly the rule that makes a false red expensive to dismiss. We already have one such gate (rf2-yumaq: G-8 dying because its baseline was TOO FAST) and fixing it took a worker. Adding a second, broader one before the measurement is stable would manufacture that cost at scale.

A PREMISE CORRECTION THE BEAD INHERITS FROM ME: its notes classify the Freehand benches as covering an artefact that is "NOT published". Freehand is PRE-PUBLICATION and expected to ship — docs/release-process.md forecloses only day8/re-frame2-ui, and implementation/freehand/deps.edn:29 says staying out of the lockstep inventory "leaves the release train untouched until Freehand actually ships". I propagated that error into six briefs today. So the gap this bead describes is narrower than stated: the benches cover artefacts that are not published YET, not artefacts that never will be.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS DISPATCHABLE, in order: (1) a stable measurement method — the report shows allocation via getThreadAllocatedBytes gave min = p50 = max in nearly every arm, so an ALLOCATION gate is buildable where a wall-clock gate is not; (2) a named regression the gate would have caught, because a perf gate with no historical catch is an assertion that the future will resemble a past nobody measured; (3) the alpha tag, after which "published artefact" stops being a moving target.

NOT A REJECTION. The operator has ruled that performance matters — the compiler is KEPT for performance-critical applications not yet seen. A gate is the right long-term instrument; it is the wrong instrument today because it cannot yet distinguish signal from a 37% floor.
*** THE DEFER LAPSES 2026-09-01 AND NOTHING IN THE GRAPH HOLDS THIS BEAD. DO NOT DISPATCH ON THE DATE ALONE. ***
