title: xray: 15 of 22 panel-gallery fixtures are zero-consumer, not just long-handler-buffer
description:
FILED 2026-09-04 by the mayor from worker/vest-a's out-of-scope observation on PR #9162 (rf2-6r9j.249). RELAYED, NOT VERIFIED BY ME — treat the count as a claim and re-census it.

WHAT IT REPORTED: while removing four zero-consumer helpers from tools/xray, it censused tools/xray/.../panel_gallery/fixtures.cljs and found FIFTEEN of its TWENTY-TWO fixtures have no consumer by the same method it used for the four it removed — not merely long-handler-buffer, which was the one its bead named. It recorded the observation rather than acting on it, correctly, because widening a bead's scope mid-flight is how a bounded deletion becomes an unreviewable one.

WHY THIS IS P4 AND NOT HIGHER: a fixture with no consumer is dead weight, not a defect. Nothing is wrong at runtime. The value is that a gallery of fixtures nobody renders misleads the next person who reads it as a menu of what the gallery covers.

BEFORE ACTING, TWO THINGS THE SAME WORKER LEARNED THE HARD WAY ON THIS EXACT SURFACE:
1. ITS OWN FIRST CENSUS PATTERN WAS DEFECTIVE — it excluded '/' on the left, so it could not see h/epoch-has-issues? and read ZERO where ten hits existed. The control caught it. Any census here needs a control that shares the shape of a qualified call.
2. THE NAME-COLLISION TRAP FIRED on this surface too: three of str-of's four repo-wide hits were pr-str-of-form and pr-str-of-rejection — different tokens entirely. Check the namespace and the arity, not just the symbol.

AND THE GATE FOR THIS SURFACE FAILS OPEN ON EXIT CODE: the panel-gallery compile grades a reference to a removed var as a WARNING and still exits 0 (measured, same PR). The discriminating signal is the WARNING COUNT against a zero baseline — vest-a's was 0 across 710 files. Do not gate a deletion here on exit status alone. Recorded as memory cljs-compile-gate-exit-0-over-removed-var.

FENCE WHEN DISPATCHED: tools/xray/** only. A dispatch touching tools/xray/ updates tools/xray/spec/* in the same PR or states 'spec unchanged because X' — vest-a established that none of ITS four symbols is named or contracted in that spec, with two instruments reading zero against a control reading 4, so the same check is needed for whichever fixtures this bead removes.

The reported '15 of 22' does not hold at tip - there are 21 builders (long-handler-buffer already removed) and 19 are dead, not 15. panel-gallery.fixtures is required by exactly three galleries (chrome, filters, settings), all as 'fixtures', and between them they call one var: n-cascades (17 sites). 17 builders had no caller; cascade-with-other and event-lens-simple-buffer were reachable only from other-rows-buffer and event-lens-with-interceptors-buffer, which had none either. Only cascade-evs and n-cascades survive. Both briefed traps handled: scoped by namespace because seven OTHER galleries bind the same alias to a different ns, and the empty-buffer collision (27 repo-wide hits) resolved to three unrelated vars in other namespaces. Superseded leftovers, not pending work - fixtures_epoch.cljs carries the equivalent *-history builders and 'event-lens' appears nowhere else in tools/xray. Spec unchanged because none of the 19 symbols is named or contracted in tools/xray/spec (two instruments zero, control finds panel-gallery in 4 files). title: realworld: duplicate React key warning on the article-card tag list
description:
Seen 2026-09-04 in a development build of `:examples/realworld` once the feed actually
rendered (it was invisible before rf2-2xzc's fix because no cards were ever drawn, and it is
invisible in a release build because production React does not emit key warnings).

  Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop.
  Check the render method of `li`. It was passed a child from realworld-http.co...

A `li` list rendered from realworld-http code is missing `:key` on its children - most likely
the tag list on an article card, where several cards carry the same tag string, so a
value-derived key would collide across cards rather than within one. Reproduced on the home
feed after sign-in; zero page errors otherwise.

Small, cosmetic, and entirely inside examples/real-apps/realworld_http/. Filed rather than
folded into PR #9134 to keep that diff to the defect it explains.
close_reason: PR #9155. The bead's hypothesis is REFUTED: every tag list already carries ^{:key tag} (articles.cljs:443, comments.cljs:830), and all 7 seq-producing child sites across the 13 realworld_http files are keyed. The bead's 'entirely inside realworld_http' is also wrong - the unkeyed seq comes from realworld_shared/markdown.cljs and has no call-site fix. Mechanism verified link by link at source: markdown-it marks a TIGHT list item's paragraph hidden (measured: all 3 bullets of the demo article body return paragraph_open hidden=true); impl.cljs:70-73 maps hidden -> :plain; transform.cljc:79-80 has :plain return a bare (seq ...); transform.cljc:111 has :list-item = (partial into-markup [:li]) which conj's that seq in. Result [:li ("text " [:code ...])] - an ARRAY child, which is why React names the render method of li. Fixed by a :plain renderer emitting a fragment, so children are positional siblings not a list; keys would be wrong here since prose runs have no stable identity. Fixes both RealWorld apps (shared ns). NOT observed: the warning vanishing in a live dev build - no static gate sees a React key warning and no browser was driven.

title: CLAUDE.md trap (c) quotes rollup totals of 82/83/84 from 2026-09-01; the band has been 86 all session and the figures read as current
notes:
FILED 2026-09-03 05:3x AUSEST by the mayor, from the sentinel-a report. THIS IS A METHOD-DOC DRIFT ITEM AND THE MAYOR CHECKOUT HAS A COMMIT GUARD, SO THE FIX IS WRITTEN OUT HERE RATHER THAN APPLIED.

CLAUDE.md, in the "Three mechanical traps in the merge criterion" bullet, trap (c), reads: "Measured 2026-09-01 across five PRs at once: totals of 82, 83 and 84 all occurred". A worker read that as the recorded BAND and reported that the current total of 86 is "above the 82-84 band recorded in CLAUDE.md".

STRICTLY THE DOC IS NOT WRONG: the sentence is dated, it is presented as an observation about five specific PRs mid-build, and the surrounding paragraph says explicitly that "a raw count is not comparable across PRs mid-build". So it does not ENFORCE 82-84.

BUT IT READS AS A BAND TO A CAREFUL READER, and that is the defect. The band has been 86 across every merge this session - I have re-measured it on the last five merged PRs at the top of every merge tick, more than a dozen times, and it has not moved. A reader who takes 82-84 as current will either think the trunk has grown a job it should not have, or - worse in the fail-open direction this bullet exists to prevent - will treat a genuinely short rollup as normal.

THE FIX, minimal and in the doc own voice: keep the measurement and the reasoning, and make the figures visibly historical rather than nominal. Something of the shape "Measured 2026-09-01 across five PRs at once, when the band was in the low eighties: totals of 82, 83 and 84 all occurred" - the point being that the presence of the aggregator tracked NEITHER the total NOR settledness, which is what the trap is actually about and which does not depend on the numbers at all. Then add one sentence saying the band is re-measured every merge tick and the doc figures are illustrative, never the band.

DO NOT put a current number in CLAUDE.md. That is the trap one level up: a hardcoded band in a doc is a figure that goes stale silently, which is exactly the failure this bead is reporting. The band is measured, never quoted.

The measurement and the reasoning are kept intact, because the trap is that the aggregator's presence tracked NEITHER the total NOR settledness, which does not depend on the numbers. NO CURRENT NUMBER WAS PUT IN THE FILE, per this bead's own instruction -- a hardcoded band would be the same trap one level up. WHAT DOES COVER IT, so this is a redundancy gap rather than a coverage void:

over every skill's evals.json; proven to read this tree by a planted duplicate

recurring drift class here is pinnable at all, since much of it is reasoning
about what a measurement licenses rather than a spelling that can be grepped.

title: Decide how far the api-manifest roster-completeness gate should widen: 243 namespaces sit under trees it does not cover
description:
PR #9040 restored the roster-completeness gate (orphaned since the freehand retirement c951808b47) and enrolled two source trees. This bead is the OPEN QUESTION it deliberately did not answer, recorded so the narrow scope is a decision rather than an omission.

MEASURED at 375d5dd899: 276 namespaces under implementation/ are absent from jvm-namespaces. #9040's two roots account for 33 of them (25 ssr, 8 ssr-ring), all now classified internal. The remaining 243 are in trees the gate does not read:

  core 84 · machines 33 · routing 28 · hicasso 25 · resources 23 · http 17
  adapters/reagent-slim 9 · schemas 7 · epoch 5 · test-quiet 5 · flows 3
  spec-resource 1 · adapters/{reagent,test-react,uix} 1 each

A namespace in an uncovered tree is still UNSCANNED in exactly the sense rf2-8arzr.7 described: absent from the roster is not unclassified, and every manifest-derived gate is blind to it at once. That class produced re-frame.resources (rf2-ivuun), two freehand namespaces (rf2-h0b0l, rf2-cfhuv) and the three ssr-node ones.

THE COST IS THE DECISION. Enrolling a tree obliges a human classification for every namespace under it, recorded in internal-namespaces with a reason. That is real editorial work — 84 for core alone — and rf2-o8xev's original write-up made the same call for the same reason: 'Widening it to the other artefacts is a separate decision with a separate cost, not a free generalisation.'

The mechanism no longer argues against it, which is what changed: roster-covered-roots is data, so a tree is a root plus its classifications and never another mechanism. Options: (a) widen tree by tree as each is touched, cheapest and never blocks anyone; (b) one sweep, expensive but ends the class; (c) leave it at the SSR trees and accept the rest stay unscanned. Not urgent, and (a) is the de facto status quo.
notes:
MAYOR RULING 2026-09-03 06:1x AUSEST. WIDEN IT, BUT ONE TREE PER DISPATCH AND HIGHEST-RISK FIRST. Do not enrol all thirteen, and do not leave it where it is.

WHY NOT LEAVE IT. The class this gate catches is not hypothetical and the bead names its victims: re-frame.resources (rf2-ivuun), two freehand namespaces (rf2-h0b0l, rf2-cfhuv), and the three ssr-node ones. That is SIX namespaces that shipped unscanned, found one at a time, each by somebody noticing. And rf2-3ne8 added a seventh finding on top of it - of the 26 under implementation/hicasso/src, FIVE turned out to be PUBLIC AUTHORING SURFACES with no documentation page at all, which nobody had spotted because the manifest could not see them. The gate does not merely record a roster; it is the only instrument that turns "we forgot" into "the build refuses".

WHY NOT ALL THIRTEEN AT ONCE. The cost is real and it is EDITORIAL, not mechanical: every namespace under an enrolled root needs a human classification with a reason. 84 for core alone. A dispatch that tries to classify 243 namespaces will either time out or produce 243 rubber-stamped entries, and a rubber-stamped classification is worse than none because it looks like a decision.

THE ORDER, and the ordering principle is BLAST RADIUS OF A MISS rather than count:
  1. hicasso (25) - ALREADY DONE by rf2-3ne8. Proof the per-tree shape works, and the tree that yielded five undocumented public surfaces.
  2. routing (28) and resources (23) - the two trees whose namespaces are most likely to carry PUBLIC authoring surfaces an app requires directly. The route-link P0 came out of routing this session; a public surface there being invisible to every manifest gate is the same shape of exposure.
  3. http (17), machines (33), schemas (7), flows (3), epoch (5) - feature artefacts with public API.
  4. core (84) LAST, not first. It is the biggest and the most tempting, and it is also the tree whose namespaces are best known and most likely to be genuinely internal - so it has the worst work-to-finding ratio, and doing it first would exhaust the appetite for the rest.
  5. adapters/* (3), reagent-slim (9), test-quiet (5), spec-resource (1) - small tails, fold into whichever dispatch has room.

FILE ONE BEAD PER TREE as you go rather than tracking it here, each carrying its own namespace count and its own classification. This bead stays open as the parent question until the last tree lands, and it should record which trees are done.

WHAT I AM NOT RULING: whether every root eventually gets enrolled. Stop and re-ask after step 2 - if routing and resources yield nothing but internal classifications, that is evidence the remaining trees are not worth the editorial cost, and the honest answer then is to stop and record why. THE MEASUREMENT DECIDES THE TAIL, not this ruling.

AND THE STANCE POINT, because it cuts both ways here: enrolling a tree is not gold plating - it is the gate refusing to let a public surface ship unrecorded, which is exactly the ergonomics-and-low-friction goal. But rubber-stamping 243 entries to reach a green IS gold plating, of the worst kind: effort spent producing the appearance of coverage.
STEP 2 MEASURED AND REPORTED (rf2-hjj4, PR #9063, 2026-09-03). Trees done: hicasso (rf2-3ne8), routing + resources (rf2-hjj4). roster-covered-roots is now five roots.

THE MEASUREMENT THE RULING ASKED FOR: 51 unaccounted namespaces (routing 28, resources 23), ALL 51 CLASSIFIED INTERNAL. Zero public authoring surfaces, zero new manifest rows (528 -> 528), zero new docs/api pages, zero nav entries. That is the ruling's own stop signal.

BUT THE REASON MATTERS MORE THAN THE ARITHMETIC, and it should govern the tail rather than the schedule does. Routing and resources are FACADE artefacts: one enrolled door re-exports everything an app may call (27 rows and 21 rows respectively), and the siblings are the concerns it composes - handler bodies, *-meta registration maps, cofx constructors, *-sub-fn bodies, host-side caches. Hicasso is the OPPOSITE shape: its five modules are separately requirable BECAUSE they are opt-in, so its door structurally could not re-export them, which is why five surfaces could hide there. THE PREDICTOR IS NOT TREE SIZE - it is whether the artefact has a single re-exporting door.

By that test the ruling's remaining steps 3-5 look like routing/resources rather than hicasso: machines, http, schemas, flows, epoch and core each publish ONE facade namespace already in jvm-namespaces. WORKER RECOMMENDATION (not a decision taken; this bead stays open as the parent question): stop enrolling trees on a schedule, and instead enrol a tree WHEN IT ACQUIRES A SECOND REQUIRABLE DOOR - the condition that actually produces findings. The reasoning is written into gen.clj's own section header so it is met where the decision is made.

TWO CAVEATS. (1) The gate still earns its keep on the two trees enrolled: it now REFUSES a new unclassified namespace under either, which is the 'we forgot' -> 'the build refuses' conversion this bead wanted, worth the 51 lines regardless of today's zero findings. (2) adapters/* is the one part of the tail NOT covered by the facade argument - adapters are requirable by definition, so if any tree is enrolled next, that is where to look first, ahead of core.

ONE THING FOR A RULING, raised by rf2-hjj4 rather than settled by it: the four .tooling / .test-support siblings. skills/re-frame2/references/tooling/routing.md:180 tells app authors to write (:require [re-frame.routing.test-support]) - a documented direct require, the hicasso signature - yet the require is for its LOAD EFFECT and the consumer-facing names are an event id and a late-bind hook, not the one public var each namespace holds. They were classified internal on that ground, so the roster now says 'not a supported surface' about a namespace the skills tell people to require. The manifest is one row per public VAR and neither var is one, so there is nothing to row; inventing a require-for-effect vocabulary would be over-engineering. If that reads wrong, the fix is a tier on those two, not a change to the gate.
MAYOR RULING 2026-09-03 07:3x AUSEST — I AM REPLACING MY OWN ORDERING RULE WITH THE WORKER STRUCTURAL ONE. STOP THE SCHEDULED WIDENING.

WHAT STEP 2 MEASURED (rf2-hjj4, PR #9063): routing 29 namespaces / 28 unaccounted, resources 24 / 23 - and 51 of 51 classified INTERNAL. ZERO public authoring surfaces. No manifest row (528 -> 528), no docs/api page, no nav entry. That is the exact opposite of hicasso, where five of twenty-six were public surfaces with no documentation page.

MY ORDERING RULE WAS "BLAST RADIUS, NOT COUNT" AND IT WAS THE WRONG AXIS. I put routing and resources first because routing produced the route-link P0 and both looked likely to carry public surfaces. They carry none, and the worker found the reason, which is structural rather than statistical: ROUTING AND RESOURCES ARE FACADE ARTEFACTS - ONE DOOR RE-EXPORTS EVERYTHING AN APP MAY CALL. Hicasso is the opposite: its modules are SEPARATELY REQUIRABLE BECAUSE THEY ARE OPT-IN, which is precisely why five surfaces could hide behind an unenrolled root. Nothing can hide behind a single re-exporting door, because the door is already rowed.

THE RULE I AM ADOPTING, in the worker words: THE PREDICTOR IS NOT TREE SIZE BUT WHETHER THE ARTEFACT HAS A SINGLE RE-EXPORTING DOOR. Enrol a tree WHEN IT ACQUIRES A SECOND REQUIRABLE DOOR, not on a schedule. machines, http, schemas, flows, epoch and core all match the routing/resources shape, so the remaining 190-odd namespaces under them are not worth the editorial cost on present evidence - and rubber-stamping them would be the gold plating I warned against when I ruled step 2.

THE ONE EXCEPTION WORTH LOOKING AT: adapters/*. Adapters are REQUIRABLE BY DEFINITION - an app requires the adapter it uses - so they have the hicasso shape rather than the facade shape, at 3 namespaces total. That is cheap enough to be worth doing on its own evidence rather than on a schedule, and it is the only tree I would enrol next.

THIS BEAD STAYS OPEN as the standing question, now with a decision procedure rather than a queue: when an artefact gains a second requirable door, enrol it then. The recommendation is also written into gen.clj section header by PR #9063, so the rule lives beside the mechanism rather than only in the tracker.

AND THE MEASUREMENT DECIDED THE TAIL EXACTLY AS THE RULING SAID IT WOULD. I wrote "if routing and resources yield nothing but internal classifications, that is evidence the remaining trees are not worth the editorial cost, and the honest answer is to stop and record why." They did. This is that.
THE "adapters/*, THREE NAMESPACES" EXCEPTION DOES NOT HOLD AS STATED. Measured 2026-09-03 07:5x AUSEST by the mayor, at the point of filing it as the next slice, which is why it was checked rather than inherited.

THE COUNT IS 15, NOT 3. `find implementation/adapters -path '*/src/*' -name '*.clj*'` returns fifteen namespace files:
  reagent/src           1  (re-frame.adapter.reagent)
  uix/src               1  (re-frame.adapter.uix)
  test-react/src        1  (re-frame.adapter.test-react)
  reagent-slim/src     12  (re-frame.adapter.reagent-slim PLUS eleven reagent2.* namespaces — core, dom.client, dom.server, impl.batching, impl.component, impl.diag, impl.template, ratom, and their .clj siblings)

THE THREE IN THE RULING ARE THE DOORS. The fourteen-minus-three remainder is a VENDORED REAGENT FORK sitting under reagent-slim. Enrolling `implementation/adapters/*/src` in roster-covered-roots obliges a classification for every namespace beneath the root — gen.clj:248-252 says so in terms — so the real bill is eleven rubber-stamp entries for somebody else's library internals. THAT IS PRECISELY THE EDITORIAL COST THIS BEAD'S OWN RULING SAID TO REFUSE, and the ruling recommended it because the count made it look free.

WHAT SURVIVES, AND IT IS SMALL. reagent/src and uix/src are one namespace each, both already public doors, both already rowed. Enrolling just those two roots is genuinely cheap — but the VALUE of enrolling a root is that it catches a NEW namespace appearing beneath it unclassified, and beneath a root holding one door that is close to zero. So the cheap version is also the version that buys least.

MY CALL: DO NOT FILE THE SLICE. Not now and not as ruled. This is minutiae, and the stance says so — enrolling two roots to protect against a namespace nobody is adding is gold plating with a governance costume on. The DECISION PROCEDURE this bead adopted is the durable part and it is unaffected: enrol a tree when it acquires a second requirable door. reagent-slim already HAS a second door in the sense that matters (reagent2.core is requirable), which is an argument for enrolling it and immediately an argument against, because the eleven behind it are a fork rather than a surface.

SO THIS BEAD STAYS OPEN, UNCHANGED, as the standing question — with the adapters exception now correctly priced rather than standing as a cheap next step that is not one. If a future reader wants it, the question to answer first is what to do about the vendored reagent2 tree, not whether three namespaces are worth enrolling.
RE-DISPATCHED 2026-09-03 AS AN OPEN ANALYSIS QUESTION; IT IS NOT ONE ANY MORE, AND NOTHING WAS WIDENED. PR #9108 (worker/schemagate-a). This bead was briefed to a fresh worker as 'decide how far to widen', which is the reading its title still invites. The two rulings above already answered it -- the structural rule replaced the schedule at 07:3x, and the adapters exception was priced and declined at 07:5x with DO NOT FILE THE SLICE -- so enrolling any root here would have contradicted a standing ruling. No root enrolled; roster-covered-roots is unchanged at five; the gate's behaviour is identical.

WHAT LANDED IS THE ONE THING THE RULING ITSELF ASKED FOR: the rule beside the mechanism. gen.clj's section header carried the EVIDENCE (routing/resources 51 of 51 internal; hicasso 5 of 26 public) but stopped at calling the facade/opt-in distinction 'the useful predictor' -- so a reader arriving at roster-covered-roots met an open question rather than a decision, which is exactly how this bead got re-dispatched. The header now states the rule (enrol a tree WHEN IT ACQUIRES A SECOND REQUIRABLE DOOR, never off a queue), why machines/http/schemas/flows/epoch/core stay out (~190 namespaces behind one rostered facade each), and the adapters exception priced rather than inherited.

ONE FIGURE RE-MEASURED AND CONFIRMED, since the ruling itself says to re-measure rather than inherit: find implementation/adapters -path '*/src/*' returns FIFTEEN namespace files -- four doors (reagent, uix, test-react, reagent-slim) plus eleven reagent2.* files of the vendored fork under reagent-slim. The 07:5x correction holds exactly as written.

BEAD STAYS OPEN as the standing question, per the ruling. Suggestion for whoever next reads it: the title is what invites the re-dispatch, and the durable part is now a decision procedure rather than a widening plan. api-manifest suite green after the edit: 84 tests, 170 assertions, exit 0.
close_reason:
CLOSED 2026-09-04 by the mayor (backlog-reread loop) as a hold costing more than it holds. The question this bead asks has been answered twice on the bead itself and the durable half is ON THE TRUNK.

WHAT LANDED (PR #9108, a769e59978): gen.clj's section header now STATES THE DECISION PROCEDURE beside the mechanism — enrol a tree WHEN IT ACQUIRES A SECOND REQUIRABLE DOOR, never off a queue — with why machines/http/schemas/flows/epoch/core stay out (~190 namespaces behind one rostered facade each) and the adapters exception priced rather than inherited. A reader arriving at roster-covered-roots now meets a decision, not an open question.

WHAT WAS RULED: DO NOT FILE THE SLICE. The 'adapters/*, three namespaces' exception was measured and does not hold — find implementation/adapters -path '*/src/*' returns FIFTEEN namespace files, four doors plus eleven reagent2.* files of a VENDORED REAGENT FORK under reagent-slim, and enrolling the root obliges a classification for every namespace beneath it (gen.clj:248-252). That is eleven rubber-stamp entries for someone else's library internals. Enrolling only reagent/src and uix/src is cheap and buys least, because the value of enrolling a root is catching a NEW namespace appearing beneath it and each holds exactly one door.

WHY CLOSE RATHER THAN KEEP IT OPEN AS 'the standing question'. It has already cost one wasted worker cycle: PR #9108's worker was briefed from the TITLE ('decide how far to widen'), enrolled nothing, and correctly reported that the two rulings above had already answered it. The bead's own last note says so and names the cause — 'the title is what invites the re-dispatch'. An open bead whose title reliably provokes a dispatch that must then be talked back out of is not a standing question; it is a trap with a queue position. The stance is explicit that we do not litigate every last fine detail.

NOTHING IS LOST BY CLOSING. The reactivation trigger is a CODE event, not a tracker one — a tree acquiring a second requirable door — and the rule that recognises it now lives beside the mechanism where the next reader of roster-covered-roots will meet it. title: skill(re-frame-migration): guided-views-m11.md is 39,701 bytes — 2.4x the leaf ceiling, and its size is inherent rather than duplication
notes:
FILED BY THE MAYOR 2026-09-03 03:0x AUSEST, from migskill-g's report on PR #9033, so an oversized leaf is not invisible to the next size audit.

WHAT LANDED. rf2-v8ybm split SS-M-11 out of guided-handlers-state.md (62,782 -> 24,231 bytes, meeting that bead's ~24 KB acceptance) into a new sibling leaf guided-views-m11.md. THE NEW LEAF IS 39,701 BYTES — 2.4x the 16 KB per-leaf ceiling in skills/README.md.

THE WORKER REPORTED IT RATHER THAN TRIMMING TO HIDE IT, WHICH WAS CORRECT AND IS WHY THIS BEAD EXISTS RATHER THAN A SILENT REGRESSION. Its ruling said explicitly: if a half still exceeds 16 KB after the split, report the figure and stop rather than trimming to reach it. It did, and it states the size is INHERENT to the section rather than duplication — the same finding its sibling bead rf2-su7xh produced, where the dedupe seam turned out to account for ~3 KB of a ~15 KB gap.

SO THIS IS NOT A REPEAT OF rf2-v8ybm AND MUST NOT BE ACTIONED AS ONE. The obvious instinct — split again — is the thing to check rather than assume: SS-M-11 is one migration rule, and a rule split across two leaves is a SKILL -> A -> B routing problem or a reader who has to load both, either of which is worse than the ceiling breach. Establish first whether the section has a genuine internal seam the way runtime-smoke-test.md had a checklist/loop seam. If it does not, the honest options are the catalogue exemption (test: would splitting reduce total tokens loaded per session?) or an explicit recorded exception, and BOTH are family-contract calls for the mayor or Mike, not a worker.

DO NOT TRIM TEACHING TO REACH A NUMBER. That is the standing answer on both sibling beads and the stance's own position.

VERIFY THE FIGURE BEFORE ACTING — measure the leaf at whatever tip is current, LF-normalised, and against both halves of the ceiling (250 lines AND 16 KB); rf2-su7xh's leaf passed the line half by 132 lines while failing the byte half by nearly 2x, so the comfortable number is not the one that decides.

DEPENDS ON PR #9033 MERGING; until then the file does not exist on main.
MAYOR RULING, 2026-09-03 04:4x AUSEST — RECORD THE EXCEPTION, DO NOT SPLIT AGAIN. AND CHECK ME BEFORE YOU IMPLEMENT IT: SEE THE LAST PARAGRAPH, WHICH IS NOT OPTIONAL.

THE REASONING. skills/README.md's exemption bullet carries a SHAPE qualifier (catalogue-shaped) and a TEST ('would splitting reduce total tokens loaded per session?'). guided-views-m11.md is not catalogue-shaped — it is one migration rule, M-11, with its guidance — but it passes the test decisively, and for a stronger reason than a catalogue does: a reader following M-11 needs the whole rule. A catalogue reader at least MIGHT need only one entry; an M-11 reader needs M-11. Splitting a single rule across two leaves produces either a SKILL -> A -> B chain, which the family contract forbids outright, or a reader loading both halves every time plus an extra file handle. So the test's answer is NO with no ambiguity, and the shape qualifier is the part that does not fit.

WHY THAT IS NOT A LOOPHOLE. The test is what the bullet says decides; the shape is how it describes the case it had in mind. A leaf that passes the test for a reason the bullet did not anticipate is a gap in the bullet's wording, not a licence to ignore the ceiling — which is exactly why this ruling is RECORD THE EXCEPTION rather than CLAIM THE EXEMPTION. Write it as a named exception with its reason, so the next size audit reads a decision instead of re-deriving one, and so nobody generalises it to leaves that merely happen to be large.

WHAT IS REFUSED. Splitting M-11 again (a rule across two leaves is a routing problem, not a size fix). Trimming teaching to reach 16 KB — that is the standing answer across every leaf-size bead this session. And inventing a second numeric ceiling, which would be litigating minutiae.

NOW THE PART THAT IS NOT OPTIONAL, AND IT IS HERE BECAUSE I GOT THIS WRONG TODAY. On rf2-wgvyx I refused a leaf the catalogue exemption WITHOUT CHECKING WHETHER ANY RECORD ALREADY GRANTED IT. Two did, in the package's own spec, and the contradiction is now rf2-j5na, awaiting a maintainer. So: BEFORE implementing this ruling, read skills/re-frame-migration/spec/design.md and spec/authoring-prompt.md and skills/README.md for anything that already speaks to leaf size or exemptions for THIS skill. If a record already grants an exemption, say so and follow it rather than adding a second. If a record CONTRADICTS this ruling, STOP, report it, and do not resolve it by picking the newer record — that is a maintainer call. A verified 'a record already covers this' is a complete deliverable and is worth more than the edit.
close_reason: Exception recorded in PR #9039, per the mayor ruling. DID THE RULING'S LAST PARAGRAPH FIRST: no record contradicts the ruling, so no STOP was warranted. What each record said -- skills/README.md 'Leaf size discipline' carries the ceiling (250 lines AND 16 KB) and the exemption bullet, names re-frame2-pair/references/recipes.md and re-frame2-pair-retro/references/known-frictions.md as examples with only known-frictions.md 'recorded exempt', and says NOTHING about guided-views-m11.md; its closing sentence ('refactor targets unless they pass the catalogue test above') makes the TEST the discriminator, which AGREES with the ruling. spec/design.md ALREADY COVERS PART OF THIS: it records guided-views-m11.md among leaves running over the 250-LINE soft ceiling 'because their shape-catalogue / worked-example content resists further splitting', and separately that 'M-11, the largest single conversion, is its own leaf (guided-views-m11.md, rf2-v8ybm)' -- so the line half was already granted with a reason, and it is SILENT on the byte half, which is what this bead is about. spec/authoring-prompt.md restates the 250-line soft ceiling for the Type A split only; no exemption, nothing about this leaf or bytes. spec/improving.md and spec/inputs.md: NOTHING AT ALL, no size statement (a real answer, recorded as one). CONSEQUENCE: because one record already grants the line half, I EXTENDED that existing design.md record to the byte half rather than adding a second competing one -- which is what the ruling asks when a record already covers the ground. RE-MEASURED at my own base, LF-normalised: 261 lines, 39,701 bytes = 1.04x the 250-line half and 2.42x the 16 KB half. The bead's 39,701 is exact; the working file's 39,962 is pure CRLF inflation (261 lines x 1 byte), and git cat-file -s on the committed blob confirms 39,701. The bead's warning held: it clears the line half by 11 lines while missing the byte half by 2.4x. NOT split, NOT trimmed, no second numeric ceiling invented. The record states it is a named exception rather than a claimed exemption (the test answers no decisively; the catalogue-shape qualifier does not fit one rule) and forbids generalising it to leaves that merely happen to be large. Gates green: doc-slugs 0 (and a planted-fault sabotage run on this very anchor went red, exit 1, proving the gate read this worktree), mkdocs --strict 0, migration-cites 0, contract-drift 0, package-refs 0, readme-links 0.

description:
## CLAIM

`skills/README.md` §Leaf size discipline: "each leaf file SHOULD be ≤250 lines AND ≤16 KB (target ~150 lines / ~10 KB) — the byte ceiling catches leaves whose long unwrapped prose lines fit under the line count but still bloat the per-session token load … catalogue-shaped leaves … may exceed the ceiling if splitting would multiply file-handle overhead without reducing tokens-per-session. Test: would splitting reduce total tokens loaded per session? … leaves that have since outgrown them are refactor targets unless they pass the catalogue test."

## TRUTH AT TIP (`wc -lc skills/re-frame2/patterns/*.md`)

| leaf | lines | bytes | over 16 KB by |
|---|---|---|---|

| `form-action.md` | 229 | 25,307 | +58% |
| `resources-mutations.md` | 209 | 20,058 | +25% |
| `forms.md` | 211 | 17,447 | +9% |

All five pass the line ceiling and fail the byte ceiling — exactly the case the byte ceiling was added for. None is catalogue-shaped: each is one pattern with one canonical declaration, and splitting would not reduce tokens-per-session. What inflates them is the same point stated two or three times in different sections:

- `form-action.md` — the redirect-vs-navigate rule at L154-162 (in-code comment), L173 (prose paragraph), and L209 (anti-pattern); the fail-closed CSRF compare at L128-135, L181, L203; the token-not-in-the-field-schema rule at L43, L183, L204; the `:form-params` normalisation seam at L14, L68, L101, L205-206. - `resources-mutations.md` — the workflow-vs-cache axis at L41-50, L82, L192, and the watcher-reaction warning at L82, L191 plus `stale-detection.md:328`.

Bring each under 16 KB by de-duplicating, not by splitting: keep each rule's code-adjacent statement, cut the prose restatement and the anti-pattern restatement down to one line that names the section that states it. title: skill(re-frame2-pair): split the screen-read + Hicasso-evidence block out of ops.md (64 KB, 4x the leaf ceiling)
description:
## CLAIM

`skills/re-frame2-pair/references/ops.md` is 318 lines / 63,758 bytes — 4x the 16 KB per-leaf byte ceiling in `skills/README.md` §Leaf size discipline (1.3x the 250-line ceiling; the byte ceiling exists precisely for long unwrapped table rows like this file's). The catalogue exemption there is a test, not a pass: "would splitting reduce total tokens loaded per session?"

## APPLYING THE CATALOGUE TEST HONESTLY

ops.md is two things stapled together:

**Catalogue (keep together, locked):** §Read, §Frames, §Write, §Trace, §Live watch, §Signal recording, §Hot-reload coordination, §Time-travel, §Dropped from v1 — op tables plus the protocol sections that `spec/design.md:134` and `spec/authoring-prompt.md:33` explicitly LOCK into ops.md ("The hot-reload protocol and v1 → v2 surface-map both live in ops.md as sections rather than separate leaves"), and that `tests/prompts/prompt_regression_test.clj` reads from ops.md by anchor (`ops.md#hot-reload-coordination`, `section-from @ops-md "Hot-reload coordination"`). Roughly 42 KB.

**Not catalogue (split candidate):** lines 108–203, ~22 KB — §DOM source bridge, §Reading what's on screen (`read-dom` vs `read-ui`), and §Hicasso evidence (mounted boundaries / read attribution / render cause). This is a self-contained "what is on screen and why did it render" concern: the Hicasso block alone is ~10 KB of honesty-marker prose (added under rf2-6c12m, `3043d1aca4`, AFTER the file-structure lock was written), not op rows. SKILL.md's loading map already routes to it as its own task shape (`SKILL.md:186-188`: two rows pointing at `ops.md#view--rendered-content…` and `ops.md#hicasso-evidence…`), and `mcp-transport.md:84-88` links the five screen/evidence tools to those anchors.

Token test, both directions: an agent doing a read/dispatch/trace/time-travel session loads 64 KB and never reads the 22 KB screen block; an agent answering "why did this boundary render?" loads 64 KB for a 10 KB section. A split reduces tokens-per-session for every session that is not both — which is nearly all of them. That is the opposite of the "multiplies file handles without reducing tokens" case the exemption protects.

## RECOMMENDATION (one PR)

- New leaf `references/screen-reads.md` (~22 KB — itself still over the ceiling, but one concern; name is a suggestion) holding ops.md lines 108–203 verbatim: DOM source bridge, read-dom vs read-ui, Hicasso evidence.
- ops.md keeps a one-line row per moved section in its §Contents pointing at the new leaf; its own size drops to ~42 KB, and everything the design lock and the prompt-regression test name stays where it is.
- Update the anchors: `SKILL.md:186-188` (loading map), `mcp-transport.md:84-88` (five rows' "Semantics home"), `recipes.md` wherever it links `ops.md#dom-source-bridge` / `#read-dom…` / `#hicasso-evidence…` (grep before moving), and `spec/design.md:119` + `spec/authoring-prompt.md:34` file-structure listings (add the new leaf; the lock is on hot-reload + v1 map, which do not move).
- Do NOT split hot-reload or the v1 map (locked + tested), and do not split the op tables (that is the catalogue the exemption is for).

If the maintainer would rather keep ops.md whole, the honest alternative is to record ops.md as an accepted exception in `skills/README.md` §Leaf size discipline with the reasoning — the current state is neither.

## GATE

`python scripts/check_skill_mcp_drift.py --verbose` (mcp-transport.md rows survive; 29 = 29); `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` (every moved anchor resolves — skills/ is in its roots; this is the gate that catches a broken `ops.md#hicasso-…` link); `bb tests/prompts/prompt_regression_test.clj` (`skill-router-still-points-at-hot-reload`, `hot-reload-*`, `ops-md-raw-eval-rows-carry-privacy-carveout` all read ops.md and must stay green — they will, since nothing they name moves). Verify by hand that SKILL.md still loads at most two leaves for the screen-read task shapes (it does: SKILL.md + the new leaf).

## ACCEPTANCE

ops.md ≤ ~42 KB with the screen-read/Hicasso block moved to one new leaf; every former `ops.md#…` anchor for that block resolves at its new home; the three gates green; `spec/design.md` §5 lists the new leaf.

title: http: re-frame.http-privacy-integration-test fails when run as a solo namespace (order-dependent fixture fragility, pre-existing)
description: Running the http artefact's privacy integration namespace ALONE — clojure -M:test -n re-frame.http-privacy-integration-test — fails 4 tests that are green in the full-suite ordering: response-body-decode-schema-sensitive-slot-redacted-in-replied-trace, response-body-whole-body-sensitive-decode-schema-redacts-all, response-body-large-slot-elided-in-replied-trace (ERROR), accept-failure-emits-category-trace-with-schema-classified-decoded. Measured 2026-08-31 during rf2-lddbk (PR #8818) on the UNTOUCHED base version of the file at trunk 95222a2c3d: solo run captured exit 1 (Ran 17 tests, 3 failures 1 error), full-suite run captured exit 0 (502 tests, 3827 assertions). The failures show schema-marked sensitive slots riding unredacted (e.g. bearer-secret at [:tags :value :token]), so some state a PRIOR namespace's load or fixture normally establishes is missing in the solo ordering — likely a registration (schemas artefact load? classification hook?) that make-reset-runtime-fixture does not itself establish. Not introduced by rf2-lddbk: reproduced byte-identically on the base file. Impact: low — CI runs the full suite — but it makes focused local iteration on that namespace read false-red and could mask real regressions behind expected noise. Fix shape: make the namespace self-sufficient (require/establish whatever the redaction path needs) or teach the fixture to establish it.
notes:
VERDICT (PR #8889, branch worker/http-robust-o9e15): FIXED. Premise reproduced exactly at trunk 24b33a618a before any edit - solo exit 1 (20 tests, 3 failures, 1 error), full suite exit 0 (508 tests, 3881 assertions) - and the guess recorded in the description turned out RIGHT, now verified at source rather than guessed.

ROOT CAUSE - the missing establishment is the re-frame.schemas NAMESPACE LOAD. privacy-body/decode-schema-marks reaches the per-slot classifier through the late-bind hooks :schemas/extract-sensitive-paths-from-schema and :schemas/extract-large-paths-from-schema, which re-frame.schemas publishes at the bottom of its facade ns (re_frame/schemas.cljc). privacy-body/extract-paths returns an EMPTY MAP when the hook is unbound, so an unloaded schemas artefact does not error - it silently classifies nothing, and every schema-marked secret rides verbatim. Probed directly under this namespace own require set: hook unbound, marks empty; after requiring re-frame.schemas the same schema yields the expected [:token] sensitive mark. In the full suite the alphabetically earlier re-frame.http-privacy-body-test - which ALREADY carries this require, commented load-bearing - binds the hooks first, which is the accidental establishment that made the full ordering green.

All four reported failures are that one cause. The ERROR on response-body-large-slot-elided-in-replied-trace is the same thing wearing a different face: contains? was called on the UNelided String and threw IllegalArgumentException.

REPAIR - declare the dependency in this namespace require, exactly as the sibling re-frame.http-privacy-body-test already does. NOT fixed in make-reset-runtime-fixture: that fixture lives in implementation/core, which must not load an optional artefact, since the whole point of the late-bind seam is that core does not depend on schemas. No assertion was weakened - these pin that secrets are redacted, and making them laxer would have converted a test-ordering defect into a silent privacy hole.

GATES on the final rebased base, captured exit codes: solo re-frame.http-privacy-integration-test exit 0 (20 tests, 49 assertions) - the red-to-green control; full suite exit 0 (508 tests, 3883 assertions) - unchanged green. The diagnostic probe was exercised in BOTH directions in one run (unbound hook yielding no marks, then bound hook yielding the expected mark), so its nothing-here answer was checked against an input it should flag.

WORTH KNOWING - CI only ever runs the full-suite ordering (jvm-http in test.yml runs a bare clojure -M:test), so no gate would have caught this, and none will catch the next namespace that acquires the same latent dependency. Related: rf2-o9e15 rode the same worker; the two turned out INDEPENDENT - shared shape, unrelated mechanisms.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #8889 (commit 54cc3e9f3e, branch worker/http-robust-o9e15). The missing establishment was the re-frame.schemas namespace load, which publishes the :schemas/extract-sensitive-paths-from-schema and :schemas/extract-large-paths-from-schema late-bind hooks; privacy-body/extract-paths returns an empty map when they are unbound, so classification silently did nothing and schema-marked secrets rode verbatim. Repaired by declaring that require in the test namespace, matching the sibling re-frame.http-privacy-body-test. Control: solo run exit 1 (3 failures, 1 error) before, exit 0 (20 tests, 49 assertions) after, with the full suite exit 0 (508 tests, 3883 assertions) throughout. No assertion weakened. title: hic: tool.cljs unjoinable-intent branch (id-less trace bundle) — reachable per Spec 009, unexercised
description: From rf2-dr90's audit. tool.cljs's merge-fragments/intent-rows (~:566-577, :587) handle a ring bundle with no :dispatch-id: it keeps its own identity, sorts last, exports :unknown. Zero exercise anywhere. Spec 009 §Dispatch correlation explicitly admits trace events with NO :rf.trace/dispatch-id ('emitted outside any in-flight run — handler registration before any dispatch, REPL evals that don't dispatch — carry no dispatch-id'), so the branch is NOT dead defensive code; what is unestablished is whether such uncorrelated events can reach read-intents' window through trace-tooling/trace-buffer's bundling, or whether the buffer drops them before the tool sees one. Task: establish that reachability first; if reachable, add the row (assert identity kept, sorted last, :unknown exported); if the buffer provably cannot deliver one, record that as the finding on this bead and close without a test.
notes:
FENCE - SEQUENCED BEHIND PR #8737 (rf2-dr90's draft), recorded 2026-08-29 10:32 AUSEST by the merge+dispatch tick. Same hicasso test surface as the live dr90 worker. Dispatch after #8737 merges, off the post-merge trunk. PLANNED SHAPE: cluster with rf2-s2ta and rf2-xofa. Whoever dispatches strikes this fence line in the same act.

REACHABILITY VERDICT (2026-08-29, hic-browser-rows cluster worker, measured at source on worker/hic-browser-rows off trunk 6eb0a2a402): NOT REACHABLE through trace-tooling/trace-buffer's bundling — closing without a test, per this bead's own terms.

THE EVIDENCE, all four legs at source:
1. read-intents' window is exactly (trace-tooling/trace-buffer fid) per frame (tool.cljs:633; explain-render's window :795 is the same door). The per-frame ring is the ONLY supplier of bundles to intent-rows.
2. The ring cannot retain an id-less event. push-to-ring! guards (when (and dispatch-id frame-id) ...) — implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/tooling.cljc:251-259 — and its docstring names the rule: frameless emits stream live to listeners only and are never retained. That is Spec 009's B3 ruling verbatim: spec/009-Instrumentation.md:879 'frameless events SKIP the rings entirely ... NEVER retained in any ring', :881 'no shared uncorrelated bucket, no fallback slot', :965 'Frameless events bypass the ring'.
3. A bundle is minted ONLY from ring run-keys: frame-ring-event-bundles maps :run-order and event-bundle seeds :dispatch-id from that key (tooling.cljc:476-488, :414-420), so a bundle's :dispatch-id is non-nil by construction. The other trace-rings writers (set-frame-events-retained! ~:204, clear-trace-buffer! ~:563, clear-trace-rings! ~:582, the inherited-default retune ~:646) resize or empty rings and mint no run key.
4. The uncorrelated events Spec 009 SDispatch-correlation admits (registry-time emits, REPL evals — spec line 72) therefore exist on the LIVE listener stream only. The :ungrouped slot at spec :798 belongs to the flat-stream group-by-event PROJECTION, not to the ring, and read-intents does not consume it.

CONCLUSION: tool.cljs's unjoinable branch (:576-577 nil-id assoc; :581-582 sorts-last; :587 exports evidence/unknown) is defensive-in-depth against a shape the buffer provably cannot deliver. The branch STAYS — it also defends the sort/export against a hypothetical manual emit carrying a non-numeric :rf.trace/dispatch-id with a :frame tag (tooling.cljc:255-257 calls that 'extremely rare - a manual emit from outside any framework boundary'), and against any future ring-side change — but no test can honestly reach it through the public path, and fabricating a windows map to force intent-rows through it would pin nothing the runtime can produce. Grepped: ::unjoinable appears only at its definition site; zero exercise anywhere, as the audit said.

description:
# hic-064 — FINAL CHECKPOINT: the §13 definition-of-done audit

**Phase**: 6 exit · **Wave**: G · **Est.**: L · **Depends**: hic-019, hic-026, hic-038, hic-048, hic-050, hic-060, hic-061, hic-062, hic-066, hic-068, hic-069, hic-071, hic-072 (re-runs the naming-ledger completeness grep — no provisional name ships)
**Surface**: read-only + final report + corrective bead files

## Goal
The independent, adversarial audit of every synth-codex §13 bullet — completeness, correctness, and quality assessed separately, by a fresh reviewer who trusts artifacts over claims.

## Review protocol
1. **Completeness**: §13 bullet by bullet, **verbatim from the spec** — package independence, small coherent language with no mode switch, explicit substrate/two-hook choices with the byte-exact shell disposition, full correctness matrix with sabotage controls, public-surface-only witnesses (incl. the hic-078 editor/grid), React-interop contract, per-surface SSR/hydration, ratified budgets met via the hic-071 reconciliation table (no silent breach rows), qualified bulk dispositions per hic-036, the warm-allocation non-claim (hic-072), native island parity vs both controls, testing ladder with honest opacity, Xray causal + privacy + erasure, every use case assigned, requirements mine + per-keystroke current, resource-demand verdict explicit (hic-050), donor independence (hic-062/076).
2. **Correctness**: clean-checkout full-suite run; re-run one sabotage per checkpoint domain (kernel, slice, native, coverage) plus the naming-census and erasure positive controls; verify the budgets reconciliation against a fresh pinned run on the physical reference profile.
3. **Quality**: the hic-069 fresh-reader result reviewed; three randomly chosen complaint ids traced id → docs anchor → recovery; the anti-cathedral check — list anything that grew beyond its witness.

## Green definition and output
**Green** = every §13 bullet green AND zero unresolved correctness/coverage rows in the hic-073 correction ledger. Anything else is a **non-release verdict** with the misses enumerated. The audit distinguishes two states explicitly: *implementation audit complete* (achievable without pilots) and *product definition of done* (red until hic-063 supplies two pilots — say so plainly). Output: `docs/design/hicasso/product/definition-of-done-audit.md` with per-bullet verdicts and the filed correction ids. Thresholds never widen to turn a bullet green.

---
[Worker context — applies to every hic bead]
PATH MAP: the normative documents are published in-tree by bead rf2-hic-000:
- docs/design/hicasso/product/decision-brief.md  (= synth.md / "the decision brief")
- docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md   (= "spec SN" / synth-codex.md)
- docs/design/hicasso/product/lanes/<name>.md    (= codex/<name>.md)
References to `fable/...` are operator-local provenance; workers do not need them.
PROPOSED-ID MAP: "hic-NNN" in any bead text = tracker id rf2-hic-NNN. The dependency manifest is authoritative over prose Depends lines.
WORKER PROTOCOL (mandatory):
1. Run the worker worktree guard before edits: sh scripts/assert-worker-worktree.sh; report WORKTREE_ROOT.
2. Read first: the path-mapped documents this bead names.
3. Gates: foreground a gate that fits inside the harness ceiling; DETACH one that does not and poll BOTH its log and its `.exit` file in a bounded loop within the same turn — never end the turn waiting for a completion event. Never pipe a gate through `tail` or any filter; redirect to a log and echo the runner's own exit code on the same command line. Commit and open the PR before ending the turn. DOC-SURFACE GATE: for an edit confined to docs/design/hicasso/, `mkdocs build --strict` is NOT the gate — mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs keeps that tree out of the site. `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` validates its markdown link targets and heading anchors, and `scripts/check_provenance_pins.py` validates changed pages under docs/design/hicasso/; nothing validates its tables, rendering or nav, so verify anchors and table column counts BY HAND and say so in the PR body.
4. Never `git stash`. Commit first, then rebase.
5. Never commit `.beads/issues.jsonl` or `.beads/metadata.json` from a worker branch — they are whole-database EXPORTS, not database files, and your branch carries the snapshot taken when its worktree was created, so committing one TIME-TRAVELS the tracker: beads closed since reopen, beads filed since vanish (PR #6677 did exactly this, 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral). Any other database-derived path likewise. The human-authored config — `.beads/README.md`, `.beads/config.yaml`, `.beads/.gitignore`, `.beads/hooks/**` — IS fair game. CLAUDE.md's Beads durability section is the authority.

A 502 FROM A MUTATING GITHUB ENDPOINT DOES NOT MEAN THE MUTATION DID NOT HAPPEN — do not retry it (2026-08-06).

WHAT HAPPENED: gh pr merge returned exit 1 with "non-200 OK status code: 502 Bad Gateway" from nginx. The PR still read state=OPEN, mergeable=MERGEABLE, mergeState=CLEAN, 0 fails, 0 pending - every signal saying "retry me". I retried three times. Each subsequent attempt failed with a DIFFERENT error: "GraphQL: Merge already in progress (mergePullRequest)".

SO THE FIRST CALL SUCCEEDED SERVER-SIDE AND ONLY ITS RESPONSE WAS LOST. The 502 was a failure to hear the answer, not a failure to act. Every retry was fighting a merge that was already running, and the PR reading OPEN was just the API not yet reflecting an in-flight operation.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE SECOND ERROR, NOT THE FIRST. A genuine "merge did not happen" retries into the same 502 or into a real refusal (CONFLICTING, failing checks). "Already in progress" is positive evidence the first attempt took. Read the error TEXT on retry rather than the exit code.

AND CHECK WHETHER THE API IS BROADLY UNHEALTHY BEFORE ASSUMING AN OUTAGE: gh api rate_limit, gh pr list and git ls-remote were all fine here, which localised it to one in-flight merge rather than a GitHub incident. That took one command and stopped me diagnosing the wrong thing.

THE ACTION IS TO WAIT ONE TICK. The merge completes on its own; the next survey shows it MERGED. This is the same family as the reaping and merging errors this session - a signal that reads as "nothing happened" when something did - but with the polarity reversed, which is why it fooled me for four attempts.

A BEAD CAN BE WIDENED BY THE AUDIT WHILE A WORKER IS ALREADY HOLDING IT, AND A CORRECT NEWEST-FIRST WALK AT DISPATCH TIME WILL MISS IT (2026-09-03).

MEASURED. A worker on rf2-6me0 did the history walk exactly as prescribed and CORRECTLY reported zero text changes — because at that moment there were none. The audit's expansion landed at 02:11:24, minutes later, while the worker was mid-task. It discovered this only because 'bd close' echoed back a title it had never seen; it re-walked the history, REOPENED the bead, and did the widened work in a second commit.

WHY THE EXISTING RULES DO NOT COVER THIS. Everything written about bead currency is about the read at the START — order by tracker timestamps, walk newest-first, the description is the oldest text. All of that is correct and all of it is a read of a SNAPSHOT. Nothing says the snapshot can move under you, and on this project it routinely can: the merged-PR audit runs continuously and reopens or rewrites beads as it goes, which is the same mechanism that makes 'this cluster is the entire remaining backlog for the lane' a false claim.

THE CHEAP DEFENCE, WHICH COST THIS WORKER NOTHING AND SAVED THE TASK: READ WHAT bd ECHOES BACK. Close and update commands print the bead's CURRENT title. If that title is not the one you have been working from, the bead moved — stop and re-walk before believing your work is complete. That is a free check on every mutation you were going to make anyway.

THE SECOND DEFENCE, for a long task: re-walk the history once more before writing the PR body, not only at dispatch. A bead held for an hour on this project has a real chance of having been rewritten.

AND THE MAYOR-SIDE VERSION OF THE SAME THING: do not treat a brief's account of a bead as durable. Tell workers the bead outranks the brief — which the dispatch template already says — AND that the bead outranks the bead as they first read it.

THE BEAD BUILT ITS OWN DELIVERABLE FIVE DAYS EARLIER AND ITS DESCRIPTION WAS NEVER UPDATED. A second commit, 858cf77e9d on 2026-08-18 (rf2-yorfi), refined it further.

WHY THIS SHAPE IS EASY TO MISS. A bead that is 'partly done' usually reads as partly done. Nothing in the tracker links the two: the commit cites the bead, but the bead does not cite the commit. And a long-lived bead with a build half and a measure half is exactly where it happens, because the build half lands, the bead legitimately stays open for the measurement, and the description keeps describing the world before the build.

If the bead id appears there, the description is describing a world that ended. Do this in addition to grepping for the alleged missing symbol — the grep tells you the file exists, the log tells you WHO built it and under which bead, which is what distinguishes 'someone else overtook this' from 'this bead already did it'.

A BLOB-HASH "MISMATCH" CAN BE MSYS PATH MANGLING, NOT A REAL MISMATCH — but I TESTED IT and the plain form is safe (2026-07-26).

THE REPORT: the viewer-404 worker hit a blob-hash MISMATCH that was "MSYS mangling : into ;". It re-verified in PowerShell and ALL FOUR BLOBS MATCHED. So the mismatch was in the measuring instrument, not the artefact.

I TESTED IT IMMEDIATELY RATHER THAN PROPAGATE IT, because three of my standing hazards proved false today. IN THE PLAIN FORM IT DOES NOT REPRODUCE: git rev-parse HEAD:scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, the quoted form, --verify, and git ls-tree ALL RETURN THE SAME HASH here. So "MSYS mangles the ref:path colon" is NOT a general truth and must not go into briefs as one.

WHAT IS LIKELY ACTUALLY HAPPENING: MSYS converts arguments that look like Windows paths, and a WORKTREE-ABSOLUTE path such as C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2-worktrees/... carries its own colon. A comparison across worktrees using absolute paths is the shape that gets mangled — not HEAD:relative/path. The worker was comparing two worktrees; I was not.

THE PRACTICAL RULE, narrow and verified: a blob-hash MISMATCH IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A CONTENT DIFFERENCE. Before acting on one, re-run it a second way. Two colon-free alternatives exist and both work here: git ls-tree <ref> <path> | awk to take the hash, or re-run in PowerShell. AND USE REPO-RELATIVE PATHS, never worktree-absolute ones, in git arguments.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A NORMAL HAZARD: I MANDATE BLOB-HASH VERIFICATION IN EVERY BRIEF as the way to confirm what landed — it is what caught a bead I closed on a merge that did not carry it, an hour ago. AN UNRELIABLE VERIFIER IS WORSE THAN NONE, because it produces false alarms on correct work and would train workers to distrust the one check that has been catching real stale merges all day. Twenty PRs today merged a state older than the worker tip; blob hash is how that is found.

AND THE DISCIPLINE THAT MADE THIS RECORDABLE RATHER THAN CARGO-CULTED: the worker did not report "blob mismatch, something is wrong". It re-measured a second way, found the instrument at fault, and said so. That is the third false signal it caught in one bead — the others being an rc=1 from Node module resolution in a throwaway dir, and a waitForSelector timeout that was a same-document hash-navigation trap.

A BY-NAME LAW IS ONLY AS TOTAL AS ITS NAMING FUNCTION — the D022 defect worth generalising (2026-07-26, PR #7081).

THE DEFECT: the disjoint-plane guard compared RAW CLOJURE KEYS, while the crossing named keyword keys by `name` and everything else by `str`. So :key / "key" / :x/key all collapsed onto ONE React prop name — as did :children / "children" and :onSelect / "onSelect" — AND EVERY SECOND SPELLING WALKED PAST THE CHECK WRITTEN TO STOP IT. The guard was not weak; it was comparing in a different space from the thing it guarded.

THE FIX SHAPE, AND IT IS THE ONE THIS ARTEFACT KEEPS CONVERGING ON: it was closed AT THE NAMING BOUNDARY, NOT PER CHECK. A host prop name is EXACT — an unqualified keyword, which is ALREADY THE LAW the declaration states for :callbacks. That makes host-prop-name TOTAL, and every by-name law total with it, SO NO NEW PER-CHECK MACHINERY APPEARS. Fixing it per-check would have added N guards and left the N+1th wrong.

THE GENERALISATION: WHENEVER A CHECK AND THE THING IT CHECKS DISAGREE ABOUT IDENTITY, FIX THE IDENTITY FUNCTION, NOT THE CHECK. Ask what canonical form the law is stated over, and make one function total for it. This is the same move as making a projector reach by SHAPE rather than by a slot roster (rf2-wd9im), and the same as keying a pairing off the WHOLE operation keyword rather than its name half (rf2-6tags) — three instances this week of "a list of cases is a roster that rots; a total function is not".

TWO PROCESS NOTES FROM THE SAME PR WORTH KEEPING. (1) IT VIOLATED A FENCE I SET, CORRECTLY: react.cljs was fenced to a live optimisation worker, but the defect lives in host-props/host-element — D022 own code. It disclosed the violation, and VERIFIED the just-merged optimisation was untouched by checking line ranges (optimisation at 187-836, host block starts at 930) and confirming none of its six changes was altered. (2) ITS NON-VACUITY ARGUMENT IS THE BEST FORM I HAVE SEEN: the browser delta +5 tests / +27 assertions is EXACTLY its file browser-mode count, WHICH PROVES NO MOUNTED ROW TOOK THE skip! PATH. A raw count would not show that. And it REPLAYED THE MOUNTED ASSERTIONS TEN FURTHER TIMES — 11 runs byte-identical — applying the flaky-green rule unprompted.

A CENSUS THAT FLAGS ALMOST EVERYTHING IS NOT A DEFECT CLASS — IT IS A BROKEN COMPARISON SET, AND IT READS AS CORROBORATION (2026-09-03).

WHAT HAPPENED. Three beads independently reported the same shape: a marker in the tree gated on a bead id that does not exist. I tried to census the class by matching every rf2-* token across implementation/, tools/, docs/, spec/ and examples/ against the tracker export. Result: 5,179 distinct cited ids, 4,997 absent. I nearly reported that as a finding.

IT IS MEANINGLESS. The tracker holds ~516 issues; the tree carries thousands of historical citations, and this repo DELIBERATELY keeps them as provenance. CLAUDE.md itself cites rf2-0yp7w as the authoritative ui/freehand retirement disposition, and rf2-0yp7w.4 — its own child — is absent from the tracker too. So 'cited but absent' is the NORMAL state of a citation older than the current tracker, and a scan that flags 96% of its subject has told you about its own scope, not about the tree.

THE SHAPE OF THE MISTAKE, which loops.md already names for the inverse: a search returning ZERO is not a check that passed. THE INVERSION READS EVEN BETTER, because a scan returning EVERYTHING looks like a rich finding rather than like silence. Ask what the instrument COMPARED, not what it answered.

THE REAL CLASS, once scoped correctly, is narrow and worth fixing: not 'a citation to a dead bead' but A LIVE CONDITIONAL GATED ON NOTHING — a PROVISIONAL marker, a pending-on annotation, a 'revisit when X lands' note whose X cannot be found. A historical citation records why something is as it is and ages harmlessly. A pending marker is a promise to revisit that nobody can discharge, and it sits in the tree forever looking like live tracking. Search the MARKER VOCABULARY (PROVISIONAL, pending, 'until rf2-', 'when rf2-', 'blocked on rf2-'), then resolve only the ids those markers gate — and expect THREE outcomes, not two: phantom id, real-and-open (leave alone), real-and-closed (the promise was discharged, so the marker is stale, which is a different fix).

A CLJS TEST DOUBLE MUST MIRROR THE ARITY *SHAPE* OF WHAT IT REPLACES, NOT MERELY THE ARITY ITS CALLER HAPPENS TO USE — and getting this wrong fails on ClojureScript while passing on the JVM from the same `.cljc` source. Measured 2026-09-05 on `tools/story` (PR #9214).

THE MECHANISM, read in the emitted JavaScript rather than inferred:
  * `prepare-variant` is a two-arity `defn` — `([variant-id] [variant-id opts])`.
  * ClojureScript compiles a one-argument call site to the ARITY-SPECIALISED entry point:
        re_frame.story.runtime.prepare_variant.cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$1(variant_id)
  * The test's `with-redefs` double was `(fn [v] …)` — a SINGLE-arity fn, which compiles to a plain JS function carrying NO `cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$1` property.
  * `with-redefs` assigns that plain function straight over the fn object, so the call site reaches for a property that does not exist:
        TypeError: …prepare_variant.cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$1 is not a function

WHY THE JVM LANE PASSES ON THE SAME SOURCE: Clojure dispatches through the VAR on argument count at run time and has no static arity specialisation, so a single-arity double standing in for a multi-arity fn is invoked perfectly happily. **A green JVM suite is therefore no evidence at all about double shape.** This is a second member of the family with "test:cljs does not report :infer-warnings": a whole class of defect that only the ClojureScript compilation path can see.

THE RULE: when you `with-redefs` a multi-arity fn in a `.cljc` test, give the double EVERY arity the real fn has — not just the one the code under test calls today. A caller added later, or a code path you did not trace, reaches an arity your double lacks and fails with a TypeError that names a mangled JS property, which reads as a build or cache problem rather than a test bug.

AND FIX THE SIBLING DOUBLES EVEN WHEN CI HAS NOT NAMED THEM — this is NOT gold-plating, and the worker proved why. It also repaired the `reset-variant` double, which nothing had yet called. With the old single-arity double in place, the CLJS negative control (reverting the fix to check the witness still catches the original defect) would have ERRORED before reaching either assertion — so the control could not have reported at all. A malformed double does not merely hide one bug; it disables the instrument that proves the test is honest.

THE DIAGNOSTIC ROUTE WORTH COPYING: when a CLJS-only failure names a mangled property like `cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$N`, READ THE EMITTED JS. The worker found `stepper_state.js:80` and `stepper_state_cljs_test.js:910` and settled the question in two reads, rather than theorising about caches or stale builds. The mangled name IS the evidence.

A HEALTHY SIGN TO LOOK FOR AFTER SUCH A FIX: the assertion TALLY RISES. Here 35 -> 37, because three assertions sitting behind the exception ran for the first time. An arity repair that leaves the count unchanged did not actually unblock anything.

RELATED: [[test-cljs-does-not-catch-infer-warnings-that-break-under-advanced]], [[harness-reported-exit-code-disagrees-with-the-captured-one]].

TRACKER INTEGRITY: where beads close on PR-OPEN rather than on merge, a CLOSED bead can describe work that never landed — and no loop will ever re-read it.

Normally benign: changes merge within the hour and the window is invisible. It becomes real when a PR cannot merge — measured 2026-09-01, two drafts held by agents that went dormant, both beads CLOSED, git cherry reporting one unmerged patch each against main.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A REVERTED CLOSURE: a reverted closure reappears in the open list, where the backlog loop reads it. This one does not reappear anywhere. The backlog reread reads OPEN items by design, so a closure that was never TRUE is read by nothing, ever. The next person to touch that surface finds the defect still present with a closed item asserting it was fixed.

THE CHEAP DETECTION, worth running whenever a change sits unmerged for an unusual length of time: for each branch with an open PR, git cherry origin/main <branch> and grep for a leading +. Any non-zero count on a branch whose bead is closed is a tracker claim the trunk cannot back.

THE SYMMETRY WORTH REMEMBERING: this is the exact inverse of an OPEN item that is already DONE. Both are the tracker disagreeing with the tree. The open-and-done direction is caught by reading the tree during the backlog loop; the closed-and-undone direction is caught by nothing, because no loop reads closed items.

A committed run.cjs / shadow-cljs bench transcript trips the portability gate. Every hicasso lane driver prints 'shadow-cljs - config: <ABSOLUTE PATH>\implementation\shadow-cljs.edn', so committing a raw transcript as a dataset makes scripts/check-no-hardcoded-paths.sh (portability.yml, no || true, no continue-on-error) exit 1 with two violations per file (literal 'miket' + personal-named path). REDACT that one line to '<worktree>\implementation\shadow-cljs.edn' with an inline marker, and state the redaction in a README beside the data and on any page calling the transcript 'unedited' — the banner is load-bearing evidence that the run read the worker's worktree and not the mayor checkout, so deleting it costs real provenance. GREP TRAP that cost a round trip: a pattern written 'C:\Users\miket' in SINGLE quotes returns a FALSE ZERO on this setup — the backslashes are eaten before grep sees them. Use grep -F, or 'Users.miket' with a dot wildcard. Verified 2026-08-16 on PR #8329 (rf2-07rnj): gate exit 1 -> 0.

CONTROL DESIGN: "a green sabotage run is a reason to stop, not to proceed" has a specific mechanism worth naming — the control SETUP can make the defect unreachable, so the control passes against the very bug it exists to detect and reads as proof.

Measured 2026-09-01, rf2-mocn3 / PR #8883, caught by the worker itself. The defect: SSR Form-2 arity detection used try (apply inner args) / catch ArityException / retry (inner), so an ArityException thrown INSIDE a correctly-invoked inner is mistaken for an arity mismatch and the inner runs a SECOND time. The control counted invocations. Its first shape used a ZERO-arity inner under a ONE-arg component — so (apply inner args) threw on the invocation itself, before ever entering the body, and the retry path was never reached. Counter finished at 1. Green against exactly the defect it was built to detect, and it would have shipped as evidence.

THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS: for that retry to bite, the arity must MATCH on the first call, so the exception has to come from the body rather than from the invocation. The control has to put the code into the state where the bug is reachable — being merely "a test of the right function" is not enough.

GENERALISE IT AS A QUESTION TO ASK OF EVERY CONTROL, before running it and again if it comes back green: does my setup actually reach the code path the defect lives on, or does it fail earlier for an unrelated reason that looks like the same red? A control that fails EARLY is indistinguishable from one that fails RIGHT, because both are red — and one that passes early is indistinguishable from a fixed bug.

The rule that saved it is the doc rule already written: a green sabotage is a STOP. The worker took the green as a reason to investigate rather than to proceed, found the setup defect, reshaped the row, and added a companion same-arity row discriminating on the argument count in the exception message (which a counter cannot express). Both then went red under sabotage on both consumers.

MAYOR CENSUS ERROR: I recorded "77 lines across 12 files" with a per-file breakdown whose rows sum to 43. Seven files were missing and the note read as a complete enumeration. A fence derived from that list would have missed them.

CAUSE: I ran `git grep -c PATTERN -- dir/ | head -12` for the breakdown and a separate `git grep PATTERN | wc -l` for the total. The head truncated the file list; the total did not. Two commands, two scopes, presented as one measurement. Nothing errored, and 12 files beside a total of 77 looks entirely plausible.

THE RULE: a count and its breakdown must come from ONE unfiltered command, or the breakdown silently contradicts the count. If a listing has to be truncated for readability, say it is truncated and give the untruncated file COUNT beside it. And the arithmetic is the free check — if the rows do not sum to the total, one of them is wrong; the worker who caught this caught it exactly that way.

THIS IS MY OWN VERSION of the hazard I brief workers about constantly (a filter silently truncating while the result reads complete), arriving through `head` rather than through a paginated API. Enforcing a rule outward is not the same as applying it inward.

RELATED, from the same worker and worth carrying into any census brief: `git grep -c` counts SYNTAX, not meaning. For the [[wikilink]] census it overcounted the actual work by about 24%, because it cannot tell a wikilink from Clojure destructuring or an :fx vector. CLASSIFY BEFORE YOU COUNT, and say which of the two numbers a brief is quoting — raw matches or genuine hits.

A COUNT I PROPAGATED WAS WRONG, AND THE FIX WAS TO STATE NO COUNT (2026-07-26). I briefed "the analyzer records NINE per-site facts" into a spec-truth dispatch, taking the number from an earlier worker report. It is EIGHT.

THE FACTS: structural-manifest projects :events with select-keys [:sid :source-coord :path :prop :classification :serializable? :sync? :handler] — eight keys, exactly what fh-struct-010.edn pins. The analyzer INTERNAL record carries two more (:site-index, :view-id) that the projection drops. So "nine" conflated the internal record with the published projection, and I repeated it without checking.

WHAT THE WORKER DID INSTEAD OF CORRECTING THE NUMBER, which is the better answer: because :source-coord is genuinely OMITTED for a declaration with no reader location, ANY count is wrong for some declarations. So the new prose states NO COUNT AT ALL — it names the five facts the fixture pins. That is the counts-drift-names-dont rule arrived at independently, on a different surface, hours after another worker reached it in CI comments. Two workers converging on it from opposite directions is the strongest signal I have that it is a real rule and not a preference.

THE RULE, now twice-confirmed: a comment or a spec sentence that COUNTS a set is a claim that rots. Name the members, or name the authority that enumerates them. Applies to co-edited-file counts, roster sizes, job counts, key counts — every instance found today was wrong or became wrong.

ALSO WORTH KEEPING from the same report — a sentence that was false on BOTH sides of the tag boundary. docs/api/README.md intro closed "Every other page on this list describes a published artefact": false TODAY for the eight rf2-snjn5 coordinates, and false PERMANENTLY for Freehand. Rewritten as "an artefact the release workflow deploys", which is true now and after the tag. When a claim is wrong in both tag states, the fix is to re-anchor it on something the tag does not move — not to pick a side.

AND A DECLINE WORTH COPYING: it left spec/API.md:311, the donor ui/custom-element row, UNCHANGED after verifying the donor validator genuinely does not carry refused-property-names. The row is accurate FOR THE DONOR; making it track the Freehand refusal would be a code change wearing a docs PR. Verified the code before deciding the doc was wrong.

A DEPENDENCY CAN BE A STRING, AND NO STATIC TOOL WILL EVER SEE IT (2026-08-11, rf2-hic-076 census, PR #7837).

THE CASE. The census had to classify every Xray, Story and Pair consumer of the donor surfaces. Pair has NO :require of any donor and NO deps.edn coordinate — a classpath scan finds it clean. It is not. view_tool.cljs:128 holds (def ^:private tier-ns "re-frame.freehand.tool"), and that STRING is interpolated into every nREPL form Pair emits. All five of Pair's view tools target the donor by wire protocol.

The worker's line is the one to remember: "A classpath scan finds Pair clean; it is not."

WHY THIS COMPLETES THE GREP LESSON. I already had a-docstring-wikilink-reads-as-a-dependency-to-a-grep: grep OVER-counts, because prose looks like code. This is the opposite failure, and it is worse: the dependency is REAL, LIVE and SHIPPED, and every static instrument — grep for :require, classpath scan, deps.edn audit, the bijection gate — reports nothing. Over-counting makes work look harder than it is; UNDER-counting makes a disposition look safe when it is not. This census exists to unblock rf2-hic-062, a bead about DELETING the donor tree. Acting on a classpath scan alone would have deleted a tree five shipped tools still call.

THE SAME WORKER MEASURED BOTH DIRECTIONS ON ONE SURFACE: 48 files matched a naive grep over tools/; 23 were load-bearing and 25 named a donor only in a comment, docstring or spec sentence — including a registry whose ten hits were all comments, four of them recording that it has NO donor dependency. And re-parsing ns forms by paren balancing with docstrings stripped caught TWO REQUIRES A LINE-ORIENTED REGEX MISSED. So the naive tool was wrong in both directions on the same files.

THE RULE: when a census or disposition asks "does anything still depend on X?", static analysis answers only "does anything NAME x in code". Also ask: is X reachable by a STRING — an nREPL form, a dynamic require, a keyword namespace, a URL, a build-id, a classpath entry assembled at runtime? Those are invisible by construction, and they are exactly the couplings a deletion breaks.

MAYOR APPLICATION: for any bead whose verb is RETIRE, DELETE, DISPOSITION or ARCHIVE, require the worker to state which dynamic-reference kinds it checked and how — not merely that the greps came back clean.

A dev warning that DEDUPES PER AUTHORING SITE (Hicasso's missing-key warning, codec/check-member-key!) fires exactly once per site for the life of a test RUN. Any render of that site taken before the console spy is installed spends the site's one warning, and the CONTROL then reads zero while the claim it guards stays green. Take the warning readings FIRST in the deftest, before any byte-equality or fairness check renders the same arm. Hit in rf2-hic-033; the dedupe made the control fail rather than the claim, which is the right way round but only because the control existed.

A differential bench arm prices EVERYTHING the plainification deletes, not the one thing its label names. rf2-vw412: the hicasso-native minus hicasso row on our-walk-against-reagents.md was read as 'the price of the intent surface / 71 intent vectors', but plainify replaces every event position, and route-link mints an [::h/navigate {...}] at 207 more of them -- so the row was three-quarters route-link and the authored surface was ~12 ns/el, not 41 or 125. BEFORE attributing a differential row, make the instrument COUNT the roster the difference actually spans; a page-level count in prose (207 links, in the same document) is not the same as the arm's own count. The 3x move then attributed cleanly to one line (69678caee6 put (set (keys m)) on a per-link-per-render path), confirmed by a one-line ablation plus a LOCAL copy of the same check as positive control -- the local copy must NOT move, or the mutation reached more than it was aimed at.
