The roster is keyed the same way: "accessibility.md", "adoption.md", "build-a-view.md".

PR #7096 moves 18 guide pages into get-running/, authoring/, host/, advanced/ and operate/. After that move the corpus sees essentially only index.md.

SO THE FIX IS THE WALK, NOT THE ROSTER KEYS: traverse recursively and key on the path RELATIVE to guide-dir, then re-key the roster to those relative paths. Updating digests alone cannot clear it, and a recursive walk still keyed on .getName would collide across subdirectories.

THE GENERALISABLE HAZARD, which is why this is worth recording beyond one PR: a non-recursive walk plus a directory restructure has TWO possible outcomes and they look nothing alike. If the check asserts "every roster row has a matching block", an emptied corpus fails LOUDLY — fine, you fix it. If any arm asserts "every corpus block has a row", an emptied corpus makes that arm VACUOUSLY TRUE and the restructure SILENTLY DISARMS the gate. Same code, same edit, opposite consequences depending on which direction the assertion runs.

SO WHEN A RESTRUCTURE TOUCHES A TREE THAT A GATE WALKS, CHECK BOTH DIRECTIONS AND PROVE NON-VACUITY AFTER THE FIX: add a page in a SUBDIRECTORY carrying an unrostered block and require the gate to RED. A gate that passes on that has been disarmed, not fixed.

This is the same family as the other gate-blindness findings here — sound machinery with one direction it cannot see — but the trigger is new: the defect is introduced by moving FILES, not by changing code or data. Any bead that reorganises a directory should ask what walks it.

A DOCSTRING [[WIKI-LINK]] READS EXACTLY LIKE A DEPENDENCY TO A GREP, AND NOTHING HERE DISTINGUISHES THEM (2026-08-11, three instances in one session).

INSTANCE 1: the rf2-6ync triage worker reported that two SSR suites ":require each other" and both reach ssr.entry. I transcribed it into rf2-6rw9 and made "give the package an SSR entry first" that bead's content. Both false — each named the other once in a docstring [[wiki-link]], and neither reached entry at all.

INSTANCE 2: the rf2-b6ja worker found and corrected exactly that, with evidence (lines 31 and 57).

INSTANCE 3, AND THE ONE WORTH REMEMBERING: the merged-PR audit of that same correction found it had made THE SAME MISTAKE IN ITS OWN PROSE — claiming ssr.entry has seven requirers including ssr/fixtures.cljs, whose two mentions are also docstring wiki-links. The audit's words: "the very false-dependency class this section corrects." Six semantic consumers, not seven.

WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING: `git grep ssr.entry` returns requires, docstrings, comments and prose identically. The habit of "grep for the symbol" is right for finding candidates and wrong for counting dependents — and the wrongness is always in the direction of MORE COUPLED THAN REALITY, which makes work look harder than it is and can stall a bead for hours.

THE RULE: when counting or claiming a dependency, grep and then READ EACH HIT, or restrict the search to require/import forms. And when writing the count down, SAY WHICH QUESTION IT ANSWERS — "six semantic consumers, excluding strings and comments" — so the next reader knows whether docstrings were counted.

MAYOR-SPECIFIC: this is the concrete mechanism behind a-workers-reading-of-a-neighbouring-file-is-a-claim. The claim that keeps being wrong is nearly always a DEPENDENCY claim, and it is wrong because the tool everyone reaches for cannot tell prose from code.

A FENCE MUST NAME A PATH — naming a SURFACE abstractly does not fence anything (2026-08-14).

WHAT HAPPENED. I fenced one worker off "the browser runner" and gave another worker a bench re-home. Both edited implementation/scripts/compile-node-test.cjs — one adding warning-tally logic (a compile that succeeds with warnings is not a green lane), the other repointing a helper path out of the tree being deleted. Both changes correct, both in different regions, and a guaranteed merge conflict.

Neither worker did anything wrong. My fence said "the browser test runner plus its selector bookkeeping", which is a DESCRIPTION. A worker cannot check a description against its own diff; it can only check a path.

THE RULE: every DO-NOT-TOUCH entry is a path or a glob. If I cannot name the path, I do not yet understand the fence well enough to issue it, and I should either look it up or say plainly "this surface is contested — tell me what you plan to touch before you touch it".

AND THE DETECTION IS CHEAP AND SHOULD BE ROUTINE AT SCALE. One command finds every collision across the whole fleet:

  for b in <workers>; do base=$(git merge-base worker/$b origin/main);
    git diff --name-only $base worker/$b | sed "s|^|$b :: |"; done \
    | awk -F' :: ' '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -d

Duplicated paths ARE the collisions. It cost one command and found a conflict neither worker had reached yet. Run it every method-reread tick, and after any dispatch that widens a worker's scope.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE AT SIX WORKERS THAN AT THREE. Fences are pairwise, so contention grows with the square of the fleet while my attention does not. A description-shaped fence that survived three workers fails at six. The sweep scales where the reasoning does not.

WHAT TO TELL THE WORKERS when it happens: keep going, expect the conflict, resolve by keeping BOTH, and verify the resolution STRUCTURALLY rather than by eye — assert each side's contribution is present and that the difference from each side is exactly the other's. On a file with two independent edits, "looks right" is not evidence.

A FENCE MUST NAME PATHS THAT EXIST AND MUST NOT EXCLUDE WHAT THE ITEM REQUIRES — and when it fails either way, the ITEM governs and the worker is right to proceed. Three instances on 2026-09-05, all three correct, all three the mayor's error.

THE THREE, and they are three DIFFERENT failures:
  * **Excluded a required path.** Fenced `spec/Conventions.md` on a Story-manifest bead whose own audit note asked in terms for a sentence in that file. The worker edited it and justified the override properly: it checked the fence's stated REASON — concurrency — by enumerating the files every open PR touched, found none held it, and proceeded.
  * **Excluded a required path, again.** Fenced `implementation/core/src/**` on a bead that enumerates `router.cljc`'s `emit-throw-reject!` as one of its three required emit sites.
  * **NAMED A PATH THAT DOES NOT EXIST.** Fenced `examples/counter*/**` on the slim-counter bundle bead. Measured afterwards: **that glob matches ZERO tracked files**, against a control of 168 for `examples/**` — the tree is `examples/substrates/reagent_slim/counter/`. **A fence that matches nothing is not a fence**, and worse, it reads as one: the worker sees a bounded scope, the mayor believes a boundary is set, and neither is true. That same brief also fenced OUT the three files the item's acceptance criteria actually mandate (`implementation/shadow-cljs.edn`, `implementation/package.json`, and the gate script), because nothing under `examples/**` can change which `:init-fn` a build uses.

WHY I KEEP DOING IT: fences get built from PEER-COLLISION reasoning — who is live, what is hot zone — and pasted without re-reading the item's required surface or checking the paths resolve. That yields a fence correct about concurrency and wrong about scope, or one made of plausible-looking globs.

THE FIX, and it is two cheap commands:
  * **`git ls-files` EVERY fence glob before pasting it**, exactly as the brief already tells workers to do for the paths it cites. A zero means the glob is wrong, not that the tree is empty. Control it against a glob you know matches.
  * **Then re-read the item's own file list and confirm every required path is INSIDE the fence.** If a required path must be excluded because a peer genuinely holds it, that is not a fence — it is a SEQUENCING decision, and the bead should be held rather than dispatched with an impossible fence.

THE RULE FOR WORKERS, which all three followed: **the item governs over the brief**; where they conflict, follow the item and say in the report what differed. When overriding a fence, check its STATED REASON rather than the fence itself — if the reason still holds, stop and report; if it is measurably absent, proceed and show the measurement. The third worker did exactly that, naming the two open PRs and confirming no worktree held the files.

A FIFTEENTH WAY A SIGNAL LIES: A GREEN THAT IS ONLY SOMETIMES GREEN, AND ONE SAMPLE HIDES IT (2026-07-26).

The rf2-6pohj worker wrote a new browser scenario, ran it, got GREEN, and then did something almost nobody does: IT REPLAYED THE REAL SCENARIO IN A LOOP. Result: 3 FAILURES IN 8 RUNS. Two bugs, both its own — a wait-predicate that THE STALE ROSTER ALSO SATISFIED (the sub is epoch-pumped, so the pre-update state passed the wait), and a regex scraping ACROSS A SPAN BOUNDARY. After the fix: 0 failures in 12 runs.

Its own words: "Had I trusted the earlier green, this would have shipped a flaky PR-smoke gate."

WHY THIS IS DISTINCT FROM EVERY OTHER ENTRY ON THE LIST: the other fourteen are deterministic — a gate that cannot see a case, a mutation that did not apply, an exit code that is not a test outcome. This one is PROBABILISTIC, and a single run cannot detect it BY CONSTRUCTION. The standard proof protocol here (plant, confirm applied, observe red, restore, observe green) uses ONE OBSERVATION PER STATE, so it is blind to this class exactly when the new assertion is the flaky one.

THE RULE: A NEWLY WRITTEN NON-DETERMINISTIC ASSERTION IS NOT PROVEN BY ONE GREEN RUN. Replay it — a loop of 8-12 is enough to expose the common shapes — before shipping it into a gate that everyone else pays for. This applies to browser scenarios, anything awaiting a settle, and anything scraping rendered text.

THE TWO SHAPES IT FOUND ARE BOTH GENERALISABLE:
  1. A WAIT PREDICATE THE PRE-UPDATE STATE ALSO SATISFIES. If the thing you wait for is already true before the action, the wait returns immediately and the assertion races. Wait for something the OLD state cannot satisfy.
  2. A REGEX SCRAPING ACROSS A SPAN BOUNDARY. Rendered text is not a string; element boundaries move with layout and content. Assert against structure, or against text within one element.

AND THE SAME WORKER CORRECTED ITSELF ON A SECOND POINT WORTH KEEPING: its first draft asserted ":generation advances on re-render". Reading the source showed :generation is the HOT-RELOAD BODY REVISION, not a render tally, and that gen 0 is correct. It re-anchored the scenario on FRESH OCCURRENCE KEYS ACROSS A REMOUNT — a fact "a projection over a static registry cannot fake". Choosing an assertion that only the live path can satisfy is the whole art of a non-vacuous browser test.

A FIFTH WAY "RAN 0 TESTS" READS GREEN: A NAMESPACE THE RUNNER REGEXP DOES NOT MATCH, HOLDING READER-CONDITIONAL TESTS THE OTHER HOST ELIDES. Found by the rf2-r8trk worker (#6435), 2026-07-19, when its own vacuity probe failed to red.
THE MECHANISM: three #?(:cljs ...) tests lived in re-frame.story.xray-preset-test. That ns name does not match the :node-test build cljs-test$ ns-regexp, so the CLJS runner never selected it. And because the bodies are :cljs reader conditionals, the JVM reader ELIDES them. NEITHER HOST RAN THEM. Not "skipped" — invisible. No count moved, nothing reported.
⚠️ THE CONSEQUENCE, and why this matters more than a missing test: one of the three asserted (false? (xray-config-available?)) under the comment "this test assumes Xray is NOT on the classpath". That was UNTRUE WHEN WRITTEN and UNCATCHABLE — a test wrong from birth, structurally unable to fail. Fixing it required moving all three into the live sibling ns (10216 -> 10219 assertions) with a self-sufficient adapter fixture, then re-probing.

THE FULL ROSTER OF WAYS "GREEN" HAS MEANT "NOTHING RAN" IN THIS REPO — put ALL FIVE in test-touching briefs:
  1. a bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` run from implementation/ (wrong dir, 0 tests, exit 0)
  2. a CLJS runner selecting nothing after a namespace rename
  3. a clojure.test MAP fixture silently swallowing the test body (cljs.test handles maps fine — JVM does not)
  4. `clojure -M:test -v ns/a ns/b ns/c` running only the FIRST var (caught only by expecting 16 assertions and seeing 6)
  5. NEW: an ns outside the runner regexp holding reader-conditional tests the other host elides — runs on NO host
⚠️ THE ONLY RELIABLE DEFENCE IS THE VACUITY PROBE, AND IT MUST BE RUN PER TEST, NOT PER SUITE: flip the assertion, confirm the FULL gate reds NAMING YOUR TEST, restore, verify byte-identical. #6435 caught mechanism 5 ONLY because its probe did not red — the probe failing to red IS the signal. Treat a non-reddening probe as a finding, never as "close enough".
⚠️ AND CHECK ASSERTION COUNTS MOVE. If adding three tests does not move the count, they are not running. #6435 verified 10216 -> 10219.

I FORWARDED A WORKER'S FINDING INTO A LATER BRIEF WITHOUT NOTICING THAT THE SAME WORKER'S PR HAD ALREADY FALSIFIED IT (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: rf2-erre5's worker reported that two things remained STRUCTURALLY UNRECOVERABLE from an allocation record - the prime region's gap steps and the absolute heap level. True, and well evidenced. I put both into the rf2-9jrhi brief as standing constraints. But rf2-erre5's whole change was to RETAIN THE RAW SAMPLES, and it had merged before I wrote that brief. The bisect worker checked at source and refuted both: samples[1]-samples[0] gives the prime-region gap, samples[0] gives the absolute heap level. It then USED that recovered heap trajectory to rule out a candidate mechanism - so the correction was not cosmetic, it was load-bearing for its verdict.

THE SHAPE, AND IT IS GENERAL: A FIX WORKER'S FINDING DESCRIBES THE WORLD BEFORE ITS OWN FIX. Its report is written from inside the problem, and its PR is the thing that ends the problem. So the report's diagnosis section has a shorter shelf life than any other part of it - specifically, it expires the moment that PR merges, which is usually minutes later and often before the next brief is written.

WHY THE USUAL GUARD DID NOT CATCH IT: I do re-verify claims at origin/main HEAD. But this claim did not FEEL like a claim about the tree - it read as a structural fact about what a JSON record can express. It was actually a claim about what the runner writes, which is exactly what the merged PR changed.

THE CHECK: when quoting a worker's finding into a later brief, ask WHAT THAT WORKER'S OWN PR CHANGED, and whether the finding is about the surface its PR touched. If it is, the finding is about the pre-merge tree and must be re-derived, not forwarded.

WORTH NOTING THE COST WAS SMALL because the premises-are-claims sentence was in the brief: the worker checked, refuted, reported, and was better off for it. That sentence keeps earning its place.

MEASURED 2026-08-21, third pattern-under-match of one session. I briefed rf2-45ti9 with 'the population is EXACTLY ONE file carrying an unregistered --self-test', derived by grepping the literal '--self-test'. worker/ceilreg-45ti9 re-derived it and found TWO: the directory carries two spellings, '--self-test' (hyphenated, the alloc_* readers) and '--selftest' (unhyphenated, ladder_band.cjs). My pattern could not have matched the second one.

THE FAILURE IS NOT 'MY NUMBER WAS STALE'. It was current. The instrument measured the wrong POPULATION, and a census that cannot see part of its population reports its remainder in the same confident voice a complete one uses. I had even carried a positive control - five registered files that DO have --self-test - and it passed, because a positive control only rules out a DEAD pattern. It cannot detect a pattern that is alive and narrow.

THE RULE: a census keyed on a FLAG NAME, an OPTION, a KEYWORD or any other spelled token must enumerate the SPELLINGS before it trusts a count. Grep the argv-dispatch site, or the token minus its punctuation, and see how many forms come back. Hyphenated against unhyphenated is the recurring pair here.

AND I WAS PARTLY WRONG ABOUT THE EXCLUSIONS for the same reason. I dismissed the *_run.cjs files as 'browser runners, legitimately in no spine'. Four are in fact reached INDIRECTLY, via registered .test.cjs files that require them - alloc_level_witness, clock_check_standard, clock_run and hd8_run. My conclusion (do not register them directly) survived; my reasoning did not, and a worker following the reasoning rather than re-deriving would have inherited the error.

SO: when a brief hands a worker BOTH a number and the METHOD that produced it, the worker can catch the method. When it hands over only the number, it cannot. Give the method every time - that is what made this recoverable.

A FOURTH VACUOUS-PASS CLASS UNDER A PRODUCTION GATE — KEY-ABSENCE WHERE THE KEY IS ELIDED WHOLESALE. Found in sub-topology-test (rf2-d2841): `no-doc-key-when-not-supplied` asserts a key is ABSENT, and `:doc` is stripped entirely under `-Dre-frame.debug=false` — so it passed because the key can never exist in that posture, not because the registration omitted it. Same false-green as an empty trace ring, DIFFERENT SUBJECT: the dev-only half is not always a trace.
The four classes now are: (1) negative over an empty trace ring; (2) a namespace that is 100% dev instrumentation, so rostering it off reports green for a namespace that executed nothing; (3) a positive assertion the gate short-circuits (`(is (true? (validate-fx! ...)))` where the fn is `(if debug-enabled? (run-validation ...) true)`); (4) THIS ONE — absence of a key the gate elides wholesale.
THE GENERAL TEST STILL COVERS ALL FOUR, and is the thing to carry rather than the list: FOR EACH ASSERTION, ASK WHAT IT WOULD DO IF ITS SUBJECT SIMPLY NEVER EXISTED IN THIS POSTURE. If the answer is 'pass', it is vacuous — whether the subject is a trace, a namespace, a validator's verdict, or a map key.
ALSO PROVEN THIS PASS: reaching for the dev-only guard FIRST costs coverage. Five negatives were re-pointed at the always-on `:errors` axis instead of being guarded, and they stay load-bearing under the gate. `emit-error-both!` lifts `:failing-id` and `:reason` onto the production record, so assertions about WHY something failed often have a production-reachable channel — check for one before guarding.

A GATE CAN BE ARMED, RUN, WALK PAST ITS SUBJECT AND REPORT GREEN — the fifth member of the vacuous-green family (2026-08-14, rf2-cujx worker, filed as rf2-2cu7f P1).

WHAT IT FOUND. `impl-src-roots` enumerates artefact roots at DEPTH 1 ONLY. The four adapter artefacts live one level deeper, at `implementation/adapters/*/src`. So they are never walked.

PROVEN BY CALLING THE SUITE'S OWN FUNCTION rather than reproducing it: 377 files walked, ZERO adapter files. POSITIVE CONTROL: the floor lint walks 835 files including 14 adapter files, and warn-once walks 425 including the same 14 — so the files exist and other walkers see them. Only the two `impl-src-roots` consumers miss them.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE ARMING HOLE IT WAS FOUND BESIDE: `adapters/*/src` DOES arm `implementation_jvm=true`. So on an adapter PR the gate is armed, it runs, it walks past the tree, and it reports green. NO ARMING CHANGE FIXES IT. Every previous member of this family failed by not running; this one fails while running.

THE FAMILY NOW HAS FIVE MEMBERS, and the shape is always the same: a gate that never runs, never inspects, never compiles, never judges, or — now — never REACHES its subject reports nothing, and absence reads as green. THE TEST IS ALWAYS THE SAME: ask what the gate actually EXAMINED, not whether it passed. Print the count of things it walked and compare it against an independent walker.

EXPECT NEW FINDINGS WHEN THE WALK IS CORRECTED. That red is the gate working for the first time, not a regression.

A gate's exit code cannot distinguish a real pass from a vacuous one; count the population. Classifying eleven donor-consuming gates (rf2-ddu3i) needed a before/after count of what each gate actually asserted, because 0-of-0 passing and 60-of-60 passing are the same rc=0. Two useful tells: a gate that exports its own tables (check-bundle-isolation.cjs exports ARTEFACTS/POSITIVE_CONTROL) can be censused in-process without running its expensive build; and a gate that is fail-closed says so in its own message ('cannot prove sentinels present (would be vacuous)') — grep for that phrasing before assuming a scan goes quiet.

A GATE'S NAME DOES NOT TELL YOU ITS SUBJECT — read the script before nominating it, and before blaming it for missing something. Measured repeatedly, three distinct instances by 2026-09-05.

THE INSTANCES:
  * `scripts/check_skill_eval_packaging.py` sounds like it validates that a skill package ships what its instructions require. It does NOT. Its entire subject is whether a skill's PROSE and its `files` array contradict each other ABOUT WHETHER `evals/` SHIPS. I told a worker it was "directly on point" and "likely the gate that should have caught this"; the worker read it and found it could not have. A follow-up bead was filed for the invariant that WOULD catch it, with the caution that a naive version would fire on every legitimate conditional reference.
  * The job named `verify-readme-links` runs TWO gates, and the one that actually checks READMEs is `check_readme_links.py --ci`, not `check_doc_slugs.py` — whose roots exclude every README beside source. CLAUDE.md records this as "nominate by PATH, never by job name", measured twice.
  * `All required checks passed` reads like a host-generated summary row and is a REAL JOB (`test.yml`'s `all-required-passed`), which is why discounting it from the band admits a rollup one job short.

THE RULE: BEFORE NOMINATING A GATE IN A BRIEF, OPEN IT AND READ WHAT IT ASSERTS. One `cat` or `head -40`. And before writing "this gate should have caught it", read it again — a gate that misses its own apparent subject matter is a FINDING worth filing, but only after you have confirmed the subject really is its own.

THIS IS THE SAME ERROR SHAPE AS the invented `design-laws.md` citation and the "five registry-ish files" misreading: a plausible inference from a NAME, repeated into briefs without opening the thing named. On this project the name is never the evidence — the file is.

A GOOD ERROR MESSAGE THAT AN ARITY ERROR PREEMPTS IS A MESSAGE NOBODY EVER SEES (2026-07-26, rf2-txe8o worker, correcting MY brief). I briefed that 18 documented reg-route examples throw at registry.cljc:455, the guard that rejects :path inside the metadata map. WRONG BY ONE STEP, and the truth is worse: all 18 sites are 2-ARG calls, and reg-route only arity is [id metadata path], so they raise a raw ArityException BEFORE reaching 455. Line 455 fires only for a HALF-MIGRATED 3-arg call still carrying :path. So the carefully-written diagnostic naming the route id and the grammar is the one a reader in this situation NEVER SEES -- what they get instead names an internal var and a number. GENERALISE: when a bead says "this input hits guard X", check whether ARITY, destructuring, or a schema gate fires first. A guard positioned after an arity boundary is unreachable for the exact malformed shape people actually write, because dropping a required argument IS the common error. This is the ergonomics half of the pre-alpha stance -- a diagnostic that cannot be reached is not a diagnostic. SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, and it is the real one: 18 was ONE VERB OF FOUR. Reading arglists off the live facade, exactly four public reg-* verbs have no 2-arg arity -- reg-resource (21 bad sites), reg-route (18), reg-flow (8), reg-mutation (8) = 55 total, so the bead as filed covered 33% of its class, and THREE of the others are in the normative spec. Filed rf2-rzuc7. THE LESSON FOR FILING: when a bead enumerates every instance of a defect FOR ONE SYMBOL, ask whether the symbol is the right unit -- the defect usually belongs to the SHAPE (here: any verb whose only arity is 3). An exhaustive count of the wrong unit reads as completeness and is not.

A MUTATION THAT COMES BACK GREEN ON SHIPPED CODE IS A DISCOVERY, NOT A NUISANCE (2026-08-06, rf2-sib23).

MUT-C AND MUT-D WERE GREEN ON THE FIRST PASS. Class tracking and escape handling in a shipped lexer had been running UNFALSIFIED — not wrong, but never tested — because NO EXISTING FIXTURE SEPARATED THE TWO READINGS: /[}]/ carries no slash inside its character class, and an escaped } sits at the same index whether or not escapes are handled. Two fixtures added; both now red; 81 -> 91 checks.

THE RULE: when you mutate a branch and the suite stays green, the FIRST hypothesis is not "my mutation failed to apply" (check that too — it has fired six times today) and not "this branch is unreachable". It is THAT NO FIXTURE DISCRIMINATES THE BRANCH. Write the fixture that does. A branch nobody can falsify is shipping on faith, and it is exactly where the next silent defect will live.

WHY THIS PARTICULAR BLIND SPOT IS EASY TO CREATE: both fixtures were reasonable and both exercised the code. They simply happened to be values on which the two readings AGREE. When choosing a negative case, ask what value would DISTINGUISH the implementations, not merely what value exercises the line — the same lesson as choosing a type mutant that is valid in a sibling category rather than obviously absurd.

FROM THE SAME PASS, three more worth keeping:

BOTH DIRECTIONS OF A LEXING DEFECT, and only one was anticipated. The masker could ERASE a genuine read (a sound driver reported as an offender) AND INVENT one (prose vouching for an unread collector, silently). The inventing arm was silent because the brace count never balances, endOfSubstitution returns -1, and maskLiterals falls through to "a lone backtick consumes nothing" and rescans the literal AS CODE. Controls judged correctly in both directions, which is what proved it a lexing failure rather than a dead check.

THE AUDIT PREDICTED THE WRONG SHAPE. It said the derail would "recreate the silent sink/handler skips". A silent sink SKIP CANNOT BE CONSTRUCTED — backticks remaining after any derail inside one template are ODD BY CONSTRUCTION, so the mask always resynchronises. The real failure is an invented read, which is worse. An audits predicted mechanism is a hypothesis; reproduce it rather than implementing against it.

A REPAIR THAT LOOKS LIKE CREEP CAN BE THE ACTUAL MECHANISM. The worker fixed an undelimitable span to blank to end-of-input rather than consume nothing, beyond the literal charge, and justified it as "the mechanism that made the charged defect SILENT rather than LOUD". That is the right test for whether an adjacent fix belongs: does it convert this defects failure mode from loud to silent? If so it is not adjacent, it is the cause.

A GREP COUNT IS NOT A FACT ABOUT THE CODE — three of my measurements were refuted by workers in one day (2026-08-14).

THE THREE, all mine, all stated to workers as measured fact:

1. "core/src and ssr/src carry LIVE RUNTIME DEPENDENCIES on Freehand" — from a directory histogram of reference counts. The mapper extracted every ns form and grepped it: ZERO requires. All thirteen references were prose in comments and docstrings. A reference count cannot distinguish a require from a comment, and I read it as though it could.

2. "hmr_remount has one native mention" — the worker found ZERO. My matches were `nativeSet` in a sibling .cjs file: the browser's own value setter, nothing to do with the native tier. A substring match on `native` is not a match on the tier.

3. "PR #8193 touches the testbed, and worker/propfix-8193 holds it" — #8193 touched impl/intent.cljs, docs and a new test, NOT the testbed; and no worktree of that name existed, because the fix worker reused the original one. I built a fence out of two assumptions and stated it as fact.

WHAT THEY HAVE IN COMMON. Each was a cheap query whose OUTPUT SHAPE I trusted without checking what it had actually matched. A count, a filename, a substring. None was wrong as a query; all three were wrong as evidence for the claim I hung on them.

THE COST IS NOT SYMMETRIC. A wrong count in a report is embarrassing. A wrong count in a BRIEF becomes a worker's premise, and a fence built on one either blocks work that was safe or permits a collision that was not. Case 3 nearly did the second.

THE RULE. Before a grep count enters a brief or a fence: (a) read a sample of the actual matches, not the number; (b) for a dependency claim, extract the requires rather than matching the name; (c) for a fence, verify the holder EXISTS — check the worktree and the PR's file list, not the branch name I remember dispatching. Where the check is more than a minute's work, ATTRIBUTE the number and tell the worker to verify it, which is already the standing rule for constants and applies identically here.

AND THE WORKERS CAUGHT ALL THREE, which is the system working. But each cost that worker time it should have spent on the bead.

A GUARD FORBIDDING A CORRECTNESS SHORTCUT PAID OFF, MEASURABLY. I dispatched rf2-wxrrp (a fast path in Freehand's cell/commit!) with the standing rule 'you may NOT weaken invariant 5 to go faster — that trade is the operator's alone'. The worker then discovered THE REPO HAD NO INVARIANT-5 COVERAGE AT ALL. It added two rows and falsified them against deliberately broken commits, one of which was EXACTLY the fast path the bead hypothesised (skip the correction when staging acquired nothing). Its verdict: 'a tear-skipping fast path would have been SILENTLY CORRECT against every other test in the repository' — 8,225 assertions, none would have moved. LESSON: when a brief asks for speed on a path that carries a correctness guarantee, name the guarantee as off-limits IN THE BRIEF and require proof it still holds. Do not rely on the suite to catch a violation; first check whether the suite covers the invariant at all. A performance bead is the most likely place for a silent correctness regression to enter, because the reviewer is looking at numbers.

A GUARD PROVEN ON CASES CAN STILL FAIL ON SEQUENCES — demand the sequence, not the cases. On 2026-07-19 I commissioned the ai/ tracking ratchet (rf2-lsp1i, #6380), accepted a three-teeth proof, merged it, and reported to Mike that his "nothing under /ai should be tracked" end-state was mechanically enforced. An independent audit (rf2-ow7dz) then showed it is a STATIC CEILING, not a ratchet: 89->61 passes (correct), and then 61->62 ALSO passes with exit 0 because 62 is still under the stored 89. Equal-count replacement admits a new path. After a decrease to zero the stale ceiling permits additions forever — i.e. the guard goes inert exactly when S7 starts removing files, which is the moment it was built for.

THE THREE TEETH WERE ALL REAL AND ALL PASSED: force-add fails and names the path; an S7-style removal passes; the unmutated tree passes. Every one tested a SINGLE transition from the pristine baseline. None tested a SECOND transition. The defect lives only in the composition.

THE RULE: when a guard carries STATE (a baseline, a ceiling, a high-water mark, a cached roster, an allowlist), case-based teeth are insufficient. Specify the SEQUENCE in the brief and demand per-arm exit codes for each step: pristine -> pass; violate -> fail; legitimately change -> pass; THEN violate again -> MUST STILL FAIL; and the degenerate end state (here, count 0) -> still guards. My acceptance bar was case-based all session while I asked every worker for mutation proofs against that same weak bar.

RELATED, SAME SESSION: rf2-wlqfq found one blanket mutation reddening three fixtures while leaving two green — certifying falsifiability it had not established for those two, because they named different levers. Both findings are the same lesson from opposite ends: A PROOF IS A CLAIM LIKE ANY OTHER AND NEEDS THE SAME SCEPTICISM AS THE THING IT PROVES. Ask what the proof does NOT cover before accepting it.

ALSO: a `bd close` can silently fail to take. rf2-r94by stayed OPEN for hours after I closed it and resurfaced as phantom work in the ready pool I was quoting counts from. An audit of 32 other closes this session found it isolated — but VERIFY A CLOSE ON ANYTHING LOAD-BEARING, and recount the pool from bd rather than from what you believe you closed.

A TEST THAT HAND-MIRRORS THE PRODUCTION LOGIC IT CHECKS ASSERTS AGAINST ITSELF, AND STAYS GREEN THROUGH THE BUG. Measured 2026-09-05 on `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp`: `elision_test/build-get-path-form` re-implemented the shape of the form production emits, then compared production's output to its own copy. The worker fixing a real defect in that emitter observed that this test **would have stayed green through the entire bug** — both sides moved together, because one side was written from the other.

THIS IS A DISTINCT MECHANISM FROM THE OTHERS IN THIS FAMILY, and worth separating:
  * A gate that inspects nothing (empty roster, wrong roots, excluded package).
  * A witness with zero assertions (an optional namespace never loaded).
  * A check that grades the WRAPPER rather than the resource (the npx wrapper, not the JVM).
  * **And this one: a check whose ORACLE is a copy of the thing under test.** It executes, it asserts, it has a real assertion count — and it is structurally incapable of failing for the reason you care about.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is quick: **ask where the expected value comes from.** If it was written by reading the implementation, the test pins "the implementation still does what it did", which catches accidental regressions but never a defect present when the mirror was written. If it comes from an INDEPENDENT source — the spec, react-dom's own bytes, a real run, a fixture captured from behaviour — it can find the defect.

THE FIX IS NOT ALWAYS TO DELETE IT. A lockstep mirror has real value as a drift alarm, and the worker here kept it updated rather than removing it. What it must NOT be is the ONLY witness. Pair it with one that drives production directly and derives its answer from behaviour — that worker's new witness "derives its answer from the emitted form rather than canning one", noting that **a canned expected value would have passed on the defect, since the relay was never the bug.**

A KILLED GATE CAN REPORT EXIT 0 — THE WRAPPER'S STATUS IS NOT THE RUNNER'S (2026-08-03, rf2-2rtt6.73).

THE MECHANISM, and it is worse than the pipe trap because nothing in the command looks wrong. A worker's spine ran past the 10-minute tool cap. The WRAPPER was SIGTERM'd, but the underlying sh.exe SURVIVED and kept running. The completion notification that arrived carried EXIT CODE 0 — the wrapper's own status, not the runner's. The worker nearly read that as a pass. The tell was that the LOG NEVER REACHED A 'PASS' LINE.

TWO COMPOUNDING CONSEQUENCES:
1. A green that never happened. 'exit 0' from a timed-out tool call means the wrapper exited, not that the gate passed.
2. A SECOND SPINE. Believing the first was dead, the worker launched another — so TWO spines ran in one worktree against one .shadow-cljs, which is exactly the contention that produces phantom failures in test_quiet_shadow_node_cljs_test. Two workers hit that shape today; one wasted a cycle diagnosing failures it had caused itself.

THE RULES THAT FOLLOW:
• NEVER trust an exit code that arrives with a timeout or cancellation. Confirm the run's OWN terminal marker in its log — 'PASS fast PR spine', a test summary line, whatever the runner prints on success. Absence of that marker beats presence of exit 0.
• BEFORE relaunching a long gate, CHECK FOR SURVIVORS by process ancestry. Do not assume a killed wrapper killed its children. The worker here found both alive, killed both, and then ran one clean spine, blocking in-turn with repeated foreground waits.
• This is the same family as: a pipeline's exit status is its last command's; a two-valued probe recording a crash as a rejection; a bench arm exiting 0 on :undeclared-var warnings. FOURTEEN instances in one week. The general form is: THE INSTRUMENT REPORTED ON ITSELF RATHER THAN ON THE SUBJECT.

MAYOR NOTE: when briefing, 'foreground to completion' is not sufficient guidance on its own — add 'if a gate is killed or times out, treat its exit code as MEANINGLESS and check the log's terminal marker; check for surviving processes before relaunching'.

A LIVE FILE IS NOT A LIVE WITNESS — a citation census that checks whether the cited file EXISTS passes silently on a file that exists but no longer covers the claim it is cited for. Found 2026-09-05 on `docs/design/hicasso/product/naming-packet.md`.

THE SETUP. A page's Witness column cited test suites; five citations named files that `git ls-files` could not resolve, and repairing those was the bead. Both the mayor and the bead framed the census as EXISTENCE. The worker ran that census, then went further and READ the surviving suites — and found two rows whose witness file is present and green while no longer witnessing the row's subject at all: one now reads only a different API, another drives a raw React construct rather than the authoring form the row is about. **Of the rows in that bucket, exactly ONE had both subject and witness still alive.** An existence census scores those two as fine.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE SESSION'S OTHER VACUITY FINDINGS and belongs beside them: a poison test whose disposer was never called; a hermetic-cleanup check grading the wrapper instead of the process; two serialisers sharing one roster so their parity test agreed with itself; a witness reporting 2 tests and 0 assertions. In each case the instrument was PRESENT and INSPECTED NOTHING. Existence is the weakest possible form of that check, because a file path is the easiest thing to verify and the least informative.

THE RULE: WHEN AUDITING CITATIONS, RESOLVE THE PATH **AND** READ THE TARGET FOR THE CLAIMED SUBJECT. Two axes, and the second is the one that finds things. Cheap version: `git grep -c <the row's subject symbol> -- <the cited file>` and treat a 0 as a finding, controlled against a file you know does mention it.

AND THE COROLLARY THAT SAVED THE REPAIR ON THIS BEAD: when a citation IS dangling, find out WHY before writing the correction. Four of the five files were deleted in one cut that RETIRED a surface; the fifth went in a different cut hours earlier that retired suites "measuring the programme rather than the product" and DELIBERATELY PRESERVED WHAT THEY MEASURED in a surviving document. So "the witness is retired, full stop" — correct for four rows — would have been WRONG for the fifth, whose row should now point at the surviving record. Same symptom, different cause, different repair. Two deletions on the same day are not one event.

A MOVE-ASIDE DOES NOT SIMULATE A DELETION FOR GIT-READING GATES — MY PROBE INSTRUCTION WAS WRONG (2026-07-26).

I briefed the rf2-ddu3i worker to classify eleven donor-facing gates by MOVING implementation/ui/ ASIDE, running each, and moving it back. That is the right probe for gates that stat the filesystem. IT IS BLIND FOR GATES THAT READ GIT.

MEASURED: check_donor_inventory.py HELD rc=0 THROUGH THE ENTIRE MOVE and only reported its 73 STALE ROWS once the deletion was STAGED IN THE INDEX. A filesystem move leaves the git index untouched, so anything reading git ls-files, git show or the index sees the donor exactly as before.

SO THE PROBE MUST MATCH WHAT THE GATE READS. For a filesystem gate: move aside. For a git-reading gate: STAGE THE DELETION (git rm --cached -r, or a real staged rm) and read the gate against the index, then restore. Deciding which without checking is how a whole class reads as unaffected.

THIS IS THE TWELFTH INSTANCE TODAY OF ONE ERROR OF MINE: A PROXY THAT DOES NOT MEASURE THE REAL THING. Directory count for tree integrity; grep hits for schema count; the word "pending" for a table column; sample coverage for fence containment; and now a filesystem move for a deletion. Every one was cheap, plausible, and blind in a specific direction. BEFORE PRESCRIBING A PROBE, ASK WHAT THE THING UNDER TEST ACTUALLY READS.

AND THE GOOD NEWS FROM THE SAME RUN, worth keeping so nobody re-derives it: the completeness gate ITSELF is not vacuous at F6e — it FAILS LOUD on a real staged deletion with pending rows. Only ONE of the eleven goes vacuous (check-elision.cjs, 60 sentinels of which 8 are donor bodies, 52 meaningful after), and even that is "a property of a careless repair, not the deletion", because elision_probe.cljs requires re-frame.ui so the BUILD fails before the checker runs.

A SECOND TRAP FROM THE SAME REPORT, filed as rf2-0dbvy: the skill gate LIFECYCLE-SOURCE-ORDER assertion NEVER FAILS — IT IS SKIPPED behind a path-list SETUP error WHOSE MESSAGE INVITES THE EXACT EDIT THAT RETIRES IT SILENTLY. An error message that tells you to make the change that disables the check is worse than no message.

A MOVED CORPUS MAY ALSO HAVE BEEN RENUMBERED — a directory swap then silently repoints citations at the WRONG document (2026-08-14, rf2-46tt9 worker).

WHAT IT FOUND. The guide moved from one tree to another AND ITS CHAPTERS WERE RENUMBERED. `draft-guide/05-interop.md` is now `09-interop.md`; `05` in the new tree is `forms.md`. Same for four more: 06-theming became 14, 08-testing became 15, 10-server-side-rendering became 18, 11-performance became 19.

SO THE OBVIOUS FIX — swap the directory prefix — WOULD HAVE SILENTLY REPOINTED FIVE CITATIONS AT THE WRONG CHAPTER. Every link would resolve. Every gate would pass. Every reader would land somewhere plausible and wrong.

THE MECHANICAL RULE THAT PARTITIONS THE TWO GENERATIONS, and it is cheap: a citation is safely repointable IF AND ONLY IF the same FILENAME exists in the new tree. If it does not, the document was renumbered and the citation needs a human to decide which chapter it meant.

THE GENERAL FORM: when a corpus moves, the move is TWO facts — the path changed, and the identity may have changed. A path rewrite assumes the second did not happen. Verify per-file rather than per-tree.

AND THE SAME WORKER CAUGHT ITS OWN METHOD BEING TOO TIGHT: its first sweep anchored on repo-top-level directories and dropped the bead's own confirmed instance, which would have produced a FALSE COMPLETION. It added a second pass resolving citations relative to the citing file's directory, and used a positive control — pass 1 found one known instance, pass 2 found all three — before trusting the output.

A NAME-AXIS SEARCH CANNOT SEE A DERIVED LIST — if a tool ENUMERATES its targets programmatically, grepping for the target's name returns zero, and that zero reads exactly like "nothing gates this". Measured 2026-09-05, where it produced a false finding that reached a bead and a dispatch brief.

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker reported "no CI workflow builds `:examples/managed-http`, so nothing gates that testbed's compile", having grepped `.github/workflows/**` and the shadow-cljs config for the build name. I believed it, filed rf2-p0b0, and ADDED MY OWN corroborating measurement — that `tools/xray/testbeds/**/spec.cjs` returns 0 against a control of 5 repo-wide — which I offered in the brief as evidence the gap was wider than the bead said.

BOTH ZEROS WERE REAL AND THE CONCLUSION WAS FALSE. `implementation/scripts/check-examples-compile.cjs` DERIVES its build list by scanning `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn` for `:examples/<name>` and `:testbeds/<name>` keys. It never names a build, which is precisely why every name-axis search returns zero. `--list` prints 58 builds and `examples/managed-http` is one of them. It runs as the `cljs-examples-compile` job in `test.yml` and unconditionally in the nightly. The classifier even arms it from both relevant directions — the testbed path AND the substrate path whose change caused the original defect.

THE THIRD WORKER FOUND IT BY SWITCHING AXES: from "search for the name" to "ASK THE TOOL WHAT IT COVERS". One `--list` invocation settled what three name-greps could not.

THE RULE: BEFORE CONCLUDING THAT NOTHING COVERS X, RUN THE COVERING TOOL AND ASK IT. A gate that takes a config-derived, glob-derived, or convention-derived target list is invisible to a name search by construction, and this repo has several: the examples-compile script derives from shadow-cljs.edn; `check_doc_slugs.py` derives from root directories; the changed-surfaces classifier derives from path globs. My standing "a census needs as many token axes as there are ways to say the thing" was necessary and NOT sufficient here — every token axis searches TEXT, and a derived list has no text to find. THE ENUMERATION AXIS IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF AXIS, not a fourth token.

AND THE SECOND LESSON, which is mine: I corroborated a worker's zero with another zero of my own and treated the pair as confirmation. Two independent searches that share a blind spot are not independent. My `spec.cjs` count was numerically correct and evidentially worthless, because compile gating in this repo does not happen via `spec.cjs` at all.

THE GOOD OUTCOME: the brief said "do not assume the answer is 'add a gate'" and asked the worker to check whether a compile WOULD have caught the original defect. It measured that too — pre-fix tree compiles clean at 0 warnings; a renamed registry fn produces 2 warnings and fails the gate — so the gate is real and non-vacuous, and the defect (a missing map key plus two legal alternate arities) was simply not a compile error in ClojureScript. Asking for the disconfirming measurement is what turned a plausible bead into a refuted one.

A NEW TOP-LEVEL JOB KEY MOVES THE CHECK BAND ONLY IF ITS WORKFLOW POSTS PR STATUS CONTEXTS (2026-08-15 18:58 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/release-gra70 (rf2-gra70, PR #8314). It added the job key deploy-hicasso to .github/workflows/release.yml — three-dot measured, +1 / -0 — and correctly concluded THE BAND DOES NOT MOVE, because release.yml is TAG-TRIGGERED ONLY (on: push: tags:) and contributes no PR status context at all. test.yml was untouched.

WHY THIS CORRECTS MY BRIEFING: I tell workers 'adding or removing a JOB KEY is a band event; changing steps inside an existing job is not.' That is true for test.yml, lint.yml and docs.yml — the three workflows carrying the required status contexts ('All required checks passed', 'Lint required', 'Docs required'). It is FALSE for a workflow that never runs on a pull request. A tag-triggered release workflow can gain and lose job keys freely without any PR's rollup changing by one.

SO THE DISCRIMINATOR IS TWO-PART, and the job-key grep is only the first half:
  1. Did a top-level job key change?   git diff origin/main...HEAD -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'
  2. IF SO, does that workflow post PR status contexts at all? Read its  block. tags-only => not a band event.
Both halves, in that order. The grep alone over-reports.

THIS COMPOSES WITH THE ALREADY-RECORDED ORDERING RULE and does not replace it: the PR's OWN TOTAL against the band is still the direct measurement, and the job-key count is still only a proxy. This refinement says the proxy has a second false-positive mode beyond the ones already recorded.

TWO OTHER THINGS FROM THE SAME RUN WORTH KEEPING.

MERGING #8314 PUBLISHES NOTHING. Both release workflows are tag-triggered; merging starts no deploy job. It makes a FUTURE v* tag publish one more coordinate. Cutting that tag is the operator's act, and the repo has still never carried one. That distinction — wiring versus publishing — is what made the bead safe to dispatch at all.

AND A SEVENTH FALSE-GREEN TRAP, avoided rather than hit: when adding a bundle-isolation positive control for hicasso, MOST HICASSO STRINGS ERASE UNDER :advanced, so a naively chosen sentinel would be absent for the wrong reason and the control would pass vacuously. The worker chose sentinels from check_production_erasure.cjs's own controls instead. Same family as the six gates found failing green today: the check passes while verifying nothing.

A PER-LINE CENSUS IS BLIND TO CLAIMS THAT WRAP — and to phrasing its patterns never anticipated. Proved by the rf2-y27a7 worker (#6420) on 2026-07-19: it ran the adapter-disposition scanner over origin/main pre-edit spec/004-Views.md and got **0 defects** while NINE were present. Two causes, both worth knowing:
  (1) the stale text was 004A-appendix PHRASING no pattern matched — the census was rostering the file and matching the wrong shapes;
  (2) some of it was SPLIT ACROSS A LINE WRAP, which a per-line scan structurally cannot see.
So "the file is rostered by the gate" does NOT mean "the gate would catch a defect in it". Rostering blocks REINTRODUCTION OF THE MATCHED SHAPES ONLY.

⚠️ THE DISCIPLINE: before claiming a gate covers your fix, RUN IT AGAINST THE PRE-FIX TEXT and confirm it reds. #6420 did exactly that and reported "no gate covered any of the nine" rather than implying protection. Compare rf2-gx2n7 (#6396), which re-seeded retired wording into Conventions and found EVERY GATE STILL PASSED, and rf2-kc4kl (#6382), which proved on real history that a document-wide census stayed green through an entire falsehood because it could not see WHERE a claim sat.
⚠️ FOR MULTI-LINE PROSE, a line-oriented scan needs a joined/normalised view or it will miss wrapped sentences. If you write a prose census, decide explicitly whether it scans lines or paragraphs, and say which in its docstring.

AND THE JUDGEMENT #6420 GOT RIGHT: it DECLINED to add a 004A pattern to close the gap, because doing so "would immediately red-light four sibling docs I am fenced out of — that is a ruling, not a determinable fact." Widening a census beyond your fence turns your PR into someone else emergency. Name the uncovered sites, do not arm a gate you cannot satisfy.

A CONFLICT THAT PERSISTS AFTER A REPORTED REBASE MAY MEAN THE REBASE WAS NEVER PUSHED (2026-08-14).

WHAT HAPPENED. I merged a PR, its neighbour conflicted, I asked its worker to rebase. It did — locally — then went straight into re-running gates and never pushed. The remote branch still carried the PRE-REBASE commits. GitHub re-reported the ORIGINAL conflict against a branch that had not moved, and I read that as a SECOND collision and messaged the worker again about a cause that did not exist.

I GUESSED THE CAUSE WRONG THREE TIMES TODAY ON CONFLICTS: twice naming the wrong file, once naming a collision that never happened. Each time the worker checked and found otherwise. The pattern is that I diagnose from what MERGED RECENTLY rather than from the conflict itself.

THE CHECK, and it costs one command: compare the PR's head SHA against the worker's local branch tip. If the remote head is older than the local ref, the rebase exists but was never pushed — and no amount of re-rebasing will help, because the thing GitHub is judging never changed.

  gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid   vs   git rev-parse worker/<name>

SAME SHAPE AS THE STRANDED SWEEP'S CORRECTION: the remote is a LAGGING indicator of a worker's state, because a briefed worker pushes at milestones rather than continuously. There, reading the remote produced a false STRAND signal. Here, reading it produced a false CONFLICT diagnosis. Both fail in the direction of imagining a problem that is not there.

AND TELL THE WORKER TO READ THE CONFLICT RATHER THAN TRUST MY DIAGNOSIS. That instruction is what produced the correct answer here — the worker checked, found the unpushed rebase, and said so plainly.

A POSITIVE CONTROL CAN SILENTLY FAIL TO APPLY, AND THEN IT PROVES NOTHING WHILE LOOKING LIKE PROOF (2026-08-06, rf2-z8oiq).

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker mutation-proved check_doc_slugs.py by deliberately breaking an anchor. The control returned 0 — no finding. It would have been entirely reasonable to report "the gate does not resolve same-file anchors". THE REAL CAUSE WAS THAT THE SUBSTITUTION NEVER LANDED: the file is CRLF and the match string used a bare \n. Second attempt asserted the substitution had applied first, and the gate then redded correctly with BROKEN ANCHOR ... :85. Its own words: "Had I stopped there Id have reported a green that proved nothing."

WHY THIS IS A NEW MEMBER OF A FAMILY I ALREADY TRACK: I have recorded five times that A MUTATION THAT DID NOT APPLY IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT DID NOT FIRE. Every one of those was about proving a gate CATCHES something. This is the mirror: it was a POSITIVE CONTROL proving a gate CAN SEE a class at all, and its failure produces the opposite wrong conclusion — not "my fix is unproven" but "this gate is blind, so I need not rely on it". That conclusion then justifies skipping the gate, which is worse than an unproven fix.

SO THE RULE COVERS BOTH DIRECTIONS: confirm the edit APPLIED — git diff --stat AND grep the token back out AND confirm the replacement token is absent — before believing ANY verdict, red or green, from a mutation OR a control.

AND THE CRLF DETAIL IS THE RECURRING MECHANISM ON THIS REPO: a bare \n in a match string does not match a CRLF file. That has now silently no-opped edits in three separate lanes (a bench mutation harness, a perl substitution, and this control). On this checkout, any programmatic substitution against a tracked file must account for CRLF or assert its own application.

FROM THE SAME PASS, two things worth keeping. THE AUDIT NAMED TWO OCCURRENCES AND THERE WERE THREE — the third sat in the pages PROVENANCE section, outside the charge, concluding "no figure on this page moves" while the tip instrument now prints NO REPORTABLE MAGNITUDE. Counting occurrences before editing is what found it; that is the fourth time today an enumeration under-counted its own class. AND THE SEMANTICS WERE ONLY VERIFIABLE IN CODE: I briefed this as prose reconciliation, but the instruments own docstring is headed "## The five verdicts" and lists :moot second with reason :no-published-figure-bears-it — so the pages four-verdict table had been wrong against an instrument that documented five all along. A page-versus-page reconciliation would have missed it.

A POSITIVE CONTROL CAN BE REAL AND STILL VALIDATE THE WRONG INSTRUMENT (2026-08-14, rf2-7cuns worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker deleted a docs tree and needed to find every inbound link. It ran `check_doc_slugs.py`, which named 18 broken targets across 11 files — including one it had not predicted. That is a GENUINE positive control: the gate demonstrably found things, so its zero would have meant something.

CI THEN CAUGHT A NINETEENTH. The `verify-readme-links` job runs TWO scripts, not one. The second, `check_readme_links.py`, has a DIFFERENT CORPUS — the READMEs outside docs, spec, skills and migration. The worker's own words: "My positive control was real (the gate named 18 files including one I hadn't predicted) but I VALIDATED THE WRONG INSTRUMENT'S COMPLETENESS."

THIS IS THE NEXT LAYER OF THE RULE I HAVE BEEN BRIEFING ALL DAY. "Produce a positive control before trusting a zero" stops a broken query. It does NOT stop a working query aimed at the wrong corpus. A control proves the instrument WORKS; it says nothing about whether the instrument COVERS.

THE ADDITIONAL CHECK: before trusting a gate's verdict on completeness, ask WHAT CORPUS IT SCANS and whether the CI job that owns it runs MORE THAN ONE script. Read the job, not the script. Here the job name named neither script.

AND THE SAME PASS FOUND WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND LINKS: deleting the tree removed THE ONLY CLASSIFIER ARM lighting `docs/core`, leaving all 60 files in that tree arming nothing and reddening a repo-wide invariant. Nothing predicted it; it surfaced only by running the classifier's own test. A deletion's blast radius includes the RULES that mentioned it, not only the files that linked to it.

A positive control needs POWER, not just a verdict. Compute where its EXPECTED ratio sits relative to its band floor in units of the run's own round-to-round sd BEFORE trusting either a pass or a refusal. rf2-4t36: the topology tournament's windowed arm sat 0.70 sd above its floor, so under the strict every-round rule a perfectly healthy instrument certified it ~1 run in 4 (0.758^5). A PASS would have been as uninformative as the refusal. Also: (1) subtracting a fitted additive floor cannot rescue such a control — the band admits floor estimates over a ~2x range, so it tests the estimate not the instrument, and this holds even if the floor IS additive; (2) BATCHING CANNOT CURE A PER-OPERATION FLOOR — ratio (c+P*s)/(c+s) is independent of batch size; batching only fixes clock quantisation; (3) check whether the clamp is actually binding before blaming it — batch-k commits share ONE now-ms pair, so the reading may be tens of quanta clear.

A PR's GREEN CAN BE STALE: GitHub reports the checks it last RAN, against the BASE IT RAN AGAINST. If a sibling PR merged since, that green may no longer describe the merged result. Caught live: PR #7133 (a flushSync FIX) showed 42 SUCCESS / 0 fail, but its baseRefOid was 9a654d86c0 while main had moved to bb37a2ab5c — and the intervening merge (#7131) ADDED a test pinning the very defect #7133 fixes. Merging on that green would have red-ed main. BEFORE MERGING, compare `gh pr view N --json baseRefOid` with `git rev-parse origin/main`; if they differ, ask whether anything merged in between can invalidate this diff — especially a test that pins behaviour the diff changes. A stale base is harmless when the diffs are disjoint (verified by checking the merged PRs' file lists), and lethal when they are the mutually-invalidating pair. Related: [[rebase-merge-makes-a-worker-branch-look-unmerged]].

A PR with ZERO scheduled checks ('no checks reported') = check .mergeable FIRST: GitHub builds pull_request runs against the test-merge ref, which does not exist while the PR is CONFLICTING — no YAML debugging needed. Empty-commit nudges and close/reopen do nothing in this state; the fix is always a rebase. (Hit on W13 #6674, 2026-07-22.)

A PROFILING INSIGHT WORTH MORE THAN THE OPTIMISATION IT CAME FROM: A CANDIDATE CAN MEASURE INERT BECAUSE ANOTHER DEFECT IS MASKING IT (2026-07-26).

THE STORY IN TWO PARTS. The compiled-tier study (rf2-lnecd) profiled the interpreter, saw self time naming clojure.string/replace, guessed the uncached react-style-name, MEMOISED IT, AND MEASURED NOTHING. It reverted the guess and took the caller-attribution-named fix instead — an uncached react-prop-name running twice per element — worth -23%. That produced the rule I have been briefing all day: SELF TIME NAMES THE FUNCTION; ONLY CALLER ATTRIBUTION NAMES THE FIX.

THE SEQUEL INVERTS IT. The follow-up (rf2-xu6rx) found react-style-name WAS CORRECT ALL ALONG — it measured inert only because UNCACHED caller-key-slot OWNED NEARLY ALL OF clojure.string/replace at the time. Once that was fixed, the residual str/replace is essentially all react-style-name, and it became THE LARGEST OF SIX CHANGES: put-style! 4.59% -> 0.93%. Its "under 1%" estimate had been taken from the PRE-FIX profile.

SO THE RULE NEEDS ITS OTHER HALF: A NULL RESULT FROM AN OPTIMISATION IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE PROFILE YOU MEASURED IT IN, NOT ABOUT THE CANDIDATE. When one hot frame dominates a shared primitive, every other consumer of that primitive reads as inert. RE-PROFILE AFTER EACH LANDED CHANGE AND RE-TEST THE CANDIDATES YOU PREVIOUSLY DECLINED — the earlier rejection was correct AND the candidate was right, which sounds contradictory only if you forget the profile moved.

THE METHOD THAT MADE THIS VISIBLE, worth copying: caller attribution over ONE SAVED CAPTURE, offline, so EVERY FRAME IS JUDGED AGAINST THE SAME PROFILE.
