TWO RULINGS THREE MINUTES APART, AND THE LATER ONE INVALIDATED A REPAIR THE EARLIER HAD ALREADY ASSIGNED (2026-08-06, rf2-2rtt6.115 / .116).

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched .115 and .116 together, guessing they were one defect seen from two sides. Half right: same POSITION (host-entrys :else arm at an unclaimed defhost slot) but two different defects — .116 the CODE was wrong (a behaviour change), .115 the RECORD was wrong (a doc reconciliation, HD-024 row 3 over-recording by exactly one position).

THE COUPLING I MISSED, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE I GUESSED: .115s review pass adjudicated at 11:23 and assigned its execution to rf2-2rtt6.103 as R4 of the merged [:>] spec. .116s RULING LANDED AT 11:26 — THREE MINUTES LATER — and SUPERSEDES HALF OF R4. R4 specifies "a scope-note on row 3 plus the witness pinning a marked h/fn at an unclaimed door slot". After .116 the marked form DOES NOT CROSS THERE AT ALL, so that witness CANNOT BE WRITTEN; the identity witness R4 wanted is now the plain-fn row beside the new refusal.

So the worker could do neither "both together" nor "only the one that stands alone": writing R4s scope-note as recorded would have put a sentence in decisions.md that its own code change falsifies IN THE SAME TREE, and leaving row 3 untouched would ship a knowingly-false record beside it. It did .116 in full plus the RECORD half of .115, and left .115 open with its closure still assigned to .103.

THE GENERAL RULE: ON A FAST-MOVING BOARD, A RULING CAN INVALIDATE A REPAIR ANOTHER BEAD HAS ALREADY ASSIGNED TO A THIRD, AND NEITHER BEAD KNOWS. Before executing an assigned repair, check whether anything ruled AFTER the assignment touches the same position — timestamps, not just status. Minutes are enough. This is the sibling of the blocked-bead rule (when a blocker clears, RE-DERIVE the blocked beads answer from the post-blocker tree) arriving from the other direction: here nothing was blocked, and the later ruling still moved the earlier ones ground.

AND THE CORRECTION TO MY DISPATCH: I told the worker both were open questions needing adjudication. NEITHER WAS. .116 was already ruled with a seven-point brief down to the error id and data keys; .115 was already adjudicated by three independent reviews with code authoritative. It executed rulings rather than making them, which is right — but I had not looked, and a worker told to adjudicate an already-ruled bead can easily re-open a settled question. CHECK FOR AN EXISTING RULING BEFORE ASKING FOR ONE.

MUTATION SHAPE WORTH COPYING: mutation B (callback? -> fn?) reddened the workers own plain-fn control PLUS TWO PRE-EXISTING WITNESSES. That is the both-directions proof done properly — it shows the refusal does not reject valid usage, using rows the worker did not write and therefore could not have tuned.

A SECOND HOST-EXHAUSTION FALSE SIGNAL, AND IT WEARS A DIFFERENT MASK (2026-07-26).

Recorded because two workers hit host exhaustion today and it presented DIFFERENTLY each time, so pattern-matching on the first will miss the second.

CASE 1: scripts/test-fast-pr.sh exited rc=1 while the WRAPPER reported 0. Cause: "The paging file is too small" with three JVMs resident from the worker own before/after proof. Caught only because the brief mandates capturing rc=$? immediately and cross-checking against the log own verdict line.

CASE 2 (new): a spine run reported "FAIL implementation JS harness helpers". NOT A REAL FAILURE — git init and git hash-object exited 3221225794 = 0xC0000142 = STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED, which is WINDOWS REFUSING TO START A PROCESS, with a 2 GB resident JVM on the host. The digest roster covered none of the workers paths. Standalone re-run: rc=0, 7 passed.

SO THE TELL IS AN EXIT CODE THAT IS NOT A TEST OUTCOME. 3221225794 / 0xC0000142 is not a test framework failure code; neither is a paging-file message. When a gate fails, LOOK AT THE EXIT CODE ITSELF before believing the label — a test-shaped FAIL line can be a process that never started. And the standing rule that a failing test on a touched surface is never a flake still holds: the discriminator is whether the failure names a deftest and an assertion, or names an OS condition.

WHY THIS IS LIKELY TO RECUR: six workers run concurrently by default here, each capable of a cold shadow-cljs compile and a multi-GB JVM. The same worker also reported the spine WRAPPER hitting the harness 10-minute ceiling on a cold :node-test compile (141s for that step alone) and ran every step individually instead of trusting a truncated run. That is the right move and worth briefing when the fleet is saturated.

ONE MORE GATE HOLE FROM THE SAME REPORT, worth its own line: test-fast-pr.sh SOFT-SKIPS mkdocs when mkdocs is not on PATH — and it is not on PATH here, though it IS installed as python -m mkdocs. Any worker touching docs and trusting the spine gets a green that never checked the docs. Brief "run python -m mkdocs build --strict directly" whenever a dispatch touches docs or spec.

A second 'shadow-cljs watch' anywhere on the machine silently steals a gate's :dev-http port. shadow starts the dev-http servers for EVERY build in shadow-cljs.edn, so any watch in any worktree binds 8061/8765/etc; the second process logs ::dev-http/http-start-ex + BindException and carries on, and a gate's HTTP probe still gets 200 — from the OTHER process. The page then runs the other tree's bundle and registers with the other tree's worker, so saves made here reach nothing. If the foreign watch is a leftover from the SAME worktree the gate goes GREEN on code this run never compiled. Detect it by comparing the served bundle's bytes with the one this watch wrote: shadow bakes a per-process proc_id and server_token into every dev bundle, so two watches can never write the same bytes. Found while reproducing rf2-odh3; fixed in implementation/scripts/serve-and-run-hicasso-hmr-testbed.cjs (assertOwnBundle).

A SHELL SCRIPT COMMITTED WITHOUT THE EXEC BIT (100644) PASSES LOCALLY ON WINDOWS AND FAILS CI ON LINUX. Found by the #6457 story-package fix-worker, 2026-07-19.

THE MECHANISM: a new .github/scripts/*.sh invoked DIRECTLY (./script.sh on PATH) needs the executable bit on Linux. Committed at git mode 100644 it gives "Permission denied" / exit 126 in CI. But WINDOWS-LOCAL GIT HAS core.filemode OFF, and bash runs the script regardless of the bit, so the author's local run exits 0. This is the exact local-green-≠-CI gap, and it is SPECIFIC to this repo's cross-platform setup (Mike develops on Windows; CI is Linux). The .github/scripts/_preflight-story-package.test.cjs harness gate went red on all 10 cases with "env: './...preflight-story-package.sh': Permission denied  126 !== 0" while test:script-policy had passed on Windows.

THE FIX (satisfies policy, changes zero content): git update-index --chmod=+x <script> — flips 100644 -> 100755, blob hash unchanged. Match the passing sibling's mode.

⚠️ IT IS ALSO A REAL BUG BEYOND THE TEST: the same script was invoked directly by release-story.yml, so the missing bit would have broken the actual release path, not just the harness self-test.

RULES:
1. Any dispatch that ADDS a .sh under .github/scripts/ (or anywhere invoked as ./script) must set the exec bit — check `git ls-files -s <script>` shows 100755, and mirror a passing sibling's mode.
2. A brief that adds a shell script must say: run the FULL CI harness command (npm run test:script-policy && npm run test:script-helpers), not just test:script-policy — CI runs both after &&, and test:script-helpers / the new .test.cjs is where a mode/policy break surfaces.
3. This joins the cross_platform_maintainers memory: file MODE, line endings, and path separators are all invisible-on-Windows / enforced-on-Linux. When a gate is green locally on this Windows box but red in CI, SUSPECT A PLATFORM-VISIBILITY DIFFERENCE (exec bit, CRLF, case-sensitivity) before assuming a flake.

A FORK OF SHIPPED CODE IN A TEST TREE CAN GO STALE SILENTLY — it compiles, so nothing reds (2026-08-14, rf2-z7cfs worker, filed rf2-u9o8k).

WHAT IT FOUND. `implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/bench/hicasso/front/controlled.cljs` is a parallel fork of the shipped controlled-element path. It has ONE commit — the re-home — and has tracked NONE of four subsequent fixes. Measured: `file-input-value?` appears 0 times against 7 in the shipped file; `toLowerCase` 0 against 4; 745 lines against 888.

SO IT STILL CARRIES THE PRE-FOLD EXACT COMPARE AND NO FILE-INPUT REFUSAL AT ALL — it walks straight into the DOM exception that a merged bead exists to replace.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: THE FORK COMPILES. It is not red on main. A stale copy of working code is syntactically fine forever, and every gate that runs it reports green about the copy rather than about the original.

THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE DUPLICATED LOOKUP FOUND HOURS EARLIER, AT WHOLE-NAMESPACE SCALE. A duplicated path is a duplicated coverage question; a duplicated NAMESPACE is a duplicated maintenance question, and neither file says which it is. Whether this fork is a DELIBERATE FROZEN BASELINE or four-fixes-stale DRIFT is unanswered by either file — and that ambiguity is the defect, more than the staleness.

THE RULE: when a fix lands on a shipped namespace, grep the tree for OTHER copies of the same function names. If a fork exists, it either needs the fix or needs a line saying why it does not. And a bench or baseline fork should SAY SO IN ITS FIRST LINE, because a reader who finds it cannot otherwise tell it from live code.

ASKING A WORKER FOR STATUS AND NAMING A DEFECT IN THE SAME MESSAGE IS A DISPATCH — count it as one, or you will dispatch the same work twice (2026-08-21).

WHAT HAPPENED. During the stranded sweep I found ceilinf idle with PR #8609 open. I sent it a status-check message and, in the same message, flagged that docs/design/hicasso/studio/README.md lines 133-134 still contradicted its own merged pages. It replied 'Yes - I am done' AND had in the meantime fixed the README and opened PR #8612. Meanwhile I had spent those minutes deriving a fence, extracting the three verbatim blocks and writing a full brief to dispatch rf2-6o5lx - the SAME README rows - to a NEW worker, idxalign. Two executors, one file. I caught it only because ceilinf's completion notification arrived seconds after the Agent call returned.

THE FENCE DERIVATION WAS NOT THE FAILURE AND FIXING IT WOULD NOT HAVE HELPED. I derived it properly: gh pr list --json files across all open PRs, git status --porcelain inside the peer worktree, and I even verified echoself's copy of the README was byte-identical to main. Every source was blind because at derivation time NO PR, NO branch and NO working-tree change existed - ceilinf created all three in the interval. This is exactly the same-tick blindness the dispatch rule already names for a peer dispatched in the same message, and the carve-out for it is 'name it from what you just dispatched, because that is the only evidence that exists'.

SO THE RULE EXTENDS: THE CARVE-OUT COVERS A WORKER I JUST RESUMED WITH A TASK IN IT, NOT ONLY ONE I JUST SPAWNED. A SendMessage that names a defect and asks the worker to handle it is functionally a dispatch, and it produces a peer invisible to all four derivation sources for exactly the same reason.

THE CHECK THAT COSTS NOTHING: before dispatching a bead, re-read the messages I sent THIS TICK. If any of them names the same file or the same defect, that work is already assigned. My own outbox is a dispatch source and I was not reading it.

SECOND-ORDER: the stand-down cost was near zero only because the worktree was still clean when I caught it - 0 porcelain lines. Message the duplicate IMMEDIATELY on discovery rather than finishing the current thought; an editing worker is far more expensive to unwind than an idle one, and the window is a single tool round.

A TEST FIXTURE CAN MAKE AN ABSENCE ASSERTION UNSATISFIABLE — the inverse false green. Found by the rf2-vxgfnd.299 worker (#6416) on 2026-07-19.

THE CASE: an elision gate asserted a sentinel ABSENT from an :advanced production bundle. After the fix landed, the sentinel STAYED PINNED AT 2. The gated library call HAD correctly folded to nil — but the FIXTURE own probe, `(:build-digest (client/descriptor ::probe))`, kept the keyword alive in the bundle as Wk.g(null). The assertion was measuring THE FIXTURE, NOT THE LIBRARY, and could never pass however correct the fix. Fixed by having the fixture export the whole descriptor via clj->js instead of destructuring the sentinel key.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN SPECIES: every other false green this session was a check THAT COULD NOT FAIL. This is a check THAT COULD NOT SUCCEED. Both are the same underlying error — an assertion decoupled from the thing it names — but the failure mode is inverted, and the tell is different: a permanently-red arm that survives a correct fix is as suspicious as a permanently-green one. If a fix is right and the arm still reds, SUSPECT THE HARNESS BEFORE RE-FIXING THE CODE.
RULE FOR ANY ABSENCE ASSERTION: check whether the TEST CODE ITSELF references the symbol being asserted absent. A probe that names the thing it is proving gone will root it.

RELATED, AND THE RIGHT SHAPE FOR A NON-VACUITY FLOOR (same PR): the floor must witness that THE NAMESPACE UNDER TEST IS ACTUALLY IN THE SCANNED ARTIFACT, otherwise an absence is attributable to the namespace having been dropped entirely rather than to the gate. #6416 floor is a STRING LITERAL (Closure never rewrites them — the property that killed the function-name oracle), UNGATED, ROOTED FROM init, and reached through an UNGATED CLIENT REGISTRY READ. Verified discriminating on the same bundle with the same grep: floor at 1 while a known-absent sentinel reads 0.

A TEST THAT CONSUMES A LEAK AS A PRECONDITION GOES QUIET, NOT RED, WHEN THE LEAK IS FIXED (2026-09-01, found by the genpool worker on rf2-cq0yi, PR #8887).

THE SHAPE: make_frame_generation_pool_window_jvm_test (rf2-rt4jz) used a generation-pool leak as a SETUP STEP -- it asserted as a control that a destroyed frames row still named pool V1. Fixing the leak (releasing the row at destroy-frame!) removed that precondition. The test did not fail. It kept passing while no longer pinning anything.

WHY THE OBVIOUS REPAIR IS NOT ENOUGH: the worker restated the control to pin the RELEASE instead, reasoning that an absent row would redden the reproduction just as hard, since nil reads as the live source store and zero-matches that frames explicit include-ns composition. That argument is well-formed and WRONG. Re-sabotaging showed 0 failures: the zero-match is swallowed by the resilient flush, so the constructors generation survives and the pin stays quiet exactly where it exists to shout.

THE RULE: when a fix removes a state some test consumed, restating that tests control by REASONING about the new state is not enough. The restatement has to be RE-SABOTAGED -- revert the original defect and confirm the restated test goes red. Only a fresh red proves the pin still has teeth.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS: nothing signals it. The suite stays green through the fix, through the restatement, and through the regression the pin was meant to catch. A restatement that reads perfectly can have removed a regression pins teeth entirely, and code review cannot see it because the test still looks like it asserts something.

CONFIRMING MEASUREMENT FROM THE SAME WORK: after planting the precondition explicitly instead, the same test read 2 failures under the pre-rf2-rt4jz ordering (the original defect reproduced) and 0 with the ordering as shipped -- verified in BOTH directions, which is what a restored pin looks like.

GENERALISATION WORTH CARRYING: this is the sabotage discipline applied to a case people do not think of as sabotage. The gate-mechanics block already says a green sabotage run is a reason to stop rather than proceed. The uncovered case is that FIXING A BUG can silently convert a live pin into a vacuous one, so any test whose setup depended on the buggy behaviour needs its control re-proven, not re-argued.

A TEXT-GREP GATE CANNOT DISTINGUISH A MENTION FROM A DEPENDENCY (2026-07-26). The "Assert no dependency on the re-frame.ui donor" step is a bare git grep for re-frame\.ui / re_frame/ui / re-frame2-ui over implementation/freehand, admitting no exceptions and not excluding comments. A worker adding a guard to Freehand wrote a test comment explaining that the guard needs NO donor dependency — naming the namespace in order to say so — and the gate reddened on the sentence asserting the very property it enforces.

THE GATE IS RIGHT AND SHOULD NOT BE WEAKENED. A donor-dependency gate that admitted comment exceptions would be defeatable by a comment, and the artefact already has an idiom that avoids the problem: substrate.cljs:80 says "the donor substrate" and never names the namespace. The worker reworded to that idiom rather than touching the gate, which is the correct resolution.

WHAT TO PUT IN BRIEFS TOUCHING implementation/freehand: you cannot write the literal strings re-frame.ui, re_frame/ui or re-frame2-ui ANYWHERE under that tree — including comments and docstrings — because a text gate enforces it. Say "the donor" or "the donor substrate" instead. This also means a well-intentioned comment explaining an absence of coupling will fail the gate that checks for coupling.

FAMILY THIS BELONGS TO: it is the mirror of the gate-blindness class found four times yesterday (a fixture declaring :large as an app-db path; resources absent from the manifest roster; the 009 ratchet pinning the Channel column but not trace ops; :query-defaults never drawn by the prism generator). Those were gates that could not SEE a real case. This is a gate that sees a case that is not real. Both come from a proxy standing in for the property — text for dependency, one fixture shape for a class — and both are worth checking for when a gate result surprises you.

DIAGNOSTIC VALUE: my hypothesis for this red was "existing tests asserted the old unguarded behaviour and need flipping". It was wrong, and I only learned that because the worker read the failing STEP rather than the failing JOB. A job name is not a diagnosis: JVM freehand (clojure -M:test) contains a test step AND several assertion steps, and the test step was green.

A THIRD VACUOUS-PASS CLASS UNDER A PRODUCTION GATE: a POSITIVE assertion that is green because the gate SHORT-CIRCUITS the thing it tests. Found in routing triage (rf2-o5dbf): `(is (true? (validate-fx! ...)))` legs were already green under -Dre-frame.debug=false because `validate-fx!` is literally `(if interop/debug-enabled? (run-validation ...) true)` — they would have stayed green IF THE SCHEMA WERE DELETED OUTRIGHT. The two previously-recorded classes are NEGATIVE assertions over an empty trace ring, and namespaces that are 100% dev instrumentation. This third one is nastier because it LOOKS like a positive proof.
THE SHARPEST INSTANCE WAS A PRIVACY ASSERTION: `(is (not (re-find #"SECRET-100" (pr-str payload))))` certifying that a secret did not appear in an egress copy THAT WAS NEVER MADE under the gate. A privacy guarantee proving nothing, indefinitely.
GENERAL TEST, covering all three: for each assertion ask WHAT WOULD THIS DO IF ITS SUBJECT SIMPLY NEVER EXISTED IN THIS POSTURE? If the answer is 'pass', it belongs inside the dev-only arm or needs a production-visible witness. Twenty such assertions were found in one artefact, plus four deftests that would have executed nothing at all.

A THIRTEENTH WAY A SIGNAL LIES HERE, AND IT IS THE SHARPEST FORM OF THE CANNED-VALUE CLASS (2026-07-26).

A TEST THAT REDEFINES THE PRODUCER TO MATCH THE CONSUMER GUARDS NOTHING. Found by the rf2-2nbck worker: tools_test.clj:4676 redefined reg-variant* to throw a FABRICATED ex-data carrying a bare :rf.error — THE VERY KEY THE RELAY READ. Meanwhile all three real registrar throws (registrar.cljc:324, :360, :401) use :rf.error/id, and NO ex-info anywhere sets the bare key. So the consumer arm was PROVABLY DEAD, and a GREEN TEST STOOD GUARD OVER A SLOT NEVER POPULATED IN PRODUCTION.

WHY THIS IS DISTINCT FROM THE EIGHTH CLASS ALREADY RECORDED: that one was a canned VALUE asserting what a producer cannot emit — a literal in a fixture. This one is a canned PRODUCER: the test replaces the emitting function itself, so the fabricated output and the consumer expectation are the same authored decision. There is no independent side. It is the same failure with the seam moved one level up, and it is harder to spot because the test LOOKS like an integration test.

THE TELL, and it generalises: if a test redefines, stubs or with-redefs the very function whose OUTPUT SHAPE is the thing under test, the test cannot fail for the reason it exists. Ask what independent authority establishes the shape. For this repo the answer is usually "drive the real boundary" — the same worker proved its fix by running server/run-loop! and reading the encoded response back, which is what showed the BEFORE/AFTER difference honestly.

THIS IS THE THIRD TIME TODAY THAT DRIVING THE REAL BOUNDARY OVERTURNED A UNIT-LEVEL BELIEF: (1) rf2-jquiy headline repro DID NOT REPRODUCE because a guard sat in front of the traced relay; (2) rf2-2z9u3 boundary proof confirmed a sibling fix had been MASKED and invisible until it landed; (3) this one. Brief for boundary proof whenever a bead is about what a consumer receives.

ALSO RECORD: the donor-inventory ledger has THREE dispositions, not two. I have been reasoning with MOVE and DELETE. The third is REPLACE — legend: "the job is real but Freehand does it differently on purpose; THE DONOR REALIZATION IS NOT CARRIED ACROSS". That is what made rf2-qe9xk moot: implementation/ui/src/re_frame/ui/tool.cljc is REPLACE | F4 | done, so the defect is NOT carried into Freehand — whereas MOVE (which made rf2-yumaq NOT moot) would have carried it. MOVE versus REPLACE is the difference between inheriting a defect and leaving it behind. Ask which one before ruling on donor mootness.

A TWELFTH WAY A SIGNAL LIES HERE, AND IT IS ABOUT MUTATION TESTING ITSELF (2026-07-26).

A MUTATION THAT DOES NOT APPLY IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT DOES NOT FIRE. The gate-scope worker first M4 attempt had a LEADING SPACE in its match string, so the edit silently did not apply — and the gate stayed green. Read naively that is "the gate failed to catch the planted defect", which is the exact conclusion mutation testing exists to produce. It is the opposite: nothing was planted.

THE RULE: after planting a mutation, CONFIRM THE DIFF APPLIED before reading the gate verdict. git diff --stat, or grep the mutated token back out of the file. The worker did this and stated it explicitly, which is why its other three mutation verdicts are trustworthy.

WHY THIS BELONGS ON THE FALSE-GREEN LIST even though it is procedural: mutation proof is now the standard I require for every gate, fixture, census and CI-arming bead — I measured today that beads closed on ARMING rather than CATCHING are the largest category the merged-PR audit reopens. So mutation testing is load-bearing across the whole programme, and a silent no-op inside it corrupts the evidence I close beads on. This is the first entry on the list that attacks the VERIFICATION rather than the thing verified.

SIBLING ENTRY FROM THE SAME DAY, on the false-RED side: the G-8 perf gate dies with "baseline p95 must be a positive finite number: 0" when the measured baseline rounds to zero — the gate fails because the thing it measures is TOO FAST. Filed as rf2-yumaq. Eleven of the twelve entries are greens that should have been red; that one is the first red that should have been green, and this mutation entry is the first that is neither — it is a measurement of a measurement going wrong.

A "VERIFIED NOTHING-TO-DO" MUST BE VERIFIED BY MAKING THE EXISTING ASSERTION RED, NOT BY READING IT (2026-08-11, rf2-7b4m finding 2).

WHAT HAPPENED, and it is the best form of this outcome I have seen. A twice-relayed audit claim said an Xray hidden-retained / visible-connected / unmounted assertion was still missing. It was not: rf2-hic-023 had landed it in commit 7c45f3ca95 UNDER AN UNRELATED SUBJECT, which is exactly why the claim still read open — nobody had re-checked, and the commit's subject gave no hint.

THE WORKER DID NOT STOP AT READING IT. It inverted both assertions and confirmed each went red at a named line, and dropped the underlying fields (`:hidden-retained` from `host-projection`, then `visibility-note`) and confirmed three more panel reds. Only then did it report nothing-to-do. Its own phrase: "A verified nothing-to-do — but verified by making it red, not by reading it."

WHY THAT MATTERS. Reading an assertion tells you it EXISTS. Making it fail tells you it DECIDES something. This repo has found the difference three times in one day: a row asserting a label plus "nothing has happened yet" that a dead timer satisfied for weeks; a row asserting an fx was in the REGISTRAR, which a never-reached fx satisfies perfectly, with a real shipped bug underneath; and testbed rows that passed whether or not an intent ever arrived. An unverified "already covered" would have left any of those in place.

SO THE BRIEF SHOULD SAY: if you conclude the work is already done, PROVE THE EXISTING COVERAGE BITES before closing — invert it, watch it red, restore, verify the restore by hashing bytes. A close on a read is a close on an assertion nobody has ever seen fail.

TWO SUPPORTING NOTES FROM THE SAME RUN:
  - AN ARITHMETIC CONSTANT CAN BE LOAD-BEARING FOR A REASON THE ROW DOES NOT STATE. `(= 4 distinct-regs)` was not a count for its own sake: it proves `into #{}` counted four IDENTITIES, because a value-collapsing set would have answered 1. Changing 4 to 5 was the instrumentation control; neutralising the release call was the runtime control. Both were needed and they test different things.
  - AN AUDIT PHRASE CAN BE TRUE-SOUNDING AND ANSWERED. The audit said "no Xray lifecycle view/change landed". Today that reads as still-open if judged by "does Xray distinguish the three states?" — it does NOT, and correctly: the tables cannot, so the door states the distinction as `:host-opaque` and refuses to fabricate it. THAT REFUSAL IS THE LANDED ANSWER. When re-checking an audit item, ask whether a deliberate refusal already discharges it.

A WORKER CAN CREATE A node_modules JUNCTION INTO THE MAYOR CHECKOUT AND SAY SO — CHECK THE REPORT, NOT JUST THE FILESYSTEM. The composing-18216 worker (rf2-drpa3.182.16, PR #7201) had no node_modules in its worktree and junctioned `implementation/node_modules` to the mayor's, then flagged it in its final report unprompted: the junction MUST be `cmd /c rmdir`-ed BEFORE `git worktree remove`, or the removal follows it and deletes the mayor's real node_modules (canary: 101 entries). That is the exact failure recorded in reference_worktree_removal_emptied_mayor_node_modules.
THE OPERATIONAL POINT: my hygiene sweep already detects junctions two ways (PowerShell LinkType/Target, plus a non-following `[IO.Directory]::Delete(path,false)` that refuses a real populated directory). Both would have caught this. But the cheapest signal was the worker TELLING me — so read final reports for infrastructure notes, not only for the deliverable. A worker that sets up its own environment may leave something the hygiene loop has to know about, and it is likelier to say so than the filesystem is to make it obvious.
ALSO: worktrees are created without node_modules by design, so any worker needing a browser or node gate will either `npm ci` (slow, safe) or junction (fast, dangerous). If a brief needs those gates, say which one to do — I have been silent on it and got lucky.

A WORKER CAN DIE BETWEEN ITS LAST COMMIT AND ITS PR — CHECK ORPHANED BRANCHES, NOT JUST OPEN PRs. The record-corrections worker stalled mid-gate-run with BOTH beads complete, committed and pushed, and no PR. From the mayor's usual sweep (gh pr list) it was invisible: no PR, no worker, nothing to merge — the work would have sat on the branch indefinitely and a later hygiene run would have found a branch with unmerged commits and correctly refused to touch it, forever.
THE SWEEP TO ADD, cheap and worth doing whenever a worker dies or the PR queue looks empty: for every origin/worker/* branch, `git cherry origin/main origin/<branch> | grep -c '^+'` > 0 AND `gh pr list --head <branch> --state all` == 0 means COMPLETE WORK WITH NO PR. Recover it by opening the PR yourself from the worker's OWN commits — that is durability, not authorship, and it does NOT violate 'never build a commit from someone else's uncommitted work' because nothing uncommitted is involved. Say in the PR body that the mayor recovered it and why, and defer the gates to CI rather than claiming a run the worker never finished.

A WORKER RETURNING "BLOCKED BY SCOPE" IS A REQUEST ADDRESSED TO ME, NOT A STATUS TO RECORD (2026-07-26).

rf2-3bjs8 — migrate examples/ off the donor — SAT BLOCKED FOR TWO DAYS AND THE BLOCKER WAS MY OWN FENCE. I dispatched it with an examples/-only fence. The worker went at it, correctly returned STRUCTURALLY BLOCKED, and proved it with FOUR MEASURED REDS, each rc captured: check_donor_inventory.py --ci drifts; implementation/ui scaffold-smoke fails; the shadow-config contract fails; and .github/workflows/test.yml:2281 is the CI harness for the second. NONE OF THOSE FILES WERE INSIDE THE FENCE I GAVE IT.

So the bead was not blocked by the work. IT WAS BLOCKED BY THE BRIEF, and it came back with the evidence and the exact fence it needed. I recorded that faithfully on the bead — and then left it, because "blocked" READ AS A STATUS rather than as an action item assigned to me.

THE RULE: WHEN A WORKER RETURNS BLOCKED-BY-SCOPE, THE NEXT MAYOR ACTION IS TO GRANT THE FENCE OR RULE THE SCOPE — IN THAT PASS, NOT LATER. It is the same shape as a green PR waiting to merge: the work is done, the cost of delay is entirely mine, and nothing downstream moves until I act. A blocked-by-difficulty return is different — that one genuinely waits.

HOW RARE, MEASURED: only three beads in the whole tracker carry sequencing/fence-bounce language. So this is not systemic — it is rare and EXPENSIVE, which is exactly the profile that escapes notice. A defect that happened twenty times would have been fixed; one that happens three times sits.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IN A REPORT, so I catch it next time: a blocked-by-scope return names FILES OR SURFACES IT COULD NOT TOUCH and usually offers the exact fence. A blocked-by-difficulty return names a QUESTION IT COULD NOT ANSWER. The first is mine to unblock in the same pass; the second waits for evidence or a ruling.

AND THE SAME LOGIC APPLIES TO A PHRASE I PUT IN MOST BRIEFS: "say so and I will sequence". That is a promise. If a worker takes it up, honouring it is a same-pass obligation — otherwise I have invited a report and then not read it as a request.

A WORKER's `bd close` is reverted by the mayor's `git checkout HEAD -- .beads`, and the loss is SILENT on both sides. Measured three times on 2026-09-03/04: rf2-6r9j.52 once, then rf2-6r9j.37 and rf2-6r9j.28 together.

MECHANISM, and why the CLAUDE.md bullet does not fully cover it. That bullet warns the MAYOR not to checkout .beads after its OWN `bd close`. But workers run `bd close` from the mayor checkout too, at a time the mayor does not control. So the sequence that loses data is: worker closes a bead -> mayor's checkpoint exports (may or may not catch it) -> mayor runs `git checkout HEAD -- .beads` -> the export reverts -> the NEXT checkpoint writes that revert back over the Dolt database. The close is gone from BOTH the export and the database, along with its close reason. Nothing errors. `bd list` looks normal. The worker's completion report still says "CLOSED", so the mayor believes it.

THE DETECTOR, and it must be built carefully because the obvious form fails open. For every OPEN bead, look for a payload commit on the trunk:

  git log origin/main --oneline -E --grep="<escaped-id>([^0-9A-Za-z.]|$)"

Two traps, both of which produced a WRONG answer in this repo:
- `jq -r '.[].id'` on Windows emits ids with a TRAILING CARRIAGE RETURN. Fed through a `while read` loop every grep misses and the sweep reports a clean zero over 48 ids. A control using hardcoded literals PASSES while the pipeline returns nothing - the control must share the shape of the target, i.e. come through the same pipeline. Pipe through `tr -d '\r'`.
- An unanchored grep treats `.` as a wildcard, so `rf2-6r9j.1` matches `.101` and `.161`. Escape the dots AND anchor the trailing boundary, or the sweep reports a page of false positives.

Run BOTH controls every time: a known-closed id that IS on the trunk (must hit) and a nonsense id (must miss).

A HIT IS A POINTER, NOT A VERDICT. Most hits are legitimately open: deliberate partials, a bead whose code half landed while its spec half waits on an unmerged PR, epics, and beads held for Mike. The revert signature specifically is: a worker's completion report SAYS closed, the payload is on the trunk, and the bead reads OPEN in both `bd show` and `git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl`.

RECOVERY is cheap and complete: re-close with the full reason reconstructed from the worker's report, then run `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` IMMEDIATELY, before any `git checkout HEAD -- .beads`. Verify in both places afterwards - `bd show` and the committed export - because verifying only one is how the second occurrence went unnoticed.

MITIGATION for the mayor's own loop: run the closes, then checkpoint, and only then do the checkout/rebase/push sequence. Never close a bead between the checkpoint and the checkout.

A worker that returns its bead from in_progress to OPEN is often making a deliberate, correct decision — not a tracker glitch. Read the completion report before inferring from timestamps. On 2026-08-21 the verdictlbl worker (rf2-egdaq) un-claimed its bead 'so it doesn't read as held', because only half the bead was shippable and the other half was Mike's operator call; closing or holding it would have buried that. I read the one-second in_progress->open gap in bd history as a machine re-import, wrote that wrong inference onto the bead as a note, and re-claimed it — undoing a considered choice. A one-second flip is NOT evidence of a machine write; bd history timestamps cluster tightly because bd checkpoints frequently. The general rule: tracker status changes made by a live worker are signals FROM that worker, and the completion report is the authority on what they meant.

A WORKER'S READING OF A FILE IT DID NOT EDIT IS A CLAIM, NOT A MEASUREMENT (2026-08-11).

WHAT HAPPENED. The rf2-6ync triage worker classified all 69 prototype suites — excellent work, independently reconciled by the merged-PR audit against the pre-port tree. In passing it also stated that two suites :require EACH OTHER and that both reach a bench SSR namespace with no package counterpart. I transcribed both into a note on rf2-6rw9 and made them THAT BEAD'S STATED CONTENT: "the package needs an SSR entry first."

BOTH WERE FALSE. The rf2-b6ja worker checked at the source: the two files name each other exactly once each, in docstring [[wiki-links]] (lines 31 and 57) — no code dependency — and neither reaches ssr.entry at all; they use React's own react-dom/server directly. So a bead I wrote described runtime work that does not need doing, and would have sent a worker to build an SSR entry for nothing.

THE DISTINCTION I MISSED: a worker's findings about the files IT EDITED are backed by the gates it ran. Its remarks about NEIGHBOURING files are ordinary reading — often right, sometimes not, and never gate-checked. I apply "verify the premise at the source" to code claims and to audit findings; I had not applied it to a worker's incidental observations, because they arrive inside a report whose main content IS verified.

THE RULE: when a worker's report supplies the CONTENT of a new bead — particularly a blocker, a dependency, or "X must happen first" — verify that specific claim before writing it down, or write it as REPORTED rather than as fact. One grep is usually enough; here `git grep ssr.entry` would have settled it in seconds.

AND WHEN IT TURNS OUT WRONG, correct the bead loudly rather than quietly amending: the wrong version may already have shaped a brief or another bead's framing. In this case it had also mis-assigned a third suite to the wrong bead.

SISTER RULE: the same shape as rows-must-be-discriminating and witness-derived-from-fix — the common thread is that CONFIDENCE TRAVELS FURTHER THAN EVIDENCE. A verified report lends its authority to the unverified sentences sitting next to it.

I RELAYED A WORKER'S JUSTIFICATION WITHOUT CHECKING IT, AND IT WAS WRONG (2026-08-14).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker declined to fold a case-insensitive comparison, saying it sat on a HOTTER PATH than the sibling it had just fixed — one that "runs for every controlled input rather than only file ones". I wrote that into the follow-up bead and then into the follow-up brief, twice, as the reason the decision was hard.

THE NEXT WORKER READ THE SOURCE AND REFUTED IT. The sibling predicate's fold ALREADY runs for every controlled input with a string type, not only file ones — both predicates sit behind the IDENTICAL gate. They differ in CALL COUNT (2 versus 1), not in POPULATION. The path is about twice as hot, not categorically hotter.

So the decision I framed as a genuine cost trade-off was, once measured, about 0.1% of a render — and the worker folded it, correctly.

THE LESSON IS NOT ABOUT THAT WORKER, WHOSE REFUSAL WAS REASONABLE AND WHOSE DELIVERABLE WAS EXCELLENT. It is that A REPORT'S REASONING IS A CLAIM, EXACTLY LIKE ITS NUMBERS. I have been treating worker COUNTS as claims to re-derive while treating worker EXPLANATIONS as established. An explanation is the easier thing to get wrong, because nothing in the gate machinery checks it.

THE RULE: when relaying a worker's reasoning into a bead or a brief, either verify it at source or ATTRIBUTE IT AS THAT WORKER'S READING and tell the next worker to check it. I attributed the count and not the argument, which is backwards.

AND THE MEASUREMENT DISCIPLINE THAT SETTLED IT IS WORTH COPYING: medians of seven runs of a million calls, taken twice, against React's own 13 microsecond render-and-commit for the same field. The worker also reported an HONEST NON-RESULT — the whole-render red/green comparison could not resolve the delta, because run-to-run spread was two orders of magnitude larger — rather than dressing it up as a measurement.

A WORKTREE PINS ITS BRANCH — SO A FIX-WORKER CANNOT CHECK OUT A BRANCH ANOTHER WORKTREE STILL HOLDS (2026-08-11).

WHAT I DID: dispatched a fix-worker with `git worktree add <new path> worker/native-hic030` to repair a red PR. That branch was still checked out in the original worker's worktree. GIT REFUSES TO CHECK OUT ONE BRANCH IN TWO WORKTREES, so my dispatch could not even complete its setup step.

AND I COULD NOT SIMPLY FREE IT. The original worktree held an UNCOMMITTED modification to spec/009 — the previous worker's local experiment, partially reverted despite its report claiming a verified clean revert. scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh REFUSED with REMOVE_REFUSED_KEEP, correctly: the file is not build output. And the method forbids building a commit from another worker's uncommitted work, because only its author knows whether it forms a coherent change.

THE CORRECT DISPATCH FOR A FIX-WORKER ON AN EXISTING BRANCH — use a detached checkout at the REMOTE head and push with an explicit refspec:

  git worktree add --detach <path> origin/worker/<branch>
  ...work, commit...
  git push origin HEAD:worker/<branch>

That updates the PR's branch without the branch ever being checked out, so it works whether or not the original worktree is still around. Verify afterwards that gh pr view's headRefOid equals the local rev-parse HEAD.

THE CHECK TO RUN BEFORE DISPATCHING TO AN EXISTING BRANCH: `git worktree list | grep <branch>`. If anything holds it, either reap that worktree first (only on a quotable completion report, and only if it is clean) or dispatch detached. Do not discover this in the worker's setup step.

THE SAME MECHANISM AS reap-before-merge-avoids-the-orphaned-branch: the worktree pins the branch, and nothing else does. There it cost an orphaned remote on every merge; here it cost a dispatch that could not start.

SECOND FINDING, WORTH ITS OWN LINE: the original worker reported "reverted both files with a verified git checkout -- (reverted-clean: True '')" and spec/009 WAS STILL MODIFIED. Its verification either ran before a later edit or checked the other file. So a worker's claim of a clean tree is not evidence of one — git status in the worktree is. Check it before reaping, which is exactly what the removal script's guard does and why the guard exists.

PASSING A FLAG A GATE DOES NOT ACCEPT PRODUCES ARGPARSE'S EXIT 2, WHICH READS EXACTLY LIKE A GATE FAILURE. Measured 2026-09-05: `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py --ci` exits **2** from argparse; the correct invocation is BARE. The worker that hit it said it "nearly banked that as a finding" — i.e. nearly reported a clean tree as red.

WHY THE CONFUSION IS EASY AND THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC: the sibling gate `scripts/check_readme_links.py` DOES take `--ci`, and the two are routinely named together in the same breath (both run in `test.yml`'s `verify-readme-links` job). So the flag transfers by habit. And exit 2 is a plausible gate-failure code — the api-manifest generator's `--check` arm genuinely uses exit 2 for a real finding — so nothing about the number says "you invoked me wrongly".

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE OUTPUT, NOT THE CODE. Argparse writes a usage line to stderr and names the unrecognised argument. A real finding names a FILE, a LINE and what is wrong. **Read the first line of stderr before believing any non-zero exit** — the same discipline as reading a count line rather than an exit code on `check_provenance_pins.py`, arrived at from the opposite direction.

THE GENERAL RULE, now measured in four different ways on this project: **AN EXIT CODE IS A HINT, NOT A VERDICT.**
  * exit 0 with a real finding printed (`check_provenance_pins.py` on a fabricated pin)
  * exit 0 with an EMPTY log on success, so a plant is needed to prove liveness (`check_doc_slugs.py`)
  * exit 0 having done nothing at all (`gh pr edit`; `cmd /c` junction ops from Git Bash)
  * and now non-zero for a reason that is not a finding at all (argparse)
In every case the fix is the same: **read what the tool SAID, and check the world rather than the status.**

MEASURED TWICE IN ONE SESSION, 2026-08-21, both times while I was AUDITING something. A zero misled me in two different ways and neither announced itself.

CASE 1 — A FLAG THAT DOES NOT EXIST. I ran `python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py --list-files` to test which files that gate scans. There is no --list-files flag. The command printed nothing, my `grep -c` returned 0, and I read it as 'the gate does not scan that file'.

CASE 2 — THE RIGHT COMMAND, THE WRONG OUTPUT SHAPE. I then ran the real flag, `--verbose`, and grepped its output for a PATH. It returned 0. But --verbose prints PER-ROOT COUNTS and never prints a single file path: 'scanning 752 markdown files across 11 roots: docs 410, spec 52, skills 173...'. So the pattern could not have matched however many files were scanned. I was one step from recording a false drift finding against my own briefs — that check_doc_slugs.py does not cover docs/design/hicasso/studio/.

WHAT SETTLED IT WAS A PLANTED FAULT, FROM A WORKER RATHER THAN FROM ME. worker/rowfix-l43ft planted broken link targets in both studio pages it was editing and the gate returned EXIT 1 naming both by path and line. That is positive evidence the gate reads those files, and it is the only kind that would have done.

THE RULE, which the gate-mechanics block already states and which I did not apply to MYSELF: a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed. Before believing a zero, run the pattern once against something it MUST find. And when the zero is about a TOOL's output, read the output's SHAPE first — a grep for a path in output that only ever prints counts is a dead pattern dressed as a finding.

THE SHARPER LESSON: I was auditing my own enforced rules when this happened, which is exactly when a false negative is most expensive — it would have sent a worker to 'fix' a correct clause in five briefs, and the repair would have made every future brief UNDERSTATE coverage, the very direction rf2-butkd's carve-out sentence exists to prevent.

A ZERO-HIT GREP IS NOT PROOF OF ABSENCE WHEN THE CORPUS WRAPS LINES — I filed a method-gap bead whose central claim was itself unverified (2026-08-11, rf2-owmq).

THE IRONY IS THE POINT. I filed rf2-owmq saying "nothing tells the mayor to verify its OWN brief's factual claims", and cited `grep -c` returning 0 on dispatch-prompt-template.md as the evidence. THE BEAD ITSELF CONTAINED AN UNVERIFIED CLAIM. Its worker found the gate half of the rule had been in that file since commit 81ce0ba455 (2026-07-31), at line 151: "Never nominate a gate that does not cover the surface being edited ... a gate run over an excluded path exits green having verified nothing ... Read the exclusion config before naming the gate." That is my proposed clause and its one-line reason, near-verbatim, already present.

TWO MORE OF MY GREPS WERE FALSE NEGATIVES IN THE SAME BEAD:
  - Shape 3 already ends "not every finding is actioned" — my grep missed it BECAUSE THE PHRASE WRAPS A LINE.
  - bootstrap.md:340 already carries "Read the current source at the named site before dispatching. A verified 'nothing to do' is a good outcome; an assumed one is not."

THE MECHANISM: these method files are hand-wrapped prose at ~78 columns. Any phrase longer than a few words has a NEWLINE SOMEWHERE INSIDE IT at an unpredictable point, so a multi-word `grep` pattern misses it. `grep -c "verify the premise"` returns 0 against a file that says exactly that, wrapped.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD when checking whether a prose corpus already says something:
  - Grep for SINGLE DISTINCTIVE WORDS, not phrases — `nominate`, `exclusion`, `premise`, `claim` — then read the hits.
  - Or use `grep -z` / `rg --multiline` so the pattern can cross a newline.
  - Or, best for a small corpus: READ THE SECTION. These files are a few hundred lines; a claim about what they do not contain is worth the read.
  - And state the method in the bead, so the worker can judge whether the search could have found the thing.

THE WIDER RULE, and this is the fourth variant of it today: DO NOT ASSERT FROM MEMORY OR FROM A WEAK SEARCH WHAT A DOCUMENT CONTAINS. The three earlier variants were naming the wrong gate for a surface, claiming the method carried a discipline it never had, and quoting an advisory ledger row as a settled ruling. This one is subtler because the evidence LOOKED mechanical — a grep with a number attached reads like proof, and a false negative reads exactly like a true one.

THE OUTCOME WAS STILL GOOD, because the worker was told the brief's premises are claims: it cross-referenced the existing line instead of restating it, preserving single-source. The honest residual gap was real and narrower than I filed — nothing told the mayor to check its own assertions, and that clause is what landed.

READING A BEAD LIST THROUGH head/tail AND THEN REASONING ABOUT WHAT IS NOT THERE IS A FALSE-NEGATIVE GENERATOR (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: I ran 'bd list --status open --limit 0 | tail -32' on a 31-item backlog. The trailer line said 'Total: 31 issues' and I read 27 rows, because tail had cut four rows off the TOP. I then noticed rf2-0moc4 was 'gone' from the list and started investigating an operator-ruling bead I thought a worker had wrongly closed. It was open the whole time. 'bd show' settled it in one command.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS ARITHMETIC AND IT IS FREE: the list prints its own total. COUNT THE ROWS YOU ACTUALLY SAW and compare against that total before believing anything about absence. 27 != 31 was visible on screen and I read past it.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT AS 'a search returning zero is not a check that passed', one level up: there the pattern was wrong, here the VIEW was clipped, and both answer 'not present' in the same voice as 'not there'. A pipeline that truncates is a filter, and the rule against piping a gate through a filter has the same root.

CHEAPEST FIX: when the question is about absence rather than about a particular row, do not pipe at all. When context forces a pipe, pipe BOTH ends (head and tail) and reconcile against the printed total.

ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE FROM THE TREE IS SOMETIMES THE METHOD WORKING — check how a witness was produced before scoring it a Gap (2026-08-14, rf2-2ius2 worker).

TWO CELLS WERE SCORED "GAP" AND BOTH WERE WRONG, for opposite reasons, and both errors are worth recognising by shape.

MIGRATION was scored Gap on the grounds that only the in-repo corpus was covered. In fact the migration bead ran ALL THREE repositories with recorded hashes, plus two controls. The external repositories are CLONED READ-ONLY AND NEVER VENDORED — so their absence from the tree IS THE METHOD WORKING, not missing evidence. A reader looking for the corpus in the tree finds nothing and concludes nothing was done.

ACCESSIBILITY was scored Gap on the grounds that no bead owns an axe run. But axe appears in NO acceptance column: the relevant acceptance is names, roles, keyboard, and virtualized/overlay focus. The bead that mentions axe is an explicit DECLINE, axe-core is in neither the manifest nor the lockfile, and the not-bundled posture is recorded. So the cell was measuring against a requirement that does not exist.

THE COMMON SHAPE: a Gap is a claim about the RELATIONSHIP between a requirement and its evidence, and it can fail at either end. One cell had evidence it could not see; the other had a requirement that was never there. Neither error is visible from the cell alone — both need reading the acceptance and the method.

SO BEFORE SCORING ANY ROW A GAP: read what the acceptance ACTUALLY REQUIRES, and read HOW the witness was produced. If the witness is produced by a method that deliberately leaves no artefact in the tree — a read-only clone, an external run, a scripted probe — its absence proves nothing.

AND THE SAME PASS FOUND THE INVERSE, which is the cheaper error to catch: a pointer whose obligation had been DISCHARGED. The cell warned that two documents contradicted each other; a merged bead had reconciled them. The right repair was to retire the pointer entirely rather than re-point it.

ABSENT FROM THE BEADS TRACKER DOES NOT MEAN "NEVER CREATED". THE TRACKER IS GARBAGE-COLLECTED, AND I BUILT A WHOLE BEAD CLASS ON THE OPPOSITE ASSUMPTION (measured 2026-09-03 by the phantom-a worker; the false bead was rf2-cu5h, filed by me).

THE MEASUREMENT THAT KILLED IT: the tracker held 10,444 rows on 2026-07-11, 2,149 on 2026-07-19, and 539 today — against 14,551 ids EVER EXPORTED (union of 13 snapshots across all 11,413 export commits). So roughly 96% of ids that ever existed are absent from a "bd show" today, BY DESIGN. Of 204 absent ids found gating live-conditional text, 200 were verified REAL-THEN-COLLECTED and the other 4 were a regex truncating longer tokens. NET PHANTOMS: ZERO.

WHY MY CHECK LOOKED RIGOROUS AND WAS WORTHLESS: I verified each id with "bd show" returning "no issue found" (exit 1) AGAINST A CONTROL THAT RESOLVES, and against every id in the CURRENT export. Both halves are real checks. Neither can distinguish "never existed" from "existed and was collected", because the current export is a WORKING SET, not an archive. A control drawn from the working set can only ever confirm that the working set is readable.

THE ARCHIVE IS GIT HISTORY OF .beads/issues.jsonl. That is where an id's existence is decidable — a union over export commits answers the question the tracker cannot.

AND THE CORRECTED READING OF WHAT THOSE CITATIONS ARE: they are DISCHARGED PROMISES, not phantoms. rf2-k0rbk — the one I cited as the worst instance — was real, was literally "confirm or rename the provisional error id", and was CLOSED 2026-08-06 with "the id stands... Remaining touch: the provisional stamps' removal is a one-line comment/docs touch". So a PROVISIONAL marker pending it is not gated on nothing; it is gated on something that RESOLVED, and the remaining work is to record the resolution. A completely different remedy from the one I ruled.

THE MECHANISM WAS NEITHER HYPOTHESIS I WROTE ON THE BEAD: tracker GC, plus one bulk bead-ref strip commit (2d64e1f7c2) that replaced an id INSIDE backticks and left a dangling "see bead" fragment standing. Its commit message reports every gate green, because no gate looks at this.

THE RULES:
  1. Before calling an id a phantom, search the git history of the export, not the tracker.
  2. "Absent, plus a control that resolves" is not proof of non-existence when the corpus is collected. Ask what the control can actually discriminate.
  3. A citation to a CLOSED bead is provenance and is wanted. A live conditional pending a bead that RESOLVED is a discharged promise: record the resolution, do not remove the citation.
  4. No tooling for this class — a linter would flag 292 legitimate sites.

AN ABSENT REMOTE BRANCH IS THE SIGNATURE OF A COMPLETED MERGE HERE, NOT OF WORK THAT WAS NEVER PUSHED — measured 2026-09-04 closing rf2-7ngc.

THE FALSE ALARM. A stranded sweep reported "304 insertions of documentation work survive only as a local commit in one working tree", filed it P3, wrote a decision dossier, and held it for the operator across two days and several ticks. The work had merged five days EARLIER as PR #8812. The branch tip was byte-identical to that PR's headRefOid, and the PR read state=MERGED.

THE TWO INSTRUMENTS THAT AGREED AND WERE BOTH WRONG, which is why it was believed:

1. `git ls-remote --heads origin <branch>` returned 0, with a positive control on `main` returning 1 — so the zero was a genuine check, correctly run, and it MEANT the opposite of what it was read to mean. This repo deletes the head branch on merge, so a merged branch's absence from the remote is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a branch that was never pushed. The sweep even recorded "there are ZERO codex/* branches on the remote at all" — which was the tell, read as corroboration.

2. A three-dot `git diff --stat` against the merge-base showed 14 files, +304 -34, and was read as "the diff has not been overtaken by trunk movement". A three-dot diff reports the branch's OWN content whether or not that content also sits on main; it can NEVER detect absorption. Re-running it later against a newer trunk feels like re-verification and re-confirms nothing.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT SETTLES IT is `git cherry origin/main <branch>`: a leading `-` means contained, `+` means not proven contained. It was applied to the three OTHER branches in the same sweep and not to this one. Cheaper still where a PR exists: compare the branch tip to `gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid` and read `state`.

CONTROL THE CHERRY BEFORE BELIEVING A `-`. On the same day, from the same checkout, `git cherry origin/main worker/receipts-hic081` returned `+` on all three of its commits — so the instrument discriminates here and now, which is what makes the `-` evidence rather than a default.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the reusable half: TWO INSTRUMENTS AGREEING IS NOT CORROBORATION WHEN BOTH ARE BLIND TO THE SAME THING. Absence-from-remote and a three-dot diff are both silent about containment, so running both feels like triangulation and is one measurement taken twice. Ask what a NEGATIVE result would look like under the alternative hypothesis; here the merged case and the never-pushed case produce byte-identical output from both.

AND CHECK WHETHER A BEAD ALREADY RULES ON IT. rf2-7ngc's second ask ("does this spike still matter?") was already ruled KEEP, with a release condition, by rf2-lafmr — closed a fortnight earlier. A BRANCH sweep never looks at beads, so a disposition recorded on a bead is invisible to it and gets re-derived as an open question. Search the tracker for the branch name before filing a branch for decision.

RELATED: [[flattening-does-not-undo-a-mid-token-line-break]], [[census-piped-through-head-reports-the-cap]].

A SINGLE ACTIVITY READ CAN CATCH A GENUINE LULL — USE THE TIP COMMIT TIMESTAMP AS THE TIEBREAKER (2026-08-14).

WHAT HAPPENED. At 12:33 all five live workers read zero touched files in an 11-minute window, and the processor queue read 0.00, so the box was idle. Both of the stranded sweep's signals — a still tip and a quiet worktree — pointed at five simultaneous strands. I re-measured with a 90-second find budget to rule out a timeout artifact; still zero. I was about to message all five.

THE TIEBREAKER THAT SAVED IT. `git log -1 --format=%cI worker/<name>` showed three of the five had committed within the previous TWO MINUTES, and all five carried commits ahead of main. They were alive and between operations. The zero was real and meant nothing.

WHY THE EXISTING SIGNALS BOTH FAILED AT ONCE. A worker that has just committed and is deciding what to do next writes no files and moves no tip. That state is normal and can last minutes. When several workers hit it together — which is likely, since they were dispatched together and run similar phases — the fleet looks dead. An IDLE BOX makes it look worse, because idleness rules out the usual benign explanation of being inside a gate.

THE ORDER TO USE: read the tip SHA; if unchanged, read worktree activity; if that is also near zero, read `%cI` of the tip and the ahead-count BEFORE concluding anything. A commit within the last few minutes is definitive liveness and costs one command. Only when the tip is old AND the worktree is quiet AND the box is idle does the strand reading hold.

NOTE THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS WORTH THE EXTRA READ: messaging a live worker costs almost nothing, but redispatching over one violates the no-concurrent-workers-on-one-branch rule and can destroy uncommitted work. So the tiebreaker is not about avoiding a message — it is about not letting five simultaneous false positives push toward step 3.

ADVISORY-SCOPED-TO-CHANGED-FILES BEATS A BLOCKING GATE when most findings are legitimate (2026-08-14, rf2-46tt9 worker's answer).

THE QUESTION I ASKED: should the mechanical path-token sweep — extract every backticked path token from a page, test each against the tracked file list — become a gate? It finds real defects NO EXISTING GATE CAN SEE, because these are prose tokens rather than markdown links, so the link checker has nothing to resolve and passes green over all of them.

THE ANSWER, AND ITS REASONING IS THE VALUABLE PART: an ADVISORY scoped to CHANGED FILES, not a blocking gate.

  Measured: 370 distinct unresolved tokens across 107 files. OVERWHELMINGLY LEGITIMATE HISTORICAL RECORDS — pages that correctly describe what was true when measured.
  A gate that reds on those GETS DISABLED WITHIN A WEEK. That failure mode is already documented in a sibling checker's own docstring.
  The worker TRIED to find a syntactic rule separating pointer from record and COULD NOT. The closest — filename preservation — partitions one sub-family; the rest need judgment.

SO THE SHAPE THAT WORKS is the one a sibling gate already uses: --changed-since scoping. Fire only on pages a PR touches, REPORT RATHER THAN BLOCK, and let the author decide — they are the one person with the context to tell a pointer from a record.

THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, worth applying to every future gate proposal here: A GATE'S VALUE IS ITS PRECISION ON THE POPULATION IT WILL ACTUALLY SEE, not on the defect it was designed for. A check that is right about a real defect and wrong about a hundred legitimate cases is a check that will be turned off, and then it protects nothing.

AND IT PAIRS WITH THE STANCE: "trust the programmer" is exactly what routing an ambiguous finding to the author — rather than refusing their PR — looks like in practice.

SHELL HYGIENE FOR bd CONTENT — I have now broken this twice in one session (2026-08-11).

THE FAULT: passing bd text that contains BACKTICKS through a double-quoted string or an unquoted heredoc lets bash run the backticked span as command substitution. First instance: a bd remember whose backticked 'needs:'/'if:' ran as commands (bash printed 'needs:: command not found'). Second instance: a bd close whose backticked 'run: npm run build:hicasso-release' did the same, silently deleting that fragment from the close reason of rf2-rbdc.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN IT LOOKS: the bd command still SUCCEEDS. The text lands, minus whatever the shell ate, and the only signal is a stray 'command not found' line mixed into output I am often grepping. A close reason or a memory with a hole in it reads as complete.

THE RULE: for ANY bd text — remember, note, close --reason, create --description — write it to a file with a SINGLE-QUOTED heredoc and pass it with $(cat file):

  cat > /tmp/x.txt <<'XEOF'
  ...text, backticks and all, taken literally...
  XEOF
  bd close <id> --reason="$(cat /tmp/x.txt)"

The quoted delimiter is what matters — <<'XEOF' takes the body literally; <<XEOF does not. I already do this for long text; the lapses were both on text I judged 'short enough to inline'. Length is not the discriminator — CONTENT is. If it contains a backtick, a $, or a !, it goes in a quoted heredoc.

CHEAPER ALTERNATIVE when the text is genuinely one line: drop the backticks. They add nothing in a tracker field that renders as plain text.

A ONE-SYMBOL EXTENSION BEYOND A BEAD'S LETTER IS ACCEPTED WHEN IT IS THE SAME GRAMMAR, INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCED, AND WITNESSED (2026-08-11, rf2-ka4d / PR #7843).

A worker fixing areduce in hic lint's direct-view-call roster also added amap, flagged it in the PR body, and invited a trim. Accepted. areduce and amap are the same grammar one argument apart - both bind an index symbol and an accumulator symbol, which is exactly the shape the roster mishandled - and the worker REPRODUCED the identical false ERROR with amap at the pin and landed a witness (self-call-in-amap) rather than reasoning by analogy.

THE GENERAL RULE: for a ROSTER or CLASS bug, class-completeness is the deliverable, not sprawl. Trimming a reproduced sibling to honour the letter of a bead written before anyone knew the sibling existed is scope discipline used against the point of the work - it knowingly ships a build-blocking false ERROR one line from the fix.

THE LINE THAT KEEPS THIS FROM BEING LICENCE - all three conditions, not one: SAME GRAMMAR (not merely related), INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCED (a failing case of its own, not analogy), and WITNESSED (a test that goes red without the fix). A symbol that only felt related, or one added without its own failing case, gets trimmed.

AND THE WORKER'S CONDUCT IS THE PATTERN TO WANT: take it, flag it prominently, offer the trim. That gives the mayor a real decision instead of a silent widening or an unfixed sibling.

WHEN A LOWER LAYER **CAPTURES** AN ERROR INTO A DATA CHANNEL, THE CALLER'S EXCEPTION BRANCH BECOMES UNREACHABLE AND THE CALLER CONCLUDES SUCCESS. The branch is present, correct and never taken — so a reader auditing the caller sees error handling that looks complete. Three instances measured on 2026-09-05, in three unrelated subsystems, which is why it belongs as its own entry rather than as a note on any one of them.

THE THREE:
  * **Story's Start.** `run-loaders!`/`run-events!` deliberately CAPTURE a throwing `:loaders`/`:setup` handler onto `[:rf.story/assertions]` and return normally. So `prepare-ctx!` completed without throwing over a frame whose `:setup` never ran, `prepare-variant` resolved `nil`, and the step debugger published "ready · N steps" at cursor 0 **over a failed preparation**. `begin!`'s `.catch` branch needed no change — it existed; nothing ever reached it.
  * **The improver skill's storage cofx.** A supplier that throws is converted by the framework into `:rf.error/coeffect-exception` plus `:rf/skip-handler? true`, so the handler silently never runs. A "fail loudly" recommendation there would buy OBSCURITY, not diagnostics.
  * **A defect filed as silent** whose error was in fact raised loudly at source and discarded one layer up — the shape the mayor-method README already records.

THE DIAGNOSTIC QUESTION, and it is cheap: **for each failure mode, does it arrive as a THROW or as DATA?** If some arrive as data, the caller must inspect that data — a `try/catch` or `.catch` alone is a half-check that will pass the exact cases the lower layer was careful about. Ask it per failure mode, not per function: the Story case is precisely that **only HALF the prepare failures arrived as a throw**, so the branch worked for one half and was dead for the other.

AND THE LIFECYCLE COROLLARY, recorded by the worker that found it: a CAPTURED setup failure can leave the frame reading `:ready`, so **a check must key on the ASSERTION, never on lifecycle state.** The state machine is telling the truth about itself and lying about the outcome.

THE FIX SHAPE THAT WORKED: inspect the data channel at the seam where the promise resolves, and reject there — not at the print site, and not by converting the capture back into a throw, which would break the callers that rely on capture.

MAYOR 2026-08-16 00:35 — I PROPAGATED A REFUTED BOUND INTO A LIVE WORKER'S BRIEF, AND THE AUDIT CAUGHT IT BEFORE THE WORKER PUBLISHED. Recording the error and the correction.

WHAT I DID. rf2-3l6hf's window recovered two of three terms and reported the third, reader membership, as "bounded: < 0.006 ms/commit, under 1% of the commit half". I read that as a finding, wrote it into rf2-07rnj's dispatch brief as guidance — "quote the BOUND, not a figure ... Publish that bound" — and reported it to the operator the same way.

WHY IT IS WRONG, per the merged-PR audit of #8328, whose reasoning I have checked and accept. Let an observed delta y equal an unknown positive true cost t plus estimator error e. A reading of y = -0.0062 proves only that the negative error excursion exceeded 0.0062 + t. It does NOT establish that +/-0.0062 is a calibrated, symmetric floor, and it CANNOT upper-bound t. A most-negative observation is a statement about the error term, not about the quantity.

THE SECOND HALF, same shape: comparing the most-negative readings from DIFFERENT positive-cost arms at 4 frames and 32 frames cannot prove an 8x floor scaling. Two error excursions from two different arms are not two measurements of one floor.

SO READER MEMBERSHIP IS UNRESOLVED, NOT BOUNDED, until a genuine null/control arm exists or another valid bound is derived. And rf2-07rnj stays BLOCKED: rf2-3l6hf owned resolving the decomposition, one of its original terms still does not resolve, and a decomposition with an unresolved term is not one - which is rf2-07rnj's own founding argument turned on itself.

*** THE GENERAL RULE, WHICH IS THE PART TO CARRY. *** An impossible reading tells you the instrument's error reached at least that far. It does not calibrate the error, and it does not bound the thing being measured. Treating "the worst negative I saw" as "the floor" is the same move as treating "no test failed" as "the code is correct" - it converts an absence into a guarantee. Whenever a worker reports a bound derived from readings that should have been positive, ASK WHAT NULL ARM PRODUCED IT. If the answer is "the impossible readings themselves", it is not a bound.

HOW IT REACHED A WORKER, and this is the process failure rather than the arithmetic one. The premises-are-claims sentence was in rf2-07rnj's brief, and it did not protect against this, because I passed the bound as GUIDANCE ("publish that bound") rather than as a premise to check. That is exactly the failure mode docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md already names for a LEAN: a worker reads guidance as instruction and a premise as a claim, so anything phrased as guidance bypasses the check. A NUMBER I ASSERT IS A LEAN TOO. Demand the evidence that produced it before writing it into a brief - here, one question would have caught it: what null arm produced that bound?

RECOVERY: the live worker was messaged the moment the audit was read, before it published. It was told to keep every measurement it had taken, publish no bound, not chase the term by widening the window, report, and leave rf2-07rnj open and blocked.

AN INSTRUMENT'S OWN POSITIVE CONTROL CAN BE WRONG BY ARITHMETIC. A worker predicted 8 B/double for a JS double array; retention priced the SAME object at 16.002 B/double, identical on 20 and 40 copies with residue 0. Cause: `.slice()` of a HOLEY double array does not take V8's packed fast path. "A SIGNAL THAT CANNOT CHANGE WHEN THE DEFECT APPEARS IS NOT A SIGNAL" (2026-08-11, rf2-qdqf / PR #7857).

I pushed hard for a particular fix to a fail-open gate: make it ANNOUNCE what it skipped, on the reasoning that converting an invisible hole into a visible one is the cheap half of the fix. I briefed it as the option I wanted argued seriously rather than dismissed. The worker argued it seriously and DEFEATED IT ON MEASUREMENT, and was right.

Two numbers killed it. First, 538 of 721 corpus files carry a fence, so the announcement fires on three quarters of the corpus - a permanent nag, and 88 of the noisiest lines would report an idiom already ruled good. Second and decisive: THE ANNOUNCEMENT'S TEXT IS IDENTICAL BEFORE AND AFTER A DOC LINK APPEARS INSIDE A FENCE. It says "I skipped N blocks" either way. So it cannot distinguish the healthy state from the defective one, which makes it not a warning but wallpaper.

THE GENERAL TEST, and it applies to any "surface the gap" proposal: ask what the output looks like WITH the defect present and WITHOUT it. If those two outputs are the same string, the signal carries no information no matter how visible it is. Visibility is not the property that matters - DISCRIMINATION is. This is the same rule the repo applies to test rows ("what single narrowing would let this row pass while the law is broken?"), turned on a diagnostic instead of a test.

ALSO WORTH KEEPING - the tuple I misread. FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES is NOT a "validate links inside fences here" roster. It is a "a markdown doc link inside a fence is ITSELF A FINDING here" roster, because a fenced block is verbatim and a link inside one renders literally. So widening it does not mean "resolve links in a prompt full of placeholders" (my worry, which made me favour the announce option) - it means BAN them there, which is correct for a text fence whose idiom is already backticked bare paths. I had the semantics backwards, and that error is what made the wrong option look necessary.

METHOD NOTE: the worker established this from the block comment and from `git log -S` on the constant - ONE commit had ever touched it - rather than from the code's behaviour alone. Intent lives in history; when a constant looks arbitrary, read the commit that introduced it before proposing to widen it.

ADDING ANY NEW FILE TO A SURFACE THE ALIAS CAMPAIGN HAS BASELINED REDS THE RATCHET UNLESS ITS REQUIRES ARE CANONICAL — **FIVE occurrences in one session**, none by a worker doing anything wrong, and each cost a full fix-worker cycle.

WHAT HAPPENS. `scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py` holds each surface at a floor in `scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn`. A new file's `[re-frame.x.y :as y]` bare-leaf requires count as violations, so a branch that merely ADDS a test file pushes its surface above the floor and reds `Require-alias dialect ratchet` — plus `Lint required`, which is `lint.yml`'s `if: always()` aggregator carrying it. It is ONE defect, not two: the aggregator's only failing step is "Fail if any required lint job failed", it runs in ~5s, and one worker read its job log showing `needs results: success, success, success, skipped, success, failure`.

THE FIVE, all 2026-09-04/05:
  * PR #9191 — 8 new edges in a new hicasso test file: implementation/hicasso 1025 vs floor 1017.
  * PR #9200 — 2 new edges, same surface: 1019 vs 1017.
  * PR #9204 — 3 new edges in a new flows test file: implementation/flows 158 vs floor 155.
  * PR #9207 — 5 new edges in a new ssr test file: implementation/ssr 404 vs floor 399.
  * implementation/core's floor is ZERO, so a single bare-leaf alias anywhere under it reds immediately.

THE FIX IS ALWAYS TO CANONICALISE, NEVER TO RAISE THE FLOOR. `--write-baseline` is MONOTONIC — a floor may only FALL — so raising it is unavailable and would regress finished campaign work. Spell new aliases dotted (`:as rf.<leaf>`) per spec/Conventions.md §Require-alias dialect. THE RATCHET'S OWN OUTPUT NAMES THE WANTED SPELLING ON EACH LINE (`-> :as rf.hicasso.impl.codec`), so the repair is transcription, not judgement.

AND THE RATCHET IS TWO-SIDED, which is the part that bites the FIXER rather than the author: it exits 1 on a surface BELOW its floor as well as above. The log lists every pre-existing violation too — hundreds on an unmigrated surface — and canonicalising any of THOSE reddens it from the other direction. Land at EXACTLY the floor. That exit 0 is itself the two-sided proof that main sat on the floor and the branch added exactly N. Three fix workers hit this and all three correctly left neighbouring aliases alone.

PUT THE WARNING IN EVERY BRIEF THAT MIGHT ADD A FILE — WHICH IS MOST OF THEM. This is not a case-by-case judgement: three of the five briefs above were written BEFORE this memory existed and all three reded; the two written after it carried the warning and did not. One sentence in the original brief replaces a whole fix-worker cycle. Treat it as default boilerplate for any implementation dispatch, alongside the stance and the fence.

DIAGNOSING ONE: `gh api repos/<o>/<r>/actions/jobs/<job-id>/logs` with an EXACT job-name match (two jobs can share a substring). Grep the log for the surface's own new file to isolate the delta from the pre-existing listing, and control the grep against a file you know is in the log.
