CLEANUP MUST PARSE `git worktree list`, NEVER CONSTRUCT NAMES (2026-07-19, second instance of this root cause in one session).

BUG: my hygiene loop derived a worktree branch as "worker/<dirname>" and derived the worktree from a branch by the same rule. WORKTREE DIRECTORY NAMES AND BRANCH NAMES ARE INDEPENDENT. Concrete case in this repo: the directory re-frame2-worktrees/core-handbook-html has branch worker/codex-audit-live checked out. Consequences of the wrong derivation, both live:
  (a) core-handbook-html resolved against a NONEXISTENT branch worker/core-handbook-html -> no PR found -> any decision keyed on that lookup is meaningless, and had a same-named PR existed it would have acted on the WRONG branch.
  (b) worker/codex-audit-live appeared to have NO worktree -> nominated for deletion WHILE CHECKED OUT. A belt-and-braces re-check (git worktree list | grep -c <branch>) aborted it; the primary scan was simply wrong.
Also missed: a detached-HEAD worktree (fix-6365-consumers) has NO branch at all, so any name-derived lookup silently returns nothing rather than erroring.

CORRECT SOURCE: `git worktree list` prints "<path> <sha> [<branch>]" or "(detached HEAD)". PARSE THAT. Path and branch are BOTH given — never construct either from the other, and handle the detached case explicitly.

SAME ROOT CAUSE AS THE WORKTREE I DESTROYED EARLIER TONIGHT (see memory: i-destroyed-a-live-worker-worktree): there I keyed a destructive action on a BRANCH NAME that collided with a historical merged PR. Both bugs are one mistake — DERIVING IDENTITY FROM A NAME INSTEAD OF READING IT. Names are not unique across time (bead ids repeat across sessions) and not unique across dimensions (dirname != branch). Key destructive operations on read identity: the SHA, the parsed branch, the PR headRefOid.

STANDING CHECKLIST for any destructive worktree/branch operation:
  1. Live-worker skip list first, unconditionally.
  2. Parse identity from `git worktree list`; never construct.
  3. Require merged-PR headRefOid == worktree HEAD before removal (name match proves nothing).
  4. Require 0 commits ahead of origin/main OR state==MERGED before branch deletion.
  5. Canary `ls implementation/node_modules | wc -l` (baseline 101) before and after every batch.
  6. Re-verify immediately before the destructive call; if the re-check disagrees with the scan, ABORT and investigate — the scan is the thing that is wrong.

CLEANUP GAP: "0 commits ahead + clean + no PR" MATCHES BOTH A DEAD-STALE WORKTREE AND A FRESHLY-STARTED LIVE ONE. Found 2026-07-24 before it caused damage.

THE SITUATION: my hygiene pass reaps worktrees that are 0 commits ahead of main, clean, and have no PR — the profile of a worker that never started. That is correct for STALE ones. But a worker that started SECONDS AGO has exactly the same profile: it has created its worktree and not yet committed anything. A worktree named pr-audit-6756, belonging to a DIFFERENT session audit loop, sat at 0-ahead/clean/no-PR while actively running.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS FRESHNESS, NOT SHAPE. A dead-stale worktree is parked on an OLD main commit and its files have not been touched in hours. A live one sits at or near CURRENT origin/main and has filesystem activity within minutes.

ADD TO THE STANDING CHECKLIST, as a rule that fires BEFORE any 0-commit removal:
  (a) Is HEAD at or very near current origin/main? Stale ones are behind by many commits — check `git -C <wt> rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main`. A large number means genuinely abandoned; ~0 means it just branched.
  (b) Any filesystem activity in the last ~30 minutes (excluding node_modules and .git)? `find <wt> -maxdepth 2 -newermt "-30 minutes"`. If yes, IT IS LIVE — skip unconditionally.
  (c) Is the worktree one I dispatched this session? If I cannot account for it, assume ANOTHER SESSION owns it and skip. Concurrent sessions independently create worker/* worktrees and branches in this repo; my dispatch list is not the full roster.

⚠️ THIS IS THE THIRD TIME THE SAME ROOT CAUSE HAS THREATENED LIVE WORK: I destroyed a live worktree by matching a HISTORICAL merged PR on a branch NAME, and separately nominated a checked-out branch for deletion by deriving the worktree from the branch name. All three are the same mistake — INFERRING LIVENESS OR IDENTITY FROM A PROPERTY THAT DOES NOT CARRY IT. A name is not identity; a commit count is not liveness.

STANDING RULE, unchanged and reinforced: reaping is only ever safe on (1) a merged PR whose headRefOid EQUALS the worktree HEAD, or (2) a worktree that is BOTH zero-commit AND demonstrably cold AND accounted for. When in doubt, leave it — an unreaped worktree costs disk; a reaped live one costs a worker its work.

AFTER A /clear, TaskList RETURNS NOTHING WHILE PRE-CLEAR BACKGROUND WORKERS ARE STILL ALIVE AND WILL STILL NOTIFY (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED. A fresh mayor session started with /clear. Two worker worktrees stood under the worktree parent: residue4-o9yo4 and workcount-n1b9h. TaskList returned 'No tasks found'. I checked both trees and each read: zero commits ahead of origin/main, clean git status --porcelain, and NO remote branch. I concluded both workers were dead, that there was nothing to salvage, and redispatched BOTH beads to new workers.

BOTH WERE ALIVE. residue4-o9yo4 reported done 25 minutes later with PR #8496 and two beads' worth of work including a refusal. workcount-n1b9h had 5,036 files touched in the last 30 minutes — a worker mid-gate. I had two duplicate executors out, and one of the pairs was BENCH-CLASS, where two concurrent runs WEDGE rather than fail.

EVERY SIGNAL I READ WAS TRUE AND NONE OF THEM MEANT WHAT I TOOK IT TO MEAN.
- TaskList empty: the harness's task registry does not survive /clear, but the AGENTS do. An empty TaskList after /clear is a statement about the registry, not about the fleet.
- Zero commits / clean tree: this is the EXPECTED reading for the commonest healthy state. A worker inside a long gate commits nothing by design. loops.md says exactly this and I read it an hour earlier.
- No remote branch: a worker pushes at milestones, not continuously. Absence of a remote ref is not absence of a worker.

THE ONE SIGNAL THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, AND IT COSTS ONE COMMAND:
  find <worktree> -newermt '30 minutes ago' -type f | grep -v '/\.git/' | wc -l
Near-zero is a strand. Thousands is a live gate. Run it on EVERY worktree before concluding anything about EVERY worker, and run it FIRST — before the commit count, before the remote check, before TaskList.

RULE FOR A POST-/clear MAYOR: enumerate git worktree list, sweep each tree for recent file activity, and treat any tree with activity as HELD by a live worker you cannot see. Do not redispatch its bead. TaskList is blind to it, SendMessage cannot reach it by a name you no longer have, and its completion notification WILL arrive — the agent id survives even though your listing does not.

COST HERE: two duplicate dispatches, both caught and stopped before they made any edit, so zero lost work. The catch was the pre-clear worker's own completion notification arriving and naming a bead I had just redispatched. That is luck, not a control.

CLJ-KONDO LOCAL/CI VERSION SKEW — the local binary reports NINE PHANTOM ERRORS that CI does not. Quantified 2026-07-24 by two workers independently.

LOCAL on this machine: clj-kondo v2025.10.23. CI PINS: 2026.04.15.

The older local version reports 9 errors of the form `Expected: throwable, received: boolean/nil` in `implementation/ui/test/**` — DONOR TEST CODE — which CI version does not report at all. A worker reproducing a lint failure locally will chase nine non-existent failures in code it did not touch.

THE RULE: when a lint or gate verdict must be AUTHORITATIVE, read CI OWN JOB LOG rather than trusting a local run.
  gh pr checks <PR> --json name,state,link      # find the job id
  gh run view --job=<id> --log-failed           # what CI actually said
If you must reproduce locally, pin the CI version first. And run CI exact invocation from .github/workflows/lint.yml — same flags, same lint paths — not a convenient approximation of it.

⚠️ THIS COMPOUNDS WITH THE PIPED-EXIT-CODE TRAP (see piping-a-gate-into-tail-discards-its-exit-code). Together they produce the worst case: a local run that reports failures CI does not have, through a pipe that hides the exit code, so a worker can conclude either "I broke something" or "I am green" with equal confidence and be wrong both times. Capture to a file, echo the exit code, and when it matters read CI log.

MAYOR NOTE — A SEQUENCING ERROR I MADE ON THE SAME INCIDENT, worth not repeating: several PRs were red on clj-kondo. One worker reported that a specific open PR carried the fix, so I instructed another worker to STAND DOWN and wait for that PR to merge. Wrong on two counts: (a) the fix had ALREADY landed on main as a separate direct commit, and (b) the PR I named was a different change. The correct remedy was simply A REBASE ONTO CURRENT MAIN. Had the worker obeyed, its gate would have stayed red and we would have lost a cycle; it had already rebased and told me so.
GENERALISATION: when a gate is red because of something INHERITED, the fix is almost always "rebase onto a main that has the remedy", NOT "wait for a specific PR". Verify WHERE the remedy actually is (git branch -r --contains <sha>) before telling anyone to wait on anything.

scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py READS THE clj-kondo VERSION PIN OFF lint.yml's INSTALL STEP BY ITS LITERAL COMMAND SHAPE (2026-08-11, rf2-rkl9 / PR #7888).

WHY THIS BIT. The rf2-rkl9 worker replaced lint.yml's two-hop clj-kondo install with a direct fetch of the pinned release archive. That is a one-file change by every obvious reading — and it broke a REQUIRED gate in a second file. check_fast_pr_gap.py knew only the `install-clj-kondo --version <pin>` shape, so with the installer gone `--check` exited 1 with "the clj-kondo version pin could not be read". Separately, the new lines stopped matching SETUP_PATTERNS, which misreported the installer as an unrun CI gate and moved the undecided-check count from 96 to 97.

BOTH FIXES WENT AT THE PARSER, not at the workflow: the pin now anchors on `clj-kondo/releases/download/v<pin>/`, which is a TIGHTER anchor than the old one, and the self-test fixture moved to match.

THE GENERAL RULE: a workflow edit can break a checker that parses that workflow, and nothing in the diff shows it. `.github/workflows/**` is already hot-zone for CONFLICT reasons; this is a second, independent reason to treat it carefully — the blast radius reaches scripts that read it. Before editing a workflow step, grep `scripts/` for the literal command strings in that step.

THE OTHER HALF OF THAT BEAD, worth keeping because it refutes a plausible remedy at source. The obvious fix was "pre-fetch the release zip with the same retry flags, then let the installer use it". IT CANNOT WORK. `script/install-clj-kondo` does `rm -rf "$filename"` immediately before its own `curl -o "$filename" -sL "$download_url"`, so a pre-fetched copy is deleted unread. Its curl carries no `-f` and no retry and is not configurable. **Any remedy that keeps that installer keeps the bug** — which is why the fix had to perform the download itself. I had written the pre-fetch option into the bead as the preferred, smaller remedy; only reading the installer showed it was unimplementable.

ADJACENT AND NOT A DEFECT, so nobody re-files it: test.yml's Babashka setup has the same two-hop shape, but wraps the WHOLE install in a 3-attempt outer loop, so its archive download is already covered.

A CLJS COMPILE GATE CAN FAIL OPEN ON EXIT CODE: shadow-cljs grades a reference to a REMOVED VAR as a WARNING and still exits 0. For a deletion, the discriminating signal is the WARNING COUNT against a zero baseline, not the exit status.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 by worker/vest-a while removing three superseded vestiges (PR #9162). It ran the panel-gallery compile as a check that nothing still referenced what it deleted. A planted reference to a removed var produced a warning and exit 0. Anyone gating a CLJS deletion on exit status alone gets a green over a broken tree.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY GATE QUIRK: the standing rule everywhere else is "quote the captured exit code, never the harness's". That rule is right, and it is NOT SUFFICIENT HERE — the captured code is a truthful 0 about a compile that emitted a real defect. The gate is not lying about its status; the status simply does not carry the finding.

THE RULE FOR A CLJS DELETION:
1. Record the warning count on a CLEAN baseline first (vest-a's was 0 across 710 files, and 0 across 1892 for the main build).
2. Re-run after the deletion and compare COUNTS, not exit codes.
3. The reintroduced-call check remains the strongest single probe, and there it DID bite properly: a 3-arity call gave an ArityException, a removed var gave "No such var", a removed private gave "Unable to resolve var". Those are the checks to lean on.

GENERALISE CAREFULLY RATHER THAN BROADLY: this is a property of how shadow-cljs grades undeclared/removed vars in that build, not a claim that every compile gate fails open. Check the tool's own grading before assuming either way — and note the same repository has a gate that grades a missing markdown ANCHOR at INFO while --strict promotes only WARNING, so exit 0 over a real finding has now been measured twice here through two unrelated tools.

cljs.core/pr-str has exactly TWO branches that descend into a foreign JS value and NEITHER carries a seen-set: object? (prints #js {..} by walking js-keys) and array? (prints #js [..] by walking elements). Every other branch a foreign value can take -- #inst, regex, symbol, the terminal #object[Ctor] -- is bounded and recurses into nothing.

React 19's createContext returns an object whose Provider key points back AT THE CONTEXT ITSELF ((identical? ctx (.-Provider ctx)) is TRUE, asserted in re-frame.ssr.foreign-value-hash-cljs-test). So ANY code that pr-strs a value reachable from a hiccup form carrying a context provider dies with 'RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded'. The cycle is a property of the object graph, not of React: (let [o #js {}] (unchecked-set o "self" o) o) reproduces it.

Two consequences worth carrying:

1. When a walk/serialiser must handle foreign values, stopping at object?/array? stops the descent PRECISELY where pr-str would have started it. That is the cheap, provable fix -- no seen-set threading through the walker. rf2-56iys fixed re-frame.ssr.hash/canonical-edn-into exactly that way, in two CLJS-only cond branches.

2. pr-str of a foreign object ALSO leaks JS function .name into the output (#js {:component #object[f]}), and :advanced renames those. So descending is not merely a crash risk: it silently makes any hash/digest built on it differ between dev and release builds. Same class as rf2-jsa2ml's #fn[] token.

DIAGNOSTIC/ERROR PATHS ARE THE UNDER-COUNTED SITE. (pr-str el) inside a thrown error MESSAGE explodes the same way, and the value also rides out in ex-data :extra, so a downstream logger explodes at ITS boundary instead of the emitter's. re-frame.ssr.emit + re-frame.ssr.ui-tree have ten such sites (rf2-9s68n).

MEASURING A HASH CHANGE HONESTLY: dump canonical form + hash for a corpus to a file before and after, then diff byte-for-byte. rf2-56iys's probe covered 75 entries (parity fixtures + nil-prune pairs + the Hicasso SSR corpus + 41 hand-built branch-coverage values); 61 were byte-identical and every changed entry provably contained a foreign JS value.

REMOVING A CLJS VAR THAT STILL HAS CALLERS DOES NOT FAIL THE BUILD — IT WARNS AND RETURNS undefined (observed 2026-08-07, rf2-ani6y).

WHAT HAPPENED: prop-name was moved out of front/codec.cljs into a shared .cljc. Three call sites elsewhere still asked codec/prop-name (walk_profile_app twice, walk_vs_reagent_app, plus a clock_views docstring). ClojureScript answered a removed var with an :undeclared-var WARNING and the value undefined. The compile stayed EXIT 0. The breakage surfaced only downstream, as 7 ERRORS in walk_profile_baseline_cljs_test — a test failure that looks like a test problem, at a distance from the actual cause.

WHY IT MATTERS: a refactor that moves or renames a var can leave the build green and the code broken. "npm run test:hicasso-compile exits 0" is NOT evidence that every caller resolved. The signal is the WARNING COUNT, not the exit code — four separate builds reporting "0 warnings" is what actually proves the move was complete.

THE RULE: after moving or renaming any CLJS var, grep the whole tree for the OLD fully-qualified name (including docstrings, which will not warn at all), and require the compile to report ZERO warnings rather than merely exit 0. Quote the warning count in the PR body.

SAME SESSION, SAME CLASS, WORTH PAIRING: the three cache seeds in that codec were hand-typed TWICE — once in the def and once in reset-caches! — with an :each fixture making the SECOND copy the live one. A drift introduced in the first was therefore measurably invisible: nothing read it. Duplicated constants where only one copy is live are a silent-divergence trap of exactly the kind the .cljc extraction existed to delete.

CLJS EMITS NO ARITY CHECK FOR A SINGLE-FIXED-ARITY defn — a wrong-arity call does NOT throw, it silently BINDS THE WRONG THING. Measured 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.128 worker while building the regression test for a shipped arity bug.

THE CASE: `note-failing-view!` is `[thrown view-id]`. A caller passed ONE argument. On the JVM that is an ArityException. IN CLJS IT IS NOT AN ERROR AT ALL — `view-id` landed in the `thrown` position and `thrown` became the only bound arg.

⚠️ WHAT MADE IT INVISIBLE, and this is the generalisable part: the value was then used as a WEAKMAP KEY. A CLJS Keyword IS an object, so the guard `attributable?` ACCEPTED it. The write succeeded against the wrong key. The real exception therefore carried no note, and the error report shipped `unknown-view` with `:loss {:reason :failing-view-unobserved}` — in the worker phrase, "A CONFIDENT nobody-saw-the-thrower FOR A PLAINLY OBSERVED FAILURE."

That is worse than a crash: the system emits a DEFINITE NEGATIVE about something it plainly witnessed, and every downstream consumer believes it.

THREE RULES THAT FALL OUT:
1. In .cljc, do NOT rely on arity errors to catch a wrong-arity call — the JVM raises, CLJS does not. A cross-host fix green on the JVM has NOT been exercised on CLJS (see also identical-on-a-keyword-literal, the same asymmetry in a different guise).
2. A TYPE/SHAPE GUARD THAT ACCEPTS TOO MUCH TURNS A WRONG-ARITY BUG INTO A WRONG-DATA BUG. `attributable?` was doing its job — a Keyword genuinely is a valid WeakMap key. When a guard exists to reject non-objects, it will not notice the object is the WRONG object. Prefer a guard that asserts the value IS WHAT IT SHOULD BE, not merely that it CAN be used.
3. ⚠️ WHEN TESTING SUCH A BUG, "SOMETHING WENT WRONG" IS NOT AN ASSERTION. The defect produces a well-formed report with the wrong content. A test asserting a throw, or an error, or a non-empty report, PASSES AGAINST THE DEFECT. Assert the ATTRIBUTED IDENTITY.

MAYOR NOTE: my brief asserted the runtime consequence was "the seam itself throws while a render throw is unwinding". That was JVM-shaped and WRONG on the host where the bug lived. The worker verified past me and said so. This is the standing symptoms-not-causes lesson again — I described a CAUSE I had not measured, and the correct brief would have said only "this path is untested; determine what the defect actually does on each host."

IN CLJS, CALLING A MACRO BY ITS BARE NAME WHEN IT IS ONLY `:refer`-ED INTO ITS OWN NAMESPACE IS A **WARNING**, NOT AN ERROR — the build succeeds, and the emitted call SWALLOWS THE ENTIRE MACRO BODY INTO THE UNDEFINED FUNCTION'S ARGUMENT LIST. Measured 2026-09-05 on `re-frame.core/with-new-frame`, both directions, on a minimal consumer.

THE MEASUREMENT:
    rf/with-new-frame   -> compile exit 0, 0 warnings   |  run exit 0, 4/4 assertions
    bare with-new-frame -> compile exit 0, "Use of undeclared Var" WARNING  |  run exit 1, TypeError, NOTHING ASSERTED

SO THE FAILURE IS NOT "IT WON'T COMPILE". It compiles, ships, and at run time the binding never binds and the body never executes as a body — it is passed as arguments to something undefined. A test written that way reports zero assertions and can read as a pass to anyone checking only the exit code of the compile step.

THE MECHANISM, and it is the part worth carrying: `with-new-frame` is `#?(:clj (defmacro …))`, and the CLJS branch of `re-frame.core` carries a **self-`:require-macros` with an explicit `:refer` list**. That `:refer` lands the name in `re-frame.core` ITSELF, never in a consumer's namespace. So the macro is reachable as `rf/with-new-frame` and never bare — the namespace's own comment says so. **Whether a CLJS macro resolves depends on HOW its namespace is required, not on whether the macro exists**, and a `git grep` that finds the `defmacro` proves nothing about a consumer's reach.

THIS JOINS THE CLJS-ONLY FAMILY, all measured in one session:
  * `test:cljs` does not report `:infer-warning`s, so `:advanced` property renaming is invisible in dev.
  * A `with-redefs` double must mirror the ARITY SHAPE of a multi-arity fn, because CLJS compiles the call site to `cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$N`; a green JVM suite is no evidence about it.
  * And this: an undeclared Var is a warning that silently eats the form.
**A green JVM read is never evidence about CLJS resolution.** Where a sample targets CLJS, compile AND RUN it on CLJS, and read the assertion count.

AND THE DISCIPLINE THAT CAUGHT IT: the worker's own first witness reported "exit 0, zero assertions" because `-main` never fired. It noticed and fixed it with `*main-cli-fn*` rather than banking the green. **Read the assertion count, not only the exit code** — that rule has now caught a vacuous witness four times in one session.

A CLOSE REASON DOES NOT SURVIVE A REOPEN, SO AN AUDIT NEVER SEES IT — PUT THE DISCHARGE IN A COMMENT (2026-08-14, diagnosed on rf2-hic-055 after it reopened TWICE with no new finding).

THE LOOP. rf2-hic-055 carried merged-PR audit #8140 obligation as a COMMENT. PR #8151 discharged it. The worker closed the bead; the audit of #8151 (commit d0a19bafce) reopened it. I re-closed with a long evidence-bearing close reason (commit 172dd317bd); the audit of #8154 (commit 69e02c9b40) reopened it AGAIN. Both reopens changed only status and closed_at — comment count stayed 2 both times, and the newest comment was still #8140 from 2026-08-13.

THE MECHANISM, and it is my record-keeping rather than the audit judgement. The audit reads NOTES and COMMENTS, where the unresolved-audit text sits describing a live defect. A close REASON is a different field and a reopen discards it. So every discharge I wrote was invisible to the thing that kept reopening the bead, and the audit went on doing the correct thing with an obligation that read as unanswered. It would have recurred on every future merge touching that bead family.

THE RULE. When closing a bead that carries an audit obligation in its notes, write the discharge as a COMMENT first — naming the obligation, the PR that discharged it, and the source-verified evidence — and only then close, with the close reason POINTING AT that comment. The comment is the durable record; the close reason is a pointer.

HOW TO TELL A CHURN REOPEN FROM A REAL ONE, cheaply. Diff the tracker export at the audit commit -- git show THE_SHA -- .beads/issues.jsonl -- piped through a JSON filter for the bead id, printing status and comment COUNT. A real reopen adds a comment. A churn reopen changes status and closed_at only. That distinction takes one command and is the whole discriminator: loops.md is right that most reappearances are the audit working, and this is how you find the minority that are not.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: gcchurn-reclose-misses-audit-obligations warns against re-closing a reopened bead without reading its notes. This is the opposite failure — the notes WERE read and the obligation WAS discharged, but the answer was recorded where nothing could read it. Both rules apply; neither replaces the other.

A CLOSE REASON'S 'pushed' CLAUSE IS A CLAIM, NOT EVIDENCE — TEST IT AGAINST THE REMOTE (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: rf2-hic-081's close reason ended 'Spike commits are pushed on worker/receipts-hic081 and retained as the experiment's record.' It was false when written and stayed false for seven days. git ls-remote --heads origin returned empty for that branch while the local ref carried all three spike commits. The worktree had already been reaped on the worker's FINISHED report, so the experiment's only copy was a local branch in the mayor checkout — one disk, no backup, and a bead publicly recording it as safe.

WHY IT PASSED INSPECTION: the sentence sat among clauses that genuinely were verified — 530 tests, 2465 assertions, an allocation control with a negative arm, a named erasure failure. Specificity reads as verification. It is not: every other clause described work the worker DID, where this one described a state of a remote the worker only asserted.

THE TEST IS ONE COMMAND, so there is no excuse for inferring it: git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/<branch>. Empty means not pushed. Run it on any close reason claiming a branch is retained, and on any spike or refusal bead in particular — those are exactly the beads with no PR to prove the push, because a spike that graduates nothing never opens one.

THE STRANDED SWEEP IS WHERE THIS BELONGS. A branch with commits, no remote, no PR and no worktree is indistinguishable from a strand at first read, and the remedy is the same either way: push it. Salvage costs nothing and is never wrong. Do it before deciding what the branch MEANS.

CLOSING A BEAD MAKES EVERY DOCUMENT THAT CITES IT STALE — and I proved it on myself within the hour (2026-08-14).

WHAT HAPPENED. I ruled on rf2-5q8o and closed it as a DECLINE. Ninety minutes later a worker sweeping dispositions.md for pointers to closed beads found TWO cells calling rf2-5q8o open. I had created a fresh instance of the exact defect class I had that worker cleaning up.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS. A bead close is a tracker operation and feels self-contained. But this repository's records CITE BEAD IDS AS OWNERS — 'open correction rf2-xxxx', 'awaiting rf2-yyyy', 'scheduled by rf2-zzzz'. Every one of those is a claim about a bead's STATE, and closing the bead falsifies it silently. Nothing in the tracker knows the document exists.

THE CHECK, and it costs one command before any close or ruling: grep the tracked tree for the bead id. If a record cites it, either fix the citation in the same breath or file the correction with the close. `git grep -l <bead-id>` is the whole thing.

AND NOTE WHAT MADE THIS INSTANCE SUBTLER THAN THE OTHERS: the SUBSTANCE was right — the decline is correct and the reasoning stands. Only the LIVENESS was wrong. So a reader checking the claim finds it accurate and moves on, while the pointer quietly promises that something is scheduled to happen. A half-true cell survives review better than a false one.

THIS APPLIES TO THE MAYOR MOST, because the mayor closes the most beads and writes the fewest documents — so the blast radius of a close is invisible from where the close is made.

CLOSING A BEAD WHOSE AUDIT NOTE CARRIES AN UNDISCHARGED RESIDUAL ORPHANS IT (2026-07-25, my error, caught by EP-0037 gate 1).

I closed rf2-kqxe6.10 (R6 integrated proof) on its merged SHA once its dependencies cleared. But merged-PR audit #6941 had recorded a RESIDUAL on that bead — the rf/route-link intent arm did not actually prove the two laws it named — and closing the bead left that residual with NO OPEN OWNER. Gate 1 found it independently by mutating compose-intent-handler to dispatch twice and before the caller: the full CLJS lane stayed green at 11439/57281, byte-identical to baseline. It is now rf2-kqxe6.22.

THE LESSON: an audit note is not just a record of what was reviewed; it can contain OBLIGATIONS. Before closing a bead, grep its notes for residual language — AUDIT-REOPEN, unmet, still owes, not discharged, RESIDUAL — and either discharge it in the close reason with evidence, or file it as its own bead BEFORE closing. A close reason that recites what shipped without addressing an outstanding residual reads as complete and is not.

RELATED FAILURE I HAVE ALREADY RECORDED: before closing a bead as churn, grep for AUDIT-REOPEN obligations. This is the same class arriving from a different direction — there the risk was closing something reopened for cause, here it was closing something whose reopen-cause was recorded but never satisfied.

MECHANICAL FORM: bd show <id> | grep -iE "residual|not discharged|still owes|unmet|AUDIT-REOPEN" before every close of a bead that carries an audit note. If it hits, the close must either cite evidence for that specific item or name the bead that inherits it.

CLUSTER BRANCH NAMING — always give a multi-bead cluster branch ONE bead suffix, e.g. worker/ui-test-integrity-i36h6. On 2026-07-19 I named a two-bead cluster branch worker/ui-test-integrity with no suffix; the merge loop derives the bead from the branch name (worker/<desc>-<BEAD_ID>) and correctly resolved it to "no bead", so it would have merged the PR and closed NOTHING. Both beads would have stayed open with their work shipped — invisible until a later recount. The validation step saved it from closing the WRONG bead, but not from closing none. RULE: suffix the branch with the primary bead id, and record the sibling ids in a --append-notes line on each bead at dispatch time so the state lives on the beads rather than in the mayor head. This is the same failure shape as the rf2-bbdbs2 promise I dropped for six hours: anything tracked only in my own context gets lost, while anything on a bead is re-surfaced by the loop every tick.

CLUSTER SIZE — beware whole-artefact-tree clusters (2026-06-20): the 2db7z1 docstring de-historicize 'clusters', each scoped to an ENTIRE artefact tree (machines = dozens of files, all-of-tools = ~80 files), caused the cluster PARENT agents to spawn many child sub-agents into one shared worktree and then HANG at the final 'serialize the commits' step — stranding 401 (tools) + 153 (impl-core) uncommitted files, and one (examples-skills) lost its worktree entirely (work gone). The 5-bead CAP is about bead COUNT but a single bead covering a huge file-tree is itself too big. Fix: (a) scope repo-wide mechanical sweeps as SMALLER per-directory dispatches; (b) brief cluster workers to COMMIT INCREMENTALLY per batch/surface (never defer all commits to the end) so a hang strands nothing; (c) discourage workers from spawning their own children into the shared worktree for commit-heavy work. Recovered via per-cluster recovery workers that commit the existing uncommitted edits + finish gaps. See [[dispatch-cluster-cap-mike-ruled-2026-06-20]].

`cmd /c` INVOKED FROM GIT BASH SILENTLY DOES NOTHING AND RETURNS EXIT 0 — it drops into an interactive shell instead of running the command. From PowerShell the identical command works. RESOLVES an earlier memory that recorded this as unresolved with conflicting evidence.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 on a scratch directory, three invocations of the same junction:
  Bash:        cmd /c mklink /J <link> <target>   -> printed only the Windows banner, EXIT 0, NO LINK CREATED
  PowerShell:  cmd /c mklink /J <link> <target>   -> "Junction created for <link> <<===>> <target>", link present
  PowerShell:  New-Item -ItemType Junction        -> link present, readable through
The tell in the Bash case is the output: the Windows version banner followed by a prompt string (`C:\...>`), which is an interactive shell waiting, not a command that ran.

THIS RESOLVES THE CONFLICT that made the earlier memory unresolved. One worker reported cmd /c mklink silently failing; others created junctions the same day with what looked like the same recipe. Both were right — the difference was never the command, it was WHICH SHELL invoked it. Workers using PowerShell succeeded; workers using Bash got a silent no-op and exit 0.

CONSEQUENCE FOR DISPATCH BRIEFS, and it is not only the create: EVERY `cmd /c rmdir "<junction>"` cleanup line in a brief has the same defect when a worker runs it from Bash. It reports success and removes nothing. That is the more dangerous half, because a surviving junction is what later cleanup follows into the mayor's real node_modules — the failure mode that emptied it twice historically.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF:
  create:  powershell -NoProfile -Command "New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path '<worktree>\implementation\node_modules' -Target '<mayor>\implementation\node_modules'"
  remove:  powershell -NoProfile -Command "(Get-Item '<worktree>\implementation\node_modules').Delete()"
AND VERIFY BOTH, because exit 0 proves nothing here: after creating, list the linked path; after removing, confirm the link is gone AND that the mayor's node_modules still counts what it did before (the canary reads 103 with `ls -A`).

THE GENERAL RULE THIS BELONGS TO: on this machine, a Windows-native tool invoked through Git Bash can no-op with exit 0. Do not trust an exit code from a cross-shell invocation — verify the EFFECT.

A COMMIT'S SUBJECT IS NOT ITS CONTENTS, AND THE DANGEROUS MISMATCH REVERTS RATHER THAN ADDS (2026-08-19).

Commit 799334f970 on worker/armconf-c4hhk read 'bench(p0): amend the level-assignment rule at run 3 of 70'. It carried 24 files — one studio record and 23 under implementation/core/src/ — at 611 insertions and 910 deletions, and the 23 were a REVERSION to pre-retirement content: core.cljc's + side re-introduced 're-frame.ui.frames/mint-frame-ops', a string absent from origin/main and belonging to a tree deleted weeks earlier.

MECHANISM: a worktree whose implementation/ content predated sweeps that had since landed on main, plus a git add -A or commit -a. The worker meant to commit one record file.

WHY NOTHING CATCHES IT. A revert of merged work is well-formed, compiles, and passes every gate the tree has. The five merge clauses measure whether CI is GREEN, and CI is green. The commit message is accurate about the part its author knew about. 'Scope did not sprawl' does not describe it either — sprawl is EXTRA work, which announces itself; this is files the author never edited, at content OLDER than the trunk.

THE CHEAP DETECTOR, one command: git diff --name-only <merge-base> <branch>. Read the file LIST against what the bead asked for. A path the bead does not explain is a finding whichever direction it runs. Then for any surprising file, test the DIRECTION rather than the size — a string present on the branch and absent from origin/main means the branch is older, not newer.

CHECK THE WHOLE FLEET WHEN YOU FIND ONE, and expect it to be one worker rather than a pattern: the other six live branches carried zero implementation/core/src/ paths, which is what made the finding specific enough to act on.

AND WHEN YOU CANNOT MESSAGE THE WORKER — it predates a /clear, so TaskList is empty while it provably runs — do not repair its branch under it. Record the finding and the exact fix-forward on the bead, and bind the merge loop instead: no PR from that branch merges while the offending paths are in its diff.

The CLJS lane split into two foreground phases is: (1) node scripts/compile-node-test.cjs node-test out/node-test.js (2) node out/node-test.js, both from implementation/ (this is exactly package.json's test:cljs, unsplit). CONCURRENCY COST: SATURATING WORKERS TIMES OUT A HARNESS SELF-TEST (2026-07-25). With 6-7 concurrent workers each running shadow-cljs compiles, 'npm run test:cljs' can fail rc 1 with 2 failures that are BOTH spawnSync ETIMEDOUT in re-frame.test-quiet-shadow-node-cljs-test — the harness's own subprocess self-test, which re-spawns the built runner under a 60s ceiling whose own comment says it 'returns in well under a second'. It is machine load, not behaviour, and a diff that cannot reach that surface (e.g. a single freehand test file) still trips it.

HOW TO HANDLE IT, in this order: (1) confirm the failing tests are exactly that namespace and exactly ETIMEDOUT — anything else is a real failure; (2) confirm the diff structurally cannot touch the harness self-test; (3) RE-RUN rather than declaring it green. Do NOT wave it through on the first red, and do NOT --admin past it: an ETIMEDOUT that is really contention looks identical to an ETIMEDOUT that is really a hang, and only the re-run distinguishes them. The rf2-z0blg worker handled this correctly — it flagged the rc 1 honestly, explained why it believed it was load, and re-ran rather than reporting green.

MAYOR-SIDE IMPLICATION FOR DISPATCH POLICY: the operator's saturate-at-6 target has a measurable cost — it makes local worker gates flakier, which in turn makes workers spend turns re-running and makes a genuine failure harder to see against the noise. When several workers are simultaneously in a CLJS-heavy phase, expect this and prefer sequencing the CLJS-heavy ones over adding a seventh. Related known pattern: under 40+ concurrent PRs the skill-MCP-drift and JVM-epoch CI gates flake the same way.

GATE A WORKER GATES ON AN OBSERVABLE, NOT ON MY GUESS — this is how to overlap a dispatch with a live measurement window (2026-08-14, invented for rf2-34yg and confirmed working).

THE PROBLEM: a clock measurement window needs a quiet box and refuses if the box is loud, so a heavy dispatch alongside it wastes a real measurement. But holding every dispatch until the window reports costs hours of throughput, and I had been doing exactly that all session.

WHAT I DID WRONG FIRST: inferred from a worker commit ("docs: fix a misnumbered arm reference") that its measurement rounds were finished and it had moved to write-up. That inference was WRONG — checking properly, it had opened no PR and its recent writes were .cpcache entries and out/node-test.js, i.e. a build running a gate. The doc commit was made BETWEEN runs.

THE TECHNIQUE THAT WORKED, and it survives my inference being wrong: brief the new worker to do all reading, editing and reasoning FIRST, then — before running anything heavy — check whether the measurement worker has opened a PULL REQUEST for its branch. An open PR is an observable that means the measurement finished. Tell it to poll in a bounded loop WITHIN ITS TURN, and give it an explicit escape: if the PR has not appeared after a reasonable wait, say so in the report and run anyway. Never end a turn waiting for an event.

MEASURED RESULT: the worker polled about 4.5 minutes, saw the PR appear on poll 10, and ran only then. It also sampled processor queue length on every poll and reported 0 throughout. No measurement was disturbed and no throughput was lost to my being wrong about the window state.

WHY THE ESCAPE CLAUSE IS NOT OPTIONAL: a conditional wait is exactly the shape that strands a worker — seven strandings in one day all came from waiting for an event that never arrived. The escape converts a possible strand into a reported delay.

GENERALISES: any time a fence depends on another worker s state, gate on something the new worker can OBSERVE (a PR, a merged commit, a file on main) rather than on my reading of tea leaves. My inference was wrong and the dispatch was still safe, which is the whole point.

A COSMETIC PIPE DESTROYS AN EXIT CODE EXACTLY AS A FILTERING PIPE DOES -- and it does not feel like piping a gate (2026-08-24).

WHAT I DID. Checking whether this checkout's git hooks were armed:
    sh scripts/install-git-hooks.sh --check 2>&1 | sed 's/^/  /'
    echo "exit=$?"
That $? is SED'S status, not the script's. It printed 0 and told me nothing. The guard happened to be armed, so the wrong instrument agreed with the truth -- which is the worst outcome, because nothing on screen disputes it.

WHY IT SLIPPED PAST A RULE I HAD JUST WRITTEN DOWN. The method tree says "Never pipe a gate through a filter. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, so a red runner reads green", and I had put the same discipline into two PR bodies hours earlier. But I did not read this as piping a gate: the pipe was there to INDENT output for readability, not to filter anything, and it was a guard-check rather than a test runner. Neither distinction matters to the shell. Any pipe -- sed, head, tr, cat, tee -- replaces the status you wanted with the formatter's, and formatters essentially always succeed, so the answer is a reassuring 0 whatever happened upstream.

THE CORRECT FORM, one command line, one shell:
    out=$(cmd 2>&1); rc=$?
    printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed 's/^/  /'   # format AFTER capturing rc
Capture first, decorate second. And when a --check style probe returns 0 with ZERO BYTES of output, corroborate independently rather than trusting it -- here, ls -l on .git/hooks/pre-commit (present, executable, 4585 bytes) plus the script's own header line "--check  # exit 0 if installed & current, 1 otherwise", which establishes that silence-on-success is the designed contract.

GENERALISE: I add "| sed 's/^/  /'" to almost every command for readable output. Every one of those pipes silently voids $? for the command I actually care about. If the line's purpose is to learn an exit code, it must not end in a pipe -- no exceptions for formatting.

A COVERAGE PLANT MUST NOT OVERLAP A GATE RUN (2026-08-11, rf2-eo9n / PR #7870).

Nearly every brief I write demands the same drill for silent-on-success gates: plant a bogus anchor, quote the exit 1, restore, confirm green. A worker's first fast-PR spine run went RED purely because the plant was still in the tree while the spine ran. Not a finding - the plant racing the gate.

WHY IT IS EASY TO HIT: the spine takes ~25 minutes and is therefore BACKGROUNDED (the harness kills a foreground command at 10). The plant-and-restore cycle takes seconds. So a worker naturally starts the long gate, then does the quick coverage proof while waiting - and the two overlap invisibly. The resulting red looks like a real failure in CI history.

THE RULE FOR BRIEFS: sequence them explicitly. Do the plant/restore drill FIRST, verify the restore by hash, and only THEN start the spine. Or wait for the spine's .exit file before planting. Never interleave.

AND IF IT HAPPENS: restore, hash-verify, RE-RUN, and say in the PR body that the first red was a plant race - otherwise a reviewer reading CI history is misled by a red that means nothing. The rf2-eo9n worker did exactly that, which is why it was diagnosable.

RELATED, same worker, worth keeping: plant with PYTHON rather than `sed -i`. On Windows sed -i rewrites CRLF->LF, so `git diff` and `git status` both read clean while the bytes differ - see crlf-defeats-byte-identical-restore. Restore with `git checkout --` and verify by sha256.

STEP 1 — GROUND TRUTH, before touching anything. For each worktree, git-only (never a filesystem walk):

  git ls-remote --heads origin <branch> | wc -l      # is the branch on origin at all
Classify: branch-on-origin = safe. Commits-but-no-remote = AT RISK. Zero-commits-plus-dirty-plus-no-remote = MOST at risk.

STEP 2 — MERGE ANY GREEN PR FIRST. A PR that was green when the process died is free progress and it unblocks whatever was sequenced behind it.

STEP 3 — PUSH THE COMMITTED-BUT-UNPUSHED WORK YOURSELF. This is pure durability and carries no judgement risk: the commits already exist, you are only making them survivable. Do NOT open a PR from them.

⚠️ STEP 4 — DO NOT COMMIT A WORKER UNCOMMITTED WIP YOURSELF. Tell the worker to do it. There is a recorded incident in this project where a mayor committed a worker partial work as a recovery PR and merged an incomplete state that broke main. Uncommitted files are mid-edit by definition; only the worker knows whether they form a coherent commit. The mayor pushes COMMITS, never creates them from someone else WIP.

STEP 5 — RESUME EVERY WORKER, with a message tailored to ITS state, leading with durability:
  - Say plainly it was not stopped for cause and its work is safe — a worker that thinks it failed behaves worse.
  - For the most-at-risk one, make the FIRST instruction "commit what you have (even as a WIP commit) and push, BEFORE rebasing, BEFORE gates, BEFORE anything."
  - Tell it exactly what landed on main while it was gone, and whether its rebase is EXPECTED (sequenced deliberately) rather than a surprise to investigate.
  - Re-state only the must-survive laws and traps specific to that worker — not the whole original brief.
THIS WORKED, MEASURED: the worst-off worker went from 0 commits / 12 uncommitted files / no remote branch to 3 commits pushed on its first resumed turn.

STEP 6 — clear any stale .git/index.lock left by the abrupt exit, then re-export beads FROM DOLT (never git checkout over them) and checkpoint.

PREVENTION, now standard in every dispatch brief and worth more than the recipe: "COMMIT AND PUSH AS YOU GO — not at the end", stated WITH the reason (two mechanisms have killed workers; incremental pushing is the only defence against both). Also: a bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface — saturation is right, but keep it within what one recovery pass can handle.

AFTER A CRASH, CHECK LANDED-NESS WITH A 600-COMMIT WINDOW BEFORE SALVAGING ANYTHING (2026-08-03).

Recovering from a host crash that killed ~18 workers, I found 14 worker worktrees with commits and NO remote branch — the classic 'stranded work' shape. I pushed 13 of them for durability, which the method explicitly sanctions.

Then I compared their commit SUBJECTS against main. Against 'git log --oneline -60 origin/main' only 2 of 13 looked landed. Against -600, ALL 13 had landed. The branches were pure residue: workers that had already shipped via PRs that already merged, leaving behind unreaped worktrees whose local branch ref simply predated the squash-merge onto main.

THE COST OF THE NARROW WINDOW: I nearly dispatched ~11 salvage workers to 'finalise' work that was already on main, and I did push+delete 13 redundant branches. On a repo merging this fast, 60 commits is a few HOURS of main. A 2-day-old worker branch needs hundreds.

THE RULE: before treating an unpushed worker branch as stranded, diff its commit subjects against at least 600 commits of origin/main (use 'git log --format=%s -600 origin/main' + 'grep -Fxq' per subject). A worktree with commits and no remote is USUALLY residue, not loss. Real loss looks different: UNCOMMITTED modified files (that worktree genuinely died mid-edit), or commits whose subjects appear nowhere on main.

ALSO: 'gh pr list --state open' returning 0 is a strong corroborating signal — if no PRs are open, no worker is mid-flight, so every branch is either landed or abandoned.

THIS CHECKOUT IS CRLF, SO A MULTI-LINE PATCH ANCHOR SILENTLY MATCHES NOTHING (2026-08-11, rf2-czlb / rf2-3f11).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker planting a sabotage edit found its first multi-line patch attempt matched nothing and reported no error — the edit simply did not apply. Cause: the working tree carries CRLF line endings, so any anchor spanning a newline fails to match a pattern written with LF. It found it only because it verified the restore by SHA-256 rather than by reading `git diff`.

TWO PRACTICES THAT FOLLOW, both cheap:
  - USE SINGLE-LINE ANCHORS when patching by string match. A pattern that crosses a line boundary is a coin flip on this checkout.
  - VERIFY EVERY RESTORE BY HASHING THE BYTES, never by `git diff`. This is already the standing rule for sabotage restores, and here is the reason it exists: a CRLF-flipping rewrite reads CLEAN in `git diff` while having changed every line, and the inverse — an edit that never applied — also reads clean. `git diff` cannot distinguish "unchanged" from "not attempted".

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SABOTAGE. The plant-and-restore discipline is how this project proves a guard is exact rather than merely present. If the plant silently does not apply, the sabotage run comes back GREEN and the worker concludes the guard fired when nothing was ever broken — a false proof of a real guard, which is worse than no proof at all. The same failure would make a "restored" tree quietly different from the committed one.

Brief it as: "verify the restore by hashing the bytes, not by reading `git diff` — this checkout is CRLF, and both a failed patch and a line-ending rewrite read clean there."

ON WINDOWS, `git diff` CANNOT VERIFY A BYTE-IDENTICAL RESTORE - VERIFY BY HASH (2026-08-11, found by the rf2-dly1 worker, PR #7859).

Every dispatch brief I write demands the same coverage drill for silent-on-success gates: plant a bogus anchor, quote the exit 1, RESTORE BYTE-IDENTICALLY, confirm green. A worker doing exactly that used `sed -i` to plant and restore, and `git diff` came back EMPTY while the sha256 DIFFERED. `sed -i` had rewritten the working copy CRLF -> LF. The content was identical; the bytes were not.

WHY git diff LIES HERE: with autocrlf normalisation, git compares the normalised form, so a pure line-ending change is invisible to `git diff` and to `git status`. Both report clean. The file on disk has changed for every tool that reads bytes rather than lines - and on this repo that includes the digest-pinned sample blocks under docs/core/, which hash exact block text.

THE FIX, two parts:
1. VERIFY BY HASH, not by `git diff`: record sha256 before planting and compare after restoring. The worker caught it precisely because it hashed.
2. RESTORE WITH `git checkout -- <path>`, which writes the exact checked-out bytes, rather than a second `sed -i` that re-applies the same normalisation.

PUT THIS IN THE DISPATCH BRIEF. I ask for this drill in nearly every dispatch, and until now the brief said "restore byte-identically" and let the worker choose how to check - which on Windows means most of them check with `git diff` and get a false pass. The claim "restored byte-identically, git status clean" is NOT evidence on this platform.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the same one that keeps recurring: an instrument answering from a NORMALISED view rather than the raw artefact is confidently wrong exactly about the difference you are checking for. Same family as `git branch -r` being a cache, `gh run list` returning lowercase status, and the beads export lagging the database.

A MULTI-LINE PATCH ANCHOR SILENTLY NO-OPS ON THIS REPO CRLF CHECKOUTS, AND THE SABOTAGE RUN THEN COMES BACK GREEN (2026-08-18).

Measured by rf2-0yp7w.9 slice 2 (PR #8502): "Two plants silently no-opped first and both runs came back green — a multi-line anchor does not match a CRLF working tree, and unchanged and not-attempted are the same diff. Only the hash caught it."

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN ANNOYING. The planted-fault route exists to prove a gate READ YOUR WORKTREE. The worker plants a fault, expects red, and reads green. The green does not say "the plant failed to apply" — it says, to a tired reader, "this gate does not cover my surface" or worse "the control does not bite". Both conclusions are false and both are actionable in the wrong direction: one abandons a gate that works, the other reports a hollow control that is not hollow. The evidence in the report is internally consistent either way.

THE DIFF CANNOT CATCH IT. "Unchanged" and "not attempted" produce the identical diff, so a worker verifying its restore by reading a diff sees exactly what a correct plant-and-restore looks like.

TWO RULES, AND BOTH ARE NEEDED:
1. ANCHOR A PLANT TO A SINGLE LINE WITH NO NEWLINE IN IT. Multi-line anchors are the failure; on a checkout whose line endings are translated they match nothing, with no error.
2. HASH BEFORE THE PLANT AND AFTER THE RESTORE, using version control content hashing against the COMMITTED OBJECT (git hash-object), never a plain byte digest of the working file — a checkout during a rebase rewrites the working file after you hashed it, so a plain digest reports a CORRECT restore as failed. Three hashes tell the whole story: pre-plant, planted, post-restore. If pre-plant equals planted, the patch never applied and the green means nothing.

This is the Windows/CRLF half of a rule the dispatch template already carries in general terms. It is worth its own record because the general rule reads as a caution while this is a reproducible property of every checkout in this repository, and it has now bitten twice in one run.

MY CRLF REMEDY IN BRIEFS IS THE WRONG REFLEX FOR MOST TRACKED FILES (2026-08-06).

WHAT I HAVE BEEN WRITING: "spec/** files are stored CRLF here; if the diff explodes, rebuild byte-exactly from the base blob and `git -c core.autocrlf=false add`."

WHAT THE rf2-ix9tk WORKER MEASURED on spec/004-Views.md: the override staged 2906 changed lines out of 2906 - it forced CRLF INTO AN LF INDEX. The plain `git add` gave 2/2, exactly the intended change.

THE REASON, and it is the discriminator to use: the file is `i/lf w/crlf` - LF in the INDEX, CRLF in the WORKING TREE, which is what `core.autocrlf=true` is FOR. The normalisation on add is CORRECT and is what keeps the index clean. Disabling it makes the working-tree CRLF the thing that gets stored, which is a whole-file diff.

THE CORRECTED RULE: use PLAIN `git add`. Then check `git diff --numstat`. Only if a plain add blows the diff up does the override become a candidate - and check `git ls-files --eol <path>` first to see which way the file is actually stored. The numstat check is the load-bearing half and always was; the remedy I attached to it was cargo.

WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG: it came from a real incident (a worker DID produce a ~4,200-line diff on spec/011-SSR.md for a +45-line change) and I generalised the CURE from one file to a whole tree without re-testing. Same shape as the git-grep-ref hazard I propagated for a session and the node_modules canary I quoted for weeks: BOILERPLATE IS THE LEAST-AUDITED TEXT I PRODUCE, because it is copied rather than composed. Re-test one boilerplate claim per retrospective.

ALSO CORRECTED IN THE SAME REPORT: my `.beads` hygiene check told workers to run `git diff --numstat origin/main..HEAD`. That is TWO-DOT, so it shows my own checkpoint commits as though they were the worker`s, and three workers in a row reported a false `.beads` positive. Use the MERGE BASE (or `sh scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh origin/main`, remembering it exits 0 with no base ref so the ref must always be passed).

EDITING A CRLF-STORED FILE UNDER core.autocrlf=true SILENTLY NORMALISES THE WHOLE FILE TO LF — a multi-thousand-line whitespace diff that reads as real content. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.103 worker, which caught it before committing.

THE CASE: spec/011-SSR.md is stored on main with CRLF. A normal edit produced a ~4,200-line diff on a HOT-ZONE file for a change that should have been +45 lines. Nothing warned; the diff simply looked enormous.

THE CURE the worker used: rebuild the file BYTE-EXACTLY from its base blob plus the intended change, then re-add with `git -c core.autocrlf=false add <file>`. Committed diff came out at +45 insertions and nothing else.

THE CHECK, and it is cheap: after ANY edit to a tracked file, run `git diff --numstat` and confirm the line counts match what you intended. A diff far larger than your change is a line-ending normalisation, not your edit.

⚠️ THIS COMPOUNDS WITH THE HOT-ZONE RULE. spec/ files are sequential-never-parallel precisely because they collide; a whole-file normalisation guarantees a conflict with every other branch touching that file, and buries the real change so a reviewer cannot see it. On a hot-zone file the damage is not cosmetic.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: `sed -i` on a tracked file does the same thing for the same reason on this Windows checkout — which is why briefs forbid it and require the Edit tool. This is the SAME hazard reached through an ordinary edit rather than through sed, so the sed ban alone does not cover it. Put the numstat check in briefs that touch spec/ files, not just the sed ban.

MAYOR NOTE: my briefs already say "no sed -i" and "check git diff --numstat shows only the lines you intended" — the second half turned out to be the load-bearing one, and I had been treating it as a footnote to the first.

DELETING A DECORATIVE ROW LEAVES THE CLAIM UNWITNESSED — the discriminating-row rule has a second half (2026-08-11, AUDIT #7835 on rf2-wjag).

WHAT I HAD BEEN TEACHING: for every negative row, ask what single narrowing of the implementation would let it pass while the property is broken. If such a narrowing exists, the row is decorative. That is right, and it has caught real defects all session.

WHAT I PRAISED, AND WHY IT WAS ONLY HALF RIGHT: a worker wrote a cold-probe row, found its mutation red nothing, DELETED the row and recorded the finding in the namespace docstring. Its words: "Claim real, witness not." I called that the rule applied by a worker to its own work, unprompted — and it was, as far as it went.

THE AUDIT COMPLETED IT: the row was decorative AS WRITTEN because the frame it used (a make-frame frame) had no stale projection to flush. The CLAIM was real and became UNWITNESSED by the deletion. The only thing still exercising it was a prototype-tree row — exercising the prototype runtime, not the package implementation, which is exactly the dependence the bead existed to end.

THE COMPLETED RULE: "this row cannot fail" is a finding about THE ROW'S CONDITIONS, not about whether the claim deserves a witness. The three outcomes, in order of preference:
  1. REWRITE the row with the conditions that make the mechanism load-bearing (here: an image-loaded frame rather than a fresh one). This is almost always the answer.
  2. DELETE it only if the claim is already covered elsewhere IN THE SAME ARTEFACT — and name the coverer. Coverage in a donor, prototype or sibling tree does not count when the bead's purpose is to stop relying on that tree.
  3. If the claim genuinely cannot be witnessed here, say so and say WHY, in the artefact — as the erasure worker did for defview coordinates, where a filename sentinel would be red on a correct build.

MAYOR APPLICATION: when a worker reports deleting a row, ask what still witnesses the claim. The report will usually not volunteer it, because the deletion feels like the finding — and it is a finding, just not a complete one.

VERIFYING A DELIVERABLE IS NOT THE SAME AS CHECKING FOR UNMET OBLIGATIONS — I conflated them and stranded work (2026-08-14).

WHAT I DID. rf2-d6ai8 flipped open three times with no comment attached. I applied the churn discriminator, verified its DELIVERABLE at source each time — requirements-mine.md carried the re-taken pass-1 entry, PR #8178 merged — and re-closed it. On the third pass I called it "churn (third status-only flip)".

WHAT I MISSED. The bead's NOTES carried an explicit unmet obligation added after the deliverable landed: "Keep this exact requirements-mine owner open until those false premises are corrected there." rf2-gvysu had also been closed as a duplicate OF d6ai8. So both owners were closed while all three false rows were still on main. The work was stranded, and it took a worker reading both beads to find it.

THE DISTINCTION I COLLAPSED. My own backlog-reread rule says: READ THE BEAD NOTES BEFORE RE-CLOSING ANYTHING, and grep them for AUDIT-REOPEN, unmet, obligation. I substituted a different and easier check — does the thing the bead was filed to produce exist on main? Both are necessary. A bead can have its original deliverable landed AND carry a later obligation that keeps it open, and the second is invisible to a source check on the first.

THE TELL I SHOULD HAVE NOTICED: a bead that reopens THREE TIMES is not behaving like churn. Churn is a flag flipping; three flips with a duplicate closed alongside it is a signal that something is actively holding the bead open. The repetition itself was evidence and I read it as noise.

THE RULE, GOING FORWARD. Before re-closing any reopened bead, do BOTH: (a) verify the deliverable at source, and (b) grep the full notes for an obligation added after that deliverable landed. If a sibling or duplicate bead exists, read it too — a duplicate closed against an owner that is itself closed leaves nobody holding the work.

ALSO WRONG IN THE SAME DISPATCH, and worth the same care: I told that worker the L6 machinery "landed today". It had not — PR #8187 was still OPEN at dispatch time and merged mid-pass. Stating an in-flight PR as landed is the same class of error as quoting an unverified constant: check the state at dispatch time, not from memory of a report.

bd dep tree's READY/BLOCKED BADGE COUNTS ONLY *OPEN* BLOCKERS — A DEFERRED BLOCKER IS INVISIBLE TO IT, SO THE BADGE FAILS OPEN (measured 2026-08-23 09:47 AUSEST, tip f05b2c2312).

THE DISAGREEMENT. 'bd dep tree <id>' prints a READY or BLOCKED badge beside the root. It disagrees with 'bd ready' exactly when every unclosed blocker is DEFERRED:

  rf2-hic-090  blocker t32wg (deferred)   -> badge READY    not in bd ready
  rf2-kmqx3    blocker uelji (deferred)   -> badge READY    not in bd ready
  rf2-hic-063  blocker kmqx3 (OPEN)       -> badge BLOCKED  not in bd ready
  rf2-hic-064  blocker hic-090 (OPEN)     -> badge BLOCKED  not in bd ready

Two instances of the disagreement and two controls, so the discriminator is the blocker's STATUS and nothing else. 'bd ready' is the conservative instrument and the correct one for dispatch: undone work is undone whether or not somebody deferred it.

WHY THIS IS WORTH KNOWING RATHER THAN SHRUGGING AT. The badge does not merely differ, it fails in the direction that costs a worker, and it does so on the two beads with the tracker's hardest operator gates in front of them. rf2-hic-090 is the bead that has already consumed FOUR dispatches (PRs #8312, #8395, #8445, #8560), each running its evidence families correctly and each declining to close for the same unruled reason. A mayor who opens the dependency tree — the natural thing to do when asking 'why is this blocked?' — is shown the word READY on precisely that bead.

AND IT IS A THIRD ROUTE TO THE SAME MISTAKE, which is why the existing fence does not cover it. rf2-hic-090's own note anticipates the ready-view route and says the block was once PROSE rather than a tracker edge; that hole was closed by adding the edge. The badge route survives the fix, because the edge now EXISTS and the badge still ignores it.

THE RULE: dispatchability is 'bd ready' plus the bead's own newest note. A dependency tree is for reading the SHAPE of a chain — who pins whom — never for deciding whether to send a worker.

Dependency-chain gating gotcha: workers close their bead on PR CREATION (not merge), so a 'bd dep add A B' where B closes-at-PR-creation makes 'bd ready' surface A as soon as B's PR is OPENED — BEFORE B's code is on main. If A and B touch the same files (surface-conflict sequencing), dispatching A off origin/main then conflicts when B merges. FIX: for surface-conflict gates, do NOT rely on the bd dep / bd ready alone — verify the BLOCKER PR is actually MERGED (gh pr view <#> state==MERGED) before claiming+worktreeing the dependent, and create its worktree off the POST-merge origin/main. Hit on EP-0005: rcim4m (rename, touches machines+spec/005) is dep on se70xj, whose #3473 PR was open-not-merged; bd ready surfaced rcim4m prematurely; reverted.

A BRIEF'S "YOUR SURFACE IS X" LINE IS A FILE-PATH CLAIM, AND I DERIVED ONE FROM BEAD PROSE INSTEAD OF FROM THE TREE (2026-08-21).

WHAT HAPPENED. Briefing rf2-xc0bw, I wrote that the worker's surface was implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/examples/ledger/. The worker replied: "The brief also placed my surface under .../hicasso/examples/ledger/; the bead says .../bench/hicasso/, and the bead governed." It was right. The driver actually lives at implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/bench/hicasso/ledger_frame_clock_app.cljs.

WHY IT WAS HARD TO SEE. Both directories EXIST. implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/examples/ledger/ is a real path, so nothing errored and no listing looked wrong. I had lifted it from the bead's description, which names examples/ as where section 9.4 governs the WITNESS APPLICATION -- a true sentence about a different thing. THE RULE IS ALREADY WRITTEN AND I FAILED TO APPLY IT. mayor-dispatch.md says the brief's content is claims verified at origin/main HEAD, and enumerates "a route, a constant, a FILE PATH, a threshold, a prohibition and a table". So this is an enforcement failure, not a gap in the documents. Do not "fix" the command file for it.

THE CHECK, ONE COMMAND, BEFORE WRITING THE SURFACE LINE:

That returns where the artefact actually is. Derive the surface from THAT, never from the bead's prose. The fence derivation (open PRs, worktrees, working trees) answers WHO HOLDS a file and cannot catch this, because it never asks whether the path you named is the right one.

IT COMPOUNDED A SECOND ERROR IN THE SAME BRIEF. I also double-dispatched that bead, because its description claimed no driver existed when one had already merged. THE GENERALISATION WORTH KEEPING: when a bead's description names a path, ask what that path is a path TO. A description may name a governing document's directory, a historical location, or a sibling artefact's home, all truthfully, and none of them is the worker's surface.

Design stance (Mike 2026-06-20, rf2-h9902s): re-frame2 does NOT validate that a programmer-supplied keyword VALUE is spelled correctly against a closed set — spelling is the programmer's job, per-value typo checks (:lvie for :live etc.) are overkill. This does NOT weaken the no-silent-swallow convention, which governs RECOGNISED-but-unhonourable input (a known key the system can't honour must still signal). When a quality sweep (correctness #go7f5o / consistency #4pbmpt / error-model) proposes 'add validation that X is in the allowed set', default to REJECT unless it's recognised-unhonourable input.

It ran under the fence anyway because I had fenced it, and said so rather than quietly benefiting from the doubt.

It cost throughput repeatedly in one session — I held a doc cluster, an audit and a tracker pass off a box that a counter census did not need quiet.

WORKTREES ACCUMULATE BECAUSE THEY ARE DIRTY, NOT BECAUSE NOBODY TRIED TO REAP THEM (2026-08-18).

A hygiene pass reaped 9 of 11 leftover worktrees whose PRs had MERGED. The two refusals were both REMOVE_REFUSED_DIRTY - git will not remove a worktree holding modified or untracked files, and the removal script surfaces each offending path prefixed [KEEP] with the message that RETRYING WILL NEVER CLEAR THIS. That is the whole mechanism behind a pile of stale worktrees: every pass reaps the clean ones and leaves the dirty ones, so the dirty ones are all that is left.

DO NOT REACH FOR --force. The script says --force DELETES the [KEEP] paths, and its own text distinguishes them from build output: an uncommitted edit, a note, a draft. On this pass one refusing worktree held a modified deps.edn plus an untracked test and an untracked script; another held a MODIFIED .github/workflows/test.yml (hot zone), a modified .claude/commands file, and a DELETED studio record.

THE CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR BEFORE DECIDING ANYTHING: check whether the [KEEP] paths already exist at origin/main. For the first worktree both untracked files were PRESENT on main - the branch's PR had merged and the worktree was simply sitting on a pre-merge commit, so its 'untracked' files were a stale local copy of landed work, at risk of nothing. That check is two git cat-file calls and it converts an alarming refusal into a nothing.

STILL LEAVE THEM. Even when the content is provably safe, force-deleting buys one worktree and risks a draft nobody has read. Leaving two dirty worktreees costs disk and a line in git worktree list.

A MERGED PR IS STRONGER EVIDENCE THAN A COMPLETION REPORT, and it is what makes an old worktree reapable at all. The hygiene rule says reap only on the agent's own completion report - correct for a worker dispatched THIS session, where a report is obtainable. For a leftover from a prior session no report exists and never will, so the rule as literally written would freeze them forever. A verifiably MERGED PR says the work is on main, which is what the report was evidence FOR. Match on exact head-ref, and re-derive the ahead-count in the same command as the delete.

TO TELL AN AUDIT REOPEN FROM A BARE STATUS REVERT, ASK WHETHER TEXT GREW WHILE THE BEAD WAS CLOSED — compare the notes length AT THE LAST CLOSE against the NEWEST notes length. Growth means an audit wrote its reason; no growth means only the status moved. Established 2026-09-05 after two WRONG re-closes destroyed real audit findings.

THE CORRECT PROBE:
  bd history <id> --json  ->  walk newest-first, find the first snapshot whose status is "closed",
  compare (.Issue.notes | length) THERE against the same field in the NEWEST snapshot.
  grew > 0  ->  AUDIT REOPEN. Leave it open. Read the added text; it is the specification.
  grew == 0 ->  candidate revert, but see the null-field caveat below.

TWO PROBES I USED BEFORE THIS, BOTH WRONG, BOTH FAILING TOWARD "TIDY UP":

1. A MARKER GREP over a fixed pattern set — AUDIT-REOPEN, "REOPENED THIS EXACT", REOPENED, "still owed", "residual". A real audit note opened "AUDIT 2026-09-04 — MERGED PR #9187: reopened because ..." — LOWERCASE "reopened", header matching nothing in the set. I ran a control on unrelated text known to be present, saw 1 hit, and concluded the instrument was live. IT WAS. A CONTROL PROVES THE INSTRUMENT EXECUTES; IT DOES NOT PROVE THE PATTERN SET IS COMPLETE. To validate a pattern set, control against a POSITIVE INSTANCE OF THE TARGET — a bead you already know carries an audit note — not against arbitrary present text. This is the sharpest form of the standing "a search returning zero is not a check that passed" rule.

2. AN ADJACENT-PAIR LENGTH COMPARISON at the reopen boundary. This assumes the status change and the note are ONE mutation. THEY OFTEN ARE NOT: an audit commonly flips status and appends its note in a SEPARATE, LATER mutation, so the adjacent pair reads unchanged on a genuine audit. Anchoring to the boundary was an improvement over comparing the newest N — which reads unchanged on BOTH classes once a bead has settled — but it is still wrong.

THE NULL-FIELD CAVEAT: if notes is EMPTY on both sides, "unchanged" proves nothing — an absent field hashes constant and reports a clean walk in the same words a genuinely unchanged one does. Fall back to a field that DOES vary on that item (description, acceptance_criteria), and confirm the deliverable is on main in the TREE before closing.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXPOSED THE ERROR, and it is the transferable part: I ran the new probe against a CONTROL BEAD I was already confident was a genuine audit reopen. It answered "revert". That contradiction — not any new evidence about the beads under test — falsified the method. RUN A NEW DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST A CASE WHOSE ANSWER YOU ALREADY KNOW, AND BELIEVE THE CONTRADICTION OVER THE PROBE.

THE COST: two beads carrying substantive second-carrier work were closed with a confident, well-argued, wrong reason — rf2-hic-064 (four accuracy repairs against captured CI gate numbers) and rf2-2hpxo (six named epoch exports whose durable facade rationale contradicts the code). Both are now reopened with the correction recorded on them. Two others re-closed the same session were re-checked and confirmed genuine reverts; those stand.

AND THE STANDING RULE THIS VIOLATED, from docs/the-mayor-method/README.md: "read the item's notes before re-closing anything. The instinct to re-close a 'reverted' item destroys a real finding and looks like tidiness." Reading the NOTES means reading the text, not measuring it. When in doubt, print the text added since the last close and read it.

THE MECHANISM, and it is structural rather than careless. A mayor writing a brief reads the bead to find out what the work IS, and the work is described in the DESCRIPTION. That field is the OLDEST text on a bead by construction — corrections accrete into NOTES and comments below it. So the field a brief is naturally drawn from is precisely the field least likely to carry the current disposition. A head-truncated show makes it worse by returning the description and stopping before NOTES, but the trap survives reading the whole bead, because the description is what answers the question the mayor is actually asking.

mayor-dispatch.md ALREADY carries the rule that catches this — establish which text is newest by TRACKER TIMESTAMP, never by position and never by which FIELD it sits in — and the rule did not prevent three dispatches. DO NOT DISPATCH ... *** followed by why, what is established, what is actually owed and who owns it, then a --- ORIGINAL DESCRIPTION FOLLOWS --- fold. The banner is in the field the brief is drawn from, so it cannot be missed by the reading pattern that causes the failure. A `$`-ANCHORED REGEX RETURNS A FALSE ZERO ON A CRLF FILE — the line ends `\r\n`, so `$` sits after the `\r` and a pattern like `'^### Foo$'` matches nothing on a heading that plainly exists. Measured 2026-09-05 by a worker whose `rg '^### …$'` came back empty for a heading it could see in the file; a control exposed the zero immediately.

WHY IT BELONGS WITH THE OTHERS: this repo is `core.autocrlf=true`, so many files are CRLF in the worktree and LF in the index. Every `$`-anchored search over working-tree markdown is therefore suspect, and the failure mode is the worst kind — a clean exit 0 and an empty result set, indistinguishable from an honest "not present". A worker concluding "that heading does not exist" from such a zero would then ADD a duplicate heading, or report a missing anchor that is not missing.

THE FIXES, in order of preference:
  * Drop the `$` when you only need the prefix — `'^### Foo'` matches regardless of line ending.
  * Or match the ending explicitly: `'^### Foo\r?$'`.
  * Or search the INDEX rather than the worktree (`git grep`), where the blob is LF.
  * And always control it: run the same pattern against something you KNOW is there. A control caught this one in a single command.

THIS IS THE SAME CRLF FAMILY AS TWO OTHER MEASURED FAULTS: a `\n`-anchored PLANT that silently matched nothing on a CRLF-checked-out file (the gate then returned a clean exit 0), and `sed -i` silently converting a whole CRLF file to LF while "succeeding" (4637 CRs to 0). **On this box, assume line endings are CRLF in the worktree until you have checked, and never let a line-ending-sensitive pattern produce a conclusion without a control.**
