AN INTERRUPTED DOLT GENERATIONAL GC CAN ROLL THE BEADS TRACKER BACK MID-SESSION, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE CORRUPTION (2026-08-03).

SYMPTOM SEQUENCE, in one 10-minute window: 'bd export' failed with 'error opening table file: table file not found: .dolt/noms/<hash>'. Then EVERY bd command — ready, list, show — exited 1. THE MISSING TABLE NAME DIFFERED BETWEEN CONSECUTIVE CALLS (18uc3mpc..., then 5l677oov...), noms/oldgen existed but was EMPTY, and the noms/ file count went 7 -> 91 across a couple of minutes. That is a generational GC rewriting table files, not disk damage.

IT RECOVERS ON ITS OWN. Roughly two minutes later bd returned exit 0 with no intervention. DO NOT rebuild the database from JSONL while this is happening — 'bd export' failing is NOT proof of data loss, and a rebuild from a checkpoint would discard everything since it.

THE REAL DAMAGE IS A PARTIAL ROLLBACK, AND IT IS SILENT. After recovery the tracker had time-travelled: a bead closed ~20 minutes earlier was back to IN_PROGRESS with its ORIGINAL 'Updated' date, and 5 note-appends were gone. But it was PARTIAL — a second close from the same pass SURVIVED. So you cannot assume all-or-nothing; verify each write individually with 'bd show'.

WHAT SAVED IT: the worker that made the writes still had them in its transcript. When bd broke I immediately messaged it to STOP all bd use and report every close/update verbatim WITH its verification evidence, then re-applied the 7 writes by hand and checkpointed at once. WITHOUT THAT REPLY THE WORK WAS UNRECOVERABLE — the JSONL checkpoint predated the writes.

RULES: (1) a tracker-mutating worker's report is a durable artefact — make its brief require verbatim reasons + evidence, not a summary; (2) checkpoint IMMEDIATELY after re-applying, do not batch; (3) row counts move under you because an automated merged-PR-audit process also commits .beads — 'HEAD had N' changing between your own checkpoints is NOT necessarily corruption; (4) beads-checkpoint.sh's shrinkage guard is the right instrument to ask 'did I lose bulk data?' — a clean round-trip at the same row count means the answer is no.

Beads Dolt off-box remote (configured 2026-08-10, rf2-4l67v): origin = private https://github.com/day8/re-frame2-beads.git (git-backed dolt remote; data under refs/dolt/data). Recovery drill lessons: (1) dolt's git-backed fetch/pull FAILS with 'fatal: $GIT_DIR too big' when the checkout sits under a long Windows path (e.g. deep Temp/scratchpad nesting) — always clone to a SHORT path (C:/Users/miket/code/<name>) for recovery drills; (2) on the SAME machine, bd bootstrap prefers a locally-registered database/remote over the tracked sync.remote, so a same-box round-trip is NOT a true second-machine test — repoint the clone's dolt origin explicitly to test the off-box copy; (3) bd can exit 0 while printing a push/pull ERROR — always read the output text, never trust the exit code alone; (4) an empty GitHub repo must be initialized with one commit/branch before the first dolt push.

THE DONE-IN-TREE SWEEP KEYS ON THE BEAD ID, SO WORK THAT LANDED UNDER A SIBLING'S ID IS INVISIBLE TO IT.

The backlog-reread sweep is 'for each open id, git log origin/main --grep=<id>'. Measured 2026-09-04: rf2-o80n asked for a route-link row in chapter 20's translation table. The row ALREADY EXISTED at tip, added by PR #9131 in commit c05871bf0b — a PR filed against DIFFERENT beads, which merged after rf2-o80n was filed. The sweep returned NOTHING for rf2-o80n, because #9131's message never names it. A worker was dispatched and its whole deliverable was the refutation.

SO THE SWEEP HAS A KNOWN BLIND SPOT AND IT IS NOT THE FALSE-POSITIVE KIND. It cannot see work that landed under a neighbour's id, which is the common case whenever one PR fixes a surface several beads describe. The complement is the loop's own rule, one level up: CHECK THE TREE, NOT THE ITEM. For a bead that asks for a specific artefact — a table row, a section, a symbol — grep the ARTEFACT at tip, not the id in the log. That check costs a line and would have saved a worker cycle.

THE SWEEP ALSO HAS A FALSE-POSITIVE MODE, which is the safe direction: with the anchored form (dots escaped, trailing boundary class), rf2-6r9j.35 and rf2-2vpm each returned a commit whose message a literal grep -F shows does NOT contain the id. Treat every hit as a POINTER and confirm with grep -F on the commit message before believing it.

AND THE ANCHOR IS STILL MANDATORY IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: unanchored, 'rf2-6r9j.1' matched five commits naming .161, .101, .17, .104 and .121. Anchored it matched none. Escape the dots and append a trailing boundary class: --grep="<escaped>([^0-9A-Za-z.]|$)" with -E.

STRIP CR FIRST. 'jq -r .[].id' emits trailing \r on Windows and every grep in the loop then misses. A control built from hardcoded literal ids tests the grep and never the pipeline — it passed while the real sweep read a false clean over 48 ids. Pipe through tr -d '\r' and build the control from the SAME pipeline.

Donor-sweep metric mismatch: the narrow grep is NOT the ledger's signal. When de-donoring a surface for EP-0036 F6, 'git grep -E "re-frame\.ui|re_frame/ui|re-frame2-ui" returns zero' does NOT mean scripts/check_donor_inventory.py agrees. Its DONOR_EVIDENCE_RE (check 4, DONOR-LEDGER-DRIFTED) is deliberately LOOSER and also matches re_frame.ui, re_frame2_ui, implementation/ui, node-test-ui, check-ui-, run-ui-, test:ui. Measured 2026-07-26 on worker/examples-freehand: a fully migrated examples/ui/minimal-counter still held the gate GREEN because README.md retained one 'implementation/ui' PATH string — the narrow grep was already zero. Consequences both ways: (a) a sweep that satisfies the narrow grep can leave a still-pending ledger row silently green, so 'zero donor references' is not proof the row is disposable; (b) finishing the job (rewriting that path) FLIPS the gate to rc=1 naming the exact ledger line, so any complete de-donoring MUST be paired with the row's status change in spec/conformance/freehand/donor-inventory.md in the SAME PR. Also note the census (checks 2/3) is narrower still — CENSUS_REQUIRE_RE needs a libspec bracket and CENSUS_COORD_RE needs 'day8/re-frame2-ui {' — so three different donor definitions are in play. Always run 'python scripts/check_donor_inventory.py --ci' and read the rc; never infer disposition from a text grep.

MIKE: DRIVE THE OPEN COUNT TO ZERO, AND MEASUREMENT BEADS RUN WHEN THE BOX IS QUIET (2026-08-14).

His words: 'Drive that number to 0. If you run out of beads to do, then do the measurement ones because the box will be quiet.'

THIS RESOLVES A CONSTRAINT I HAD BEEN TREATING AS A BLOCKER. Several hicasso beads are TIMING MEASUREMENTS — tau, the interpreter-walk mount cost, allocation constants, a reader-array cost, a profile re-take, three budget gates. They cannot run honestly while five workers compile, so I had parked them as 'needs a quiet machine' with no rule for when that arrives.

THE RULE IS NOW: THE BOX IS QUIET EXACTLY WHEN NOTHING ELSE IS DISPATCHABLE. So measurement beads are the TAIL of the queue, not a separate track. Dispatch everything else first; when the dispatchable pool empties, the fleet drains, and the machine becomes the quiet box those beads need. The scheduling constraint and the priority order agree.

PRACTICAL FORM:
  While non-measurement beads remain dispatchable, saturate with those.
  When the pool empties, STOP dispatching and let the fleet drain to zero workers.
  Then dispatch measurement beads — ideally ONE AT A TIME, because two concurrent measurement workers reintroduce exactly the contention that makes the numbers worthless.

AND THAT LAST POINT IS THE ONE TO BRIEF: a measurement bead's whole value is a trustworthy number. Running two at once, or running one beside a compile, silently corrupts the deliverable in a way no gate detects. A measurement worker should say what else was running while it measured.

THIS SITS UNDER THE PHASE ORDER RATHER THAN BESIDE IT: measurement beads are stage 1-3 work (complete / correct / good quality code), so they lead the queue by stage — but they execute last by scheduling. Both are true and they do not conflict.

WHEN COLLAPSING DUPLICATE BEADS, THE SURVIVOR IS THE EARLIER OWNER WITH MORE CONTENT — not the one with the sharper framing (2026-08-15 16:54 AUSEST).

MEASURED ON MYSELF. rf2-15bqc and rf2-4ncab were the same finding: same four -h-fn recovery keywords, same emitters (impl/intent.cljs, impl/controlled.cljs), same Spec 009 lines. At 15:47 I closed 15bqc AS A DUPLICATE OF 4ncab. An audit then closed 4ncab AS A DUPLICATE OF 15bqc — the opposite direction.

THE AUDIT WAS RIGHT AND I LEFT IT STANDING. My reason was that 4ncab 'carries the sharper framing' — it states the CONSTRAINT ('the ids move with their emitters, or not at all') rather than only the symptom. The audit's reasons were stronger:
  - 15bqc is the EARLIER exact owner
  - it already carried the authoritative complaints.md ruling, the full emitter list, the one-pass repair AND the troubleshooting-doc tail
So it had both provenance and more content. Framing is cheap to copy forward; accumulated content and history are not.

THE RULE: prefer the earlier owner, and prefer the bead carrying more verified content. If the loser has a better framing sentence, COPY THE SENTENCE ONTO THE SURVIVOR — that costs one note. Do not close the richer bead to keep the better-worded one.

WHY NO DAMAGE WAS DONE, and this is the part that made it safe: BOTH closes carried the loser's unique evidence forward. Mine moved 15bqc's two extra surfaces (troubleshooting.md, hicasso.cljc) onto 4ncab; the audit's moved 4ncab's bench-mirror evidence onto 15bqc. Net result is one bead holding everything. THE CARRY-FORWARD IS WHAT MAKES A COLLAPSE REVERSIBLE — a close that merely says 'duplicate of X' is not.

DO NOT RE-CLOSE THE SURVIVOR. The method's own rule applies directly: the instinct to re-close a 'reverted' bead destroys a real finding and looks like tidiness. Read the notes first. Here the reopen was an audit converging on the better survivor, and the correct action was to leave it alone and record why.

CONTEXT ON WHY DUPLICATES ARISE AT ALL HERE: these two were filed HOURS APART by DIFFERENT workers approaching the same residue from opposite directions, neither visible to the other because both were mid-flight. That is rf2-a30v2's blind window one level up.

DUPLICATE deftest — CLJS WARNS, THE JVM IS SILENT. rf2-9e4lf (#6349, 2026-07-18) verified this with a standalone probe rather than assuming: a Clojure namespace defining the same deftest twice, with the FIRST body deliberately failing, reports 'Ran 1 tests... 0 failures' and emits ZERO diagnostic output. Clojure's 'already refers to' warning only fires ACROSS namespaces, so there is no JVM equivalent of shadow-cljs's :redef-in-file. CONSEQUENCE: a duplicate deftest in a .cljs/.cljc file is detectable (shadow-cljs warns on every build — rf2-qo5xk's went unread for months); the same defect in a .clj file is COMPLETELY INVISIBLE. Only the test count reveals it. PROOF TECHNIQUE (use this, not a green suite): to show a resurrected test body actually executes, temporarily INVERT one of its assertions and confirm the suite reds AT THE NEW SYMBOL NAME — that is impossible while the body is being replaced. Then revert and gate on the reverted tree. A green suite plus a +1 count is weaker: the count can rise for unrelated reasons and green proves only that nothing failed. Both instances found so far (qo5xk, 9e4lf) were genuinely DISTINCT tests collapsed onto one symbol by different causes — a rename sweep and a copy-pasted parallel test block — so archaeology first, never assume the cause from a sibling case.

WHEN DUPLICATION KEEPS RECURRING, THE DEFECT IS DISCOVERY — not the duplication (2026-08-14, rf2-040s1 worker).

THE SITUATION. A bead said two scripts independently parse the same build-summary line and asked whether to unify them. THE WORKER FOUND THREE. The third had been doing it for eleven days BEFORE the bead was filed, reached the identical verdict, and recorded the SAME reason for not reusing the others. So the bead's own trigger — 'unify when a third lane wants the line' — HAD ALREADY FIRED, unnoticed by its author.

IT REFUSED THE UNIFICATION, ON A REASON NEITHER AUTHOR HAD RECORDED: one gate's pattern is a FILTER, not merely an id capture — it deliberately FAILS on any summary whose id was not requested. An id-agnostic shared pattern would hand that gate every id the compiler prints and reopen a settled question across 54 builds. And what actually differs between the three is the SELECTION POLICY, not the regex: reconcile a requested set / every row must read zero / take the last row so a dependency's summary is not mistaken for the lane's. A shared module would remove three regexes and leave three policies.

IT ALSO ESTABLISHED THE DUPLICATION CANNOT FAIL QUIETLY: all three refuse an unreadable summary, so a compiler reformat yields three RED gates rather than a silent pass. Duplication that fails loudly is far cheaper than an abstraction that hides a policy.

THE REAL FIX WAS DISCOVERY. Two authors solved one problem against one wall and neither found the other. So the roster of readers is now stated IN ALL THREE FILES, with the full argument in one and short pointers in the others — one owner for the prose, so it cannot drift.

AND IT REPLACED THE COUNT WITH A POLICY TEST. The bead said 'unify when a third wants it'; three had arrived and the count was still wrong, so the count was never checkable. The new rule: a lane whose selection policy one of the three already implements CALLS that reader's export; a lane with a genuinely new policy writes its own and adds itself to the roster.

GENERALISE: before proposing to unify duplicates, ask what they share and what they DIFFER on. If the difference is policy rather than mechanism, unification hides the policy. And if the same duplication keeps appearing, the thing to fix is how the next author FINDS the existing one.

WHAT HAPPENED: in PR #6978 it wrote a canned MCP response envelope containing :classification :callback. THERE IS NO SUCH MEMBER — the vocabulary is closed at seven (:vector :options :ui-event :handler :fn :dynamic :spread). WHY EVERY SUITE STAYED GREEN, which is the whole lesson: a canned stub asserts the CONSUMER's wire handling. Nothing checks the stub against the PRODUCER's closed vocabularies. So a fixture can depict output the producer cannot emit, and the tests that read it will pass forever — while the stub sits in the one place an agent reads to learn the shape. Its own words: 'a canned stub is documentation with a test's authority.'

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER SEVEN: (1)-(6) are misreading a verdict; (7) is a stale compile cache computing a verdict from stale input; (8) is a verdict computed correctly over INVENTED INPUT. No exit-code discipline catches it, and no cache-clearing catches it either.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when a diff adds or edits a canned envelope, fixture, sample response or documented example payload, check every VALUE in it against the producing source's vocabulary — not against the consumer's prose, and not against a docstring sentence. Closed vocabularies are the specific hazard: if a keyword is drawn from a fixed set, find the set. And check the combination, not just the members: two individually-valid values can name a state the producer cannot reach.

DISPATCH IMPLICATION: brief workers touching MCP descriptors, tool catalogues, canned envelopes or documented payloads to verify values against the producing source. The Pair tool catalogue is exactly this shape — tool-descriptors.edn, descriptors_data.cljs, registry.cljs, 003-Tool-Catalogue.md and the mcp-conformance end-to-end must all move together, and a fabricated value in any of them is invisible to all of them.

(1) EMPTY-ROLLUP TRAP: 'gh pr view --jq fail=0 pending=0' reads GREEN even when total=0 checks (CI not yet registered) — that is NOT green, it is 'no CI yet'. ALWAYS check total=N>0 before merging; bake 'total=[1-9]' into the merge guard. A force-push/new-branch PR sits at total=0 for a while. (2) CO-EDIT RATCHET: renaming/removing a public symbol cascades into gates that assert the catalogue matches the code — the error-catalogue-channel-conformance test (spec/009 rows), the Public-API manifest drift-check (spec/api-manifest*.edn + metadata sidecar), and the doc-slug/mkdocs-strict validator (anchor links break when a heading slug changes). These CANNOT be deferred to a follow-up even though spec/009 is hot-zone — they must land in the SAME PR or CI goes red. When a rename/removal PR is red on JVM-core/Docs/Lint, suspect these three first. (3) The big-sweep failure shape is ALWAYS 'worker's named gates green locally, a cross-cutting CI gate red' (manifest / doc-anchor / skill-drift / mkdocs-strict — the worker skipped them locally) — fix with a Shape-5 fix-worker on the EXISTING branch running the ACTUAL failing gate, NEVER --admin past it. (4) bd-create DESCRIPTIONS must not contain backticks — bash command-substitution runs them; quote/avoid. See [[pre-alpha-no-deferred-removal-mike-2026-06]] + [[worker-liveness-windows]].

EP-0002 carried-frame pattern for DEFERRED dispatch (event handlers / async): a React :on-click (or any callback firing LATER) runs OUTSIDE the render's dynamic extent and any with-frame scope, so a bare (rf/dispatch [...]) resolves no frame -> :rf.error/no-frame-context (runtime never synthesises a frame from absence). FIX: carry the frame into the deferred dispatch — capture it at RENDER time via (:dispatch (rf/frame-handle)) (the reg-view resolves the frame-provider's frame through React context during render; the handle closes over it), OR default {:frame fid} for single-frame apps. Used for the reagent adapter testbed + SCI playground smokes (#3662). UIx/Helix use the same frame-handle pattern.

EP-0002 frame-resolution has TIERS: tier 1 = ambient dynamic-var re-frame.frame/*current-frame*; tier 2 = React-context (frame-provider). Tier 1 WINS when bound. GOTCHA (rf2-6z9clg): the reset-runtime test fixture binds an ambient *current-frame*=:rf/default around the test body, so React-context DOM tests (cross_spec_dom, frame_provider_context_dom) resolved :rf/default at tier 1 and NEVER exercised the tier-2 context they were testing (and frameless cases didn't fail closed). FIX: context-tier DOM tests must clear the ambient frame — (binding [frame/*current-frame* nil] ...) around the render, or the :ambient-frame nil fixture opt. This is by-design tier ordering, NOT a runtime bug.

ER-01 (v/$ vs compiled Hiccup) settled by evidence, 2026-07-26: at matched semantics v/$ allocates 1.011x compiled Hiccup (8 fresh JVMs, 0.00% within-run spread) so there is NO render-work case for the fork; and the compiled analyzer REFUSES a $ body ('outside the compiler's audited expression set'), so the two front ends are disjoint - the composable v/$ that dissolves D010's cliff is exactly the one that forfeits manifest + :view-cell :elided + build-time refusal. Recommendation: keep v/$ a non-goal. Also: on JVM structural renders ~80% of allocation is the OUTPUT TREE all front ends share, so compiled-vs-interpreted tops out near 0.80 - any front-end change competes under that ceiling. Report: docs/design/freehand/studio/er-01-architecture-comparison.md

Event-handling pipeline atomicity (Mike CONFIRMED 2026-05-24). Architecture: interceptors (incl. the path std-interceptor) mutate the :db/:fx EFFECTS in interceptor context; app-db gets a SINGLE deferred install only after the ENTIRE chain (all :after interceptors + the flow transform) is done. Flows run at the OUTERMOST :after (framework-prepended :rf/flows, fires last) because flows read full-app-db :inputs and path's :after reshapes :db. CONTRACT: ANY throw BEFORE install (cofx, handler, interceptor :after, flow) => the deferred install simply does NOT happen => app-db UNCHANGED, NO :rf.event/db-changed, NO :fx. No partial commit (a flow throw must NOT commit prior flows' writes). The :db install is the atomic commit boundary. The ONLY post-commit stage is :fx: an fx throw surfaces an error but does NOT wind back app-db (fx side-effects http/nav/dispatch may already have fired and are irreversible). Uniform: flow-throw behaves like every other pre-install throw.

TO ASK WHETHER A BRANCH HAS A PR, USE THE API'S EXACT head= FILTER RATHER THAN SCANNING PR PAGES (2026-08-23).

THE COMMAND: gh api -X GET repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls -f state=all -f 'head=<owner>:<branch>' 
It queries the WHOLE pull-request set by exact head ref and returns [] when there is none. No paging, no substring matching, no window to be wrong about.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. The hygiene loop's rule is 'never delete a branch whose PR is not verifiably MERGED, keyed on exact headRefName equality'. I had been answering it by pulling gh pr list --state all --limit 400 and equality-filtering in Python. That is correct as far as it goes and it has TWO failure modes the head filter does not:

1. THE WINDOW. 400 PRs covered #8326-#8726. Both orphan branches' tips date from 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-15, whose PRs would sit BELOW that window -- the scan's zero was a zero over the wrong range, and it read exactly like a zero over the right one. Widening to pages 5-6 reached #8126 and still could not prove absence, only extend it.

2. THE COST. Each widening is another API round trip and another chance to mis-set the range. The head filter answers in one call and its answer is total.

MEASURED: head=day8:worker/receipts-hic081 and head=day8:worker/retire-delete each return 'NO PR of any state', confirming what the paged scan could only suggest. Both branches therefore carry genuinely-new work (git cherry '+' counts 3 and 1) that has never been proposed for merge, and under the rule they can never be deleted on evidence -- only on the operator's explicit word.

THE GENERAL SHAPE: when a rule says 'compare for equality yourself', prefer an instrument that takes equality as INPUT over one that returns a page you then filter. The filter is right; the page is the risk.

A NON-CODE EXCLUSION THAT STOPS AT COMMENTS LEAVES STRING BODIES SEARCHABLE — AND THE FIX IS TWO PROJECTIONS, NOT ONE (2026-08-06, rf2-t4j7c, PR #7620).

THE DEFECT: a gate blanked COMMENTS so prose could not stand in for a call. It deliberately KEPT string literals, and it had to — the scans own targets include the strings release, --config-merge and the require path. So the same `resetLaneBuildCache(IMPL, BUILD)` text SITTING IN A LOG LINE stood in for the call exactly as comment text had. Reproduced on unmodified main: a rider with no executable reset, carrying that text in a const string and repeated in a template, returned null from requires, clearsFirst, noLiteralId AND sameBuildId — 40 tests, 40 pass, exit 0.

THE FIX SHAPE, and it generalises: ONE SOURCE, TWO BLANKED VIEWS, both the ORIGINAL LENGTH so offset comparisons still hold across them. `code` (comments blanked, strings kept) feeds discovery, the require check and the spawn-side reads that legitimately need string text. `exec` (comments AND string bodies blanked) feeds the clear call and its build-id argument, which must be executable to count. The question is never "what is not code" in general — it is WHAT MUST THIS PARTICULAR SCAN NOT SEE, and different scans in one gate can have different answers.

THE REVERSE MUTATION IS WHAT PROVED BOTH HALVES LOAD-BEARING, and it is the better half of the proof: pointing sameBuildId back at `code` makes it FALSELY report a correctly-wired probe carrying a decoy log line as "clears DECOY but releases BUILD". So the split does not only close a false GREEN, it prevents a false RED. A projection change that only ever tightens is suspicious; check whether the looser view was also inventing findings.

AND IT WROTE THE UNCOVERED EDGE INTO THE HEADER rather than leaving it for the next audit: spawn-side reads must still see string text, so that half is deliberately unprotected. It also re-argued the failure-direction claim for the SECOND view rather than assuming it carried over, and bounded it honestly as "a direction, not a proof". When you add a projection, the safety argument does not inherit — restate it per view.

THIS IS THE THIRD ROUND ON THIS ONE GATE (comment text, then regex-in-substitution, now string bodies), each found by an audit of the previous fix. The pattern is not incompetence: each repair narrowed the aperture and revealed the next-widest way a token could masquerade as a call. Expect a masking gate to take several rounds, and expect each rounds audit to find the shape the last one made visible.

FACADE-EXPORT CLASSIFICATION is a CI-ONLY gate (Public-API manifest drift-check, .github/workflows/lint.yml → clojure -M -m re-frame.api-manifest.gen --check). It does NOT run in a worker's local 'npm run test:cljs' or the fast-pr spine, so a new public facade export (re-frame.core / re-frame.flows / etc. defn re-export) added WITHOUT a :classification sidecar in spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn passes local gates + a mayor fail=0 merge check, then lands as DRIFT on main and reds the NEXT PR's manifest gate (happened 2026-06-21: #4857/en00bk added flows/flow-meta-at unclassified → surfaced by Mike's #4859 → fixed by #4860). MAYOR RULE: when merging any PR that adds a public facade export, verify it added a matching api-manifest-metadata.edn :classification entry (mirror the nearest precedent, e.g. app-schema-meta-at {:tier :tooling :owner <spec-num> :status v1}); don't trust fail=0 alone since the gate may not have run on that branch. Classification of a new tooling-introspection export mirrors its precedent (not a fresh Mike ruling); genuinely-novel surface tiers still go to Mike.

FALSE-GREEN VECTOR — test-fast-pr.sh SOFT-SKIPS ITS OWN MKDOCS STEP (2026-07-25, found by the rf2-2jomv worker): scripts/test-fast-pr.sh logs 'mkdocs not on PATH ... local soft-skip OK' and still exits 0. So a green fast-PR spine does NOT mean mkdocs passed, and a docs-only change can read as fully gated while its only real gate never ran. Fix for briefs: any worker touching docs/ or spec/ must run 'python -m mkdocs build --strict' SEPARATELY and report its own exit code; do not accept the spine's rc as covering it. This is the THIRD distinct exit-code false-green found in one session, alongside (1) piping a gate through tail/grep returning the pipe's status and (2) a compound/backgrounded command's trailing echo supplying a 0 while the log said FAIL. Common lesson: an exit code only means what the LAST thing to set it did — cross-check every rc against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines before believing it.

FAN-OUTS DEFEAT PRE-LOOP GUARDS — a check taken BEFORE a loop does not fence the loops later iterations. Found by rf2-sdeae (P1, #6361, 2026-07-18). rf2-qfrh4 had fenced every epoch-restore SEAM on the exact-ownership token, but three of those seams are fan-outs: the guard ran once, then the loop kept invoking callbacks that could seat a successor mid-flight. Three interleavings were constructed on the same thread, inside the callback, between the read and the write. Sharpest: the quiesce chain first hook (:machines/on-frame-restored!) destroys frame A and seats B; A second hook (:http/abort-in-flight-for-frame!) then aborts B in-flight requests — a dead frames tail mutating a live successor. RULE: when auditing an ownership or liveness guard, ask whether the guarded region contains ITERATION or CALLBACK RE-ENTRY. If it does, the guard must travel INTO the region (widen the token through the loop) rather than gate its entry. FIX SHAPE that worked: an ORDER fix, not a new gate — detach-slots! removes slots in one swap-vals!, THEN aborts the detached values, so no host side effect runs inside the retriable swap. The sibling timers/release-frame! already did this; the work-ledger table was the odd one out, so the fix converged on established local discipline instead of inventing a mechanism. BONUS SIGNAL WORTH COPYING: the adversarial re-entrancy case exposed unbounded amplification — a callback re-entering release-frame! re-read the not-yet-dropped slot and re-aborted it 1101 times in the red run. If a re-entrancy test produces a COUNT rather than a boolean, the count is the evidence. Related: rf2-uhouu (#6339) collapsed two reads into one atomic decision; this is the same discipline in the opposite direction — the decision existed and had to travel.

A DISPATCH FENCE IS NOT ALWAYS SPELLED "DO NOT DISPATCH" — the pre-dispatch grep needs the POSITIVE forms too. Measured 2026-09-04, the third gap found in this instrument in one session.

THE CHECK. Before dispatching any bead, grep its notes for a hold, because `bd ready` reads dependency EDGES and can never see a PROSE fence. The pattern I had been using was: FENCED | DO NOT DISPATCH | SEQUENCED | RELEASE CONDITION | HOLD UNTIL | Mike rules | STILL MIKE | DOSSIER | RECOMMENDATION | operator call.

WHAT IT MISSED. rf2-i6kh carries, in capitals: "DISPATCH ONLY AFTER rf2-2hpxo's PR HAS MERGED, never merely opened." The old pattern returns ZERO on that bead. I dispatched it; the worker read the bead, found the line, and correctly STOPPED without a PR, having first measured the surface and banked the results. One worker cycle spent, nothing damaged.

WHY THE GAP IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. Every term in my pattern was a PROHIBITION ("do not", "hold", "fenced"). A precondition can equally be written as a PERMISSION with a condition attached — "dispatch only after X", "once Y merges", "after Z lands" — and those share no substring with the prohibitions. A keyword list built from the prohibitions will therefore keep missing the permissions, and adding one more term does not fix the class.

THE WIDENED PATTERN, verified to fire on rf2-i6kh where the old one was silent (it returns "DISPATCH ONLY", "AFTER rf2-2hpxo's PR HAS MERGED", "precondition"):

  grep -o -i -E '(DISPATCH ONLY|ONLY AFTER|DO NOT DISPATCH|FENCED|SEQUENCED|RELEASE CONDITION|HOLD UNTIL|precondition|MUST MERGE|after .{0,20} HAS MERGED|Mike rules|STILL MIKE|operator call|DOSSIER|RECOMMENDATION)'

TWO THINGS THAT MAKE THIS SURVIVABLE RATHER THAN A LOOMING FAILURE. First, the grep is a cheap FILTER, not an authority — a hit means read the bead, a miss means nothing. Second, the real backstop is the worker: the preamble's "check your dispatch preconditions before you begin" plus "premises are claims, not findings" is what caught this, as it has caught every mayor-side gap this session. So widen the pattern, and keep the clause in the brief that makes the worker check independently.

AND NOTE THE TRACKER ITSELF WAS WRONG AT DISPATCH TIME: rf2-i6kh WAS in `bd ready` when I read it, and a dependency edge was added afterwards, so it is correctly blocked now. Both instruments failed together; only the worker did not.

RELATED: [[grep-notes-for-a-fence-before-every-dispatch]], [[jq-output-carries-cr-and-poisons-every-loop]].

A FENCE NEEDS BOTH SIGNALS, AND I DROPPED THE OLD ONE BECAUSE THE NEW ONE HAD JUST BITTEN (2026-08-15 14:15 AUSEST). WHAT I GOT WRONG. I briefed worker/stale-uvazt that 'skills/reagent-migration/** is FREE — verified at dispatch against every open PR and every live worktree.' IT WAS NOT. origin/worker/mount-7mtcf held SEVEN of the twelve files, including evals/evals.json. The worker found it, tested liveness properly (merge-base --is-ancestor says NOT merged, so not a rebase leftover; tip 1d576c2a8b at 13:29; bead still open; no PR yet) and correctly REFUSED half the cluster as blocked. HOW I MISSED IT, AND THIS IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. I ran inside each live worktree and read mount-7mtcf as CLEAN. It WAS clean — because it had COMMITTED its work. The committed three-dot diff (git diff --name-only origin/main...worker/) is the signal that would have shown those seven files, and I did not run it for that path. SO I INVERTED THE VERY TRAP I HAD JUST LEARNED. Earlier today rf2-42bj2 established that a worker at ZERO COMMITS looks empty by three-dot diff while holding real working-tree edits — so I started checking porcelain. Then I quietly stopped checking the diff, because porcelain was the signal that had recently caught something. The two signals answer DIFFERENT questions and neither subsumes the other: git diff --name-only origin/main...worker/
-> what the worker has COMMITTED git status --porcelain (inside the worktree) -> what it has NOT yet committed A worker mid-task flips between them: uncommitted early, committed at milestones, and CLEAN-BUT-COMMITTED for the whole stretch between a commit and its PR. That last state is invisible to porcelain and is exactly where mount-7mtcf sat. THE RULE IS THEREFORE: RUN BOTH, ALWAYS, AND UNION THE RESULTS. Adding a third check (PR state) separates a live holder from a rebase-merged ghost, but it does not replace either of the first two. WHY IT COSTS: an omitted holder is a stale-NARROW fence, which mayor-dispatch.md itself names as the expensive direction — two workers on one file merge-conflict and can silently revert each other. Here it cost half a cluster instead, only because the worker re-derived rather than trusting me. GENERAL FORM, since this is the second time today I have done this shape: WHEN A NEW CHECK IS ADDED BECAUSE THE OLD ONE FAILED, THE OLD ONE IS STILL REQUIRED. The new check exists because the old one was insufficient, not because it was wrong. Same error as clause 5's job-key count, where zero turned out to be necessary and not sufficient.

MY FENCES ARE ENUMERATIONS, NOT RULES — AND A WORKER CROSSED ONE SILENTLY (2026-08-11).

WHAT MY BRIEFS SAY: "Your surface is X. You are fenced out of spec/*, .github/workflows/*, package.json, shadow-cljs.edn. Worker A holds Y, worker B holds Z." That is a NAMED SURFACE plus a LIST OF FORBIDDEN PATHS. A file that is in neither is UNDEFINED, and the worker has to guess.

WHAT HAPPENED: rf2-hic-030's worker was fenced to native.cljc|.cljs plus new test files, and out of the four hot-zone paths. It edited implementation/hicasso/resources/clj-kondo.exports/.../config.edn — neither named nor forbidden. I found it by reading its PR diff, not from a report.

I ALMOST GOT THIS WRONG IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION. The directory belongs to another live worker (areduce-ka4d), so at a glance it read as a collision and I nearly told it to back the change out. Reading the actual FILE list showed no overlap — areduce holds hooks/*.clj, the README and the fixtures; config.edn is untouched by it. And the change was RIGHT: :lint-as clojure.core/defn because defcomponent is defn-shaped, with n/$ and n/props deliberately getting nothing so the grammar is not restated in a second place that can drift. Enforcing the fence mechanically would have destroyed a good decision.

THE TWO FAILURES THE ENUMERATION ALLOWS: a worker crosses silently into a contended file (a real collision nobody sees until the merge), or a worker DOESN'T make a correct small change because it was not obviously permitted.

THE FIX, one clause added to the fence paragraph in every brief:

  "Your surface is <X>. Anything outside it: if the change is trivially additive and the file is held by nobody, make it and SAY SO IN YOUR REPORT. If it is contended, hot-zone, or more than trivially additive, STOP and report instead."

That converts a list into a RULE, makes the crossing visible either way, and keeps the judgement with the worker — which is the stance. I already write the stop-and-report form for ANTICIPATED crossings (a new build id, an npm script, a new :rf.error/* id); this generalises it to the unanticipated ones, which are the only ones that surprise me.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a diff shows a file outside the brief's surface, READ THE FILE LIST OF EVERY OTHER LIVE WORKER BEFORE REACTING. Directory-level overlap is not collision. I check this now; I nearly did not.

A POLLING PROCESS IS INVISIBLE TO THE STRANDED SWEEP'S WRITE CLOCK — IT MOVES EXACTLY ONE FILE, $GIT_DIR/FETCH_HEAD (measured 2026-08-23 10:28 AUSEST).

WHAT SIX SWEEPS GOT WRONG. The worktree pr-audit-8445 was read on seven consecutive stranded sweeps and reported each time as silent for hours: file-tree newest write 03:13:10, git index 03:38:20, both static. Each sweep correctly declined to reap it, but on the reasoning 'cannot tell from spacing alone'. It was in fact alive the whole time. Reading .git/worktrees/pr-audit-8445/FETCH_HEAD three times gave 10:26:44, 10:27:26, 10:28:08 — 42 seconds apart, twice. Something in there runs git fetch on a 42-second cadence.

THE MECHANISM. A process that only polls neither edits a file nor touches the index, so the two clocks a sweep naturally reaches for never move. But a fetch is a write, and it lands in exactly one place: FETCH_HEAD, which is PER-WORKTREE ($GIT_DIR for a linked worktree is .git/worktrees/<name>, so a fetch run from the mayor checkout writes .git/FETCH_HEAD and never the worktree's). That per-worktree property is what makes it usable as a liveness probe.

THE CONTROLS MAKE IT A DISCRIMINATOR RATHER THAN AN OBSERVATION. Every worker worktree HAS a FETCH_HEAD — hotzone 08-21 09:37:38, repoint 08-21 09:15:58, specsize 08-22 00:29:33 — each frozen at the moment that worker died. Only the live one moves. Worktrees created by a different harness had none at all. So the file's PRESENCE says nothing; two reads a minute apart say everything.

WHY IT MATTERS AND IN WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILS. The blind spot makes a LIVE process look STOPPED, which is the direction that authorises reaping. The existing guidance gets you to the right suspicion and then stops one step short: it says a worker that is only READING touches nothing. A poller is not merely reading — it writes, once per interval, to a file the sweep was not looking at.

HOW TO RUN IT: stat .git/worktrees/<name>/FETCH_HEAD twice, 30-60 seconds apart. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration. Absence of movement is still not proof of death — it only restores the situation the older clocks described.

FOOTNOTE ON THE TWO OLDER CLOCKS, since they disagree and both are real: .git/worktrees/<n>/index moves when the worker stages or commits; the file tree moves when it edits or checks out. Neither is wrong, they answer different questions, and the earlier sweeps' recorded numbers were the index clock.

THE HEAD==origin/main VERIFICATION CAN READ A STALE origin/main FOR SEVERAL COMMANDS RUNNING, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE DIVERGENCE (2026-08-16 01:44).

WHAT I SAW. The merge sweep's closing check printed 'local==origin: NO' with local=e56fc00ccb and origin/main=401bd15991. I then ran, in order: rev-parse both refs (same mismatch), 'git fetch origin main -q', rev-parse both again (SAME mismatch), 'git pull --ff-only origin main' which printed 'Already up to date' and exited 0, and rev-parse a third time (STILL the same mismatch). Three consecutive reads agreed that the refs differed.

THEY DID NOT DIFFER. A fourth check resolved it: git rev-parse HEAD and git rev-parse origin/main both returned e56fc00ccb75a3f4f8098a5b62a515a6d1f9832d, merge-base --is-ancestor answered YES in BOTH directions, and rev-list --count was 0 both ways. The refs were identical the whole time and the SHORT read was showing a stale remote-tracking ref.

THE MECHANISM: 'git fetch origin main' and 'git pull origin main' NAME A BRANCH, so git writes FETCH_HEAD and does not necessarily update refs/remotes/origin/main. The pull can therefore be genuinely up to date while the tracking ref a later rev-parse reads still holds the previous tick's value. CLAUDE.md's rule to NAME THE REMOTE AND BRANCH on the pull is right for the pull itself — it stops the bare form no-opping against a racing audit push — but it is exactly what leaves the tracking ref behind for the verification that follows.

WHY IT MATTERS: the mayor's post-merge verification IS 'git rev-parse HEAD must equal git rev-parse origin/main'. If that comparison can read a stale ref for several commands in a row, a clean tree reports as divergence, and the remedies for real divergence — pull --rebase, force-with-lease, resetting — are all destructive against a tree that was never wrong.

WHAT SAVED IT is already written in CLAUDE.md and I nearly did not apply it: 'one mismatch is not yet evidence either ... read both refs again before believing it.' I read them a fourth time with the FULL SHAs and ancestry rather than the short form, and the phantom vanished. Note the rule says read AGAIN, not read TWICE — here it took four.

THE RELIABLE CHECK, and use this rather than repeating reads: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/main' AND the reverse, or 'git rev-list --count' both ways. Ancestry resolves the objects rather than trusting a possibly-stale ref label, and it answers the question the mayor actually has — is the checkout the same tree as the remote — instead of the question the short SHAs answer, which is whether two ref labels happen to print the same characters right now.

TO FORCE THE TRACKING REF FORWARD when you do want it current: 'git fetch origin' with NO branch name, or an explicit refspec ('git fetch origin refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main'), which is the form already used in this session for worker branches and which does update the ref.

MERGE-LOOP HAZARD: the draft interlock does NOT protect a fix worker. The method has workers publish as a draft and mark ready as their last act, so the merge loop cannot merge out from under a live author. A FIX worker dispatched onto an EXISTING branch inherits a PR that is already marked ready — by its original author, who has finished — so nothing in the rollup or the PR state says a second worker is currently inside that branch. The merge criterion tests the change, the change goes green, and the merge lands while the fix worker is still running.

Observed 2026-09-01: PR #8873 was merged on a clean five-clause pass while its fix worker (dispatched ~34 min earlier onto worker/routing-encoding-j3tud) was still live and had not reported done. Nothing was lost — its commits were what went green and they landed — but that was luck about timing, not a guarantee: had it been mid-way through a second commit, the merge would have taken a partial change.

THE ASYMMETRY TO REMEMBER: for an ordinary dispatch, draft/ready is a reliable liveness signal. For a fix dispatch, it is stale by construction and says nothing. The mayor holds the only live-worker knowledge (the dispatch ledger and the agent listing), so on a PR that has a fix worker assigned, check the agent is finished before merging rather than trusting the PR state. Candidate method-doc gap; raise at the next method-reread rather than acting on it here.

A FIX WORKER CANNOT 'git worktree add <path> <branch>' WHEN ANOTHER WORKTREE STILL HOLDS THAT BRANCH — git refuses two checkouts of one branch, and the fix is --detach, never --force.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 on PR #9147. I dispatched a fix worker onto the existing branch worker/census-a while the original census-a worktree was still registered (deferred from reaping because its PR was open). The recipe in my brief — 'git worktree add <newpath> worker/census-a' — FAILED for that reason.

THE CORRECT RECIPE, which the worker found and which should go in every fix-worker brief:
  git -C <mayor> fetch origin
  git -C <mayor> worktree add --detach <newpath> origin/<branch>
then commit on the detached HEAD and publish with an explicit refspec:
  git push origin HEAD:<branch>
When the branch has not diverged that is a plain FAST-FORWARD — no --force and not even --force-with-lease. And --detach avoids the alternative of forcing a second live checkout onto one branch, which is the thing the ban on concurrent same-branch workers exists to prevent.

TAKE THE TIP FROM THE REMOTE, NOT THE LOCAL REF, AND THIS IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL. Measured twice in one session. On #9147 the local worker/census-a was 940ea6c299 — the same three commit subjects on an OLDER base — while origin/worker/census-a was 09e72fa9eb. On #9142 the local ref was 5f05dd6698 while the remote had already been rebased to a3cd526469. A worker branching from the stale local ref silently drops remote-only work, and the diff afterwards looks entirely reasonable.

RELATED HYGIENE INTERACTION: this only arises because the loop DEFERS reaping a reported worktree whose PR is still open (free insurance). That deferral is correct and should stay; the recipe is what has to change.

FLAKE PROOF — a run count is not always the right evidence; sometimes a MARGIN is. I briefed rf2-ybqse to prove stability with 20+ consecutive runs. Its worker (2026-07-18) correctly pushed back: focused runs could not exercise that flake at all (the bug lived in the gap between namespace LOAD and render, which a focused run collapses), and full-suite runs cost ~4 min each. It ran 20 focused + 3 full and supplied the better proof — the measured margin between the fixture's :stale-at and the render-time clock: +30461ms pre-fix (29.5s of a 60s horizon already burned), -13700ms when deliberately shrunk to falsify (reproducing the reported failure string verbatim), +60000ms post-fix. At a constant 60000ms the failure is UNREACHABLE rather than merely unobserved. RULE FOR BRIEFS: ask for proof the failure is unreachable, and let the worker choose the instrument. Repeated green runs prove absence-of-observation; a margin, an invariant, or a falsification run can prove absence-of-possibility. Demanding N runs can also mislead — N greens on a test that structurally cannot fail in that mode is a false-green about a false-green. ALSO: this class of flake (wall-clock captured in a top-level def, compared against a render-time clock) is invisible in isolation and only appears when a bundle loads all namespaces before executing any.

FLATTENING WHITESPACE DOES NOT UNDO A RENDERER'S MID-TOKEN LINE BREAK — and the break is not only a FALSE ZERO, it MANUFACTURES IDENTIFIERS THAT DO NOT EXIST. Measured 2026-09-04, three times in one session, the third time inside a dispatch brief.

THE MECHANISM. `bd show` hard-wraps its output. It breaks lines at spaces AND inside tokens, at hyphens and at underscores. Flattening with `tr -s ' \n' ' '` turns that break into a SPACE, so the token is now two words and neither is the original.

INSTANCE 1 — THE FALSE ZERO. Probing a freshly appended note for `ls-files` returned 0 after flattening. The text was intact; the renderer had split `git ls-` / `files`, so the flattened form read `git ls- files` and the token genuinely did not occur. This is the dangerous variant precisely BECAUSE flattening is the documented remedy for wrapped text: a zero that SURVIVES the fix reads as strong evidence of real damage, and the next move after that is a recovery from git history that was never needed.

INSTANCE 2 and 3 — THE FABRICATED IDENTIFIER, which is worse and which the earlier version of this memory did not cover. Extracting file paths from `bd show` output with a flattened regex produced `oke_dom_cljs_test.cljs` — a fragment of `per_keystroke_dom_cljs_test.cljs` split at an underscore. I PUT IT IN A DISPATCH BRIEF as a real file. The worker had to spend effort establishing that it "does not exist and never did"; the bead had never named it. The same extraction later yielded `mine.md` and `keystroke.md` from `requirements-mine.md` and `per-keystroke.md`. Verified: all three fragments return 0 from `git ls-files`, both real names return 1.

SO THE FAILURE IS BIDIRECTIONAL. A mid-token break can make a present token invisible (false negative) OR mint a plausible token that was never there (false positive). The false positive is the expensive one, because it propagates into work instructions where a person or agent will try to act on it, and a well-formed filename carries no signal that it was assembled by a line wrap.

THE RULES.
1. NEVER extract identifiers — file paths, symbols, ids — from RENDERED output. Take them from the source of truth: `git ls-files`, `git grep -l`, `bd show --json`. Rendered text is for reading, not for harvesting.
2. If you do harvest from rendered text, VALIDATE EVERY EXTRACTED PATH before it reaches a brief, a bead or a report: `git ls-files <path>` returning 0 means you invented it.
3. A zero that survives flattening is NOT proof of absence. Probe a substring with no hyphen, underscore or dot, or print the neighbouring text with `grep -o -E '.{0,80}<anchor>.{0,120}'` and read it. That costs one command and settles it outright.
4. A positive control proves the INSTRUMENT works, not that the TARGET can be spelled the way you spelled it. Both instances passed their controls.

FREEHAND API-MANIFEST IS A SERIAL LANE for public-verb beads — the biggest merge-friction in the Freehand build wave (2026-07-23). re-frame.freehand is a FULLY-ROWED manifest surface: adding ANY public verb requires FIVE co-edited files in ONE PR — implementation/freehand/src/re_frame/freehand.cljc (facade block), spec/api-manifest.edn (REGENERATE, never hand-edit), spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (classification row), spec/API.md (roster row + remove the declared-vacancy prose), docs/api/re-frame.freehand.md (member heading + remove vacancy prose). FOUR gates enforce it: the api-manifest gen --check entry point, api-md-check, doc-api-check, and the CLJS manifest probe under npm run test:cljs.

THE TRAP THAT COST THREE REBASES (presence PR 6713, measured — the most important part): git rebase AUTO-MERGES the generated spec/api-manifest.edn with NO conflict markers, merging the var ROWS correctly while leaving a STALE :var-count HEADER (observed 517 against a set of 519). The file looks cleanly merged and is SELF-INCONSISTENT. The drift gate then reds with "var set identical; :meta or formatting differs — regenerate", which READS LIKE a formatting or toolchain problem and sends you hunting the wrong cause. IT IS NOT A TOOLCHAIN TRAP. Cure: run the plain generator (no --check flag) to overwrite byte-exact, then --check must exit 0 AND git diff spec/api-manifest.edn must be EMPTY after that fresh run — the empty diff is the proof the committed file equals the generator output.

RULE: for a GENERATED file, a clean auto-merge is NOT evidence of correctness. Treat every rebase touching api-manifest.edn as resolve-by-REGENERATE whether or not git reported a conflict.

OTHER OPERATIONAL FACTS: (a) verb-adders are a SERIAL LANE — merge one, rebase the next onto it, and HOLD the lane still for the worker you are waiting on or it rebases forever against a moving main. (b) doc-api-check requires a member heading in docs/api for every new advanced or front-porch var. (c) the CLJS manifest probe CACHES the metadata namespace across a metadata-only edit — clear .shadow-cljs to re-verify locally. (d) INTERNAL-only beads (manifests/elision, the checker, the test surface, cell/shell correctness fixes) do NOT touch this surface and parallelize freely — dispatch those alongside verb work to keep saturation without lane contention.

MAYOR PLAYBOOK: brief every verb-adding bead with "add your metadata row, REGENERATE the manifest, add the API.md row and the docs/api member IN THE SAME PR or the gate reds", treat it as a serial-lane occupant, and hold the lane still while it rebases. RESOLVED 2026-07-23 by PR #6700 — the fixture-cache warning is NO LONGER needed in Freehand worker briefs. Freehand conformance fixtures are now a shadow-cljs build dependency, so a fixture-only edit invalidates the cache and the compiled test sees the new expectations.

WHAT THE BUG WAS, kept because the shape recurs: re-frame.freehand.conformance/fixture inlined its .edn at MACRO-EXPANSION time, and shadow-cljs had no dependency edge from a test namespace to the fixture it inlined. A fixture-only edit therefore did not invalidate the build cache, and the compiled test kept asserting the PREVIOUS expectations. A green CLJS or browser conformance run after a fixture change was worthless. The JVM side was never affected.

MEASURED TWICE, INDEPENDENTLY, by two workers with no stake in each other's finding — which is why it was believed rather than argued about. The route-link slice mutated a fixture and got 484 tests / 2746 assertions / 0 failures, green on a fixture that MUST fail; its probe passed TWICE before it cleared the cache. The CI-classifier slice separately flipped FH-CALL-001 :predicates :view? true->false and saw a warm cache recompile 1 file and report 0 failures, versus 124 files and 1 failure after clearing.

⚠️ THE GENERAL LESSON, WHICH OUTLIVES THIS FIX AND IS WHY THIS MEMORY SURVIVES: a table-driven gate whose expectations are INLINED AT COMPILE TIME can silently decouple from its data. Whenever test expectations live in a separate file that a macro reads, ASK WHETHER THE BUILD SYSTEM KNOWS ABOUT THAT EDGE — and prove it the only way that counts: mutate the data WITHOUT clearing any cache and require RED. A fix verified only after a cache clear proves nothing, because that is the broken state's own behaviour.

TWO SEPARATE HOLES EXISTED ON THIS PATH; both are now closed and neither alone sufficed. rf2-drpa3.66 (#6699) made the CI jobs RUN on a fixture change — the classifier had no route for spec/conformance/freehand/fixtures/** so both newly-required host jobs skipped. rf2-drpa3.65 (#6700) made the compiled test SEE the change. Scheduling and compilation are independent failure modes; check both when a data-driven gate looks green.

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched a bead to fix a "stale" voice instruction, telling the worker that the operator's directly-stated preference in the loop body governs over the command file. THE WORKER REFUSED AND REFUTED THE PREMISE.

The command file says ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English for chat. That is accurate against TWO LIVE bd records dated 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-10, the second recording "ASKED THREE TIMES". GATE EXIT-CODE TRAP, SECOND VARIANT (2026-07-25, found by the rf2-kqxe6.20 worker): a BACKGROUNDED or compound gate invocation can report 'exit code 0' while its log says FAIL. The worker's first scripts/test-fast-pr.sh run was reported exit 0 while the log read 'FAIL CLJS node integration' — the 0 belonged to a TRAILING ECHO in the compound command, not to the runner. This is distinct from the known pipe variant (piping a gate through tail/grep returns the PIPE's status). So the rule needs both halves in briefs: (a) never pipe a gate through tail/grep; (b) never read the exit status of a compound or backgrounded command as the runner's — capture the runner's own status immediately into a variable (rc=$?) on the line after the runner, echo THAT, and cross-check it against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines before believing either. A gate that reports success while its log says FAIL is the single most dangerous failure mode available to a worker, because it produces a confident false green.

RELATED ROOT CAUSE worth briefing alongside it: a FRESH worker worktree has no node_modules, so shadow-cljs is not on PATH and any CLJS/node arm dies for environmental reasons that look like test failures. Fix is 'npm ci' under implementation/ inside the worktree (NOT a junction into the mayor tree — a junction makes git worktree remove destroy the mayor's real node_modules). Multiple workers hit this today. Also observed: rewrite-local-root-coord and 'implementation JS harness helpers' flake on Git-Bash fork exhaustion (0xC0000142, 'fork: Resource temporarily unavailable') when several JVMs are live, then pass uncontended — load-sensitive, not a real failure.

THE DEFECT. scripts/check_gate_scheduling.py answers "is this gate scheduled to run in CI?" by searching the workflow YAML. It searched the RAW file. test.yml carries paragraph-long job comments that NAME the commands they explain, so A COMMENT MENTIONING A COMMAND MARKED THAT GATE AS SCHEDULED. Measured: only 39,567 of 511,152 chars of the workflow corpus is executable — 8%. The gate was reading its answer out of the other 92%.

THE SHARPEST INSTANCE, and it is the reason this is worth a memory rather than a bug report: the test:mcp-conformance disposition pinned its ci-runs-it-directly probe on the JOB ID mcp-conformance-re-frame2-pair, which appears 8 TIMES IN RAW YAML AND ZERO TIMES IN ANY run: VALUE. Its premise had never once been confirmed by anything CI executes. A scheduling claim resting entirely on prose, in the checker whose whole job is to verify scheduling claims.

THE FIX SHAPE: derive reachability from run: VALUES ONLY - inline, block/folded scalars, and the "- run:" first-key form - excluding name:, if:, with:, the defaults: run: mapping, and comments at every level. Transitive closure preserved, no new dependency, still pure-static.

THE LOAD-BEARING VERIFICATION: identical counts before and after on the live tree (40 gates / 34 scheduled / 6 declared). That is what proves nothing real was leaning on prose, so the tightening cannot red main. A tightening that CHANGES the live counts is telling you something was depending on the loophole - read it before shipping.

WHY THIS GENERALISES. This project has found the "a comment justifying an omission is an unverified assertion" pattern five times. THIS IS THAT PATTERN ONE LEVEL UP: not a human trusting a comment, but a MACHINE CHECK trusting one. Any checker that greps a file containing both executable content and prose has this defect available to it. Ask of every static checker: WHAT SUBSET OF THE FILE IS IT ENTITLED TO READ, and is it reading only that?

TWO SEPARATE gh HAZARDS, OFTEN CONFLATED — keep them distinct (2026-09-03, corrected same day).

=== HAZARD 1: the 100-file cap is REAL, and it truncates a PR's FILE LIST ===
'gh pr view N --json files' and 'gh pr list --json files' return at most 100 filenames, silently — well-formed JSON, no marker. MEASURED on day8/re-frame2 PR #9103: 'gh pr view 9103 --json files --jq .files|length' = 100; 'gh api --paginate repos/day8/re-frame2/pulls/9103/files --jq .[].filename | wc -l' = 401.

It matters because the mayor's overlap check is
  comm -12 <(git diff --name-only <merge-base> origin/main | sort) <(gh pr view N --json files ...)
so on a PR over 100 files the right side is a truncated sample and a real overlap in files 101..N reads as NO OVERLAP. Fails OPEN.
FIX: gh api --paginate repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<N>/files --jq '.[].filename'
DETECTOR: 'gh pr view --json changedFiles' reports the TRUE total even when files[] is capped. changedFiles != (files|length), or a length of exactly 100, means truncated.

=== HAZARD 2: gh/git LISTINGS CAN RETURN A STALE VIEW — this is NOT the cap ===
DO NOT attribute a missing PR to the 100-file cap. A worker A/B'd it: 'gh pr list --state open --json number,headRefName' and the same call WITH files both returned the same 3 PRs. The cap truncates a PR's file list; it does NOT drop PRs from a listing. Its 'git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/worker/<prefix>*' pattern form was also control-tested and works.

What actually happened: at one instant, THREE independent probes — two different 'gh pr list' shapes and one 'git ls-remote' — all returned a view stale by 3-9 MINUTES, missing a PR created 9 minutes earlier and a branch that existed on the remote. The worker read their agreement as corroboration when it was CORRELATED STALENESS. Root cause not reproduced; do not invent one.

THE DEFENCE FOR BOTH: a NEGATIVE from any listing needs a POSITIVE CONTROL THROUGH THE SAME COMMAND SHAPE — 'does this return something I know exists RIGHT NOW?' Independent probes agreeing is not corroboration when they share a stale cache. This is the census-control discipline applied to listings, and the listing is usually the load-bearing negative.

=== AND: PR-vs-TRUNK OVERLAP IS NOT PR-vs-PR OVERLAP ===
The mayor's tick checks each PR against the trunk. That never sees TWO OPEN PRs editing the same file. Measured: #9108 and #9105 both edited tools/template/spec/005-Repo-Split.md and neither worker nor the tick knew, because no one compared the two PRs to each other. When several PRs are open, cross-check them pairwise with the paginated file lists before choosing a merge order.

(2) I was discarding stderr with >/dev/null 2>&1 on the merge call, which hid the reason. CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION FAILS CLOSED ON A CASE MISMATCH BETWEEN TWO gh COMMANDS (2026-08-13).

gh pr checks --json state returns UPPERCASE: SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS.
gh run list --json status returns lowercase: completed, queued, in_progress.

mayor-merge.md clause 4 said 'runs whose status is all COMPLETED'. A literal test of .status != "COMPLETED" therefore counts every FINISHED run as nonterminal. It reported all six open PRs as blocked (runs@sha=5 nonterminal=5, identically) when all five runs on each were completed/success. Caught only by dumping the raw JSON.

USE (.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED".

TWO THINGS WORTH KEEPING. First, the direction: unlike every other trap in the merge criterion this one fails CLOSED, so it never ships a bad merge and never announces itself either - it presents as a CI queue that will not drain, which is entirely believable and can burn ticks indefinitely. The identical reading across all six PRs was the tell; real CI does not stall six branches in lockstep.

Second, the neighbouring fail-OPEN version of the same clause: --commit takes the FULL 40-char headRefOid. An abbreviated sha matches nothing and returns [], which reads as 'no live runs' and passes clause 4 vacuously. Same clause, one argument away, opposite direction.

`gh run view --log-failed` RETURNS ~81 BYTES WHILE A RUN IS STILL IN PROGRESS — that is "not finished yet", NOT "this machine cannot fetch logs". Measured 2026-09-04, and I misdiagnosed it in a dispatch brief.

WHAT HAPPENED. PR #9188 had one failing check. `gh run view <id> --log-failed` returned nothing; `gh run view --job <id> --log` returned 81 bytes. I concluded the log fetch was broken on this box, wrote that into the fix worker's brief as a machine quirk, and told it to obtain the text some other way. The worker ran `gh api repos/day8/re-frame2/actions/jobs/<job-id>/logs` and got the full log immediately. The run had simply still been in progress when I asked; GitHub does not serve a complete job log until the job finishes.

WHY THE MISREADING WAS TEMPTING. This box genuinely does have several instrument faults that return empty (grep -iF aborting, jq CRLF, sed range collapse), so "the tool is broken here" was a live hypothesis with precedent. But it was the WRONG hypothesis, and the cost was that the brief told a worker something false about its own environment.

THE RULE: BEFORE CALLING A FETCH BROKEN, CHECK WHETHER THE THING BEING FETCHED EXISTS YET. For a CI log that means reading the run's own status first — `gh run view <id> --json status,conclusion`. An in-progress run has no complete log to serve.

AND THE WORKING FORM IS WORTH KEEPING: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/jobs/<job-id>/logs` returns a finished job's full log directly, including per-step boundaries, which is what made the real cause visible — the failure was in step 7 (a generated-artefact drift check), not step 6 (the test suite), and only the step breakdown showed that.

THE TWO gh COMMANDS IN THE MERGE CRITERION USE OPPOSITE CASE VOCABULARIES, AND A FILTER WRITTEN FOR ONE SILENTLY MISCLASSIFIES THE OTHER (2026-08-10).

  gh pr checks <pr> --json state    -> UPPERCASE:  SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS
  gh run list --commit <sha> --json status -> lowercase: completed, in_progress

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION USES THE SECOND ONE. I wrote its check as
`select(.status != "COMPLETED") | length` — copying the case from clause 2's vocabulary —
so it matched NOTHING and counted EVERY run as nonterminal. On PR #7774 it reported
"clause4 not-COMPLETED: 5" for a PR whose five runs were all `completed/success`.

THIS ONE FAILED CLOSED, WHICH IS WHY IT COST ONLY A MINUTE. An over-blocking clause 4
refuses a green PR; the method already names that failure ("a guard that blocks forever is
not safe, it is differently wrong") but it is far cheaper than the fail-open direction.
Had I written the inverse test — count runs EQUAL to "COMPLETED" and require the count to
match the total — the same typo would have passed a branch with live runs on it.

WHAT SAVED THE EARLIER MERGES. I printed the run list and read the statuses BY EYE for
every merge before this one, and lowercase `completed` reads correctly to a human. The
defect only bit when I switched from printing to counting. So: a filter you cannot eyeball

TO ASK 'DOES THIS BRANCH CARRY ANYTHING MAIN DOES NOT HAVE?', USE git cherry — NOT git rev-list --count (2026-08-13, third rev-list miss in one session).

I escalated to Mike that two guide-rewrite branches were COMPETING WHOLESALE REWRITES that conflicted and needed him to pick one. They were not competing. They had landed as a deliberate SEQUENCE, and every branch tip was PATCH-EQUIVALENT to main.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..BRANCH   read 1     <- misleading
  git cherry main BRANCH                     prints '-' <- already landed

A rebase-merge leaves the ORIGINAL commit object unreachable from main while its PATCH is fully present. rev-list counts OBJECTS; the question is about CONTENT. git cherry marks '-' for patch-equivalent and '+' for genuinely unlanded.

THE PATTERN IS BIGGER THAN THIS ONE COMMAND. A rev-list count misled three separate times in one session:
  1. liveness  - the ahead count is INVARIANT UNDER REBASE, so a working worker read as stalled (rf2-0vvw)
  2. the check band - a mid-run rollup total is a FLOOR, not a count; 92 became 93 when it settled
  3. unlanded work - object reachability is not patch equivalence (this one)

Each time the number was real and the QUESTION IT ANSWERED was not the question I was asking. Before quoting a count, say out loud what set it counts and whether that is the set you care about.

COST HERE: a false P2 escalation to the operator, a bead held at 'needs Mike' for several ticks, and three further beads fenced behind it that were never actually blocked.

GIT CHERRY'S '+' IS NOT PROOF THAT WORK IS ABSENT FROM THE TRUNK. Its '-' IS reliable; its '+' is not.

MEASURED 2026-09-04, and I got this wrong in a stranded sweep. `git cherry origin/main worker/retro-b` reported one commit '+', so I concluded six files of skill-layout work had never reached the trunk, pushed the branch to make it 'durable', and REOPENED a closed bead on it. All of that was wrong: the deliverable was already on origin/main at commit 0093c1858c — same author date, same message, same stat. The worker sent to re-land it found the truth in one directory read.

WHY CHERRY SAID '+'. It compares PATCH-IDS, and a patch-id is computed over the hunk INCLUDING ITS CONTEXT LINES. The trunk's copy and the branch's copy differed in the blob index line and TWO CONTEXT LINES — a neighbouring sentence that had since gained a fourth skill in a list. Same change, different patch-id, so '+'.

SO THE ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE POINT, and it is the safe direction that is trustworthy:
  '-' means an identical patch is on the trunk. Reliable. Use it to authorise a branch delete.
  '+' means NO IDENTICAL PATCH was found. It does NOT mean the content is absent — the trunk may carry the same change with one line of drift around it.

THIS DOES NOT RESTORE --is-ancestor OR git branch -d. Under `gh pr merge --rebase` every merged branch is rewritten, so ancestry reports merged work as unmerged and the ahead count agrees with it. Cherry remains the better instrument for containment; it is simply not a proof of ABSENCE.

THE DECISIVE TEST IS THE SOURCE AT TIP, and it is the loop's own rule one level up — CHECK THE TREE, NOT THE RECORD. Before declaring anything stranded, `git show origin/main:<path>` and look for the content. One command. I skipped it because cherry felt authoritative, which is exactly how a well-formed wrong answer gets believed.

AND THE COST OF BEING WRONG HERE IS NOT ZERO: re-landing a stale copy of a region silently REVERTS whatever landed in it since. The cherry-pick the worker attempted conflicted on exactly that sentence — the trunk named four skills, the stranded hunk three — so the 'salvage' would have deleted a sibling's work while passing every gate.

RELATED: a branch whose cherry reads all '-' is still safe to delete, so the hygiene loop's branch rule is unaffected.

MECHANISM. The files are stored and checked out with CRLF terminators, so a `\r` sits between the last literal character and end-of-line. `git grep` matches against that `\r`; `^` is unaffected, and `.*$` is unaffected because `.` matches the `\r`. Only literal-text-then-`$` fails, and it fails SILENTLY as "no matches".

MEASURED, on `.claude/commands/mayor-posture.md`:
  leading `^` only ........................ 1 hit
  `.*$` .................................... 1 hit
  full literal line + `$` .................. 0 hits  <-- FALSE
  same literal line, no `$` ................ 1 hit

The entire surface the method-reread loop audits is affected.

The method-reread loop's duplicate-block check ran `git grep -l "^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$"` and returned EMPTY — for a heading that demonstrably exists at `dispatch-prompt-template.md:478`. Unanchored, it returns exactly 1 file, which is the correct answer. Had a second copy of that block existed, the check would have reported clean.

WHY NO DISPATCH WAS EVER HARMED. The block extraction uses `sed`, not `git grep`, and `sed` on this Git Bash STRIPS the `\r` on read — `sed -n '/^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$/,/^```$/p'` still returns its 51 lines, and the extracted text is clean LF. So the paste path is sound and only the VERIFICATION path was blind. Do not "fix" the extraction.

THE RULE: never end a `git grep` pattern with a `$` straight after literal text on this repo. Drop the `$`, or use `.*$`. And this is the standing "a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed" rule biting the mayor's own audit — run a positive control on any census whose zero you are about to believe.

`git grep` with a pattern that STARTS WITH `/` is MSYS path-mangled on this Windows host and silently returns ZERO for everything — including patterns that certainly match. Found by a worker on 2026-09-04 and reproduced by the mayor on the same tree:

  git grep -c "/client-root" -- 'examples/real-apps/realworld_http/*'   -> no output, exit 0
  git grep -c "client-root"  -- 'examples/real-apps/realworld_http/*'   -> core.cljs:1
  grep -rn "client-root" examples/real-apps/realworld_http/             -> 1 hit

MSYS sees a leading `/` as a Unix path and rewrites it to a Windows path before git ever sees it, so the pattern searched for is not the pattern written.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG: it fails OPEN and it defeats the standard control. A census over qualified names — `/render!`, `/mount!`, `"/client-root"` — is a normal thing to write when looking for a var by its unqualified tail. The zero looks exactly like "this symbol is not used", which is usually the conclusion the census exists to support. And a control that SHARES THE SHAPE of the target (the advice that catches most census bugs) is mangled identically, so the control reads zero too and confirms the wrong answer. Only a SECOND, DIFFERENT instrument catches it — `grep -rn` is not MSYS-mangled the same way.

WHAT TO DO:
- Never start a `git grep` pattern with `/`. Anchor on the namespace side instead (`census.clj` not `/census`), or match the bare tail and filter, or escape as `[/]client-root`.
- Keep the two-instrument rule for every census, and make the second instrument a DIFFERENT TOOL rather than a different pattern in the same tool. This is the case that proves why "two independent instruments" means independent in mechanism, not just in wording.
- The already-recorded sibling trap is the pathspec one: `git grep -- 'implementation/*/src'` matches NOTHING because a git wildcard pathspec matches the whole path — use `implementation/*/src/*`. That is a PATHSPEC bug; this one is a PATTERN bug. They are different and both fail open.

RELATED, from the same worker: every file in `migration/reagent-to-hicasso/codemod/` is pure CRLF and carries non-ASCII, so edits there need byte verification (crlf==lf count, UTF-8 decode) and emitted EDN is worth hex-checking for U+FFFD. `git log --grep=<bead-id>` IS A PREFIX MATCH, AND THE BACKLOG REREAD'S CHECK 5 RUNS ON IT — measured 2026-09-04.

CHECK 5 of the backlog reread asks, for every open bead, "is this already DONE in the tree?" and the prescribed instrument is `git log origin/main --oneline --grep=<id>`. That instrument OVER-REPORTS on any hierarchical id, because the pattern is an unanchored regex and `.` matches any character.

MEASURED: `--grep=rf2-6r9j.24` returned THREE commits, none of which mention rf2-6r9j.24. Two were siblings whose ids merely START with it — rf2-6r9j.244 and rf2-6r9j.249 — and the third carried its id in the commit BODY where `--oneline` does not show it. Anchored as `--grep='rf2-6r9j\.24[^0-9]'` the same query returns ZERO. This repo's ids are dotted and hierarchical (rf2-6r9j.24 / .53 / .161 / .244 / .249), so every short-numbered child of a large epic is exposed.

THE DIRECTION OF THE FAILURE IS THE PROBLEM. Check 5's action on a hit is to consider CLOSING the bead. So a false positive pushes toward closing an open item on the strength of a commit that was about a different bead entirely — and the commit will look plausible, because a sibling of the same epic is usually adjacent work in the same files. It fails toward "looks done".

THE FIX IS THE ANCHOR, and it costs nothing: `--grep='<id>[^0-9]'`, or `--grep='<id>\b'` where the id does not end in a digit. Escape the dots too — `rf2-6r9j.24` as a regex also matches `rf2-6r9jX24`, which is harmless here but free to rule out.

THE RULE THE LOOP ALREADY CARRIES SAVED IT ANYWAY, and this is why that rule is written the way it is: "a hit is a POINTER, confirm in source before closing". On the same sweep, rf2-6r9j.53's single hit was GENUINE — Mike's own commit 866e452d37 naming the bead in its subject — and confirming it meant reading the corrected docstring at tip, not trusting the grep. One instrument found both a false positive and a true one in the same run; only the source read told them apart.

AND NOTE WHAT THE TRUE HIT WAS: an operator ruling that landed as a COMMIT rather than as a note on the bead. No other loop would ever have found it — dispatch reads `bd ready`, merge reads PRs. That is the whole reason check 5 exists, so keep running it; just anchor the pattern.

git rm --cached DOES NOT PROTECT FILES FROM A LATER CHECKOUT — and this will bite rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 at 85 files. Found by the ai/decisions untracking worker (#6424) on 2026-07-19, in its own worktree.

THE HAZARD: `git rm --cached` leaves the file on disk IN THE BRANCH WHERE IT RUNS — but the COMMIT RECORDS A DELETION. Any later rebase, checkout, or `git reset --hard` ACROSS that commit removes the working-tree copies too, silently and with no warning. The worker rebased onto post-#6422 main and its four dossiers vanished from disk; it caught this only on a final on-disk verification and restored them.
⚠️ THE SAME THING HAPPENS IN EVERY OTHER CHECKOUT WHEN THE COMMIT MERGES. The mayor loop `git reset --hard origin/main` after a merge will delete the operator working copies. On 2026-07-19 I backed the four dossiers up to the scratchpad BEFORE merging #6424 and restored them after, so they end up UNTRACKED BUT PRESENT — which is what "should not be tracked" means. "Untrack" is not "delete".

⚠️ rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 WILL HIT THIS AT 85 FILES (ai/findings/new-substrate-synthesis + new-substrate-codex). Its brief MUST carry:
  1. Back up the full tracked ai/ set to a location OUTSIDE the repo before the untracking commit.
  2. A POST-REBASE ON-DISK RE-VERIFICATION step — after any rebase or checkout, confirm the files are still present, not just that the index is right.
  3. The same restore step in the mayor merge sequence, or the operator local working material disappears from every checkout that pulls.
  4. State explicitly whether the operator wants them KEPT on disk or genuinely DELETED — do not infer. Mike instruction was "this path should NOT be tracked", which is about the index, not the filesystem.

GENERAL FORM: an index-only operation still produces a tree-changing commit. Whenever you `git rm --cached` anything a human is still using as working material, the deletion propagates to every working tree that later checks out that commit. Back it up first; verify on disk afterwards; and say plainly to the operator that the files will vanish from their checkout unless restored.

GitHub splits a markdown TABLE ROW on every `|`, INCLUDING pipes inside a backticked code span. So writing a gate name, a shell alternation or any `||` inside a code span in a table cell silently adds columns to that row and breaks the table's rendering. Nothing in this repo catches it: no gate validates prose, tables or rendering at all, and the two link gates strip fences before extracting.

Caught 2026-09-04 by a worker's own hand check before it landed — its first draft of a TESTING.md row wrote the gate as a code span containing `||`, which took that row to 5 pipes against the table's 3. Reworded as prose. This is the concrete case for the standing rule that table column counts are verified BY HAND and said so in the PR body: the check is not ceremony, it has caught a real defect.

If a pipe is genuinely needed inside a table cell, escape it as `\|`. Prefer rewording to prose.

RELATED, same worker, same run — the harness's reported exit code disagreed with the captured one on TWO of three sabotage runs: the harness said "exit code 0" while the file the runner wrote read 1. Both were deliberately sabotaged runs, so believing the harness would have read as "the control does not bite" and inverted the conclusion. Quote the number the runner itself wrote to a file; never the harness's report about the same run.

GREPPING A GATE LOG FOR 'FAIL' HITS ITS OWN SELF-TEST CONTROL LINES — count them against a known-good run before believing a failure (2026-08-15 20:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/release-gra70 (rf2-gra70, PR #8314). Its fast-PR spine log contained 35 matches for FAIL while the run exited 0. Those 35 are CONTROL LINES of the form 'PASS ... FAILS' — a self-test asserting that a deliberately-broken input fails. The worker's discriminator was simple and right: THE SAME COUNT APPEARED IN A RUN THAT EXITED 0, so 35 is the baseline rather than a signal.

WHY THIS MATTERS: the standing rule is already 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's'. This is the mirror failure — reading the LOG instead of the exit code, and being misled in the opposite direction. One makes a failure look like a pass; the other makes a pass look like a failure. THE EXIT CODE FROM THE RUNNER'S OWN LINE IS THE VERDICT. A log grep is at best corroboration, and only against a known baseline.
