GREP -F COMBINED WITH -i SILENTLY RETURNS ZERO ON THIS PROJECT'S GREP BUILD (measured 2026-09-03 by the xray-b worker, and its CONTROL is the only reason it was caught).

MEASURED, same needle, same tree, same invocation shape:
  grep -ri  <needle> -> 43 hits
  grep -rFi <needle> ->  0 hits

No error, no warning, exit status of an ordinary no-match. So a census written with -F for literal safety AND -i for case-insensitivity reports ZERO and looks exactly like a clean tree.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG: -F is the flag careful people add. It is the correct instinct — a needle containing regex metacharacters (a dot, a question mark, brackets, and this repo is full of names like machine-has-tag? and :rf.error/...) must be matched literally. So the census that combines -F and -i is the one written BY the person being careful, and it is the one that lies. The reward for care is a false zero.

THE DEFENCE IS A CONTROL THAT BITES, AND NOTHING ELSE. A search returning zero is not a check that passed. Every census in this project must be run alongside a needle KNOWN to be present, drawn from the same pipeline with the same flags; if the control also reads zero, the instrument is broken, not the tree. The xray-b worker had exactly that control at 43 and caught its own broken census on the first read. A worker without one would have reported 'premise does not hold, zero carriers' with complete confidence.

RELATED FAILURES OF THE SAME FAMILY ALREADY RECORDED HERE: bd --json emitting CRLF so grep -F matches nothing (fixed with tr -d '\r'); a whitespace-collapsed pass and a line-oriented pass disagreeing 97 vs 117 with neither a superset; a punctuation-final needle missed by a word-boundary pattern. The generalisation is one sentence: A CENSUS IS AN INSTRUMENT, AND AN INSTRUMENT IS NOT TRUSTED UNTIL IT HAS BEEN SEEN TO MOVE.

BEFORE DISPATCHING ANY BEAD, GREP ITS NOTES FOR A FENCE — `bd ready` IS A DEPENDENCY VIEW AND CAN NEVER BE A HOLD VIEW. Measured 2026-09-04, having made this exact mistake while knowing the rule.

THE TWO QUESTIONS ARE DIFFERENT AND ONLY ONE HAS AN INSTRUMENT. "Is this bead unblocked?" is answered by `bd ready`, which reads dependency EDGES. "Is this bead held?" is answered only by reading the bead's NOTES, where sequencing fences, operator holds and release conditions are written as PROSE. A fenced bead therefore appears on the raw ready list looking perfectly dispatchable, and nothing in the dispatch path contradicts it.

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched rf2-hic-064 after confirming its dependency edges were clear and seeing it on `bd ready`. Its newest note reads, in capitals, "FENCED — DO NOT DISPATCH UNTIL: rf2-hic-063 closes". I never opened the notes.

THE AGGRAVATING DETAIL, and the reason this is a PROCESS defect rather than a lapse: I HONOURED THE SAME KIND OF FENCE ON A DIFFERENT BEAD IN THE SAME TICK. rf2-xtqs carried a prose fence; I waited for its PR to merge, and I wrote in my own dispatch notes that "bd ready CANNOT SHOW THIS — it filters dependency blockers only; a prose hold is invisible to the scheduler". Forty minutes later I dispatched a fenced bead without applying the sentence I had just written. KNOWING A RULE IS NOT THE SAME AS HAVING A STEP THAT EXECUTES IT.

AND THE FENCE'S AUTHOR HAD ANTICIPATED EXACTLY THIS. The note's own rationale reads: this fence exists "because this bead APPEARS ON THE RAW READY LIST WITH NO ACTIVE BLOCKERS and is not dispatchable". A previous mayor saw the failure coming, wrote the warning on the only surface that could carry it, and it still did not fire — because the dispatch path reads a list, not a bead.

THE FIX IS ONE COMMAND PER DISPATCH CANDIDATE, not a resolution to be careful: grep the bead's notes for FENCED / DO NOT DISPATCH / SEQUENCED / HOLD / release condition, and read what it says. Do it for every candidate, including the ones that look obviously clear — the fenced one looks identical to the rest, which is the whole problem.

WHAT SAVED IT was the preamble clause "THIS BRIEF'S PREMISES ARE CLAIMS, NOT FINDINGS — check each at source". The worker applied it to my assertion that its dependencies were clear, found the fence, reasoned about whether it should hold, ran anyway on the bead's own Green definition, and reported the tension instead of hiding it. That clause has caught a mayor error in three separate dispatches in one session; it is the highest-yield sentence in the dispatch template.

POSTSCRIPT ON THE RULING: the fence should not in fact have held — its stated concern (unclosed PROSE dependencies) was discharged, and its release condition sat behind a deferred operator decision, so read literally it fenced the audit indefinitely. Getting the right answer by not looking is still not looking.

grep -iF ABORTS and grep -oiF SILENTLY RETURNS ZERO on this Windows/Git-Bash build — measured 2026-09-02 by the setupskill-a worker, whose first flattened census returned zero FOR EVERYTHING INCLUDING ITS OWN CONTROL.

WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY TOOL BUG: the method's standing defence against a false zero is 'run the search once against something it should find'. That defence assumes the control and the target go through a WORKING instrument. Here the instrument was broken, so the control returned zero too — and a reader who checks only 'did my census return zero?' sees a confirmed premise. The worker caught it because it noticed the CONTROL had also failed, which is the only signal available. A zero control is not a weak result; it is evidence the instrument is broken, and it must never be read as 'the control does not apply here'.

THE REMEDY THAT WORKED: re-run the census in Python, once line-oriented and once flattened. Do not reach for another grep flag combination.

BOUNDS: measured on this repo's Git-Bash on Windows 11. The -F (fixed-string) flag is implicated in both failures; plain grep and rg were not observed failing this way. Re-measure before asserting the scope is wider.

THIS IS THE SECOND INSTRUMENT IN ONE DAY that answered 'nothing here' while broken — the other was the surface classifier, which reports every surface unaffected when handed revisions where it wants PATHS (hit by three separate workers). Same class, different tool: any instrument that can answer 'nothing here' gives that answer when misused, and raises no error.

I RECORD worktree -> agentId -> BEADS AT DISPATCH AND NEVER READ THE BEAD COLUMN BACK. Twice in one session that produced a duplicate executor (2026-08-21).

CASE 1, rf2-6o5lx. I sent worker ceilinf a status check that ALSO named a defect and asked it to handle it. It did, and opened a PR. Minutes later I dispatched a second worker at the same file under the same bead. My outbox was the dispatch source I failed to read.

CASE 2, rf2-xc0bw, AND THIS ONE IS WORSE BECAUSE THE RECORD WAS ALREADY ON DISK. I dispatched ledgerdrv to build a per-frame driver. That driver had ALREADY LANDED as PR #8605 from worker framedrv, merged hours earlier. ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv carried the line "framedrv <agentId> 2026-08-21 05:45:21 rf2-xc0bw" -- I had written that bead id myself, at dispatch, exactly as the hygiene rule prescribes. I never grepped it. The bead's description was stale against the tree and I briefed from it.

THE FILE HAS A BEAD COLUMN AND I ONLY EVER WRITE TO IT. Its documented purpose is recovering a completion report across a /clear. But the same line answers a second question for free: HAS THIS BEAD ALREADY BEEN DISPATCHED? Nothing else answers that -- bd ready still lists such a bead, its status still reads open because dispatches do not claim beads, and gh pr list shows nothing once the earlier PR has merged.

THE CHECK, AND IT IS ONE COMMAND BEFORE EVERY DISPATCH:
  grep <bead-id> ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv
A hit means a worker has already been sent at this bead. That is not automatically a refusal -- work legitimately continues across PRs -- but it means READ THAT PR AND THE TREE BEFORE BRIEFING, because the bead description is now presumed stale.

WHY THE EXISTING RULES DID NOT CATCH IT. The file-ownership fence derives from open PRs, worktrees and working trees. All four sources are blind to a MERGED PR whose worktree has been reaped -- which is precisely the state a completed predecessor is in. The premises-are-claims rule would have caught it had I applied it to the bead's central premise ("topo has no driver", "the slice has no per-frame driver") rather than to its file paths. I checked paths and not the claim.

BOTH WORKERS HANDLED IT CORRECTLY AND THAT IS NOT THE POINT. ledgerdrv refused to build a second driver, said the tree governed over the brief, and landed the one item genuinely still owed. The waste was a full dispatch cycle, and the near-miss was a second driver landing beside the first.

GUARD REGIONS — a document-wide census cannot see WHERE a claim sits, and that is a false-green generator. rf2-vxcl7 (#6348, 2026-07-18) proved it in situ: deleting ONLY spec/004's Abstract sentence while leaving the body correct kept the document-wide test GREEN; only a region-bound guard (section-text slice of the Abstract) went red. Same defect class rf2-yho9j hit, where two guard rows were satisfied by a second occurrence of the same phrase elsewhere in the file. RULE: when a guard pins a claim that must hold in a SPECIFIC place, bind the region, not the document. Also: vxcl7 found the existing rows were blind because they keyed on the noun 'AST' while the retired formulation said 'template representation', and its quantifier sat outside the emitter alternation — so when adding a census row, check the row matches the WORDING you are retiring, not just the concept. CRLF TRAP (same PR, near-miss): a region extractor using "\n## Heading\n" returns nil on this Windows CRLF checkout. It surfaced only because subs-on-nil THROWS; an extractor returning an empty region instead would have made every row VACUOUSLY GREEN on the LF CI runner and nowhere else. Normalize line endings inside any section-slicing helper.

THE HARNESS'S OWN COMPLETION NOTICE CAN REPORT "exit code 0" FOR A COMMAND THAT FAILED (2026-08-10).

WHAT HAPPENED. The rf2-2rtt6.143 worker ran sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh as part of a compound command ending in a grep. The spine FAILED - its own $? was 1, on "CLJS node integration: Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js". The harness's completion notice for that run reported EXIT CODE 0, because the status it surfaced was the trailing grep's, not the script's. The worker caught it only because it read $? directly, as briefed.

THIS IS THE PIPELINE-EXIT-CODE TRAP ONE LEVEL UP. Every brief in this repo says "never pipe a gate through tail/head/grep - a pipeline's exit status is its last command's, so a red run reads green". That rule is usually explained as a risk to the WORKER. It is also a risk to the MAYOR: the tool result I read can carry the same lie. A green-looking completion notice is not evidence a gate passed.

THE ONLY TRUSTWORTHY FORM: run the gate alone, redirect to a worktree-local log, and echo $? into its own file on the very next command.
    sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > gate-spine.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > gate-spine.exit
Then read gate-spine.exit. Never append a filter to the same command line as the gate, not even to shorten output for a report.

A SECOND TRAP IN THE SAME INCIDENT, worth as much as the first. The worker's EARLIER spine run had genuinely passed - because cljs_node_test was FALSE and that whole tier was SKIPPED. Touching the classifier is what armed the tier, which is what exposed the missing implementation/node_modules in a fresh worktree. So a green spine in a worker worktree can mean "the tier that would have failed did not run". When a diff changes what CI selects, every prior gate result on that branch is stale - re-run after the classifier change, not before.

THE HARNESS EXIT-CODE DISCREPANCY HAS A MECHANISM, AND IT IS NOT A BUG (2026-08-14, rf2-5gka worker).

ALL DAY workers reported the harness saying exit 0 while their captured value said 1 — five consecutive runs for one worker, all three red runs for another, a spine run for a third. I recorded it as a harness defect and briefed workers to distrust the harness number. The mechanism is simpler and it is our own doing:

  THE TRAILING `echo "EXIT=$?"` OWNS THE SHELL'S STATUS.

Every brief in this repository tells workers to redirect a gate to a log and echo the runner's exit code on ONE command line. That trailing echo succeeds, so the SHELL exits 0 — and the harness reports the shell's status, correctly. The gate's own status was captured into the log by `$?` a microsecond earlier.

So the harness is not lying. It is reporting the last command in the pipeline, which is the echo we asked for. Both numbers are true about different things.

THE RULE IS UNCHANGED BUT ITS REASON IS NOW CORRECT: for any redirected gate, the harness number is MEANINGLESS — not wrong, just answering a different question. Quote the captured one. And do not go looking for a harness bug: there isn't one to find, and workers have spent time wondering.

WORTH SAYING IN BRIEFS AS THE REASON RATHER THAN THE RULE, because a worker who understands why will apply it correctly to shapes we have not anticipated — a pipeline ending in `tee`, a compound command ending in a cleanup, anything where the last command is not the gate.

THE HARNESS HARD-KILLS A FOREGROUND COMMAND AT 10 MINUTES — so 'run the gate in the foreground to completion' is UNSATISFIABLE for the fast-PR spine (2026-08-11, measured by the catalogrows-vkle worker).

ITS WORDS: 'a foreground run is not achievable here — the harness hard-kills foreground commands at 10 minutes, and my first foreground attempt died exactly there (exit 143, mid-JVM tier).' Exit 143 is SIGTERM. I hit the same class myself at the mayor's own 2-minute tool ceiling when chaining bd export behind other measurements under six concurrent workers.

CONSEQUENCE FOR BRIEFS, and this supersedes the bare 'foreground only' line: the spine must be DETACHED to finish. That is not a violation and must not be briefed as one. What matters is not foreground-ness — it is (a) unpiped output, (b) the exit code captured on the SAME command line into a file, (c) the gate root line checked against the worker's own worktree, and (d) THE WORKER STAYING IN ITS TURN, polling the log and .exit file until it exits, rather than ending the turn to wait for a notification that may never arrive.

The catalogrows worker did exactly this and said so plainly: 'The run is detached only so it can finish; the output is unpiped and the exit code is captured the way you specified, and I am waiting on it rather than reporting around it.' That is the correct shape.

SEE ALSO brief-must-carry-the-poll-fallback-for-long-gates — same defect, this is the measured number behind it.

THE HARNESS'S REPORTED EXIT CODE DISAGREES WITH THE RUNNER'S OWN, AND IT ERRS TOWARD GREEN — measured directly 2026-09-05, TWICE IN ONE WORKER, both times the harness reporting 0 where the worker's own `.exit` file read 1.

This is no longer inference. Every worker brief in this project carries the instruction "quote the number you captured, never one the harness reports about the same run", and until now that rested on scattered observations that every disagreement surfaced as exit 0. One worker on rf2-xpd8 hit it twice in a single session and said so plainly: "The harness disagreed with my captured exit code twice, both times reporting 0 where my .exit file read 1. I quoted mine."

WHY THE DIRECTION MATTERS. A disagreement that errs toward RED is self-correcting — the worker investigates and finds nothing wrong. A disagreement that errs toward GREEN is silent: a failing gate reads as passing, the worker reports success, and the merge decision fails open. Both observed instances were the green direction.

THE PROCEDURE, unchanged but now evidenced:
  * Redirect the gate to a log and echo the runner's own `$?` to a `.exit` file, ON ONE COMMAND LINE IN ONE SHELL — never piped, because a pipeline's status is its LAST command's.
  * Quote the number from that file. An ABSENT exit file is NO VERDICT, not a pass.
  * Name the artefacts for the worktree AND the attempt, and confirm the file you read is your own current attempt's — a peer's run can overwrite a generic name, and a killed shell's orphan keeps writing to the file a restarted run is using.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE BOX'S OTHER SILENT-SUCCESS FAULTS, and the family is now large enough to state as a rule: ON THIS MACHINE, A REPORTED SUCCESS IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT SOMETHING HAPPENED. `cmd /c` junction create/remove exits 0 having done nothing; `pkill` anchored on a bare verb exits 0 having killed nothing; `grep -c $'\0'` returns a plausible count from an empty pattern; `grep -iF` aborts with empty stdout that reads as a clean zero; `gh run view --log-failed` returns 81 bytes while a run is in progress. CHECK THE WORLD, NOT THE STATUS.

AND A SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, the mirror image — A TEST CAN PASS WITH ZERO ASSERTIONS. Its first witness reported "2 tests, 0 assertions, exit 0" because `re-frame.schemas` is optional and late-bound, so the ns never loaded and the deftest bodies never ran. It caught this itself and fixed it by putting the require in the ns form. READ THE ASSERTION COUNT, NOT ONLY THE EXIT CODE: a green with an implausibly low assertion count is a vacuous run, and this repo's suites report both numbers.

A COMMITTED FILE WHOSE CONTENT HASH IS CITED MUST BE PINNED `text eol=lf` IN .gitattributes, OR THE RETENTION VERIFIES WRONG ON WINDOWS. Found by the rf2-rguy1 worker, 2026-08-08, and the audit that commissioned the work did not name it.

THE MECHANISM. This box runs core.autocrlf=true. An unpinned .json is CRLF-rewritten ON CHECKOUT, so the bytes in a Windows working tree are not the bytes that were committed. A reader who recomputes the digest to check the page's claim gets a DIFFERENT hash and concludes the evidence is corrupt — or, worse, a later pass "corrects" the published digest to the CRLF one and the Linux/CI reader then disagrees instead. Either way the retention looks done and verifies wrong.

WHY IT IS THE NASTY CLASS. The whole point of retaining evidence and citing its hash is that a fresh clone can verify a claim WITHOUT trusting the page. A silently platform-dependent digest defeats exactly that property while leaving every visible sign of success: file present, size right, page cites a hash, gates green. It is the same shape as a gate that exits 0 having verified nothing.

THE FIX, and it must be tested rather than assumed:
  1. Pin the path in .gitattributes: `path/to/*.json text eol=lf`
  2. Round-trip it: delete the file, `git checkout -- <path>`, re-hash, confirm the digest is unchanged and the file carries zero CR bytes.
Copying with `cp` and comparing with `cmp` is NOT sufficient — that tests the copy, not the checkout. Re-verify out of the git index: `git cat-file blob <rev>:<path> | sha256sum`.

WHERE IT APPLIES BEYOND THIS CASE: any committed artefact whose bytes are load-bearing — retained benchmark datasets, golden files, fixtures a test hashes, provenance sidecars. If a doc anywhere cites its sha256, it needs the pin.

RELATED, from the same worker: bind evidence to its inputs at BOTH ends. Forward, the producer should hash what it actually feeds the browser (the dist bundle the server hands out) before launching Chromium, and refuse a stale or absent dist rather than measuring it. Backward, a retained run gets a provenance sidecar whose digests are RE-HASHED FROM THE SURVIVING ARTEFACTS, never copied from the prose they are meant to corroborate.

I HAVE NOW TWICE READ A TRUNCATED OUTPUT AND REPORTED THE TRUNCATION AS THE ANSWER (2026-08-18/19). Same defect, two different tools, and the second time was WHILE CORRECTING SOMEONE ELSE FOR THE SAME KIND OF ERROR.

INSTANCE 1 — the tracker. Reading beads with "bd show <id> | head -N" gave me the DESCRIPTION, which is the oldest text, and I briefed two workers from it. Both beads newest comments said the work had already landed. Recorded as never-read-a-bead-with-head.

INSTANCE 2 — a census. Slice 2 of a retirement sweep reported two donor hits in implementation/shadow-cljs.edn. I re-derived and announced a CORRECTION to five, writing it onto the bead as a mayor count-correction so the worker would not brief from the smaller number. My command was:
    grep -nF "freehand" implementation/shadow-cljs.edn | head -5
The real count is ELEVEN. Lines 923-934 are an entire second block. I did not miss them through a bad pattern - the pattern was right and I truncated its output to five lines, then published "FIVE" as a measurement. The worker found eleven with the same command minus the head.

THE SHAPE, AND IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY MISCOUNT. head -N returns exactly N lines whenever there are at least N matches, so the output LOOKS complete at precisely the moment it is not. A truncated census is indistinguishable from a full one by inspection, and the number N is one you chose rather than one the tree gave you. It fails silently and it fails toward under-counting, which is the direction that sends a worker to fix part of a problem and report it closed.

THE RULE: NEVER PIPE A COUNT OR A CENSUS THROUGH head. If the output is long, that is information - use grep -c for the number, or read all of it. head is for glancing at a file, never for measuring anything you will assert. Where the number underwrites a brief or a bead comment, take it with -c and quote the command.

THE SECOND-ORDER LESSON, which is the one I keep having to learn: a MAYOR CORRECTING A WORKER IS STILL MAKING A CLAIM. Announcing "the count is five, not two" reads as authority and gets believed - the worker had to spend effort disproving my correction as well as the original. A correction deserves MORE verification than the thing it corrects, not less, precisely because it arrives with the weight of a second opinion.

Incident 2026-06-10 (commit 7aea52459): a mayor-loop heartbeat 'git add .beads/issues.jsonl; commit' caught the file MID dolt-re-export (transiently EMPTY/truncated) and committed+pushed a 0-line issues.jsonl to main (numstat tell: 'N deletions(-), 0 insertions' where N=full file size + working-tree still shows full content = staged blob is empty). Dolt DB was intact (bd reads fine); only the git-tracked jsonl export was truncated. RECOVERY: bd re-exports the full jsonl into the working tree; re-add + commit it. GUARD (now mandatory in the heartbeat): before committing .beads, (1) wc -l .beads/issues.jsonl must be > a sane floor (e.g. >1000), AND (2) after 'git add', verify the STAGED blob non-empty via 'git show :.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l' BEFORE 'git commit' — abort the commit if either is empty. Authoritative integrity check = git cat-file -p <commit>:.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -lc (NOT 'git show origin/main:path' which can mis-resolve transiently).

A BASH HEREDOC ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP STRIPS BACKSLASHES, SO A REGEX INSIDE `python - <<'PY'` SILENTLY BECOMES A DIFFERENT REGEX AND RETURNS A FALSE ANSWER (2026-08-10).

REPORTED BY THE rf2-re0m WORKER after it nearly published a wrong number. It ran a
throwaway `python - <<'PY' ... PY` script to count Markdown links inside fenced regions.
The heredoc ate the backslashes in its patterns, so the pattern that should have matched
`](` matched nothing, and the script reported ZERO fenced links — on a tree that had seven.
It caught the discrepancy, re-ran everything from WRITTEN SCRIPT FILES, and got the true
counts.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE BACKSLASH BUG ALREADY ON RECORD. The known form is
`git worktree add` and `cmd /c mklink` losing path separators — those FAIL, loudly and
immediately, and you go fix the quoting. This form SUCCEEDS. Python compiles the mangled
pattern happily, the script exits 0, and you get a plausible number that is wrong in the
safe-looking direction: zero findings, nothing to do, ship it. A verification tool that
misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch.

THE RULE: never put a regex, or any backslash-bearing text, through a heredoc in the Bash
tool on this setup. Write the script to a file and run the file. If a throwaway script
reports a suspiciously clean result — zero findings where you expected some — re-run it from
a file BEFORE believing it.

AND THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is the reason to remember it: an ad-hoc verification script is
itself unverified. When its answer is the evidence for a claim, the script needs the same
red-first discipline as a test — prove it can report a non-zero count on known-bad input
before trusting its zero.

hicasso browser lane: an UNSETTLED promise rejection in a cljs.test async row is TERMINAL, not slow. Measured 2026-08-22 (rf2-x43z sabotage control). 2. Then ensure it is GOOD QUALITY CODE.
3. Then ensure the DOCS are complete, correct, and quality.
4. Then ensure the associated SKILLS are complete, correct, and quality.
5. Then ensure the XRAY INTEGRATION is complete, correct, and quality.
6. Then ensure the COMMENTS are complete, correct, and quality.
7. Then ensure the TESTS are complete, correct, and quality.

This is a dispatch-ordering ruling, not a licence to gold-plate: the posture (pre-alpha, elegance/power/masterpiece, NOT over-engineering, trust the programmer, don't drown in minutiae) still governs what counts as done in each phase. SHARED-BUILD-ID CACHE TRAPS SELF-HEAL — every trial must start COLD (rf2-2rtt6.20).

The hicasso P0 lane runs N different programs under ONE shadow-cljs build id
(:hicasso-bench via --config-merge), so they share one build cache entry. Shadow
derives the cache dir from the build id alone, fixed in `new-build` BEFORE
--config-merge is applied, so --config-merge can NEVER reach :cache-root.

CARRIER is `shadow-js/` (npm-conversion cache), NOT the Closure name-stability
maps. `convert-sources-simple` invalidates its index on SHADOW-CACHE-KEY /
cache-affecting-options and never on the set of npm modules the build needs.
Reagent arms cache 14 modules with no react/jsx-runtime; a UIx arm built over
that index compiles clean and dies at first execution with "Cannot read
properties of undefined (reading 'd')".

TWO METHODOLOGY TRAPS worth remembering:
1. THE TRAP SELF-HEALS. Once the shadow-js index has accumulated every arm's
   modules, replaying the poisoning builds cannot take them back out. A control
   run from a WARM cache came back ALIVE and was meaningless. Every trial must
   rm -rf .shadow-cljs/builds/<id> first. A positive result without a DEAD
   control proves nothing.
2. DON'T BLOCK A/B COMPARISONS. Running all of main's reps then all of the
   branch's confounds the variable with box load drift — the same
   block-vs-interleave fault order_guard exists to catch. REFLECT the order.
   Blocked it looked like the branch caused an M2 guard refusal (main 0,0,0 /
   branch 2,0,0); reflected, MAIN refused and BRANCH passed in the same round.

When the harness clears the cache before every rep, a "clear the cache" fix is a
literal NO-OP in that comparison: both sides emit a byte-identical bundle
(sha256-verified), so any difference is variance BY CONSTRUCTION. That logical
argument beats statistics.

COST: clearing the whole per-build cache entry is ~free — warm 34s/26s vs
cleared 33s/37s. Time is JVM start + classpath + the Closure :advanced pass, not
the CLJS compile the cache holds. "It costs a full recompile" does not survive
measurement. Bonus: always-cleared builds are byte-DETERMINISTIC.

The generalisation is not "check your diagnostics"; it is that ANY CODE HANDLING A HOSTILE VALUE MUST TREAT ITS OWN REPORTING PATH AS HANDLING THAT VALUE TOO.

I CALLED THREE ORDINARY STALE WORKTREES "HUSKS" ALL SESSION, AND HUSK IS A TERM WITH AN OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE (2026-08-24).

THE METHOD DEFINES A HUSK PRECISELY: a partial removal, where the tool deregistered the worktree and deleted its metadata, then hit a lock and stopped. Its signature is four things -- it no longer appears in the worktree listing, pruning has nothing to clear, a status check inside it FAILS AND PRINTS NOTHING, and because of that a clean/dirty test reads it as CLEAN.

MY THREE FAIL ALL FOUR, and on the decisive axis they are the exact inverse: they are LISTED, their metadata directory is PRESENT, status works fine, and it reports them DIRTY (one staged file each). They are ordinary registered stale worktrees.

WHY THE WORD MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING LOOSE VOCABULARY: "husk" ROUTES TO A DIFFERENT REMEDY. The method says the ordinary removal path refuses a husk forever and that you must reach for the tool's acknowledged-husk path, which disarms links before deleting. Someone reading my sweep reports -- me, after a context roll -- would reach for that special path for trees where the ordinary path is the correct one, and would skip the ordinary path on the belief it cannot work.

THE OUTCOME HAPPENS NOT TO CHANGE, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG. They stay either way. But the REASON differs, and the reason is what a later decision keys on: they stay because they are DIRTY and carry no completion report, not because they are unremovable-by-construction. Dirty is a state waiting never clears; husk is a state retrying never clears. Different remedies, different escalations.

NO DOCUMENT DEFECT. The definition is precise, testable in one command per criterion, and I never tested it -- I inherited the word from an earlier report and repeated it perhaps twenty times. THE CHECK IS CHEAP: does the worktree listing show it, and does a status check inside it return output? Two commands separate the two states completely.

GENERAL SHAPE: a term of art in the method carries its remedy with it. Using one loosely does not stay loose -- it silently prescribes.

CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT FILED (2026-08-11): the theoretical clock-hold leak in hm/hydrate!. Recorded so a future auditor does not rediscover it, file it, and re-litigate a decision already taken.

THE OBSERVATION, from the rf2-4mvd / rf2-w2e6 worker (PR #7883), which reported it explicitly as "not a bead": hm/hydrate! installs the page-wide virtual clock (around mounted.cljs:798) immediately before handle-for, inside a setTimeout callback with nothing between them. IF handle-for ever threw there, the clock hold would leak — and because it sits in a timer callback, the throw would not reach the promise, so nothing would surface it.

THAT IS STRUCTURALLY THE SAME SHAPE AS rf2-4mvd, which was real and is now fixed: mount! installed the clock before mint-frame! and a throw escaped before any handle existed, leaving the page-wide clock installed for the rest of the run.

WHY IT IS STILL NOT WORK:
- Both beads scope their repair to mount! in terms. Widening a bounded repair on a hunch is the exact anti-pattern this project keeps paying for.
- handle-for is map-building. It does not realistically throw, whereas mint-frame!'s :initial-events path raises :rf.error/initial-events-step-failed BY DESIGN — a deliberate, reachable throw. That asymmetry is the whole difference between the two sites: one had a documented escape, this one has a hypothetical.
- The stance rejects speculative hardening. Filing it would be gold-plating, and the worker said so itself rather than quietly widening its diff, which was the right call twice over.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER — and this is the useful part of the record. File it if any of these becomes true:
- handle-for gains a genuine failure mode (validation, a lookup that can miss, anything that raises).
- Anything else is inserted between install-clock! and handle-for in that callback, widening the window.
- A hydrate! path is observed leaving a clock installed in practice. A reproduced symptom outranks this reasoning immediately; do not argue a live symptom away with this note.

DO NOT treat this entry as authority that the site is CORRECT. It is authority that the site was LOOKED AT, by someone who had just fixed the sibling defect, and judged not worth work under the current stance. Those are different claims, and the second is the only one anybody verified.

I CREATED A DUPLICATE EXECUTOR BY INFERRING A WORKER'S DEATH FROM SHAPE (2026-07-25). A dispatched worker showed zero commits, no remote branch, and HEAD identical to origin/main after ~30 minutes, during a period when the operator had reported an internet outage. I concluded it had been killed at launch and re-dispatched a fresh agent onto ITS EXISTING worktree and branch. It was alive and mid-flight with ~203 insertions / 76 deletions plus a 147-line untracked namespace — all uncommitted.

THE METHOD ALREADY WARNS ABOUT EXACTLY THIS: 'zero commits, clean tree, no PR describes both an abandoned worker and one that started a minute ago; the discriminator is FRESHNESS, not shape.' I used shape.

WHAT SAVED IT: the second agent detected the collision from advancing file mtimes, deleted ONLY its own untracked near-duplicate file after verifying nothing referenced it, touched none of the peer's files, did not commit/push/PR, and reported. That is the behaviour to reward. The correct recovery was to SendMessage-resume the live peer and tell it to commit and push immediately — never a third executor.

MECHANICAL RULE, since 'check freshness' as a policy is what I failed to apply: BEFORE re-dispatching onto an existing worktree, require ALL THREE — (a) a recorded terminal notification for that agent (completed/failed/killed), (b) file mtimes under the worktree older than several minutes (check the newest source file, not just git state), and (c) git state showing no uncommitted work. Absent (a), assume ALIVE regardless of (b) and (c) and message it instead. An idle-looking worker costs a slot; a duplicate executor on one branch risks corrupting real work and wastes two agents.

COROLLARY: a worker that has been running a long time with zero commits is a PUSH-DISCIPLINE problem, not a liveness signal. The right intervention is 'commit and push now', not re-dispatch.

I DELETED THE MAYOR'S node_modules WITH THE DOCUMENTED RECIPE, BECAUSE `cmd /c rmdir` DID NOT EXECUTE FROM THE BASH TOOL. 2026-07-28, removing worktree composing-18216 (PR #7201) after its worker warned me it had junctioned `implementation/node_modules` into the mayor checkout.
WHAT HAPPENED, EXACTLY. I ran `cmd /c rmdir "<path>"` via the Bash tool. It printed the Windows banner and a fresh prompt — i.e. it launched an INTERACTIVE cmd shell and never ran the rmdir. The canary right after still read 101, which I misread as 'junction cleared' when it actually meant 'nothing happened yet'. `git worktree remove --force` then followed the live junction and emptied the real directory: canary 101 -> 0. Recovered with `npm ci` at `implementation/` (exit 0, ~4 min).
THE TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) `cmd /c rmdir` IS NOT RELIABLE FROM THE BASH TOOL ON THIS SETUP — use PowerShell instead: `[IO.Directory]::Delete(path, $false)` removes a junction without following it, and REFUSES a real populated directory, so it is self-verifying in both directions. (2) THE CANARY MUST BE READ AS A DELTA WITH A KNOWN EXPECTED VALUE, NOT AS A NUMBER THAT LOOKS FINE. After clearing a junction the correct assertion is `Test-Path <junction>` == False, not 'the mayor still has 101 entries' — the mayor ALWAYS has 101 entries until the moment it doesn't.
WHY THE SAFEGUARDS DID NOT FIRE. My hygiene sweep detects junctions correctly and has done so all session. This removal skipped it because the worker had already TOLD me there was a junction, so I went straight to the fix — and the fix was the untested half of the recipe. Knowing about the hazard is what let me skip the check that would have caught the failed remediation.

I DESTROYED A LIVE WORKER WORKTREE (2026-07-19) — deterministic branch names collide with HISTORICAL merged PRs.

WHAT HAPPENED: my deferred-cleanup loop removes a worktree when `gh pr list --head worker/<name> --state all` reports MERGED. I derive branch names deterministically from the bead id, so I dispatched rf2-vxgfnd.195 onto `worker/shadow-host-gates-195` — the SAME name a previous session had used for the same bead, whose PR #6030 merged on 2026-07-16. The cleanup matched that historical PR, and removed the live worktree plus the branch (local AND origin) while the worker was mid-run. Work lost, worker orphaned.

WHY THE OBVIOUS GUARDS DID NOT CATCH IT: the worktree was clean (worker had not committed yet) so the dirty-check passed; the PR state was genuinely MERGED so the state-check passed; `--state all` is what made a long-closed PR visible. Every individual condition was satisfied. This is the SECOND time I have removed a running worker worktree (the first was k8l1m), and the deferred-cleanup pattern I adopted after that incident did not prevent this one, because it addressed timing rather than identity.

TWO FIXES, USE BOTH:
1. MAINTAIN AN EXPLICIT LIVE-WORKER SKIP LIST. I dispatch the workers, so I know their worktree names — skip every one still running, unconditionally, before any state check. This is the reliable guard; the PR-state heuristic is the unreliable one.
2. REQUIRE THE MERGED PR TO BE *THIS* WORKTREE WORK, not merely same-named: compare `git -C <worktree> rev-parse HEAD` against the PR `headRefOid` (`gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid`), or require `mergedAt` to be LATER than the worktree creation. A name match alone proves nothing — bead ids are stable across sessions, so a re-dispatch of any partially-delivered bead reproduces the collision exactly.

GENERAL LESSON: a deterministic naming scheme makes names non-unique ACROSS TIME. Any cleanup keyed on a name will eventually match a historical artefact. Key destructive operations on identity (a SHA, a creation time), never on a name.

I OVERRODE A RECORDED DEFERRAL WITHOUT ACKNOWLEDGING IT — SECOND TIME TODAY — AND THE WORK TURNED OUT JUSTIFIED FOR A REASON NEITHER I NOR THE DEFERRAL KNEW (2026-07-26).

rf2-jl7gz carried a note from the #7051 audit: "STAYS DEFERRED — measured zero corpus exposure". I dispatched it anyway, in a brief that never mentioned the deferral. The worker built it and FLAGGED the override rather than silently complying — same shape as rf2-n4by4 earlier the same day, where the bead said "ENFORCEMENT NEEDS A RULING, do not pick one silently" and my brief silently picked one. Two instances in one session of the same defect: I read beads for FACTS and miss their RECORDED DISPOSITIONS. A deferral, a reserved ruling and a held decision are all instructions addressed TO ME, and a brief that overrides one without saying so leaves the tracker unable to distinguish a considered reversal from an oversight.

BUT THE DISPATCH WAS RIGHT, AND THE REASON IS THE GENERALISABLE PART: THE DEFERRAL WAS MEASURED ON ONE DIRECTION OF A BIDIRECTIONAL GATE. "Zero corpus exposure" meant no FALSE GREEN was reachable today — no bad row passing. The worker found the same miscount was ALSO COSTING EVIDENCE: the `~#js [fx]` unquote island and the reader-conditional arm pairing were ALREADY DROPPING REAL EDGES, so the FALSE-RED direction was live and had never been measured. In its words, the miscount "was costing evidence as well as inventing it".

SO THE RULE: A DEFERRAL MEASURED ON ONE DIRECTION OF A TWO-DIRECTION CHECK IS NOT A DEFERRAL. Before honouring "zero exposure" on any gate that can be wrong in both directions — a census, a redaction, a refusal, a roster — ask which direction was measured. Under-matching and over-matching have different corpora and only one of them is usually counted.

THE OTHER THING WORTH KEEPING, because it is the cleanest instance yet of a probe that cannot discriminate: the bead own axis-2 case (`#_#?(:clj (def fx …))`) REDS UNDER THE OLD READER TOO, measured not assumed. Read short it does leave `(:clj (def fx …))` standing exactly as the bead describes — but `_DEFINER_RE` is anchored to a top-level form HEAD and the survivor head is `:clj`, not `def`, so no binding registers and the row reds either way. The wrapper the miscount leaves is INERT. A TAG target discriminates because there the survivor IS the form: `#_#js (def fx …)` leaves the `def` at top level to bind the fixture, giving a silent green. The worker kept the `#?` case but RELABELLED it as a regression guard on the anchoring rather than as evidence. That is the right disposal for a case that cannot fail for the reason it was written.

AND A SELF-CAUGHT REGRESSION WORTH THE SWEEP: `##NaN` is written straight into the adapter suites, and the first draft read the second `#` as a tag over `NaN`, turning `##Inf` into `##Inf 3`. Its own extent table caught it. When extending a reader rule, enumerate the OTHER `#`-prefixed forms — `#(`, `#{`, `#"`, `#=`, `#!`, `##`, and namespaced maps `#:ns{…}` — and say which need the rule and which do not.

I BROKE THE PIPELINE-EXIT-CODE RULE I BRIEF WORKERS ABOUT, IN MY OWN MERGE LOOP (2026-08-11).

WHAT I WROTE, trying to be defensive about the known post-merge pull abort:

  git pull --ff-only origin main 2>&1 | tail -1 || git pull --rebase origin main 2>&1 | tail -2

THE `||` NEVER FIRED. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, and `tail` succeeds whatever it is fed. So the fallback was unreachable, and both merges left the checkout diverged (1/2 then 2/9) with the reassuring line "fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting." printed and ignored. No damage — I noticed on the ref comparison and rebased cleanly — but the guard I wrote was decorative.

WHY IT IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN JUST FIXING: this is the SAME defect class the method documents for gate runners, and I have put it in every worker brief tonight — "never pipe a gate through tail/head/grep, a pipeline's exit status is its last command's". I then wrote exactly that pattern into my own control flow, because I was thinking about the OUTPUT (I only wanted the last line) and not about the EXIT CODE. The trap is that piping for brevity and branching on success look independent and are not.

THE CORRECTED SHAPE, for any command I want to both trim and branch on:

  git pull --ff-only origin main > /tmp/pull.log 2>&1; rc=$?; tail -1 /tmp/pull.log
  [ "$rc" -eq 0 ] || git pull --rebase origin main > /tmp/pull.log 2>&1

Redirect to a file, capture the code, THEN trim for display. Never let a display filter sit between a command and a branch that reads its result.

MAYOR-SPECIFIC: the post-merge pull now aborts routinely, because the audit hook pushes to main asynchronously and my own beads checkpoint commits locally. So the fallback is the COMMON path, not the exception — which makes an unreachable fallback exactly as bad as no fallback. Verify the outcome by comparing HEAD to origin/main rather than trusting either the printed line or a branch that may not have run.

I PRESCRIBED AN UNSOUND FIX AND A WORKER CAUGHT IT BY MEASURING (2026-08-01, rf2-8vvdo / PR #7336). Record the lesson, not the incident.

WHAT HAPPENED. A core test reddened under load because it asserted a PROCESS-WIDE weak-map count for strict equality; the diagnosing worker filed rf2-8vvdo proposing (<= (.size m) baseline) as a STRONGER replacement, and I briefed that fix as-is while telling the implementing worker 'the fix must be stronger, never weaker' and 'prove it still catches the original defect'.

THE IMPLEMENTING WORKER REFUSED IT AND WAS RIGHT. (<= (.size m) baseline) cures the false RED by buying a false GREEN under the same load: a SIBLING entry expunging in our entry's place satisfies it while OUR entry is still leaked. It did not argue this — it MEASURED it, with a probe of (and (<= (.size m) baseline) (.containsKey m our-key)) that PASSED, i.e. the proposed assertion held with the leaked entry still in the map, before the throwable was even released. That is precisely the fail-open class my own brief forbade.

THE CORRECT SHAPE, which the bead itself had offered as an alternative: assert THE ENTRY'S OWN ABSENCE, not a population count. (= (inc baseline) (.size m)) -> (= 1 (count our-keys)); (= baseline (.size m)) -> (not (.containsKey m our-key)). It also found the bead had diagnosed only ONE of the two assertions — the sibling assertion carried the identical defect and would have left the test load-sensitive.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is mine: WHEN A BEAD PROPOSES A SPECIFIC FIX, THE BRIEF MUST TREAT IT AS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT A SPECIFICATION. I passed a diagnosing worker's proposed patch through to an implementing worker with my authority attached, which converts a suggestion into an instruction and invites compliance over judgement. Correct form: state the DEFECT and the ACCEPTANCE CRITERION (here: 'the assertion must fail when this entry leaks, whatever else the process is doing'), cite the bead's proposal as one candidate, and say explicitly that a better shape is welcome and a refusal with evidence is a complete answer.

SECOND-ORDER POINT WORTH KEEPING: an assertion about a SHARED, PROCESS-WIDE quantity can almost never state a claim about ONE participant. Prefer identity over population whenever the property is about a specific object — count-based proxies fail open under concurrency in both directions.

I REPEATED THE gh --jq --arg BUG AFTER RECORDING IT (2026-07-26). gh accepts the jq PROGRAM as the argument to --jq, so writing "gh pr list --json ... --jq --arg B \"$b\" \x27<program>\x27" makes --arg the program and the real program a stray argument. The query returns EMPTY, not an error. I hit this once on a hygiene sweep where every PR read as pr=none, recorded it, and then wrote the identical construction again on the next hygiene sweep.

THE FIX: fetch once to a file with gh --json, then pipe/read that file with the jq BINARY, where --arg is valid: gh pr list --json number,state,headRefName > /tmp/prs.json, then jq -r --arg B "$b" \x27...\x27 /tmp/prs.json.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE TYPO: both times, the broken query fed a DESTRUCTIVE decision — branch deletion gated on "is this PR merged?". Both times the gate FAILED SAFE and refused, because an empty result does not match *MERGED. That is the only reason a broken query did not delete a live branch. Design destructive gates so the empty/unknown case refuses; do not rely on the query being right.

TWELFTH WRONG MEASUREMENT THIS SESSION, and the first outright repeat. The others were varied (loose greps matching comments, row-count as a proxy for content, diffing a worktree against moved main, reading a file before the pull landed, --is-ancestor after a rebase-merge). This one I had already written down. Recording a trap is not the same as building the habit that avoids it — for shell constructions specifically, the habit that works is: never put --arg on a gh command line.

MY RECURRING BRIEF DEFECT IS OVERSTATING A GATE'S OR A FENCE'S SCOPE — TWICE IN ONE SESSION, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS (2026-08-21, found by the method-reread loop grading its own briefs).

INSTANCE 1 — THE HOT ZONE. I wrote 'spec/ is HOT ZONE and single-toucher' into a brief and carried it generally. CLAUDE.md's hot-zone bullet is an ENUMERATION of 8 named spec pages, and git ls-files 'spec/*.md' returns 52. A blanket fence covers 44 pages the tree never asked to serialise. Cost direction: COVERAGE — a worker warned off a file nobody holds declines work it was free to take, and nothing on screen says so. See [hot-zone-names-eight-spec-pages-not-the-spec-tree].

INSTANCE 2 — THE FENCED-LINK RULE. I pasted into EVERY brief this session: 'Both gates strip fenced code blocks before they read a single link... if your edit lands inside a fence, neither gate is your gate.' That is FALSE for docs/design/hicasso/ and docs/the-mayor-method/, which is where nearly every worker this session was editing. scripts/check_doc_slugs.py:1708 sets FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES = ('docs/design/hicasso', 'docs/the-mayor-method'), and its own header says: 'In the trees listed in FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES a markdown doc link inside a fence is itself reported. Everywhere else it is SILENTLY skipped.' CLAUDE.md states the exception correctly; my boilerplate dropped it.

THE SHARED SHAPE, and it is what makes this one lesson rather than two: BOTH ERRORS TOOK A GENERAL RULE AND DROPPED ITS CARVE-OUT. The hot-zone rule has a list; I used a glob. The fence rule has an exception roster; I used the general case. In each the general half is memorable and the carve-out is not, which is the same failure mode the PROJECT STANCE paraphrase has — the lenses survive a summary and the when-to-stop clauses do not.

WHICH DIRECTION EACH RUNS, because they differ and both are quiet. Instance 1 understates what a worker MAY TOUCH. Instance 2 understates what a gate COVERS, so the worker hand-checks (harmless) and then MISREPORTS coverage in its PR body — the same both-directions misreporting the fast-spine-gap clause already warns about. Neither produces an error message.

THE FIX THAT GENERALISES: when a brief states a gate's or a fence's scope, NAME THE CONSTANT OR THE LIST IN THE TREE rather than paraphrasing it — FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES, DEFAULT_ROOTS, CLAUDE.md's hot-zone bullet. A prose list drifts and this repository has been bitten by exactly that before (rf2-yxuta, rf2-8pb5k). Naming today's value alongside the constant is useful; presenting it AS the definition is the defect.

WHERE THE FIX LANDED: .claude/commands/mayor-dispatch.md, which governs how a dispatch brief is written and may name repository paths and script names freely. NOT docs/the-mayor-method/**, which is generic by design and carries no repo specifics — putting it there would be the layering error the method-reread loop exists to catch.

ANY BEAD THAT ADDS AN `:rf.error/*` ID IS A FORCED spec/009 TOUCH, SO IT IS NEVER HOT-ZONE-FREE (2026-08-10, found by the rf2-hic-007 worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched rf2-hic-007 with the surface fenced to "the macro and error
files only" and treated it as parallel-safe against five other live workers. The worker
decided, correctly by my fence, to REPORT spec-drift rather than edit a hot-zone file — and
then the fast-PR spine failed it. `check_keyword_catalogue_drift` CHECK A reds on a new
`:rf.error/*` id unless spec/009-Instrumentation.md is edited IN THE SAME PR. It is an
explicit same-PR co-edit invariant, not a nightly reconciliation.

So the edit was mandatory, and the bead was hot-zone work that neither the bead nor my
brief had classified as such.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR DISPATCH, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. spec/* is on the fixed hot-zone
list: sequential, never parallel. If two beads that each mint a diagnostic id run
concurrently, both are forced into spec/009 and they collide — and neither one's stated
surface says "spec/". The collision is invisible at dispatch time unless you ask the extra
question.

THE RULE: before dispatching, ask whether the bead can plausibly MINT A NEW DIAGNOSTIC ID.
If yes, treat it as touching spec/009 and sequence it against every other id-minting bead,
regardless of what its Surface line says. Beads that obviously qualify: a new refusal, a new
error shape, a complaint-catalogue entry, anything the guide teaches as "refuses with ...".
rf2-hic-021 (the complaint catalogue) is the clearest future instance — it mints ids by
definition.

AND THE GENERAL SHAPE: a bead's stated Surface line is what its AUTHOR expected to touch,
not what the gates will force. A repo-wide co-edit invariant can drag any bead into a hot
file. Where a gate enforces "change X and Y together", X's owners inherit Y's contention.

identical? ON A KEYWORD LITERAL IS JVM-SOUND AND CLJS-UNSOUND — it silently makes a sentinel check unreachable on CLJS. Found by the rf2-6t6qk/rf2-uoy6m worker (#6452), 2026-07-19, while making the trace deferral seam cross-platform.

THE BUG: deferred-continue marked "baseline unread" with a ::unread KEYWORD and compared it with identical?. On the JVM keywords are interned so identical? works. ON CLJS KEYWORD LITERALS ARE NOT GUARANTEED REFERENCE-EQUAL, so the check never matched — every call fell through to level-testing the LIVE predicate instead. Consequence: a cascaded :rf.event/dispatched envelope whose target-live? was unbound post-drain read FALSE and THE EVENT WAS SILENTLY DROPPED. Not an exception — a dropped event.

THE META-LESSON, the important half: this was the CLJS-ONLY FACE of rf2-eaxnai REGRESSION 1. The JVM cure shipped in PR #6365 and looked complete; the CLJS half of the same defect survived undetected because no CLJS test exercised the path. A cross-host .cljc fix is NOT done when the JVM suite is green. It surfaced here only because making the seam cross-platform FORCED the CLJS gate to run it (4 cofx_cljs_test failures), and the worker instrumented the flush to diagnose rather than working around it. Fix was a dedicated OBJECT sentinel, not a keyword.

RULE: in .cljc, never use identical? against a keyword/string/number literal as a sentinel — use a dedicated object value. And when a .cljc correctness fix ships green on ONE host, ASK EXPLICITLY whether the other host exercises the same path; if no test does, that is a GAP, not a pass. Cross-ref rf2-eaxnai REGRESSION 1, PR #6365 (JVM-only cure), PR #6452 (cross-host fix).

ALSO FROM #6452 — JVM GATE TIMEOUTS ON THIS BOX ARE RESOURCE CONTENTION, NOT HANGS. Repeated 10-minute harness timeouts on implementation/core clojure -M:test were environmental: jstack showed the JVMs actively inside clojure.test with NO Java-level deadlock and no "waiting to lock". Cause: multiple agents running JVMs concurrently, AND each timed-out run ORPHANS a ~1.8 GB JVM that compounds contention. Worker guidance: if a JVM gate times out, jstack before concluding hang, kill YOUR OWN orphaned JVMs only, re-run. Mayor guidance: saturating 6 workers that each run a full JVM suite is a real resource ceiling on this machine — a timing-out gate is a signal to check concurrency, not to assume a stuck worker.

A CLJS GUARD WRITTEN WITH identical? ON KEYWORD LITERALS IS ALWAYS FALSE IN A DEV BUILD, AND AN ABSENCE-ASSERTING SUITE STAYS GREEN OVER IT (2026-08-19).

Measured by rf2-oaksj (PR #8508). The first implementation of the client-only adoption trace used identical? to compare keyword literals. identical? is reference equality, and a DEV build emits no shared constants table, so the two literals are distinct objects and the guard never fired. Nothing was ever emitted.

WHY IT SURVIVED ITS OWN TEST SUITE, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING. Every row of the first suite asserted an ABSENCE — no event here, no event there, at most once. A mechanism that emits NOTHING AT ALL satisfies every absence assertion perfectly. So the suite was GREEN OVER DEAD CODE, and it would have stayed green forever. This is the hollow-gate shape exactly: the control could not catch its own case, and the proof of coverage was the blind spot.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: a sabotage run that came back GREEN. The worker interrogated the control instead of believing it. That is the method rule "a green sabotage run is a reason to stop, not to proceed" paying for itself on a real defect rather than a hypothetical.

TWO RULES:
1. In CLJS, compare keywords with = , not identical?. Under :advanced a shared constants table can make identical? appear to work, so this defect PASSES IN PRODUCTION AND FAILS IN DEV — the opposite of the usual direction, and it will not reproduce in a release-build check.
2. A test suite for an emitter must prove the POSITIVE case. If every assertion is an absence, the suite cannot distinguish "correctly silent" from "structurally incapable of speaking". Add at least one row that fails when nothing is emitted.

The fix taken was to switch to booleans, which REMOVES the failure mode rather than repairing the comparison — the right shape, per the rule that a hollow control is replaced rather than patched.

TO PROVE A REPRODUCED BEHAVIOUR IS CORRECT RATHER THAN DEFECTIVE, IMPLEMENT THE FIX AND MEASURE WHAT IT BREAKS. Established 2026-09-05 on rf2-f3yl, and it is the strongest form of a "not a defect" verdict this project has produced.

THE SHAPE. A bead claimed `reg-flow`, called cold outside a drain, does not materialise a new flow's initial output until some later unrelated drain — the same shape as a sibling defect (rf2-g1zb) that HAD been fixed the day before. The premise held: reproduced three ways with the db seeded first, each with an empty `:rf.event` trace proving nothing drained, including two arms the bead never predicted (a re-registration returns the PREVIOUS derive's value).

THE WORKER THEN BUILT THE SYMMETRIC FIX ANYWAY — the one the bead's own "if it reproduces" plan called for — and ran the suite: **30 failures and 69 errors**, from a green 253/6119. And the errors gave the reason rather than merely the count: `reg-flow` adds a flow that has NEVER RUN, so settling forces a first evaluation at a moment the caller did not choose; the direct form is documented for boot code that registers BEFORE it seeds; so that evaluation throws `:rf.error/flow-eval-exception` out of `reg-flow` itself. A `:derive` is not required to be total on nil.

THAT IS QUALITATIVELY BETTER EVIDENCE THAN AN ARGUMENT. "This is intended behaviour" is an opinion; "the fix produces 69 errors and here is the mechanism" is a measurement. It also protects against the opposite failure — a worker who reasons its way to "not a defect" and is simply wrong ships nothing and no one finds out.

WHEN TO REACH FOR IT: any bead whose verdict is heading toward "reproduced but correct", "works as designed", or "the premise holds but should not change". The cost is one implementation the worker then reverts; the return is a close reason a third carrier cannot reopen on reasoning alone.

TWO COROLLARIES THE SAME WORKER ESTABLISHED:
  * **A SIBLING DEFECT IS NOT A TEMPLATE.** The clear-flow case WAS a defect and this one is not, and the distinction is precise: `clear-flow` leaves a value no live flow OWNS (orphaned, incoherent), while a re-registration's stale value IS owned and is refreshed unconditionally on the next drain (merely late). "Same shape as the one we just fixed" is a hypothesis, not an inheritance.
  * **A SPEC THAT EXCLUDES SOMETHING WITHOUT SAYING WHY INVITES THE QUESTION BACK.** `spec/013-Flows.md` explicitly excluded `reg-flow` from the settle guarantee — it was not silent — but gave NO REASON, which is exactly why the question was reopened one day after the sibling landed. Recording the REASON alongside an exclusion is what stops the same bead being refiled. The worker closed that gap as its deliverable.

AND A CAUTION ABOUT FRESH CARVE-OUTS: the exclusion sentence this bead asked to revisit was ONE DAY OLD, added by the sibling's own PR as a scope fence rather than as a considered ruling. Check the age and provenance of a carve-out before treating it as settled doctrine — a fence someone erected yesterday to bound their own PR is not a decision.
