EDITING THIS TREE WITH A PYTHON HEREDOC CORRUPTS ANY NEWLY-INTRODUCED NON-ASCII CHARACTER, SILENTLY (2026-09-03, measured by worker vocabname-a).

Python's default encoding on Mike's Windows box is cp1252, not UTF-8. A heredoc edit that WRITES an em-dash emits a lone 0x97 byte — invalid UTF-8 — into a file whose existing em-dashes are correct UTF-8. It renders as a replacement character and nothing catches it: 'git diff --check' exits 0, the linters pass, the suite passes.

THE ASYMMETRY IS WHY IT HIDES: text mode ROUND-TRIPS pre-existing non-ASCII harmlessly, so a worker that edits a file full of em-dashes sees them survive and concludes encoding is fine. Only NEWLY INTRODUCED characters corrupt. So the bug appears exactly when you add prose, never when you edit around it.

REMEDY: write the file in BINARY mode with explicit UTF-8 byte sequences (an em-dash is \xe2\x80\x94), or stick to ASCII in generated prose. VERIFY with 'od -c' on the changed region — not by reading the diff, which renders the corruption as a plausible-looking glyph. Restore from the committed blob and verify by 'git hash-object' if you find one.

SAME FAMILY AS THE CRLF NO-OP, AND BOTH BITE THE SAME EDIT PATH: this tree is CRLF, so a prose edit anchored on LF silently matches nothing and the edit reports success having changed nothing. Both failures are invisible in tool output and both are caught only by re-reading the file's BYTES afterwards. Treat 'edit prose in this repo' as requiring a byte-level re-read every time.

RELATED FALSE INSTRUMENT recorded by the same worker: do NOT compare shadow-cljs compile output by fingerprint to prove 'nothing changed'. Two runs over an UNCHANGED tree give different fingerprints (measured: 142798d0 vs 6846ebbc). The valid comparison is the compiled FILE SET (sorted list diff), not bytes.

Windows unclean-shutdown can ZERO-FILL .git/config (12KB of \0), breaking ALL git ('fatal: bad config line 1'). Diagnose: od -c .git/config shows all \0; scan .git top-level for other all-null files (only config was hit). Recover: back up the corrupt file, reconstruct config from surviving data — remote URL from .git/FETCH_HEAD, committer identity from recent commit objects (read with config moved aside), core/* Windows defaults; restore beads.role via 'git config beads.role maintainer'. Verify with git fsck-lite (cat-file -e HEAD + HEAD^{tree}), ls-remote, and 'only tracked file modified is the expected one' (a zero-filled tracked file would show as modified). Happened 2026-07-08.

A WITNESS DERIVED FROM THE FIX INHERITS THE FIX'S BLIND SPOTS — five instances in one session (2026-08-10/11, hicasso).

THE SHAPE: a test or table whose STATED SCOPE EXCEEDS THE CASES IT ACTUALLY DRIVES. Each was green, each was honest, each claimed more than it checked.

1. rf2-hic-020 — a runtime/kit parity table claiming both arms of the raw escape, driving only the VALID raw component.
2. rf2-hic-007 — a completeness test claiming all six constructor fields unforgeable, running only where declaring! had already supplied real values; outside every extent the guarantee did not hold.
3. rf2-hic-012 — a comment recording the EXPECTED result as though it were the measured one, contradicted by the very row it annotated.
4. rf2-hic-021 — a round-trip check whose both directions ranged over ids THAT EXIST, so thirteen taught refusals with no id at all satisfied it VACUOUSLY (fail-open).
5. rf2-hic-022 — a shadow-detection walker whose letfn arm reads [nm params] and collects params only when the second node is a VECTOR; in multi-arity letfn it is a LIST, so every arity is missed. PR body and README both claimed letfn was covered.

WHY IT RECURS, and it is not carelessness: the witness is written FROM the fix, so it drives the shapes the author had in mind while fixing. The shapes that break it are exactly the ones the author did not think of — the same set. Test-after-fix is structurally biased toward passing.

THE COUNTERMEASURE, now standing in briefs: DERIVE THE WITNESS FROM THE GRAMMAR OF THE THING, NOT FROM THE FIX. Enumerate the legal shapes of the construct (for letfn: single-arity vector, multi-arity lists, docstring/prepost variants) and drive each. Require the PR body to state which shapes of the grammar were driven AND which were not — the second list is the valuable one, and writing it is what surfaces the gap.

SISTER RULE: see sweep-generator-defines-reachable-failure-directions — a generator's excluded shapes make a whole error DIRECTION invisible. Same disease at a different scale: coverage is defined by what the instrument can express, not by how much of it you ran.

A DEFECT-WITNESS TEST AND ITS FIX ARE MUTUALLY INVALIDATING — merging both without flipping the witness REDS MAIN, in either order. Cost a P0 red-on-main on 2026-07-24.

THE MECHANISM: a validation pilot reproduces a known hazard and writes it down as a LIVE TEST asserting the CURRENT (broken) behaviour. A separate slice FIXES that hazard. Each PR is green against a main lacking the other. Merge both and the witness test fails, because the defect it documents no longer exists.

THE CONCRETE CASE: the dropdown pilot independently reproduced the ref-composition hazard and shipped `a-behavior-and-a-top-layer-state-on-one-element-lose-a-ref` — a test that PASSES ONLY WHILE THE BUG IS PRESENT. I merged the pilot, then merged the ref-composition fix, and main went red with 2 failures. Every other gate stayed green, so it read like a mystery regression in a slice that had been CLEAN as a PR.

⚠️ WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A MEMORY IS THAT I HAD ALREADY IDENTIFIED THE PATTERN AND FAILED TO APPLY IT. Days earlier I wrote into a different brief: "both pilots assert the current REFUSAL in a test, so the blocked cell re-opens loudly. THOSE ASSERTIONS WILL START FAILING WHEN YOU SUCCEED — update them deliberately as part of this slice." I understood it for the compiled-browser refusal and did not carry it to the very next fix I merged. Recognising a hazard in one place does not transfer it to another unless it becomes a CHECK.

THE CHECK, now standing — BEFORE MERGING ANY FIX, ASK: does a merged test currently ASSERT THE DEFECT THIS FIXES? If yes, the flip belongs in the SAME PR as the fix, or main goes red the moment both are in.
  git grep -l "<hazard keyword>" implementation/**/test/
Pilot and validation suites are the usual home, because documenting current-state honestly is exactly what they are FOR.

THE REPAIR IS A FLIP, NOT A DELETE, and it has three parts:
  1. Assert the FIXED behaviour positively (both participants ran), never loosen to tolerate either outcome — that discards the only coverage of the combination.
  2. RENAME the test. A name asserting the opposite of its body is a trap for the next reader.
  3. Sweep for SIBLING witnesses in the same suite rather than discovering them one merge at a time.

⚠️ AND THE DIAGNOSTIC LESSON: the failure looked like a regression in the fix. The worker got it right by READING CI OWN LOG for the failing test NAME and MESSAGE — the name said "lose-a-ref" and the message said "one of the two refs was lost", which is the test DOCUMENTING a defect, not detecting one. A test name that describes a BUG rather than a PROPERTY is the tell. My own grep for the failure lines used a pattern chosen before I knew what the output looked like and returned only the namespace roster — capture the log to a file and read it.

GENERAL FORM: this WILL recur wherever validation pilots run alongside active development, which is the whole point of running them. It is a property of the arrangement, not a mistake by either author.

READ A WORKER'S LIVENESS CLOCK IN ITS OWN METADATA DIRECTORY, NOT AT <worktree>/.git -- AND ALWAYS PRINT THE DATE (2026-08-23, two sweeps wrong on the first, one on the second).

TRAP 1 -- THE PATH. In a LINKED git worktree, .git is a FILE containing "gitdir: <path>", not a directory. So "find <worktree>/.git -maxdepth 1 -type f -printf %T@" measures the mtime of that one-line pointer and reports it as the worker's metadata clock. It fails quiet: a plausible timestamp comes back, no error. MEASURED: on worktree pr-audit-8445 the wrong form read 2026-08-23 03:13:05 while the real gitdir clock was 21:14:02 -- an 18-hour error, in the direction that reads as DEATH. I nearly recorded a live, actively-fetching worker as quiescent.

RESOLUTION: gd=$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse --git-dir); find "$gd" -type f -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS %f\n' | sort -r | head. For a linked worktree that resolves to <main>/.git/worktrees/<name>/, holding that worktree's OWN FETCH_HEAD, HEAD, index and ORIG_HEAD.

TRAP 2 -- THE FORMAT. Printing %TH:%TM without %TY-%Tm-%Td makes a four-week-old file read as tonight. MEASURED: three frozen husks printed "20:45" beside a live worker's "22:07" in the same table, and the 20:45 was 2026-07-25. The conclusion survived only because the number contradicted an earlier reading and I re-measured with dates. In a liveness table -- where the whole question is how old something is -- a bare time is not a timestamp. ALWAYS carry the date.

WHICH FILE ANSWERS WHAT, measured on pr-audit-8445:
* FETCH_HEAD -- moves on every fetch, so it is the POLLING clock. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration; stillness proves nothing. Read it twice 30-60s apart.
* index -- moves when the worker actually stages work. Its index wrote at 11:41:02 and the commit "chore(beads): audit PR #8721" landed at 11:43:26, two minutes later. That gap VALIDATES index-mtime as the "is it producing?" clock, distinct from the fetch clock.

THE METHOD TREE ALREADY SAYS THE FIRST HALF, better than I was practising it: the fetch-head file lives in "that item's OWN metadata directory, which each linked worktree gets its own copy of", and "movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration". Both failures were mine, not the document's, so the repair is this memory rather than more text in the tree.

DO NOT confuse the mayor's .git/FETCH_HEAD with the worker's. Both move; only the worker's proves the WORKER is alive. Check the path you actually measured.

MEASURING WHETHER A WORKER IS ALIVE: compare the TIP REVISION ID, never a commit count (2026-08-13, corrected same day by an audit).

BE PRECISE ABOUT WHICH COUNT — the first version of this memory was wrong and the error reached main:
  git rev-list --count <branch>              counts EVERY reachable commit. Measured 21677.
                                             REBASING ONTO AN ADVANCED TRUNK MAKES THIS GROW. Not invariant.
  git rev-list --count origin/main..<branch> the AHEAD count. Measured 3.
                                             INVARIANT under rebase — the same commits are replayed.

The ahead count is the one a mayor naturally reads, and it is the one that misleads.

WHAT MOVES AND WHAT DOES NOT, under rebase:
  ahead count        NO
  %ar author date    NO
  %cr committer date YES
  tip revision id    YES

So record the tip id each tick and compare ids. Committer date is a usable second signal.

AN UNCHANGED TIP AUTHORISES NOTHING ON ITS OWN. That half is load-bearing: it is what stopped a healthy worker being called stranded across two ticks. The next step after an unchanged tip is to MESSAGE, and the reply shape is the real read — 'queued for delivery' means alive, 'had no active task; resumed from transcript' means idle.

SECOND TRAP IN THE SAME MEASUREMENT: do NOT read FETCH_HEAD after a fetch whose exit code you suppressed. Linked worktrees share one .git and therefore one FETCH_HEAD, so a raced or failed fetch leaves a stale value that reads as fresh. Prefer 'git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/worker/*' — one command, no shared state, no exit code to check.

WHEN TWO AGENTS DISAGREE ABOUT A COMMIT'S AGE, suspect two clocks before suspecting an error. One reported 75 seconds where another read 43 minutes; one read committer date, the other author date. Neither misread.

WORKER LIVENESS (Windows mayor loop): TaskList can return 'No tasks found' for background agents launched in a PRIOR turn even while they are actively running, AND their output-file mtime does NOT advance during a run (transcript flush is buffered). Both gave false 'dead' signals — a realm worker that TaskList showed as absent + mtime static for 9min actually completed a 624s run. NEVER infer a worker is dead from TaskList/mtime; NEVER recycle/--force-remove a worker's worktree on that basis (it clobbers live workers mid-edit). The ONLY reliable liveness signal is the completion/kill <task-notification>. To recycle, wait for that notification or confirm via a pushed branch with the expected commits.

Background workers and review agents MUST NOT create, claim, or close beads. Beads are mayor action only — filing them makes the mayor think they own the work. Worker outputs go in chat and ai/findings/ (local). Use background workers freely for parallel drafts/research; never bd create for that.

Worker node_modules junction destroyed the mayor's real node_modules AGAIN (2026-07-31, rf2-2rtt6.8 / PR #7311). A worker worktree with no node_modules cannot compile; the established repo convention (a live sibling worktree had exactly this) is a Windows junction: cmd /c mklink /J <wt>/implementation/node_modules <mayor>/implementation/node_modules. That works for the build, and then post-merge hygiene ran git worktree remove, which FOLLOWED the junction and emptied the mayor's REAL implementation/node_modules to 0 entries - breaking every local build in the repo. Repair is cheap and deterministic: cd <mayor>/implementation && npm ci (exit 0, restores the canary 101 entries; verify react + shadow-cljs are present). TWO fixes, both needed: (1) the WORKER should cmd /c rmdir the junction as its last act before reporting done, not leave it for hygiene; (2) HYGIENE must cmd /c rmdir <wt>/implementation/node_modules BEFORE git worktree remove, and re-check the mayor canary (~101) after each removal batch. This is the second recorded instance of the same class.

Worker path-leak mechanism (CONFIRMED 2026-07-17, rf2-r09qj + flagged by rf2-klyw5): a subagent that Reads MAYOR-checkout absolute paths during exploration can have its SUBSEQUENT Edit tool-calls carry that mayor path — so edits land in the mayor checkout, NOT the worktree. Invisible in the worker's OWN git status (the worktree looks clean); visible only from the mayor side. MITIGATION that works: the boundary-block's post-write BOTH-TREES check catches it — the worker self-recovers (git checkout-restore the mayor file, copy completed work into the worktree, verify mayor clean). HARDEN BRIEFS: instruct workers to Read AND Edit only worktree-absolute paths (never the mayor checkout, even for exploration reads), re-verify rev-parse per edit, and run the both-trees check after the first edit + any new file. Mayor-side detection: 'git status --short | grep -v .beads' in the mayor checkout should be empty; a stray modified file there = a live leak (capture the diff, don't blind-revert if the worker may be mid-recovery). This is a REAL Agent-subagent mechanism, distinct from the Workflow args-undefined misdiagnosis.

Worker PR-creation hang gotcha (2026-06-09): a worker (B6/vzld77) completed + committed + pushed its work, then hung ~1h LOOPING on 'gh pr create' with a heredoc body containing backticks/parens (bash kept mis-parsing). Mayor salvaged by opening the PR from the pushed branch. LESSON: in worker briefs, tell workers to create the PR with a SIMPLE body or '--body-file', avoid backticks/parens/heredocs in the inline body; and if a worker is committed+pushed but PR-less + idle, the mayor can open the PR for it (git -C <wt> push; gh pr create --head <branch>) rather than killing the work.

worker/receipts-hic081 IS NOT STRANDED -- do not delete it, and do not re-file it as hygiene residue (rf2-fuuqd, triaged 2026-08-15).

It is a DELIBERATELY RETAINED spike record. rf2-hic-081 ('Spike: capability receipts') closed with the verdict SPLIT and its close reason ends: 'Spike commits are pushed on worker/receipts-hic081 and retained as the experiment's record; nothing from them lands on main.' The 3 commits are pushed, have no PR and never will -- that is the design, not an oversight.

The conclusions are fully promoted and verified on main: the capability-receipt DESIGN is in docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md, decision-brief.md and lanes/left-field-ideas.md (rf2-eoo9, PR #7898); the erasure-gate reachability rule is in check_production_erasure.cjs and siblings (rf2-nkr3, PR #7878); impl/receipt.cljs is correctly ABSENT from main.

THE GENERAL LESSON for the hygiene loop: 'pushed + unlanded + no PR' is a heuristic, not a verdict. Before filing a branch as stranded, check whether a CLOSED bead retained it on purpose -- spike branches are the class where the finding lands on main and the diff deliberately never does.

Worker recovery hazard (learned 2026-06-22, the #4910/#4913 xray-testbeds incident): (1) A worker coming to rest is NOT proof it finished. The xray-testbeds worker came to rest waiting on a gate it launched; the mayor misjudged it as done, committed its UNCOMMITTED partial work as a recovery PR (#4910) — but it had not yet written standard_epochs/core.cljs, so #4910 merged an incomplete state that crashed the two-frame surface on load and left a red gate on main. RULE: only recover/commit a worker's work after a genuine final report with a PR URL; an idle worktree mid-task is not a completion signal. (2) NEVER git worktree remove --force a worktree whose worker may still be live — it destroyed the live worker's workspace AND emptied the mayor implementation/node_modules via the node_modules junction cascade (the worker had to npm install to restore the mayor tree). RULE: only remove a worktree for a worker that has genuinely completed (final report received); the junction-rmdir-before-remove step does not protect against removing a still-active worktree.

"WORKTREE-LOCAL" IS ONLY HALF THE RULE FOR WORKER SCRATCH FILES — IT MUST ALSO BE GITIGNORED (2026-08-09).

THE SEQUENCE. Earlier in the day two concurrent workers overwrote each other's helper files and PR-body drafts in the SHARED scratchpad, and one nearly published another bead's PR body. The fix put into later briefs was "write every file you create inside your own worktree". Both workers complied exactly. Both worktrees then REFUSED to reap: REMOVE_REFUSED_DIRTY, each holding one untracked pr-body-<bead>.md that the disposability classifier will not accept as build output.

SO THE TWO HAZARDS TRADE OFF AND THE BRIEF MUST CLOSE BOTH. dispatch-prompt-template.md already says it: put EVERY gate artefact where git ignores it, and warns that one leftover is enough to make a tree unreapable (nine accumulated that way once). The ignored extensions are *.log, *.exit and *-exit.txt. A file named pr-body-something.md is worktree-local, safe from collision, and still blocks the reap.

THE COMPLETE INSTRUCTION FOR A DISPATCH BRIEF: write every file you create inside your own worktree AND give it an ignored name (*.log / *.exit), or delete it before you report done. Never a shared temp directory; never an unignored leftover.

RESOLVING IT WHEN IT HAPPENS IS CHEAP BUT MUST NOT BE BLIND. --dry-run prints each offending path tagged [KEEP] or [build output]; a PR-body draft whose content is already published on the merged PR is genuinely disposable, so --force is correct AFTER looking. Do not reach for --force-disposable (it refuses anything not recognised as build output) and never spray a blanket --force across a sweep list: when that guard was written, one worktree held four analysis files for an OPEN bead and three others carried uncommitted source and doc edits.

A WORKTREE YOU DID NOT EXPLICITLY DISPATCH MAY BE YOUR OWN WORKER SPAWNING A SECOND WORKTREE — not a concurrent session. Misdiagnosed 2026-07-24. I dispatched a 4-bead cluster to ONE worker; it did 3 beads in worktree A (PR one) then created worktree B for the 4th bead (PR two). My hygiene scan found worktree B, had no record of creating it, and I concluded a concurrent session was also dispatching workers. WRONG — it was my own worker branching per bead. THE COST: the false belief made me over-cautious about that surface being externally contested. THE DISCRIMINATOR before concluding concurrent-session: a branch named worker/<desc>-<beadid> whose bead you assigned to a live worker IS that worker, even as a second worktree. Check worker completion reports and open PRs first — a worker report names every worktree and PR it created. Track by BEAD ownership (who did I give this bead to), never by worktree count: one worker is NOT necessarily one worktree or one PR. The genuinely-separate process here (the pr-audit loop) FILES beads, it does not dispatch code-editing workers, so it never contests a code surface. No harm done — I correctly did not touch the worktree or re-dispatch the bead.

A WORKER STRANDS BY ENDING ITS TURN ON A BACKGROUNDED GATE, AND IT WILL DO IT REPEATEDLY UNLESS THE BRIEF SAYS HOW TO WAIT. Observed again 2026-08-08 on rf2-2rtt6.142, twice in a row after a resume.

THE SHAPE. A gate exceeds the tool's foreground time ceiling. The worker detaches it — correctly — and then ENDS ITS TURN "waiting" for a completion notification. Nothing is guaranteed to wake it. It reports "still progressing, continuing to wait", the turn ends, and the same thing happens on the next nudge. The work is usually fine; only the waiting is broken.

WHAT DOES NOT FIX IT: telling the worker again that gates must be foreground. It already believes that, which is exactly why it detached and then waited politely. The instruction it is missing is what to do INSTEAD of waiting.

WHAT FIXES IT — put this in every brief, not just the ones with long gates:
  "If a gate exceeds the tool's time ceiling, run it detached and BLOCK ON IT INSIDE THE SAME TURN by polling its exit file in a loop. Never end a turn with a gate outstanding."
and give the literal shape:
  for i in $(seq 1 240); do [ -f gate-<id>.exit ] && break; sleep 15; done; cat gate-<id>.exit

TWO RIDERS THAT MATTER AS MUCH AS THE LOOP:
- The detached invocation must use an ABSOLUTE path to the gate script. These scripts derive their repo root from BASH_SOURCE, and a relative invocation that gets detached adopts whatever cwd the shell really has — one did that inside ANOTHER live worker's checkout and produced a complete, internally consistent verdict about somebody else's diff. Check the run's "gate root:" first line names your own worktree.
- If the invocation writes no exit file at all, that is the real defect, not the waiting. Re-run as: sh <ABS>/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > g.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > g.exit

MAYOR-SIDE RECOVERY, cheap and reliable: check the ground truth yourself rather than nudging twice. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` and a remote-vs-local sha comparison in the worktree tell you whether the work is durable; `ls *.log *.exit` plus the log's mtime tell you whether the gate is genuinely still running or dead. On this occasion the work was already committed AND pushed, so nothing was at risk — the only outstanding step was reading an exit code.

DO NOT MISREAD THE SPINE LOG WHILE CHECKING. test-fast-pr.sh prints lines like "ok  unexpected extra dependency -> FAILED" from a negative-test harness confirming its own mutations fail correctly. Those are PASSES. The verdict is the echoed exit code, never a line in the log.

WORKER TRAP — git mv then edit (2026-07-25, found by the misc-cluster-a worker on PR #6946): after 'git mv old.cljc new_cljs_test.cljc', a subsequent 'git add <path>' does NOT pick up content edits made after the mv. The worker's first pushed commit therefore carried the RENAMED file with the OLD ns name still inside it — a commit that would not compile. It was caught only by noticing a stray 'M' in git status, then fixed by rebuilding both commits from the base and force-pushing with --force-with-lease. This is the exact shape of the rf2-dn6v7 / rf2-lgozq lane-suffix work (rename file + edit ns in one change), so it will recur. Put in briefs for any rename-plus-edit bead: after a git mv, re-run 'git add' on the path AFTER the content edit, and verify with 'git diff --cached' that BOTH the rename and the content change are staged before committing; a rename-only commit of a .cljc test file is a non-compiling commit.

A FRESH WORKER WORKTREE CANNOT RUN THE FAST-PR SPINE'S NODE TIER WITHOUT THE node_modules JUNCTION (measured 2026-08-13).

A worker on a clean worktree captured exit 1 at 'FAIL CLJS node integration' with 'Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'. Nothing in its diff could reach shadow-cljs resolution. THE CAUSE WAS THE MISSING implementation/node_modules. Creating the junction turned the SAME spine green with no source change.

SO THE BRIEF'S INSTRUCTION 'run scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' IS INCOMPLETE for a doc-only worker that never expected to need npm. The failure looks like a real red, and a worker that trusts it will hunt a defect that does not exist - or worse, report a red PR as blocked.

SAY THIS IN BRIEFS THAT NOMINATE THE SPINE: if the node tier fails on module resolution, create the implementation/node_modules junction, re-run, and REMOVE THE LINK with cmd /c rmdir as your last act. Never a recursive delete - it follows the junction and empties the mayor's real tree, which has happened twice. Re-verify the canary with the script's own instrument either side.

THE SAME WORKER ALSO HIT THE HARNESS-DISAGREEMENT TRAP ON THAT RUN, which is the sixteenth observed instance: the harness reported 'completed (exit code 0)' while the runner's own .exit file read 1. It quoted the file. Had it trusted the harness it would have shipped a red spine as green. EVERY observed disagreement so far has surfaced as a harness-reported 0.

A FRESH WORKER WORKTREE HAS NO `implementation/node_modules`, AND THE SPINE FAILS ENVIRONMENTALLY THERE — the harness then misreports it (2026-08-11, rf2-gxry).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker ran `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh` in a newly-created worktree. It captured exit **1** on `CLJS node integration`, with `Cannot find module 'shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'` — nothing compiled, because the worktree had no `node_modules`. **The harness announced "completed (exit code 0)" against that captured 1.** The worker junctioned `node_modules` at the mayor's real one, deleted the stale `.exit` and `.log`, re-ran the gate whole, and captured **0** with `[:node-test] Build completed. (2307 files, 2306 compiled, 0 warnings)`.

THE HAZARD IS NOT THE FAILURE, IT IS THE SHAPE OF IT. A missing-module error is not a test failure, but it PRESENTS as a red gate, and if a worker reads the harness's number instead of the captured one it presents as a GREEN gate over a build that never ran. Both readings are wrong in opposite directions, and the second is the dangerous one: a green that compiled nothing.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF for any worker that will run a compiling gate:
  - A fresh worktree has NO `implementation/node_modules`. If a gate needs one, create the junction to the mayor's real tree, and REMOVE THE LINK (never its target) as your last act — a later `git worktree remove` follows it and empties the shared tree. Canary the mayor's count before and after.
  - `Cannot find module` or `command not found` from a gate is ENVIRONMENTAL, not a verdict. Fix the environment and RE-RUN THE GATE WHOLE. Do not report the first number, and do not report it as a failure of the diff.
  - DELETE the stale `.exit` and `.log` before the re-run. A stale `.exit` survives the next run's `>` on its log, so the pair can disagree and the older verdict is the one you quote.

TWELFTH SIGHTING TODAY of the harness reporting a captured 1 as exit 0. The rule stands and is now in the method: THE NUMBER YOU QUOTE IS THE ONE YOU CAPTURED.

Worker worktrees have NO node_modules, so browser/shadow-cljs gates cannot run there by default. Do NOT junction into the mayor checkout's node_modules to fix it — that is the configuration that destroyed the mayor's real node_modules once and nearly again. THE SAFE ANSWER IS `npm ci` INSIDE THE WORKTREE (one worker did exactly this today, exit 0, no junction created, canary unmoved). Cost is a few minutes; the alternative is deferring every browser gate to CI. Put this in any brief whose gate menu includes `npm run test:browser`, a shadow-cljs build, or an adapter testbed spec.cjs — otherwise the worker hits 'shadow-cljs is not recognized', concludes the gate is unrunnable, and defers coverage that actually matters (the real-DOM gate catches repaint bugs test:cljs structurally cannot see). Related: [[windows-junction-detection-two-wrong-answers-before-the]].

Workers can get stuck in a monitor-wait loop on slow test suites (rul3ov burned ~770K tokens over 3 segments re-arming a Monitor for the full CLJS conformance run before committing). Recovery: SendMessage the agentId with a firm 'do NOT arm another Monitor — commit FIRST, push, gh pr create NOW; CI runs the full suite so CI is the gate, not your local terminal.' Over-cautious 'won't PR until local green' is the anti-pattern; the PR's CI is the real gate.

CONCURRENT WORKERS SHARE THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD AND OVERWRITE EACH OTHER'S FILES — including PR bodies (2026-08-09).

WHAT HAPPENED. Six workers ran in parallel on the hic-* Wave A set. The rf2-hic-004 worker reported that its verify.py and pr-body.md were BOTH overwritten mid-run by the rf2-hic-005 worker. Same filenames, same shared scratchpad directory. Its PR body survived only because gh had already read the file before the overwrite landed. A slower run would have published another bead's PR body under its own PR number.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT COVER IT. The brief said 'use worktree-local log paths', and every worker complied FOR GATE LOGS — they all wrote gate-slugs.log inside their own worktree. The collision was in the HELPER FILES nobody thought to fence: scratch scripts, PR-body drafts, temp verification output. The known hazard was written narrowly as a gate-log hazard; it is really a shared-temp-directory hazard and applies to every file a worker writes outside its worktree.

THE FIX FOR FUTURE BRIEFS. Say: write EVERY file you create - gate logs, helper scripts, PR-body drafts, scratch output - inside your own worktree, never in a shared temp or scratchpad directory. If you must use a shared directory, prefix every filename with your bead id.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A WRONG GATE LOG. A clobbered gate log yields a plausible-but-wrong exit code, which the echo-the-exit-code rule catches. A clobbered PR body is published verbatim to GitHub under the wrong PR and nothing checks it.

THREE WORKERS IN ONE NIGHT STALLED WAITING FOR A "COMPLETION NOTIFICATION" THAT DOES NOT EXIST (2026-08-10).

WHAT THEY EACH DID. rf2-8a6s: "Still running. I'll stop here and resume when the watcher fires - no more polling." rf2-hic-009: "The spine is still running ... I have a waiter armed on its exit code and will report the moment it lands." rf2-hic-016: "The fast-PR spine is still running; I'll wait for its completion notification rather than end the turn" - and then the turn ended. All three had briefs that said, in terms, run gates in the foreground to completion and never background one.

THE BELIEF IS SPECIFIC AND WRONG, WHICH IS WHY THE EXISTING WORDING DOES NOT PREVENT IT. They do not think they are abandoning the task. They think a watcher/notification will wake them. Nothing does. A stopped subagent resumes ONLY when the mayor sends it a message, and the mayor only knows to because the completion report reads oddly. "Run gates in the foreground" does not contradict the belief - a worker can believe it ran the gate in the foreground AND that something will tell it the answer later.

THE WORDING THAT ADDRESSES THE BELIEF, not the behaviour: "There is no completion notification. No watcher wakes a stopped worker. If you end your turn waiting for a gate, the task stops until a human notices. Run the gate in the foreground, block on it, read its exit code yourself. A long foreground gate is fine; an unfinished turn is not."

THE REAL COST IS UNPUSHED WORK, AND IT VARIES. rf2-8a6s had committed AND pushed - fully durable, only the PR was missing. rf2-hic-009 had pushed and opened a PR - only the spine result and PR body were missing. rf2-hic-016 had THREE COMMITS AND HAD NOT PUSHED - one lost worktree from losing an entire three-engine browser suite. So the recovery order is: check `git log origin/main..HEAD` and `git ls-remote` FIRST, and if it is unpushed, make PUSH step 1 of the resume message before anything else.

RECOVERY IS CHEAP AND RELIABLE: SendMessage to the agent id resumes it from its transcript with full context. All three resumed and continued correctly. Do not re-dispatch a fresh worker - it would redo work that is already committed.

DETECTION: a completion report that says "still running", "I'll report when", "waiting for", or "watcher armed" is a stall, not a status. Treat it as a resume trigger immediately, and check push state before replying.

Workers strand because the long gate outlives their TURN budget, not because they disobeyed 'run foreground'. Three workers in one session (dispatch-sync, ci-test-lanes, tags-ratchet) ended their turn mid-gate with 'Waiting on the spine/watcher' — commits pushed, NO PR, nothing mergeable. A brief that says 'run test-fast-pr.sh foreground to completion, THEN open the PR' makes stranding likely on a loaded box, because the spine can exceed the budget. BETTER BRIEF ORDER: commit -> run only the FOCUSED, fast, arm-specific gates (plus any non-vacuity/mutation proof, which is cheap and is the evidence that actually matters) -> OPEN THE PR -> name the slow gates as 'deferred to CI' in the ## Quality gates section. CI runs the same surface and IS the merge gate; the local spine never was. Recovery is SendMessage-resume, which works and keeps the worker's context.

Workflow rule (Mike, 2026-06-10): beads marked in_progress are LOCKED - never update their title/description/notes/scope (a worker is executing against them). To add findings or scope to in-progress work, CREATE A FOLLOW-UP BEAD (dep on the in-progress one if sequenced). Check status with bd show before any bd update.

`git worktree add` CAN BE KILLED BY THE HARNESS FOREGROUND TIMEOUT MID-CHECKOUT, LEAVING A STALE LOCK (2026-08-11; hit by two workers in one tick).

This repo's checkout is ~5308 files, and a fresh `git worktree add` can exceed the harness's 2-minute foreground limit. When it is killed partway (~25% in one observed case) it leaves BOTH a stale `.git/worktrees/<name>/index.lock` AND a `locked` marker reading `initializing`. The worktree exists, is registered, and is unusable; the guard script fails.

RECOVERY, in this order:
1. remove `.git/worktrees/<name>/index.lock`
2. `git reset --hard HEAD` from inside the worktree, BACKGROUNDED - it re-runs the full checkout and took ~9 minutes on this box
3. `git worktree unlock <path>`
Then the worker guard passes normally.

PUT THE MITIGATION IN THE DISPATCH BRIEF: every brief I write opens with `git worktree add`, so this is a first-command failure that costs a worker ten minutes before it has done anything. Tell workers to run the create BACKGROUNDED by absolute path and poll, exactly as they are already told to do for the 25-minute test spine - the same 10-minute ceiling applies to it and nobody expects it to.

Two workers hit this in a single tick (thirdsite-fbi4 and presence-5gka), so it is not rare. Both recovered without data loss, and both reported it rather than silently retrying - which is what made it diagnosable.

Worktree cleanup: a directory can be REUSED and re-pointed at a different branch mid-session, so a name-based safe-list goes stale while you are acting on it. Observed live: a hygiene agent was handed 'ci-test-lanes-cluster - safe to remove, PR #7116 merged', but between the list being written and the removal, a worker reused that same directory on a NEW branch (worker/xray-fuzzy-regression-pin) carrying an open PR #7119. Removing by name would have destroyed an in-flight PR worktree. Re-read `git worktree list --porcelain` IMMEDIATELY BEFORE each removal and re-verify the branch AND its PR state at that moment; never trust a safe-list compiled minutes earlier. Corollary: 'PR merged' is a fact about a BRANCH, not about a DIRECTORY. Related: [[rebase-merge-makes-a-worker-branch-look-unmerged]].

Worktree hygiene: `git status` ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH to decide whether a worktree holds work. The `/ai/` tree is GITIGNORED, so findings docs, gate logs, PR-body drafts and ad-hoc probes are INVISIBLE to git status — a worktree that looks pristine can hold real content. Sweep `ai/` (and any `.worker-logs/`, `.wt-logs/`) separately and READ any non-log file before discarding. Observed: three worktrees held hidden content (20 gate logs, a pr-body.md draft, an ad-hoc probe .clj) — all correctly judged residue, but only because they were looked at. Corollary for the other direction: a hygiene brief that says 'clean tree = safe to remove' is wrong on this repo.

A WORKTREE'S INDEX CLOCK MEASURES THAT WORKTREE, NOT THE FUNCTION IT WAS DISPATCHED FOR (2026-08-24, correcting my own reading across ~six sweeps).

WHAT I HAD BEEN SAYING. Every stranded sweep reported the pr-audit worktree as "alive, polling on a ~40s cadence, index still 11:41, so nothing audited since 11:43". The first half is right. The second half quietly asserted that the AUDIT FUNCTION had produced nothing, and that does not follow.

WHAT THE PARENT CHAIN SHOWS.
* 10ade546c4 "audit PR #8721", 11:43:26, parent ebc7e737bd -- which IS that worktree's HEAD and its branch tip. So that commit was made from that revision, and the index write at 11:41:02, two minutes earlier, is genuine evidence of it staging. That inference was sound.
* d1c824098d "audit PR #8730", 01:22 the next morning, parent 3c9e358a0f -- a revision that worktree has NEVER been at (its branch reflog has exactly two entries: created, then one fast-forward to ebc7e737bd, and `git cherry` reads 0 ahead).

SO AUDITS KEPT HAPPENING WHILE THAT WORKTREE DID NOTHING BUT FETCH. Tonight's audit filed a bead against my own merge and pushed a commit, from a checkout at main's tip, not from there. At least two things perform this role, and the worktree I was watching is not the one that has been working.

THE CORRECTION, and it is about the shape of the claim rather than the number: an index mtime is evidence about ONE CHECKOUT. Reading it as a health signal for the capability that checkout was dispatched to provide is a category error, and it fails in the reassuring direction -- "nothing has been audited" was false every time I said it, while the audit was in fact catching my own defects.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE PARENT CHAIN, not the clock: take a commit the function produced and ask whether its PARENT is a revision that checkout has actually been at. Its branch reflog answers that in one command and cannot be faked by a fetch.

STILL TRUE, and worth keeping: FETCH_HEAD movement proves that worktree is alive (measured twice, 40 seconds apart, against a mayor clock that stayed still), and it remains unreapable and unmessageable because no dispatch row records an agent id for it.

THE 'NEVER WRITE THE WORKTREE PATH INTO A COMMITTED FILE' RULE IS NARROWER THAN THE RISK, AND THE CI GATE DOES NOT CLOSE THE GAP (2026-08-18).

Adopted into mayor dispatch practice on the report of the worker on rf2-f5cma, which was fixing that very rule and is the best-placed reader of it.

THE GAP: a PR body and a bead close reason are both DURABLE and PUBLIC, and neither is a committed file. The 'No hardcoded personal/home paths' CI gate does not see either. So a worker that obeys the rule as written can still publish an absolute home path where it persists. That worker kept paths out of both only by extending the rule on its own initiative.

ADOPTED WORDING for every dispatch: report the printed WORKTREE_ROOT to the mayor in your completion message, and never write it, or any absolute home path, into any COMMITTED FILE, PR BODY OR TRACKER TEXT.

AND CARRY THE POSITIVE FORM, which the template now has and my briefs lagged a revision behind: if the deliverable is itself a written record, what makes the guard evidence is that it RAN and exited 0, not the machine-specific path it printed. A worker told only what not to write still has evidence to produce and will improvise something.

SEPARATE OBSERVATION FROM THE SAME REPORT, not yet actioned: the guard prints an MSYS-style root (/c/Users/...) while the boundary block in every brief states the worktree as C:/Users/.... A worker comparing the two LITERALLY sees a mismatch, on the one rule where a directory-level error is expensive. Every worker so far has resolved it from context. If it ever bites, the fix is to state both forms in the boundary block rather than to change either producer.

GENERAL SHAPE: the worker fixing a rule is the best reviewer of the brief that carries it. Ask. Two of the three improvements here came from asking one worker whether its own setup instruction was well worded.

WRITE EVERY DISPATCH BRIEF TO A FILE BEFORE SENDING IT, BECAUSE THE POSTURE LOOP'S FIDELITY CHECK IS OTHERWISE TESTIMONIAL RATHER THAN MECHANICAL (2026-09-03).

THE PROBLEM. loops.md section 4 asks the mayor to confirm that every dispatch since the last posture tick pasted the stance VERBATIM and carried the boundary and gate-mechanics blocks. If the brief was assembled inline in the Agent call and never written down, there is nothing left to check against afterwards — the mayor's own recollection is the only witness, and a mayor that had summarised the stance would recall having pasted it. That is precisely the failure mode the loop exists to catch, so the check silently degrades to self-report at exactly the moment it matters.

THE FIX IS ONE EXTRA STEP AND IT COSTS NOTHING. Build the brief mechanically into a scratchpad file — stance header, then the extracted preamble / boundary / gates blocks appended, then the task body — and dispatch by telling the worker to read that file as its FIRST action. Then the posture check is three greps with counts, run against bytes that still exist: grep -c on a distinctive line of each block. Anything other than 1 is a defect you can name.

TWO SECOND-ORDER WINS, BOTH REAL. (1) Telling the worker to cat the file is MORE faithful than pasting, because the bytes it reads are the extractor's output rather than anything that passed through the mayor's hands again. (2) The file survives compaction. Measured this session: four dispatches made before a compaction could not be re-verified at all, because their briefs had only ever existed inside the Agent call, and the only surviving evidence was one worker's report happening to describe gate-block-specific behaviour (planted-fault runs, git blob-hash restore). That is corroboration, not verification, and it was luck.

THE ANCHOR-DUPLICATION DETAIL. Repeat the worktree path, branch, base oid, bead ids and the premises-are-claims sentence INLINE in the Agent prompt as well. A worker that fails to read the file then contradicts an anchor visibly instead of improvising a task silently — the failed read becomes detectable rather than silent.

DO NOT read this as licence to skip the extractor. The file is where the extractor's output lands; it is not a substitute for extracting. See never-retype-a-verbatim-block.

WRITE THE DISPATCH LEDGER ROW IN THE SAME TOOL CALL THAT SPAWNS THE AGENT — never in "the next step". Measured twice on 2026-09-05, same cause both times, by the mayor.

THE MECHANISM, and it is structural rather than forgetfulness: the Agent spawn returns, and a background task-notification for a DIFFERENT worker arrives in the same turn. The notification is substantive — a completion report worth acting on — so attention moves to it, the turn ends on that thread, and the ledger write is never made. Both misses (`exserve-a`, then `httpcancel-a` + `exsubstr-a`) happened exactly that way. A worker was live, working, with NO row in `ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv`.

WHY IT MATTERS: the ledger is the only route from a worktree back to its agentId, and the reap test requires the agent's own report. A worktree with no row cannot be routed to, so at reap time it looks like a tree with no owner — which is the state that invites reaping on a refused proxy (a merged PR, a clean tree, elapsed time).

THE FIX, in order:
  * **Write the row in the same call as the spawn**, or immediately after in the SAME turn, before reading any notification.
  * **Then verify by name-keyed read** — `rows=1 fields=5` per live worktree. That read is what caught both misses; without it the omission is invisible until reap time.
  * A `rows=0` on a worktree you know you dispatched is a MISSING ROW, not a wrong key — but check the key form first, because `/c/Users/…` against a stored `C:/Users/…` also reads 0 for every row, uniformly, which looks exactly like an answer. Keep a control: query one key you know is present.

**AND DO NOT ADDRESS FIELDS BY INDEX.** Read by name. CLAUDE.md's ledger contract records that a positional parse is right about one row in eight and wrong with a well-formed answer on the rest.

RELATED: [[the-ledger-key-is-the-stored-path-form]], [[a-uniform-zero-reads-exactly-like-an-answer]].

WSL bash.exe DOUBLE-EXPANDS a -c command string. Found by rf2-sefx0 (#6357, 2026-07-18) with a decisive probe: bash -lc with FOO=hello then printf of the escaped dollar-FOO prints the literal dollar-FOO under Git Bash (single pass) but prints hello under WSL bash (an outer pass already substituted it). CONSEQUENCE: any -c string that READS BACK a variable the SAME string assigns is broken under WSL — the outer pass substitutes the not-yet-assigned name to empty. That is how a PATH= assignment referencing a FIXTURE_DIR assigned immediately to its left silently produced /bin:<real PATH>, so stub executables were never found and 15 of 15 cases failed before reaching the code under test. Pre-existing vars (PWD, PATH) survive both passes, which is why the bug looks selective. FIX SHAPE: build one env-prefixed command whose every dollar-NAME already exists in the parent environment; let the child script read the rest from its own environment rather than from the command string. DISPROVED on the way: the semicolon separator is fine, and double-quoting is fine — do not chase those. TESTING LESSON (the important half): a BEHAVIOURAL test for this cannot protect you, because Git Bash and the Ubuntu CI runner both expand ONCE — a reintroduced self-reference stays green on CI while breaking only for Windows contributors. sefx0 pinned the STRUCTURE instead (assert the command references only pre-existing variables) with a non-vacuity guard. Generalise: when a defect is invisible on the platform your CI runs, a structural pin beats a behavioural one.

A RULING DETAIL WAS EMPIRICALLY WRONG: notifications CAN arrive before dispatch returns on the stock-Reagent adapter (found 2026-08-07, rf2-ynved).

THE RULING SAID (item 8) that notifications never arrive before dispatch returns. FALSE on this adapter: :flush-render! is (fn [f] (f) (r/flush)), so dispatch-sync DRAINS THE QUEUE ITSELF. A test written to assert the ruling literally went red.

HOW IT WAS HANDLED, and this is the part to copy: the worker did not quietly conform the test to observed behaviour, and did not quietly conform the docs to the ruling. It reported the ruling was wrong, and changed the DOCS to say the re-feed rides a Reagent flush rather than an inline callback inside the app-db write — while telling the author to code as though it lands on the FOLLOWING commit. That last clause is the useful part: teach the WEAKER guarantee even when the stronger one currently holds, because the stronger one is an implementation detail of one adapter.

SECOND FINDING from the same run: a sibling unmount COMMIT re-runs a surviving tracker against an unchanged value, so the survivor takes one idempotent re-feed. The DOM-free counterpart drives the identical release with NO React commit and sees no duplicate. So it is a property of the commit cycle, not of the recipe — and the assertion was rewritten property-based with the reason recorded.

GENERAL RULE: when a test contradicts a recorded ruling, the ruling is a hypothesis like anything else. Report the contradiction, establish which is true FROM THE ADAPTER SOURCE, and fix whichever is actually wrong. Do not assume the ruling wins; do not assume the observation wins.

title: flows: direct clear-flow leaves dependent materialized outputs stale until an unrelated drain
description:
## Scope

Correct the plain/direct `re-frame.flows/clear-flow` lifecycle path when it is called outside an active event drain. Clearing a producer flow must not return with other registered flows still materialized from the producer value that was just removed. Keep the existing id/opts API, frame scoping, leaf-only vacation, and the already-correct `:rf.fx/clear-flow` behavior.

## Verified finding

At HEAD 52b2579e9b53816abddd3406f72db5a5278bed1c, a live JVM probe registered producer `:probe/a` (`[:x] -> [:a]`) and dependent `:probe/b` (`[:a] -> [:b]`), then seeded `{:x 2}`. Before clear, app-db was `{:x 2, :a 2, :b 2}`. Calling `(flows/clear-flow :probe/a {:frame :probe})` returned with `{:x 2, :b 2}`: the source slot was gone but its dependent still published the value derived from that removed slot. Only a later unrelated no-op dispatch changed it to `{:x 2, :b :absent}`. The probe exited 0 and used the package's plain-atom runtime.

This follows directly from `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc` `clear-flow` / `vacate-output-path!` (currently lines 798-891): outside a drain it writes the vacated live app-db immediately, removes the registry/cache row, and returns; no flow pass is requested. The next ordinary drain finally dirty-checks `:probe/b` against nil and repairs it.

## Impact and ergonomics

This is an observable split-brain app-db state, not a trace-only detail: a view, handler, test, or per-tenant setup reading app-db immediately after the documented synchronous function returns can trust a dependent value whose declared input no longer exists. `docs/core/flows.md` lines 325-341 explicitly advertises the plain functions for boot code, tests, and per-tenant setup, while `docs/api/re-frame.flows.md` lines 55-73 describes `clear-flow` as a synchronous deregister-and-vacate function. Requiring each such caller to invent an unrelated event to repair the dependency graph recreates the ceremony already removed from the effect route.

The existing direct-clear test, `implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_test.clj` `clear-flow-removes-from-registry-and-vacates-output-slot` (lines 102-118), checks only the cleared producer row and leaf. The stronger dependent-flow behavior exists only for the effect route in `implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_settle_on_dispatch_test.clj` `settle-runs-once-and-recomputes-dependents` (lines 85 onward), leaving the plain function gap untested.

## Bounded recommendation

After a successful out-of-drain direct clear, settle the selected frame's remaining flows through the existing private/ordinary flow-pass machinery before the synchronous call completes, so dependents observe the producer's absence without an application-authored nudge. Reuse the established settle/error semantics where practical; do not add a public settle command, option, alternate clear API, fixed-point engine, or general scheduler. Preserve in-drain behavior, where `clear-flow` already queues the vacation for the current pending-db flow pass, and preserve no-op behavior for an unknown flow or absent frame.

The precise internal bridge (for example, reusing the private settle transport after releasing the drain lock versus a smaller exact-owner helper) is intentionally left to implementation review. It must not deadlock/re-enter the current serialization gate, and it must retain the exact-incarnation fences around direct vacation and teardown.

## Posture rationale

Flows are deliberately a small convenience, so the right fix is one consistent lifecycle boundary, not more API. The effect form already guarantees cleared inputs and their dependents settle together. Making the documented plain function honor the same observable invariant removes a surprising manual drain and keeps boot/test/per-tenant use low-friction for people and generated code without broadening flows into a dataflow system.

## Duplicate and history search

Searched all tracker statuses across titles, descriptions, and notes for `flow`, `clear-flow`, `direct clear`, `outside a drain`, `dependent flow`, `initial output`, `settle`, and `unrelated event`. No issue owns this direct-clear/dependent-output boundary. Closest is closed `rf2-kh73v`, which fixed automatic settling only for `:rf.fx/reg-flow` / `:rf.fx/clear-flow`; its scope and tests are effect-specific and its non-goals explicitly exclude static/direct registration work. Closed `rf2-pt637` fixes only the cart example's hot-reload callback.

History confirms the split: `clear-flow` dates to 691c892564e; direct path vacation was added in 7e83e7c691 and later exact-owner-fenced by b5c4599df0/a3ca268cdc0/5c660f2fda. Commits 47e90cf3b4 and 7b6d1e75a3 added and ordered private settling for lifecycle effects without changing the plain direct path.

## Uncertainties

The spec currently states direct clear's deregistration/vacation but does not explicitly say whether dependent flows settle before return; the public synchronous shape and advertised outside-handler use make the current inconsistent graph the actionable defect. The fixing worker should record the chosen direct-call failure boundary if a remaining dependent's derive throws, aligning with the existing private settle semantics rather than inventing rollback behavior.
acceptance_criteria:
- A focused CLJ regression reproduces producer A -> dependent B and proves that after direct `(flows/clear-flow A {:frame frame-id})` returns: A is unregistered, A's output leaf is absent, and B has recomputed once against that absence without any unrelated/app-authored dispatch.
- The regression has a negative control: it fails against the current implementation with B retaining the pre-clear value.
- Unknown-id and absent-frame direct clears remain silent no-ops; clearing one frame does not settle or mutate a sibling frame.
- In-drain direct clear and `:rf.fx/clear-flow` keep their current one-settle/topological behavior; existing settle ordering tests remain green.
- The implementation does not expose a public settle event/function/flag, add fixed-point iteration, or change `clear-flow`'s public arities.
- Exact-incarnation loss cannot let an old direct clear or its settle tail mutate a same-id successor frame, and the implementation does not deadlock by dispatching while holding the drain lock.
- Spec/API/core guide wording states the observable direct-clear boundary and its downstream behavior; JVM and CLJS coverage is added in proportion to the cross-host `.cljc` lifecycle code.
notes:
PR #9204 audit follow-up (2026-09-05): the direct settle itself repairs dependents synchronously, but the specified failure boundary is not represented truthfully by the exception diagnostic. `settle-frame-flows!` invokes the ordinary `run-flows-on-db`; `flow-eval-failure!` still hard-codes that the derive ran "during the drain", "the event aborts before the :db install", and "app-db [is] unchanged". Those statements are false for this newly added caller: direct `clear-flow` has already deregistered the producer and committed its output-path vacation, which intentionally stands when a dependent throws.

Deterministic JVM probe at merge commit 27762aa6f9fa1a32db32a59994aa85a5ab0472b8: producer A (`[:x] -> [:a]`), dependent B (`[:a] -> [:b]`) that throws on nil, seed `{:x 2 :a 2 :b 2}`, then direct clear A. The thrown message said "during the drain; the event aborts before the :db install (no partial commit, app-db unchanged)", while immediate state was `{:x 2 :b 2}` and A was absent from the registry. Thus app-db did change (A's leaf was vacated), no event existed, and the clear did not abort. The same mismatch exists for the `:output-write` branch.

This is the exact remaining edge of rf2-g1zb: its original description explicitly required the implementation to record the direct-call failure boundary, and PR #9204's spec/API prose does so correctly. Keep the existing error category and phase taxonomy, but make the user-facing diagnostic context-aware (or neutral across drain/direct callers), and add a focused cross-host regression proving both the propagated exception wording/data and the intended post-failure state: clear stands, settle candidate is unwritten, dependent retries later. Do not add a new error category or rollback the clear.
Diagnostic edge closed on PR #9257 (branch worker/flowsettle-a). settle-frame-flows! now runs its pass under a private *pass-caller* binding, and flow-eval-failure! varies only the two clauses that describe the caller's commit boundary: where the evaluation ran, and what its failure left behind. Error id, :derive/:output-write phase discrimination, trace tags, ex-data and :recovery are byte-identical across callers; no new error category and no rollback of the clear.

Reproduced first, at origin/main, on BOTH phases. :derive -> app-db {:x 2 :a 2 :b 2} became {:x 2 :b 2} with :probe/a deregistered, while the message asserted 'during the drain; the event aborts before the :db install (no partial commit, app-db unchanged)'. :output-write -> {:x 2 :v [1 2] :a 2} became {:x 2 :v [1 2]} carrying the same three false clauses plus 'the pending app-db' for a db that is committed rather than pending.

New cross-host regression implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_direct_clear_settle_failure_cljs_test.cljc: 3 tests / 43 assertions. Measured RED against the unmodified source (exit 1, 9 failures) and green after (exit 0). It proves the propagated wording and ex-data on both phases and the intended post-failure state — clear stands, settle candidate unwritten, dependent retries on the next drain — and its third test is the control that keeps the DRAIN's own sentence intact, without which the fix could have been satisfied by deleting that sentence.

Gate: clojure -M:test from implementation/flows, exit 0, 261 tests / 6187 assertions. CLJS arm relied on CI (sibling workers live; a second shadow-cljs build wedges).
close_reason:
MERGED as PR #9257 (rebased; mayor fast-forwarded to dec77429ce). Five clauses: 87 checks, 0 non-terminal, 87 passed-or-skipped, 0 live runs at head oid, 0 structural workflow lines on trunk since merge base.

WHAT CLOSED IS THE BEAD'S NOTE, NOT ITS DESCRIPTION. The description's defect — direct clear-flow leaving dependents stale — was fixed and merged earlier as PR #9204. The live instruction was the PR #9204 AUDIT follow-up note, which the worker confirmed by a controlled bd history walk: exactly ONE text mutation in 388 entries, notes 0->1768 chars at 2026-09-05T02:05:29, everything newer being checkpoint/status noise.

THE REMAINING EDGE, reproduced at origin/main before editing, on BOTH phases. :derive — app-db {:x 2 :a 2 :b 2} became {:x 2 :b 2} with :probe/a deregistered, while the thrown message asserted 'during the drain; the event aborts before the :db install (no partial commit, app-db unchanged)'. All three clauses false for this caller: app-db DID change (the leaf was vacated), no event existed, and the clear did not abort. :output-write carried the same three plus 'the pending app-db' for a db already committed.

THE FIX IS CONFINED TO THE HUMAN :reason. A private *pass-caller* var names the caller's commit boundary and only the two clauses describing it vary. Error id, phase discrimination, trace tags, ex-data and :recovery are IDENTICAL across callers — asserted as hard as the difference, which is the part that keeps this a diagnostic repair rather than a contract change. Dynamic var chosen over a threaded parameter because the hot loop already carries seven args, there is one read site, and the settle is synchronous.

EVIDENCE: new file flows_direct_clear_settle_failure_cljs_test.cljc, 3 tests / 43 assertions, exit 1 with 9 failures against unmodified source and exit 0 after. Its third test is the CONTROL that keeps the drain's own sentence intact, so the change cannot silently neutralise the original wording. Full flows artefact suite exit 0 at 261 tests / 6187 assertions, delta +5 tests / +51 assertions. The docs gate was proven non-vacuous rather than trusted: a planted broken anchor took check_doc_slugs.py to exit 1 naming spec/013-Flows.md:508, exit 0 on restore. CLJS arm relied on CI and declared in the PR body — correct, with five siblings live.

title: flows: direct reg-flow does not materialize a new flow's initial output until an unrelated drain
description:
Sibling of the fixed rf2-g1zb, found while fixing it. NOT yet reproduced with a live probe — the evidence below is source-level, so the first task is to measure it.

CLAIM (verify at source): `re-frame.flows/reg-flow` called as a plain function OUTSIDE an event drain registers the flow and returns without running a flow pass, so the new flow's INITIAL output is not materialized until some later, unrelated drain. Source evidence: `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc` `reg-flow` writes output marks, mutates the registry, drops the dirty-check row and emits traces — it contains no call to `run-flows-on-db` and no settle. That is the same shape as the clear-flow defect rf2-g1zb fixed. Its own comments note the asymmetry: a DIRECT cold `reg-flow` does not inherit the router's exact-owner predicate that the `:rf.fx/reg-flow` route does.

WHY IT IS FILED SEPARATELY AND NOT FIXED IN PR #9204: rf2-g1zb's scope and bounded recommendation were explicitly clear-flow-only, and its acceptance criteria named no reg-flow arm. PR #9204's spec wording therefore says in terms that the new Spec 013 subsection governs clear-flow only and that reg-flow's direct path is out of scope, so symmetry is NOT read into it — see spec/013-Flows.md, the subsection 'The same boundary for a direct clear-flow'. That sentence is what this bead would revisit.

WHAT IS ALREADY SPECIFIED: Spec 013 §Sequencing is NORMATIVE that a flow registered by `:rf.fx/reg-flow` has its initial output materialised, and every dependent recomputed, by the time the dispatching event settles. It is silent on the direct function, exactly as it was for clear-flow before rf2-g1zb.

FIRST STEP: reproduce. Seed app-db FIRST, then `reg-flow` a flow whose inputs are already present, then read app-db with no dispatch in between — the trap is that a probe which registers against an EMPTY db proves nothing, because there is no value to derive. Use the witness harness from `implementation/flows/test/re_frame/flows_direct_clear_settle_cljs_test.cljc`, which already carries the machinery: adjacency, a derive counter, a whole-stream :rf.event trace recorder with its own in-run positive control, and a drain-equivalence assertion. If the premise does not hold, that finding with its evidence is the deliverable.

IF IT REPRODUCES: the fix is likely one line reusing the seam PR #9204 added — `registry/set-settle-fn!` publishes an exact-owner settle installed by the facade, and `reg-flow` could call it under the same three fences clear-flow uses (inside the registration's exact-owner postcheck, out-of-drain only, inside the serialized region). Note the docs promise to reconcile: docs/core/flows.md currently states in prose that reg-flow's direct form does NOT make the matching promise about initial output and points readers at `:rf.fx/reg-flow`; docs/api/re-frame.flows.md documents the settle boundary on clear-flow only. Both would need updating alongside the spec subsection.

Consider also whether reg-flow's error surface changes: reg-flow already throws `:rf.error/flow-frame-not-live`, so a settling derive throw propagating to the direct caller is less of a departure there than it was for clear-flow.
notes:
Post-merge audit — PR #9222 (correctness + completeness): the new rationale overclaims the safety of the effect route. `spec/013-Flows.md` and `flows_direct_reg_deferral_cljs_test.cljc` say `:rf.fx/reg-flow` runs inside a drain “where app-db is by construction the application's live seeded state, so the hazard cannot arise.” A drain does not guarantee that a new flow's declared inputs exist. On merged commit `fc306b82b6434b676e34e70d1e4036e063732adb`, a fresh default frame with `{}` app-db and an event whose only effect is `[:rf.fx/reg-flow [:audit/double {:inputs [[:n]] :output-path [:out]} (fn [n] (* 2 n))]]` calls the derive once with nil, leaves db `{}`, keeps the flow registered, and emits `{:error :rf.error/flow-eval-exception, :event [:rf/settle-flows], :flow-id :audit/double, :phase :derive}`. Thus the very absent-input hazard used to justify direct-call deferral can arise through the effect route; it is merely surfaced at the effect's explicit settle boundary. The main direct-reg-flow contract and its three new behavior tests remain sound. Bounded fix: correct the false sentence in the normative spec and test docstring (and user guide if needed) to explain the actual distinction: an effect registration requests immediate evaluation, so its event must establish/precede the inputs or can fail normally; a direct registration deliberately waits for the caller's next drain. A focused effect-before-seed witness would keep that caveat executable, but no lifecycle redesign or removal of effect settling is implied.
Resolved on PR #9257 (branch worker/flowsettle-a) as the AUDIT note directs, not as the description does. The description's premise — that a direct reg-flow's missing initial-output settle is a defect to fix by symmetry with clear-flow — is superseded: PR #9222 already ruled the opposite way and landed it as NORMATIVE (Spec 013 'Why a direct reg-flow does not settle': a direct reg-flow registers without evaluating and MUST NOT settle). Nothing in that ruling was disturbed.

MEASUREMENT of the audit's claim: it REPRODUCES. The sentence ':rf.fx/reg-flow ... runs inside a drain, where app-db is by construction the application's live seeded state, so the hazard cannot arise' is false. A drain evaluates against the EVENT'S OWN pending app-db, which may be empty. Witness effect-reg-flow-evaluates-immediately-even-against-an-unseeded-db: default frame, app-db {}, one event whose only effect is [:rf.fx/reg-flow [:audit/double {:inputs [[:n]] :output-path [:out]} derive]] -> derive called exactly once with nil, app-db still {}, flow still registered, always-on record :rf.error/flow-eval-exception with :flow-id :audit/double and :phase :derive. Paired witness effect-reg-flow-succeeds-when-its-own-event-seeds-first shows the other half: the same registration on an event that seeds first yields {:n 21 :out 42} by the time the dispatch returns.

Note for any port or re-measurement: the derive is spelled with an explicit refusal on nil, not arithmetic. (* 2 nil) throws on the JVM but evaluates to 0 in CLJS, so the arithmetic form would go green on one host for the wrong reason.

FIX is prose only, three sites in one commit: the normative sentence in spec/013-Flows.md, the same reasoning in the witness file's docstring, and the user guide parenthetical in docs/core/flows.md (which now says the effect evaluates right then, so that event needs its inputs present or must seed them). The rule is unchanged; only its justification moves — from safety to RESPONSIBILITY: an effect registration is issued from inside an event, so that event is the place to establish the inputs and it requests evaluation now, a failure being an ordinary event failure at the effect's explicit settle boundary; a direct registration has no such event to be responsible for, so it declares and waits. docs/api/re-frame.flows.md documents the settle boundary on clear-flow only and needed no change. No lifecycle change, no removal of effect settling.

Gates: clojure -M:test from implementation/flows exit 0 (261 tests / 6187 assertions); check_doc_slugs.py exit 0, proven non-vacuous by a planted broken anchor that took it to exit 1 naming spec/013-Flows.md:508; check_readme_links.py --ci exit 0. CLJS arm relied on CI.
close_reason:
CLOSED via PR #9257 — but NOT as the bead was written, and the correction matters more than the fix.

THE BRIEF'S FRAMING DID NOT HOLD, and neither did the bead's own description. Both asked whether a direct reg-flow's deferred initial output is a defect to be fixed by making reg-flow settle. PR #9222 had ALREADY RULED THE OPPOSITE WAY and landed it as normative: a direct reg-flow MUST NOT settle. The worker found this by a controlled history walk — description set at creation, then notes 0->1540 chars at 2026-09-05T04:30:33 — and established that the note is an audit of PR #9222, not of #9204 as the bead's own text implies. It disturbed none of the ruled behaviour, which is correct.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG WAS A SPEC JUSTIFICATION, AND IT REPRODUCES. Spec 013 claimed :rf.fx/reg-flow 'runs inside a drain, where app-db is by construction the application's live seeded state, so the hazard cannot arise'. That is false. Measured: default frame, app-db {}, one event whose only effect is :rf.fx/reg-flow — derive called exactly once with nil, app-db still {}, flow still registered, :rf.error/flow-eval-exception with :phase :derive. Paired positive witness: the same registration on an event that seeds first yields {:n 21 :out 42}. So the rule survives and its stated REASON does not; the fix is prose across three sites in one commit, moving the justification from 'safety' to 'responsibility'. docs/api/re-frame.flows.md needed no change — it documents the settle boundary on clear-flow only.

ONE TRAP WORTH CARRYING FORWARD, recorded because it would silently half-pass: the witness spells its derive with an EXPLICIT refusal on nil, because (* 2 nil) THROWS on the JVM but evaluates to 0 in CLJS. The arithmetic form would have gone green on one host for the wrong reason — a cross-host control that is right for a reason that does not transfer.

This is the second bead this wave whose deliverable was a refutation rather than an implementation. Both were worth more than the work would have been.

title: bug(trace,xray): Xray Clear-buffer resets trace retention; add a policy-preserving 0-arity clear-trace-buffer!
description:
_Filed 2026-09-05 12:37:46 AUSEST by the API-review wave-3 coordinator from trace-epoch.md (ref trace-epoch.4); parent epic rf2-kuky. Local-only dossiers: ai/findings/API-review/{fable,codex}/ (gitignored; may be deleted)._

## Problem

Xray's user-facing "Clear buffer now" (Settings popup) and its automatic reveal→redact scrub both run `retroactive-scrub!` (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/trace_collector.cljs:350-365`), whose first act is `(rf.trace.tooling/clear-trace-rings!)` (`:360`). That fn (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/tooling.cljc:575-585`) is documented as a "Test-fixture / `clear-all!`-shaped helper" and does three things: drops every frame's ring, **resets `process-events-retained` to `default-events-retained`** — silently undoing the user's `(rf/configure! {:trace-buffer {:events-retained N}})` and every ring's `:override?` flag (the rings map is reset to `{}`) — and clears the B4 hot-reload dedup table (so the next hot reload re-emits every registration trace into the buffer the user just emptied). The per-frame clear `clear-trace-buffer!` (`:557-573`) deliberately does none of that: it re-empties the ring with its `effective-retained` and preserves `:override?` (rf2-va65k). Two clears, two policies, and the user-facing one is the fixture one.

The trace ring's retention has no reader (fable use case 6: `re-frame.epoch/current-config` exists, its trace twin does not), so the user cannot even see that their setting was reverted.

## Evidence (tip 6445d0611b)

- `trace_collector.cljs:339` comment and `:360` call; `:381` registers `retroactive-scrub!` as the toggle-off callback; `:427-434` `reset-for-test!` also calls `clear-trace-rings!` (that one IS a fixture — it stays).
- `tooling.cljc:575-585` `clear-trace-rings!` body: `(reset! trace-rings {}) (reset! process-events-retained default-events-retained) (clear-dedup-table!)`.
- `tooling.cljc:557-573` `clear-trace-buffer!` preserves `effective-retained` + `override?`; pinned by `implementation/core/test/re_frame/trace_buffer_test.clj:219,274` (rf2-va65k findings 1 and 2).
- `clear-trace-rings!` consumers: Xray `:360`, `:433`; 9 test files; `tools/xray/spec/013-Trace-Consumer.md:331-337` documents the scrub as clearing the rings (it does not mention the policy reset).
- Xray setting writes: `settings/effects.cljs:491` `(rf/configure! {:trace-buffer …})` — the very knob the button reverts.

## Target API

```clojure
;; re-frame.trace.tooling (re-exported unchanged on the facade as rf/clear-trace-buffer!)
(clear-trace-buffer! frame-id)   ; existing — empty one ring; retention + :override? preserved
(clear-trace-buffer!)            ; NEW 0-arity — empty EVERY ring the same way:
                                 ;   each frame → (empty-ring (effective-retained rings fid) override?)
                                 ;   process-events-retained UNTOUCHED, dedup table UNTOUCHED
(clear-trace-rings!)             ; unchanged — the fixture reset (rings + process default + dedup)
```

Dedup-table treatment is chosen deliberately, not inherited: the table holds registrar shapes keyed `(kind, id)` (`tooling.cljc:296-321`), not trace payloads, so a data clear — including a privacy scrub, whose subject is sensitive *events* — has no reason to touch it. Xray `retroactive-scrub!` `:360` → the 0-arity data clear (spelled `rf/clear-trace-buffer!` if @trace-epoch.1 has merged — the file already requires `re-frame.core` — else `rf.trace.tooling/clear-trace-buffer!`); the rest of the scrub (frameless ring, app-db slot, suppressed counters) unchanged. `reset-for-test!` `:433` keeps `clear-trace-rings!`.

## Corroboration

One-reviewer area; codex's own doc proposes precisely this shape and calls the Xray call path "actionable evidence": "Keep the existing per-frame clear; add its useful all-frame case … `(rf/clear-trace-buffer!) ; clears retained traces, preserves retention policy`" and "Migrate Xray's user clear/scrub to data clearing, while preserving its additional frameless-buffer, displayed-cache and privacy cleanup. Do not claim the existing button only empties history; the inspected call path currently does more." Fable's Grok cross-check concurs ("Add an all-frame data clear that preserves retention and override flags. Keep `clear-trace-rings!` … as the fixture operation"). Codex's caution, honoured: `clear-trace-rings!` is NOT relabelled as the 0-arity, and no epoch clear is invented (`epoch/clear-history!` also drops in-flight capture buffers — it is a fixture op; item A of @trace-epoch.5).

## Deletion list

None. (`clear-trace-rings!` stays; its docstring gains one sentence pointing data clears at `clear-trace-buffer!`.)

## Consumers to migrate

- Xray `trace_collector.cljs:360` (the scrub) → 0-arity data clear; `:339` comment; `:427` docstring unchanged in substance.
- Nothing else: 0 tool-code callers of per-frame `clear-trace-buffer!` (9 JVM test sites via `rf/` unchanged); the 9 `clear-trace-rings!` test files unchanged.

## Spec, docs, examples, skills, tests

- **Spec (hot-zone):** `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` §`trace-buffer` API table (`:910-915`) — add the row `(rf/clear-trace-buffer!)` `() → nil` "Empties every frame's ring. Retention policy — the process default and each frame's explicit override — is preserved, and the hot-reload dedup table is untouched; the fixture-grade reset that also resets policy is `re-frame.test-support`'s concern, not a public verb"; `spec/API.md:621` row (signature gains the 0-arity, same sentence). No Tool-Pair change (`:513`, `:602` name the read, not the clear).
- **Manifest:** `clear-trace-buffer!` rows unchanged (arity is not a manifest axis) — `gen --check` + `api-md-check` confirm.
- **Docs:** `docs/api/re-frame.core.md:1016-1026` (signature + one example); `docs/core/observability.md:165` (the clear paragraph).
- **Xray spec (mandatory with any `tools/xray/` change):** `tools/xray/spec/013-Trace-Consumer.md:331-337` item 1 → the data clear, and one sentence stating what the scrub deliberately does NOT reset.
- **Skills:** `skills/re-frame2/references/cross-cutting/api-cheatsheet.md:170` row mentions `clear-trace-buffer!` — add the 0-arity in passing if @trace-epoch.1 has not already rewritten the row; otherwise leave.
- **Tests to add:** in `trace_buffer_test.clj` beside the rf2-va65k pins: `(rf/configure! {:trace-buffer {:events-retained 7}})`, frame B with `:rf.trace/events-retained 3`, dispatch in A and B, `(rf/clear-trace-buffer!)` → both rings empty; dispatch 10 more in each → A retains 7, B retains 3, B's `:override?` still true; then `(rf.trace.tooling/clear-trace-rings!)` → default back to 50 (the existing fixture contract, pinned so the two verbs' difference is a test, not a docstring). Xray: a CLJS unit test in `tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/` that `retroactive-scrub!` leaves a configured `:events-retained` in force (observed behaviourally: configure 3, scrub, dispatch 5, `(count (trace-buffer fid))` → 3).

## Sequencing and hot-zone

Touches `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` and `spec/API.md` → serialise with @trace-epoch.3 and with the other areas' API.md beads. Prefers @trace-epoch.1 merged first (facade spelling on CLJS) but does not require it.

## Risks

- Xray's scrub semantics: a sensitive event can live only in the rings, the frameless ring and the app-db slot (`trace_collector.cljs:337-343`); the data clear still empties all three, so the privacy contract (009 §Privacy §Retroactive-scrub) is unchanged — assert it in the Xray test (`buffer-for-test` empty after scrub).
- `empty-ring` / `effective-retained` are private (`tooling.cljc:142,153`); the 0-arity lives in the same ns, so nothing is exposed.

## Local dossier

`ai/findings/API-review/codex/trace-and-epoch-inspection.md` §A clear operation is not a fixture reset; `ai/findings/API-review/fable/trace-and-epoch-read-surface.md` (local-only pointers).
